You bought this game thinking it was your average tactical strategy squad-based shooter. Until you realised this is an actual
and every soldier that returns home in a coffin is another blow in your already shattered heart.
Enter
, or
, an organisation funded by all the goverments in the world with the sole purpose to defend Earth against the alien invasion. Your job as the man in charge is to guide this organisation to victory through research, experimentation, building your base and commanding your troops in battle. Do well and the nations will make it rain on you with them precious dollars. Do poorly, and the nations will pull out, leaving you with reduced resources to fight.
Every aspect of the game is all about making the right choices, as there's no such thing as fully upgrading everything. Will you keep a soldier in battle to upgrade his skills or will you pull him out to undergo psychic training? Will you buy more satellites to spot alien aircraft faster or will you buy more interceptors to deal with the ones you find? Everything has a price to pay and tensions will rise very soon once the main bulk of the game reveals itself.
Combat-wise, as your soldiers take part in more missions, they get more experience, which allows them to unlock certain skills. It's a well-made system, because it allows you to tailor your troops as you see fit and adjust them to your playstyle. You can also rename your soldiers and change their appearance. Later in the game, you will have the option to unlock their psionic powers or turn them into cyborgs for greater efficiency. All these combined, give a sense of personality on each soldier and you will feel differently about them, mostly sympathetic. That means that their deaths can leave you in a state of sadness, since you know that from now on you will only see them in the dead troopers' records. And that's the game's magic, you will develop a bond with the men and women that are ready to sacrifice everything for victory.
The missions are pretty difficult, especially in higher levels, requiring careful planning and tactics to pull them off. The alien enemies have different races, skills and weapons at their disposal, meaning that each enemy requires different approaches to defeat. You will always have the feeling that the aliens are two steps ahead of you and you are struggling to keep the organisation alive between demanding nations, alien spaceship assaults and dogfights on the Earth's atmosphere. It's brutal, harsh and unforgiving, granting a huge level of immersion.
The game looks beautiful, colorful and well-made. By the time each mission finishes, the map will be full of debris, exploded cars, crushed walls and dead bodies (alien or not). Your soldiers look incredible in their special battle armors, even if some players might find them slightly cartoonish. It really does a nice job giving you a feel of the battlefield as you see the firefights and explosions everywhere. Better yet, even though everything can be used as cover, that means cover will often be destroyed by gunfight, leaving an unpredictability factor in the game, forcing you to think on the fly to save your precious soldiers.
On the downside, the fact not all your soldiers can't reach the highest point of their abilities, means you won't have much room to make the most out of their abilities. You rarely will see a trooper fully-upgraded, let alone one with all his psionic powers mastered, for example. This is, in my opinion, a major failure of the game. True, it adds a "survive" feel to the game, but you will never feel overpowered and badass against the aliens. Despair and anxiety are realistic factors, but overdoing it is just not gonna work that nicely.
Now excuse me, I got to bury a soldier that looks like my nasty boss. Huh, this game has good moments after all...

Although NEO Scavenger doesn't have the fancy graphics of titles with huge budgets and numerous developers, it manages to do a lot more with a lot less. Scraping by and surviving in a world in which almost everything and everyone would rather see you dead (and in which death is permanent) may not sound fun on paper, but the game manages to create that addictive just-one-more-turn quality that's a sign of a great game. Thanks to the excellent music and writing, the game also manages to pull off an impressive amount of immersion and atmosphere with the limitations of the isometric, hexagonal world.
Unlike a lot of early access games with more staff and so less of an excuse, the developer has been communicative and responsive throughout which I can only think has led to a better game.
NEO Scavenger is a testament to what one guy with vision and dedication can do.

I beat this game a few months and purchased it during a bundled JRPG sale.
Honestly, this game is pretty fun for being about 7ish hours (that was my play time at getting everything to 100% with some small grinding invovled). The story is simple, but enjoyable.
Gameplay wise, it had it's ups and downs. Overall the need to grind doesn't really exist. You can break bosses by using one spell over and over without taking any damage to the party. Random encoutners do not exist in this game as the mobs just wander around like npcs, so basically you clear an area and then reset and do it again if you want to grind. However, grinding isn't really needed since, agian, you can just break the boss with one spell. There isn't really any in terms of customization, but that was fine. Items aren't something you really need (mostly heal pots). This didn't really bother me as I could just keep going with the game and didn't have to worry about gear.
Characters were a let down. Things start off like you're going to learn a lot about them, but then ends up flopping right on you. So that was kind of meh. The main character is fleshed out abit, but overall character development wasn't really there.
World. Meh. It's small, easily traveled. There isn't much to the world at all and that was lame. But for a short game that you can do in one sitting no issues, I guess it works.
Story. Again simple. Nothing complex and there were a few turns that I didn't seem coming which was a nice relief due to all things mentioned above.
Overall the game was fun and I don't regret playing. I'd like to do a Let's Play on this game as it's short. A lot more could have been done with the game, but I don't know much about the developer to say why or why not it was done as it was. Hopefully at somepoint they can expand upon the world / characters more in a sequel or something. Again, no regrets and recommended if you're looking for something to pass the time (great for in between LoL ques or something of the like).

Storm of Spears is an RPGmaker game developed by Warfare Studios and released mid 2016.
At this time I've played around 4-5 RPG maker games, most were mediocre, and one was absolutely terrible. This one has a few things I liked, but it's definitely a play and forget.
The story is the weakest aspect of Storm of Spears... Well, that's not really fair to say without elaboration. Clearly someone has tried their best to write up a story, but the story didn't engage me at all.
I cared so little that I skipped 90% of the text by spamming my Z/Enter key. Normally RPG maker games punish you for doing this because you don't know what to do next.
But Storm of Spears actually has a quest log! This is the first time I've ran into an RPG maker game which tracked quests and side quests for me. So let me sincerely say: "THANK GOD". It was my favorite feature, and let me complete the game much faster by skipping lackluster dialogue.
"But Atratzu, you haven't really explained what was so bland about the story yet" Good observation projected thoughts of my review reader! Specifically my problems lie with the protagonist, "Sura". She is passed off as some charismatic leader of a group of mercenaries known as "Knight Watch" or "night watch", or "edgy-impressive-sounding-nitey-night-knight-watch-wach-swatch" or something.
She has no interest in joining the rebellion, instead she wants to hide away with her younger brother. She is obsessed with protecting him, and won't risk doing anything which could put him in danger.
(and being a mercenary is a good way to keep him safe? The plot has more holes this swiss cheese being used for target practice at a shotgun rally, lets ignore that part, and smile and nod)
Well as you might imagine, she gets sucked into the conflict, and then there's a type of reconciliation because she was "tricked" to force her to lead the rebelion, and then she's like "oh, that's okay. You helped me see the error of my ways, I'm totes... *skip skip skip skip*  ....Waffle Walrus... *skip skip skip* ...and I forgive you.
...uh huh... Cuz forgiving someone IMMEDIATELY after finding out they made a crazy lie and then living with that lie for... days? months? realistically it should have been months to rally everyone to get to that point.
I'd be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥(seriously, pi-ssed is a filtered word?). and THAT would have made the protagonist more relatable! If she said "oh yeah? So I've been fooled into this, well peace out. now we don't need to continue dancing this dance, time to go find a peaceful part of the land and live the rest of our lives out in peace"
And then it takes some other REAL crisis to break her out of her apathy, THAT would be more compelling and would make the protagonist more interesting for me. But nope, "you've taken away my burdens", oh, okay, sure, fine.
standard RPGmaker controls and mechanics. There are three difficulty settings, however my impression is that the different difficulties will just reduce damage given, gold and experienced gained after combat, annndddd minor other differences.
I doubt it makes too much of a difference, but at least the developer gave me a baby-easy-mode to blast through so I can move on to another game.
The store page says it has 10 hours of gameplay, and if you intend to do all the things, you probably could sink 10 hours into it. But if you want to run past enemy fights and play on the easiest difficulty you can easily beat Storm of Spears RPG in 3-4 hours.
Another praise I have for the game is the lack of random encounters. Oh thank you so much for not including them, I've been random encountered out from most RPGmaker games.
There are NPC battles, but you move much faster then them, and can easily bypass them quickly if you time it right.
(I don't know how much this would impact the level curve. At higher difficulties the gearing and exp might be more required... but on easy difficulty I was speedy gonzales.)
reviewing my review (that's a funny sentence), I feel that I had more negative to say about Storm of Spears RPG, but that's probably because like I summarized at the start: "The game is utterly forgettable".
If you want to add an easy 100% achievements completed game to your library you can pick this up, if you're starved for RPGmaker games, this one isn't that bad... but it isn't that good either.
Until steam lets me give reviews a thumbs-side-ways, I'll just mark this one "recommended", but only because it didn't hold me hostage for 10 hours... 10 hours and I'd be a salty satly bastage.

I think this game is super unbalanced in terms of how much luck you need to get through it. It's really hard to survive combat without one of the combat traits but in taking combat traits you loose the survival traits that keep you alive over the long haul. It's not uncommon to spend a couple hours building yourself and your camp up up just to get wrecked by a dog you couldn't out run. Ultimately the scavenging and crafting are alright but the combat system is really what gets me. There is no consistant means of escape and no way to tell how much health your opponent has or has lost during the battle.
On a side note I'm really interested in the story elements of the game. I want to see the robot facility and I want to find out whats in the middle of the swamp but I just feel like I'm spending all of my time dealing with malnutrition and water poisoning. This is again another luck based flaw. If you can't find a tin can or a pot to boil water in your as good as dead within the first day or so. In all honesty I think the best way to fix that would be to have more set, consistent points in the game. That way I"m not forraging through settlement after settlement just to have varying results of survival gear, weapons or neurishment which leave the players superunder capable of surviving.
Maybe I"m missing things that others figured out but there isn't even a tutorial system to introduce you to the interface.

- game design glitches here and there: For instance a Pak team can pull its cannon as fast as your infantry troops can sprint. Meaning if you chase the PAK with Grenadiers the PAK can still run away (2 guys pulling a PAK!!!). This means the AI will run back with a PAK which you attack with infantry for as far as into its own base. So after you chased the PAK over all of the battlefield it is in machine gun cover of the base. The scenery looks pretty ridicolous (your own PAK will get shot of course).
- at times your own units disobey you. meaning a tank will attack infantry or a building instead of the tank you targeted, while the enemy tank shreds it in the meanwhile.
- Cheating AI: The AI outnumbers you at least 2 to 1 if not 3 to 1. Just choose an Expert AI as your ally and see how many units it will spawn. Also it doesnt matter if you deny the AI resources. It will still keep on building tanks. Since the game is about conquering resources for putting your troops at risk the AI is frustrating in a useless way.
- Commanders dont really make a difference unlike in the first COH (except for getting the tiger or kv8, for most of the units you are better of spending on regular troops).
- Units die randomly fast at times (even expensive anti infanry units get teared by cheap flame thowers).
- micro management is more important than strategic decisions apart of knowing which counter to send against which troops. The stupid behaviour of your troops requires constant baby sitting.
- I had to download a 10.2 GB patch after buying the DVD version at higher cost only to avoid this. Thumbs down for that.
Overall it can be a lot of fun to explore the different units and the atmosphere is great. Finally I would recommend the game.

Pro's
1. This is a very good program for someone who's looking into getting into rendering images, character/model creations to animations.
2. its free, try getting Autodesk ie maya, 3ds, or Maxon CD4 or any other 3d rendering programs they cost $1,500-$3,000 per year astronomical price for anyone whos a beginner.
3. Very large and active community support, from forums to youtube tutorial videos theres almost every solutuon for every how to's and questions that you may ask or get stuck on.
4. Did i mention its free?
Cons
Not everything is positive on blender so here's some
1, HUGE LEARNING CURVE AHEAD, litterly ask me how to use blender 6 months ago and ill probally look at you with a blank stare, it almost same as when you get Maxon C4D Autodes ie Maya 3ds ect, like all 3d programs they have their own learning curve and quirks and as always it has everytools that is avaliable use but learning how to use it is the mountain that a beginner needs to climb. You can always hit the forums, books, youtube video tutorials (theres tons of them) to assist you to get familiar with the program. Onces you get a hang of it its quite easy to use later on, just dont give up.
2. Crashes, yes it has bugs that causes blender to crash espically when you doing high load task ie animations (i see more crahes in animation that anything else), however theres an autosave revert function that saves every 5 mins so if it crashes just revert or save frequently.
3 Updates, Though updates are generally good there things that may change ie interfaces, UI, functions, though its gotten better there was a time were they did a radical change with the UI which made me almost relearn how to use blender but it wasnt all bad really. Also you'll need to reactivate your plugins since blender just does a clean install on to of your old version, but your save files and your work will remain intact
And there you have it folks Blender a powerful 3d program without the cost of someother ones, sure it has a few issues but it can be overseen so if you're into CG art, rendering or animation give blender a spin.

Parkour + Zombies. It sounds like a naff combination of two topics that are well past their peak, so I wasn't expecting much but ended up very pleasantly surprised by this highly engrossing, game with genuinely scary moments. There are no gameplay ruining bugs and the parkour system is well executed.
The day-night system brings an interesting dynamic to the game - a largely optional, periodic, in-game difficulty boost. During the day, tread with some level of care and you'll be fending off the horde successfully most of the time. At night, you'll be running around in a state of panic desperately trying to get to the nearest safehouse, slip up once and you get ripped to shreds. It would be a frustrating experiecing if the game forced you to play like this all the time, but you engage it on your terms: sleep through the night or go out and double your experience gathering pace - as long as you don't blow it.
The music is a refreshing change to the usual bombastic cinematic stuff - very reminiscent of John Carpenter movies and works well.
The only annoyance I have with the game and perhaps it's deliberate on the director's part, is the incoherent locale. The game is clearly set in an Middle Eastern or North African environment and other than the lead, the main characters speak with an appropriate accent but there's an abundance of characters that speak with regional UK or North American accents, signage is in English, the architecture is a confused mess from various continents and so forth.
It's as if mid way through development they had a change of heart and tried to make the game location neutral or perhaps part of the content was done by a different studio that didn't get the brief. Contrasting this with the stellar job that Ubisoft did on The Division in recreating New York, this is just sloppy.

You've probably heard it all before, but here goes:
One of the most immersive experiences one can have. The fact that the story isn't just laid out for you to read trough and must actually put tought into it, coupled with the fact that the gameplay elements themselves are an important part of it can cause a much higher sense of accomplishment and even trigger some fairly strong feelings.
The graphics and estethics are amazing. The assets were litterally painted and digitized, and it shows - almost everything looks gorgeous. There's really little to say about it, and screenshots don't do it justice, just see it for yourself.
The music fits right in. Very atmospheric, yet still at times very melodic. A better soundtrack could not be wished for.
The puzzles are varied and interesting, often times quite difficult to figure out, even. And that's just the basic ones - there are hidden puzzles within puzzles that unlock something special, and those are _really_ mindbending sometimes. Each "world" comes with it's own set of rules and capabilities, and most of them are quite amazing.
I, personally, have only two complaints about it: 1) the bunny-cat-flower things are make way too high-pitched noises, and 2) at some points there are doors (completely indistinguishable from regular ones) that break your key and don't open. That's just a cheap shot.
Other than that, I can't fault almost anything about it.
Go get it, and enjoy it - almost guaranteed you will.

Gameplay: 8/10 (Simple yet you have the skills learned on some highter levels)
Graphics: 5/10 (a simple Pixel Art, i love Retro style cuz im into those RPG Maker games!)
Support: 8/10 (fast responce from the Developer Chery-Sama when i posted up my problem!)
Price: 7/10 (not to expensive and also on sale very cheap!)
Story: 8/10 (good Story Plot. sometimes Awkward and funny and so on, but it dont misses to entertain i think)
Sound: 7/10 (not the usually 16 bit sounds, those are handmade tracks i think)
Performance: 8/10 (serveral Issues due to Core using of my FX, but that wasnt the games problem its my windows/cpu that could not get the game properly on stable 60 FPS when walking in the Free Roam)
FAZIT: 7/10 (A good RPG Maker game, worth a Try if you like comedy and VN and oldschool RPG)

The big question. Is it better than COH1? The answer is both yes and no. In its current state, COH2 is overall a great state, but that has not always been the case. In fact this is one of those games I uninstalled multiple times because I was so frustrated with it in the past. COH2 for the first year or so was a half-baked sequel to the first.
The SP game is often forced by a timer, has many poorly designed levels, and a really unnatural balance of units. The campaign has not changed, and is completely inferior to COH1.
Theatre of War is a good idea, but has the DLC feel to it. It is okay, but truly I rarely play it.
Skirmish/comp stomp is mostly awesome! Open maps are a pain as the computer micros really well, and matches will exhaust your attention. In choke point maps, turn up the difficulty and you will have some really intense combined arms attacks you must counter. Graphics, sound, unit feel, and attention to detail is incredible and makes COH1 look primative.
Muliplayer is great! Nerd rage on message boards about balancing changes is always a good sign of a fun game that has devoted fans. If the game sucked, they wouldn't rage in the first place.
I so rarely see games I despise become great with patches, but this game has! Overall, for under $20 this a, now, a fantastic game. Throw in WF, which is totally worth it, the game really shines!

Metro 2033 Redux is a survival horror first-person shooter video game, based on the novel Metro 2033 by Russian author Dmitry Glukhovsky. It was developed by 4A Games in Ukraine.
Metro 2033 is a sharp, atmospheric fps survival game. With a heavy enphasis on atmosphere and immersion, the original 2033, released back in 2010, did an an astonishing job, the polish and attention to detail is back and stronger than ever. 4A Games did not just re-release the game for next-gen consoles to grab money from the people who didn't play this before, or played it and they tried to trick them into buying the same game twice (I'm looking at you The Last of Us) this is an effort to refine and fix some of the problems with this game. Like stealth, some issues with the AI and overall improving everything else. Anyways, let's talk about a bit about the game.
In Metro 2033 Redux you star in the shoes of Artyom. Inhabiting the post-apocalyptic world of Russia, Moskow, you mostly dwell underneath the earth, into the metro system. The only hospitable place for humans to live. From time to time you will wander above the ground, into the ruins of the destroyer Moskow in a superb showcase of graphics, an upgraded skybox(from 2033), global illumination and levels being a continuos flow, where 2033 was broken into cinematic segments. Artyom's home station, VDNKh, is being threatened by the mythical creatures called "The Dark Ones" and so, he is sent on a mission by Hunter, to warn Polis about the imminent threat. Artyom's journey will get him through a variety of segments, which include gunfights, stealth segments, paranormal and horror-esque parts. You will also see how humanity has adapted after it was almost wiped out off the face of the earth. And how humans react to this hostile place, how political ideologies, survival and living on the edge of humanity affects this world.
This is where this game shined, and will shine on. Metro is such an amazing rollercoaster ride, I used this metaphore because it is not an open world experience, and in my opinion, it doesn't have to be. This game is from an Eastern Europe based studio, in an ex-communist country. These guys know best how things looked back in the cold war, and it draws heavy inspiration from that. This is what makes it believeable and tangible. Levels are packed with amazing shadow/light effects, spider webs, great props, detailed interior and exterior design. The levels feel so refined like no other game before it, honestly. I spent so much time just glaring at object scatered around me, this made the "non-violent" sections of the game such a breath of fresh air, and a bit relaxing to be honest. I legitimately enjoyed catching other human npc's interact in the game, in a manner that is  human, in the real way, they feel really fleshed out. You can feel the dread and sorrow of some, while others seem like they're built for such an opressive society. The desperation and hopelessness drips in this game. This is a serious subject and it is treated as such. You are not an unstoppable killing machine with unlimited ammo and bad♥♥♥♥♥one liners. You are a survivor, I cannot stress this enough, please, do yourself a favor and play this game on Ranger Hardcore for the ultimate experience. In the end, the game isn't just a game you play for fun, it has so much emotional value and so many interesting design choices, I can't imagine a better way to deal with such a subject matter.
Some of the more notable changes of 2033 Redux from the original are as follow:
The list goes on and on, I could babble for weeks why I love this franchise and why these devs are some of the most ambitious people to come recently into the market with something so fresh and so amazing. I will leave you with this, for 20 bucks as a starting price, and 50% off if you own the original 2033, this is such a great deal, I'm sorry, this is like the only "next-gen" remastered game I trully approve of. It is a must buy for pc shooter fans, for metro fans, for everyone. Everyone will find some delight in this game. Personal rating of 10/10.

A devloper once told me, "UI (User Interface) is like a joke; If you have to explain it, then it isn't that good."
This game fits into that category with poor UI as only one of many design flaws. Don't waste your time and money.
* Unweildy Menu Navigation
The game plays in a window by default, which in and of itself isn't a bad thing. The problem comes when trying to back out of a menu just to end up closing the entire game instead (and losing any progress in the process). The menus themselves, such as inventory, crafting and the map are not very intuitve and require a lot of trial-and-error to figure them out. Saving a game is unweildy, too, because there is only one option; "Save & Quit" from the main menu.
* Lack of Information and Direction
Very little information is given for each item beyond "condition" which is how well in a state of repair an item is. For example, when tying to compare weapons, stats such as range and damage are inaccesable to the player; You have to guess which weapons may or may not be better! Same goes for clothing; There are no stats beyond condtion that tell a player how well protected they are. Lack of stats and lack of other useful information leaves the player in the dark. Trial and error helps, but the game is so inconsitant that trial and error will only get you so far.
* Nearly Impossible Early Game
I like a challange, but this game has too many variables. The map, encounters and looting are all random, which could be a good thing. However, the game starts you out with next to nothing and already suffering from exposure to cold weather. When you need some basic supplies just to survive, and the only way to get those supplies is by a series of lucky random events, then the game becomes more about luck-of-the-draw and less about any real strategy.
* Bad Combat Encounters
On top of just trying to survive the elements, there are things out there that want to kill you, and you have next to nothing to fight back with! Your choices are fight with a poorly-designed combat mechanism or try to run and ineveitably get overrun anyway. Even if you win the fight, it's likely you will succumb to the injuries sustained in combat, because you don't have the supplies you need to properly treat yourself.
So on top on the bad, unhelpful UI design are a series of random events that will kill you rather quickly, because you never get a chance to get what you need to survive. This game is NOT fun, but rather frustrating, to have to start over and over again and get nowhere in the process. Don't waste your time - Go find a better game.

A classic real-time strategy game with excellent balance and an interesting campaign story.  Though the graphics may be well past their prime the mechanics of the game are still fun to this day.  I assume Dawn of War was truly a trendsetter in its time though this review in particular is being typed up by someone who first laid their hands on it in 2015.
There are several aspects of this game that really hooked me in.  The fact that your units are -actually- units (small bands of soldiers) was a pleasant surprise.  Each unit can be reinforced, given time and requisition (currency), so it will continue to be an active part of your army as long as you replace your losses.  This prevents replacements from clogging up your new unit construction at your base and allows you to keep pressing your advantage without worrying about logistics as soldiers arrive on your frontlines instead of far behind them.  Additionally, I enjoyed being able to personally customize my own units.  If I wanted one unit of Space Marines to excel at eliminating other heavy infantry I could deck them out with a few plasma rifles while if I was going for more an anti-vehicle/building approach with that unit I could supply them with rocket launchers instead.
Though I personally can't think of any complaints on the game as a whole other than stretching and pointing at the outdated graphics, I can say that I enjoyed the campaign far more than I did the random scenarios or multiplayer.  I found that I had a blast playing the game with objectives and a story but the Starcraft model of 'create a horde as fast as possbile and zerg the other base' got old quickly.  However, I am aware that there are -plenty- of players out there who would find that a great addition to the level of fun that they experience, not a detriment.
I recommend this game to all RTS fans especially those who enjoy the more old-school variants.  I picked it up in a sale and got almost fifteen hours out of the Game of the Year version by itself; fifteen hours that I still believe were very well spent.

The humour is extremely subtle, and without a solid grasp of theoretical physics most of the jokes will go over a typical viewer's head. There's also Rick's nihilistic outlook, which is deftly woven into his characterisation- his personal philosophy draws heavily from Narodnaya Volya literature, for instance. The fans understand this stuff; they have the intellectual capacity to truly appreciate the depths of these jokes, to realise that they're not just funny- they say something deep about LIFE. As a consequence people who dislike Block n Load truly ARE idiots- of course they wouldn't appreciate, for instance, the humour in Rick's existential catchphrase "Wubba Lubba Dub Dub," which itself is a cryptic reference to Turgenev's Russian epic Fathers and Sons. I'm smirking right now just imagining one of those addlepated simpletons scratching their heads in confusion as Dan Harmon's genius wit unfolds itself on their television screens. What fools.. how I pity them.

A classic real-time strategy game with excellent balance and an interesting campaign story.  Though the graphics may be well past their prime the mechanics of the game are still fun to this day.  I assume Dawn of War was truly a trendsetter in its time though this review in particular is being typed up by someone who first laid their hands on it in 2015.
There are several aspects of this game that really hooked me in.  The fact that your units are -actually- units (small bands of soldiers) was a pleasant surprise.  Each unit can be reinforced, given time and requisition (currency), so it will continue to be an active part of your army as long as you replace your losses.  This prevents replacements from clogging up your new unit construction at your base and allows you to keep pressing your advantage without worrying about logistics as soldiers arrive on your frontlines instead of far behind them.  Additionally, I enjoyed being able to personally customize my own units.  If I wanted one unit of Space Marines to excel at eliminating other heavy infantry I could deck them out with a few plasma rifles while if I was going for more an anti-vehicle/building approach with that unit I could supply them with rocket launchers instead.
Though I personally can't think of any complaints on the game as a whole other than stretching and pointing at the outdated graphics, I can say that I enjoyed the campaign far more than I did the random scenarios or multiplayer.  I found that I had a blast playing the game with objectives and a story but the Starcraft model of 'create a horde as fast as possbile and zerg the other base' got old quickly.  However, I am aware that there are -plenty- of players out there who would find that a great addition to the level of fun that they experience, not a detriment.
I recommend this game to all RTS fans especially those who enjoy the more old-school variants.  I picked it up in a sale and got almost fifteen hours out of the Game of the Year version by itself; fifteen hours that I still believe were very well spent.

TL;DR Snail Games bought a dead IP from 11 years ago, stuffed Ark inside its skin, and let it sit upright at the end of the bar while we all punch barrels for two hours because of the lag.
Alright so, let's kick this off with an important piece of trivia: THIS IS NOT A NEW IP. Not really. I remember hearing about Dark and Light as far back as 2006 and it was ambitious for its time: a fantasy sandbox MMO. It had one TINY dilema though: it was a pile of hot garbage and I soon forgot it existed when bigger games came down the pipeline.
Fast forward almost 11 years under a new developer, we now have the bare bones of of what is shaping up to be a solid Ark clone. That is also one of it's biggest criticisms though. It hasn't distanced itself from its big brother and it shows with both the UI, SFX, and the grinding (which has been dialed up it seems).
Another big issue is that this game has garbage netcode I'm not running cutting edge hardware, but with a 6700k @ 4.7GHz and a 980Ti, I should at least be seeing higher numbers than 30fps. When you jump off the public servers though, it's a totally different experience. On a private server, the game runs as smooth as silk. On the public realms, you're lucky if you can break a barrel open before you die of lack of sleep. Barrels take 1-2 hits to break, by the by.
Don't get me wrong, I still like this game. It has potential. I can look passed the bugged quests, the chugging framerate, and the headache inducing grind, but the hit detection and janky netcode is where I start banging on pots and pans like a six year old. If Snail Games is committed to having a successor to Ark, they need to fix the latency issues.

Simple old-school 2D RPG - an engaging story with turn-based combat. Level design is exceptional, preserving the exploration maze without luring the player to waste endless amounts of time checking every bit of scenery for hidden rare goodies. Run speed is also quick enough to not feel sluggish as well - a real asset.
Combat system is definitely skewed towards physical, as the one real spellcaster has incredibly weak spells - his physical output is more than double his magical output. There's one very prominent battle tactic - and once you learn it, you never really are in any danger of losing to any battle.
Random forced encounters are done away with, instead allowing you to dodge around them - or run head on to trigger an encounter. This is a welcome addition when attempting to explore an area for chests - or in some of the bigger levels.
Story was good, albeit brief. It draws you in, and definitely compels you to move forward at all stages - but the oldschool Final Fantasy lover in me says it felt too short, especially near the end. There's a sweet spot for longevity in this genre, and this one comes up well before the mark.
A plethora of side-quests do pad out the experience if you're one of those people who like 100%'ing a game - but you're looking at <5 hours of straight gameplay regardless. Some of those side-quests could lead into a sequel, but we'll see.
All in all, a good experience - worth the small amount of $ I dropped on it.

This game really brings back memories... while the campaign is pretty awful, the gameplay is very good. Before I got this game on Steam, I had well over 300 hours on the disc version, so for me there is no replayability problem. I especially enjoy the Galactic Conquest mode. Where this game REALLY shines, imho, is the modding community: famous mods like the unofficial 1.3 patch, Battlefront Extreme, the Total Conversion Pack, and Dark Times I and II add so much to the base game.
Pros:
+A lot of replayability (especially with mods)
+Galactic Conquest
+Space assault mode
+Modding support (no workshop, but ModDB has a great section for Battlefront 2 mods)
+Active community on GameRanger
Cons:
-Dated graphics (easily fixed by some mods)
-Horrible AI: some may say that the AI isn't that bad, but by today's standards the AI is atrocious. One of the most frustrating examples is in Space Assault: the AI will not attempt to infiltrate your hangar. For 2005 however, the AI isn't that bad. The Dark Times mod vastly improves AI in the Dark Times game mode
-Boring campaign: essentially a series of instant action battles with unique (but not necessarily fun or challenging) objectives sprinkled throughout
-Sometimes LAN play requires messing around with your network connections (I had to do that)
Unfortunately, my cons section is almost as large as the pros section... Don't let that dissuade you from this game. While overall this is an amazing classic, it can get old quickly. I highly recommend installing the unofficial 1.3 patch, Total Conversion (and the Total Conversion 2.2 patch ), and Battlefront Extreme mods; these will add at least 50 hours worth of additional content to the game.

It's the original Metro...but shinier! Better! More expanded!
While it's not as dark (I mean that literally, not in the metaphorical sense), Redux has a *lot* of improvements over the original
+ Roaming above ground looks a hell of a lot better, and prettier to boot.  Plus, the Metro itself looks great!
+ Two game modes - Survival (Classic) and Spartan (Last Light-style), with Ranger mode built in!
+ Expanded areas to explore, so wandering off into that dimly lit side tunnel is great for finding environmental stories and loot
+ Safes give you a nice loot based incentive to explore out of the way areas for their keys
But, there are a few detractors
-/+ Stealth knockouts break the game like in Last Light. You'll be overflowing with ammo and medkits, but that does make the inevitable mutant hordes easier
-  A bunch of bugs, mostly related to climbable surfaces. Hopping into broken down trains, climbing out of holes in the hub stations, etc
- If you somehow alert anyone, everyone will know exactly where you are regardless, and will hunt you down like a guided missile.
All in all, a very well put together update for Metro, worth the cash!

Company of Heroes 2 had a lot to live up to compared to its predecessor, Company of Heroes. With its deep tactical play and asymmetrical factions, Company of Heroes managed to create a balanced, varied battlefield that evolved as the match wore on. Cover was blown to bits, bodies littered key points and increased amounts of ordnance (and resulting explosions!) would be pumped onto soil and human body alike. It was a game that felt... alive with action.
CoH 2, with its emphasis on the Eastern Front, sought to replicate that balance on two unique factions. The result was a much grittier game, with more brutality than ever before. Additional mechanisms (like Truesight) help add to the tactical complexity, whereas the use of commanders (rather than skill trees) vastly changed the way players fought (and opened up massive microtransaction opportunities for Relic Entertainment). The stalwart CoH community has been slow in transitioning to this new iteration of the game, but with the Western Front Armies add-on there is little reason not to. Combat is now lively and varied as in the original CoH, but more polished and advanced than before. The Oberkommando West (OKW) forces are a great fit to my style of RTS play, with several high-value squads placing pressure on key strategic points rather than a broader, wide-front style of the numerically superior Soviet units, for example.
This is NOT to say that the game is perfect. The single-player story is confronting, but also improbable. Penal squads were not permanent fixtures (and often had frequent troop movements as individuals were sent back after serving their time), Polish allies of the Soviet cause were not executed for no good reason and there was a high emphasis on the determination of a Soviet army that often (as history told) displayed a propensity for cowardice under pressure and a lack of combat discipline, even in the higher ranks. However, no storytelling effort is perfect, and I grudgingly accept that reality. Matchmaking has been a tedious process, with matches taking a long time to start. Even when they take place, matchups are often skewed with a highly experienced player facing an absolute newbie. Match commentators/casters often lack key statistics such as units/value lost and army values on-screen, numbers which would vastly help paint a picture of the battlefield. Lastly, I would like to see replays downloadable from the actual game (linking to
as opposed to the ghetto-feeling method of popping it into our replays folder.
Despite these shortcomings, the game feels polished and fun. I've had many terrifying experiences: watching a 105mm artillery shell fly across my squad of Sturmpioneers and hit a clump of Volksgrenadiers, smashing them to a giant pink mist. I remember the King Tiger that rolled across the bridge to destroy a pair of T34-85s that were marauding my static defences and hapless infantry. I remember the clutch artillery strike that saved a key victory point, securing us victory against our opponents, who happen to be the AI (they aren't pushovers!). Prepare yourself for hours of tactical goodness and intellectual gaming, combining macro- with micro-focused gaming in a seamless experience. You'll get bombed, shot at, destroyed, and pick yourself up to get right back into the fight.
You'll love it.

Company of Heroes 2 is a Real time strategy game that incorprates the Soviet union's Red army, the Germans Whermacht and if you buy the western front DLC you get the Us army and the Oberkommando west. This game uses teamwork or brute force in most cases to over come and destroy your enemys. To create units you get 3 types of supplies Fuel, ammunition, and manpower. Having a certain number of these allows you to create units. You get differant Hqs for every type of unit. Basic infantry, support infantry, Light tanks and Heavy tanks. You must buy these aswell. Doctrines are technicaly commanders that can give you special units or abilites some can do airstrikes others flame tanks others simply boost morale in your men. They can be game changers if used right. Cover is also implemented aswell, using differant types give you men better advantages, brick walls are heavy wood is medium and if your in the open you will most likey die against a Mg nest waiting for you in a house down the street. Know your enemy aswell. If you have a rifle squad dont take on a Panzer 4 but a bazooka team will do the job.Next try and use Mgs smartly, Mgs pin down units so they cant move or shoot use that to your advantage, have a grenadier  squad with grenades chuck them at the pinned enemys while they are immoblie. If they have more exp points you can even pin down a tank by shooting its view ports. Blizzards also effect all troops, if they dont have fire or a warm house or vehicle they will freeze to death. This is a very fun game a nd i recommend it to any one who enjoys RTS or has played the original Company of Heroes.

One of my all time favourite games.
Braid tells a nice sad story. Its a perfect blend of story telling and puzzle platform action.

There is a lot of replayability to Braid. Once you complete the game normally you then have the challenges. Once you've done the challenge you have the ultimate time challenge... complete the whole game in one sitting in a time limit and the time limit leaves very little room for error. Braid is a puzzle-platformer, drawn in a painterly style, where you can manipulate the flow of time in strange and unusual ways. From a house in the city, journey to a series of worlds and solve puzzles to rescue an abducted princess. In each world, you have a different power to affect the way time behaves, and it is time's strangeness that creates the puzzles. The time behaviors include: the ability to rewind, objects that are immune to being rewound, time that is tied to space, parallel realities, time dilation, and perhaps more.
Braid treats your time and attention as precious; there is no filler in this game. Every puzzle shows you something new and interesting about the game world.

So I really, really wanted to like this game, because the amount of potential in this game is absolutely tremendous. The interplay between different systems and the really neat environment and design decisions should have made a great game.
It didn't. There's not enough content for this game to shine, and because there's so little content the problems it has are made starkly apparent. Permadeath is not an inherently good or bad decision, but what it does in a game like NEO Scavenger is force the player through the same few bits of content over and over again. That content has an optimized solution, which means the first 5-10 minutes of every play-through are doing the exact same thing, every time, with no reason or reward from deviating from it. And then you end up at one of the pieces of game content that you _did_ play before, with functionally identical choices. And then you die, fairly or unfairly (and this game _loves_ unfair deaths; there are a number of places where you can die in a narrative scene because you didn't tag a skill!), and you get to do it again.
A simulation game has to hide its brain to be deeply rewarding. This doesn't, and the narrative and the neat bits do not carry it through. Buy it for a couple bucks and play it once or twice, but at list price it is emphatically not worth your money because it will not respect your time.

This game really brings back memories... while the campaign is pretty awful, the gameplay is very good. Before I got this game on Steam, I had well over 300 hours on the disc version, so for me there is no replayability problem. I especially enjoy the Galactic Conquest mode. Where this game REALLY shines, imho, is the modding community: famous mods like the unofficial 1.3 patch, Battlefront Extreme, the Total Conversion Pack, and Dark Times I and II add so much to the base game.
Pros:
+A lot of replayability (especially with mods)
+Galactic Conquest
+Space assault mode
+Modding support (no workshop, but ModDB has a great section for Battlefront 2 mods)
+Active community on GameRanger
Cons:
-Dated graphics (easily fixed by some mods)
-Horrible AI: some may say that the AI isn't that bad, but by today's standards the AI is atrocious. One of the most frustrating examples is in Space Assault: the AI will not attempt to infiltrate your hangar. For 2005 however, the AI isn't that bad. The Dark Times mod vastly improves AI in the Dark Times game mode
-Boring campaign: essentially a series of instant action battles with unique (but not necessarily fun or challenging) objectives sprinkled throughout
-Sometimes LAN play requires messing around with your network connections (I had to do that)
Unfortunately, my cons section is almost as large as the pros section... Don't let that dissuade you from this game. While overall this is an amazing classic, it can get old quickly. I highly recommend installing the unofficial 1.3 patch, Total Conversion (and the Total Conversion 2.2 patch ), and Battlefront Extreme mods; these will add at least 50 hours worth of additional content to the game.

Enemy Unknown is a well-executed game, and especially good if you're new to the series. The whole thing feels very finely-tuned, like this is exactly the game Firaxis wanted to make. That makes it very different from the last real XCOM game, Apocalypse. You won't find any half-implemented concepts or grand overreaches in scope here. That said, Apocalypse was my favorite of the old-school XCOMs for those very reasons; despite the fact that Mythos fell short of its over-ambitious designs, the game was packed full of more detail and complexity than anything to which you could ever compare it. It was a hot mess on wheels, and yet sending my scratch-made war fleet into the alien dimension for humanity's final assault was one of the most rewarding experiences of my gaming life.
And that's why, despite enjoying Enemy Unknown as much as I did, I still don't feel quite the same sense of accomplishment. In the end, it's almost too polished for its own good. A 25-hour grand campaign in this genre is a sprint where many of us are looking for a marathon. And while those 25 hours are delightfully free of sweeping every room in a multi-acre, 9-story tenement building for that last ♥♥♥♥ing brainsucker you somehow missed, it's also free of those organic, zero-to-sixty, oh♥♥♥♥♥♥moments when that last brainsucker turned out to be six multiworms and you just realized you screwed up so bad.
I recommend Enemy Unknown to lovers of squad-level, turn-based strategy games in general, and the XCOM brand in particular. But for diehard fans of the old XCOM games, be aware that this is the summer blockbuster interpretation of some of your favorite books. It's a lot of fun, but it's over a bit too soon.

My first entry into the Metro franchise was with Last Light which I said was possibly the best single piece of media I had experienced in years. Having thoroughly enjoyed Last Light, I jumped at the chance to play the original Metro 2033 in a refined HD format.
I was initially concerned that Metro 2033 Redux would be too far different than Last Light, as I had heard that 2033 was more of a survival-horror game and less of the creepy first-person-shooter that was Last Light. Luckily, upon loading a new game in Metro 2033 Redux you are not only given the option to choose difficulty (Normal, Hardcore, Ranger, Hardcore Ranger), but you are also allowed to choose whether you would like to play in "Survivor" mode (similar to the original 2033 experience) or "Spartan" mode (closer to the action-oriented Last Light).
This made me really happy because I absolutely loved Last Light and just wanted more of *that*. All of my favorite guns and attachments are here; and i'm really glad they put the lighter/notepad and gas-mask-wiping mechanics in.

I don't think I have ever played any game that is so *unforgiving* in terms of having to do everything in a set way. As such even though it can be a lot of fun, it also becomes quite annoying when you realise that you have very little real choices in trms of how to play it. This is doubly annoying when it's not apparent that you are *doing something critically wrong* until 4 hours later when you suddenly realise you are in a dead-end game scenario with no real way out, and you realise that you have to go back to a save you made ages ago to try to make the *right choice* this time; except that the *right choice* is not obvious until prior experience tells you so.
It also becomes clear after a while that the game's design predetermines certain things to happen, no matter what you do to try to prevent it.
I admit that I like games to have choices, allowing for player creativity and multiple ways to make various strategies work; X-com just does not allow for enough freedom of play: some of the ideas were very nice, but just were not implemented well enough to allow for enough possibilities. I was continually wanting to do things that were just not possible becasue of arbitrary restrictions and simplified mechanics.
Another crappy aspect seems to be that sheer luck seems to play such a big part in it too, you can get a string of right missions (that will give you the right rescources, and allow you to build the right things and allows you to control the Countries panic ratings), but you can just as easily get a string of missions that will give you effectively nothing and create a bad domino effect, and just screws things up so bad you end up in a state of impasse.  Repeating the same missions over and over can get very tedius and severely destroys the game immersion imo.
The tactical part can be lots of fun, but with the rest of it being the way it is, just so often isn't an enjoyable playing experience overall.
Becasue of the games ridiculous rigidity, inflexibility and overly linear nature I just can not recommend it. This could be a very fun game that could be made so much better if there was a more sandbox+open ended gamelay aspect to it; a choice of missions that secured areas, rescources, tech, science so that you could strategically plan ahead and take control, and play it the way you want, instead of having to just *jump through the hoops* to get to each stage that the game expects of you.
Edit: I have been making myself play it to see if it gets any better, but no, the more I play it, the more I realise how screwed up it is: uncovering more and more critical failures in the game mechanics. I always really try to see a game through to the bitter end, even when its this messed up, but I am getting to the point where I have had enough; and its a shame because I really like certain parts of it. Very disapointed.

I haven't played an old school RPG for a long time so I thought why not? I was recommended the game by my friend as it was cheap, and one of the groups encouraged the purchase, so shoutout to them people - you know who you are!
The game hits you with hilarious humour that is present through the beginning to the end. Some people might find it cringy or weird, yet I thought it was perfect as you don't see many games that use humour as a major thing as it's risky - althought you have games such as Deadpool and this that pulled it off greatly. There are inside jokes that reflect upon the developer and her past work which was pretty interesting. The reference to the actual player and the meta aspect was very different and it felt like a breather from the actual game. The characters are very interesting with each and single one differing from one another in order to pick your favourites and to simply not be bored with the same kind of dialogue. Quests are major in RPG's and the ones that are presented in this game are unique, interesting and again - funny. There are areas that differ from another that also have their unique enemies that provide a good fight, along with a decent amount of gold and exp. The new skills that are unlocked are VERY classic such as boosting the ATK of the party, provoking an enemy to hit a specific character, hitting enemies all at once yet with a reduced amount of damage and etc. This is the most basic description of the gameplay, in a nutshell :)
I feel like if someone wants to capture the essence of this game, they need to try to immerse themselves to the fullest by blocking out the real world with a set of headphones and a comfortable seat as you'll be playing this game for a while - as exploration is key to finding cool items but also the achievements that people are desperate to get! This game is really a gem not only for the gameplay. Although this is a small indie title, the Dev's respond to every single question that the community ask regarding the game. The timing is near to instant and the first comment will ALWAYS be from the dev - attempting to sort out the problem whilst being kind at the same time.
By no means is this game perfect. There are many bugs and problems with this game as it's completely new - but it's slowly developing. The devs release updates that sort out most of the problems and when a new one occurs, they fix it in a flash. It's £0.15 (dunno how many centssss :S), you're not loosing anything and if you don't like it then oh well, maybe your friend will! But yeah I hope everybody gives this game a shot as it's worth it in my opinion. I've only played around  6 hours and I feel like I'm no where near done!

A very enjoyable and promising early access game.
A refined, High-Fantasy styled ARK, this game expands on the concept with it's unique magic, town and quest systems making it feel like a mix between a survival game and a more traditional rpg.
Played 13 hours straight with two friends and enjoyed setting out into the wild, building a home and overcoming the initial challenges of survival that we were consistently bombarded with, now that we've overcome the local surroundings we can finally think about exploring further across the map.
Running on a GTX 1070, I5 4690k and 8GB of DDRM3 RAM (Yes, I know, I should consider upgrading.) with the game installed on a HDD, initial loading is slow (Around 10 - 15 minutes to get into a server with no further loading required after) but outside of small performance hic-ups here and there the game performs smoothly on a 10 series card but I have heard otherwise for low spec cards and computers.
Bugs are an issue at points in game but I've had nothing that has stopped me from enjoying content as is expected, the largest issue I've suffered so far has been a tamed creature getting stuck on terrain and being unable to move.
After much coaxing and around thirty minutes of manipulation, bringing another creature forced our tamed friend to a different position allowing him to move freely.
Overall in it's current state I'd recommend the game with friends as it provides an enjoyable experience that's all about adventure and discovery.
If you are planning on playing the game Solo then I'd suggest perhaps waiting for some further content updates, the game itself is focused heavily on group play with the house system which you should be familiar with as  the tribes system in ARK and other similar games.
If you only wish to play polished, bug free experiences, then I'd suggest waiting until the game releases from it's Early Access state, bugs are common in these titles and as always, you're buying into a W.I.P product.
Personally, I believe I've found a game that's clicked with me more then many in recent years.
I'll be updating my review once I've spent more time in game and as Major content updates release.

This is the game where skill means a lot. And by "a lot" I mean almost everything. Sure, lucky shots happen everywhere, lags and high ping can bring you down, but a good warrior is determined not only by his accuracy, but by the way he thinks on the battlefield, and most importantly -- by the way he moves there.
And Movement is something one can spend a lifetime to master. Movement is the key element here as velocity plays a crucial role in understanding game mechanics and unbelievable tricks people are doing here and there. Remember, it's much harder to hit a fast moving target.
QuakeLIVE is an absolutely fantastic experience, it's all about pushing the limits. Your patience limits most of the times. And if you work hard on developing your skills, you'll become a much better warrior.
Just keep training, and never give it up. That's it!
Good luck on Arena!
UPD: As long as the Oct 15 update have broken the ELO ratings, prev. established friendlists and clans, UI and stuff -- the game's still a great example of how old (but gold!) decent game mechanics can work throughout the years, even in modern era of gaming.

Let's just get this out of the way;
Yes, the game cheats.
Having been quite frustrated with the gameplay I decided to have an experiment: I saved a game at a point where I had a 50% chance to hit an enemy in front of me. I then tried to shoot him, and missed. I then reloaded the game to try the 50% shot again. And I failed again. After about 10 failed attempts at a 50%  chance of probability, I only have to ask "How do you fail 10 coin flips in a row?"
Now, just saving your game before every shot would be a very poor way to play. But if even that can't win a mission, there's something seriously wrong with the game.
The probability calculation in this game is meaningless. There is some form of calculation in play behind the game mechanics that actually determines success or failure. If you make a decision which isn't considered tactically sound by the game's predefined (and very poorly defined) standards, you will fail regardless of probability.
This game is not hard.
A hard game would have low probabilites that could be raised by careful tactical choices. This game has arbitrary chances that appear to be given to us to indicate only whether or not the developers WANT us to make specific decissions. If the devs want you to fail, you will. Period. This is not a difficult game, this is not even a tactical game. This is a game of repeitition; you must experiment with various tactics until you find the one the devs decided you must use to win.
I genuinely have little to complain about in the game itself. It's fanbase is loyal for a reason; the game has excellent presentation and a genuinely fun UI. I only ask that the devs remove the percentages given to players to indicate the possibiity of success-- or at least replace them with a far more meaningful (and honest) Yes or No indication.
If you can't make a game hard without cheating, then you're not making a good game. You may make a popular game, but it won't be a GOOD game.

Star Wars Battlefront II...
A gem of a game. this is one of the games I will never forget but love all the time. Maybe some of you remember those days when you maybe had it on the PS2 and doing galactic conquest with your bud (co-op) or simply mowing down hordes of enemies with your hero.
Those were times.
So, where do I start:
The game is a shooter (obviously), so typical shootercontrols...well, not really. right click enables your secondary equipmet (grenades, mines, bots or turret; depending what your character is) and your scope/zoom is enabled by your mousewheel. the zoom isnt really needed (except for snipers) so a la CS is possible (you know, hipfire) since your shots land where you aim...well, not always. Some innaccuracy for the blasters, but the weapons come later.
Basically we have 6 classes in the game: 4 of them are the "core unit" and the other 2 are special classes.
The core units are the riflers, the rocketlauncher guys, the sniper and the engineer. Riflers are good against infantry and somewhat effetive against vehicles since the grenades do ~some~ damage against them. Rocketlauncher guys are the anti-vehicle units: By having a strong rocketlauncher and mines/grenades, they can inflict heavy damage against vehicles. Snipers...do sniping, so good anti-infantry. They also have a few grenades and a deployable turret to give them somewhat of a cover. Engineers are the supporters: they carry medi-ammo-kits and can repair/build structures aswell as vehicles(not the building part on vehicles). They carry shotguns and are extremly dangerious on close range...if known properly. They also have kind of C4's, so you could do some traps or hurt some vehicles. They also have their tool whcih repair and can slice up an vehicle, forcing the driver(s) out of the vehicles if the slicing is successful.
You see, the classes are really flexible and aren't op in any way.
The special classes depend on which fraction you're in. The republic for example has minigunners who can give teammates a defensive buff and jet troopers: hovering grenadelauncher dudes.
Yes, the game is balanced: No op units since every unit has its own weakness: Droedikas eg have powerful blasters and a shield, making them perfect tanks and damage dealers. But once that shield is gone or the Droedika has to move...the droedika is quite vulnerable since they technically have less HP than other units.
Short peek on the campaign: the story is quite alright. The objectives are always quite challenging and spice the game up if you're tired of the typical "deminish the enemy reinforcements"
Speaking of reinforcements: When fighting (surface battles), each team has a set amount of reinforcements, basically the amount the whole team can spawn again. if the counter is at 150, around 145 people can respawn since reaching 0 reinforcements (including units ON THE FIELD) is the end of the round. so if you have around 5 people on the field but the reinforcement counter is a 2...you better not lose 2 of your teammates.
But that isn't the only way to win a round: You respawn at set points on the map you or the enemy can conquer. After picking your desired spawn point and class, you are ready to go and fight your enemy! Logically, this means if you have no more points to spawn, a timer will start ticking down from 20 seconds. If your team does not conquer a point in that time, your team loses.
There arent only surface battles: There's also space battles. And oh boy, those are some fine looking space battles. Again, you also have 2 classes here: The pilot, being a weak fighter himself but repairing space ships while flying, and the soldier, having a rocket launcher and a rifle but not being able to repair space ships. Obviously, the role of the pilot is to fight in space and either fight against other vessels or destroy key parts of the enemy main space ship. and even the flyable ships have different roles and abilities! One of them is the allrounder, having fast firing lasers and usually torpedos, making them capable of fighting against other vessels and inflicting ~some~ damage on the main ship. An other one is a pure fighter, being small and unforgiving against othere vessels, usually having an even faster firing gun as the allrounder and special, hard dodgable missiles but having lower HP themselves. the last "normal" space ship is the bomber: Strong, slow firing lasers and (ofc) bombs to inflict heavy damage against the main ship. They ~can kind of~ fight against other vessles, but it's kinda hard and requires much skill.
In big battles, you'll experience a bigger, special vessel: This usually is a transporter and a strong vessel, being capable to transporting soldiers aswell as taking down several other ships. Downside: they are quite slow and so it's hard to dodge missiles or shots.
Short peek on the soldiers: They are made to infiltrate the enemy main ship and destroy it from the inside. the blaster to kill the defending units and the rocketlauncher to destroy key parts of the ship from the inside.
They key parts can be repaired by pilots if damaged. Once they are destroyed, it's too late (except the shield generator. That one can be repaired after destroyed, reestablishing your shield). And yes, the main ship has a hangar in it and a shield to prevent direct damage at the key parts of the ship.
In galactic conquest, you can buy certain classes and perks before entering a fight. Perks are eg more ammo, additional reinforcements if they run low, more HP for the units or (the all time favourite) the hero. The hero usually is devastating, mostly killing normal units really fast without having to fear any strong resistance. They vanish after some time but to stay on the field, they have to kill more enemies. If not...well, good bye hero.
You earn credits by fighting: The more planets you own and depending on if you won or not the more money you will get. Sometimes, a good perk is more devastating and helpful than an additional class.
Another small thing about surface battles: The vehicles I am talking about are the usual star wars tanks you've seen in the movies. Straight up: they are tanks. every tank is different by having other weapons: One of them has a laser, another one has rockets. OFC: depending on which side you're on.
I give this game a solid 9/10. The game always is challenging, doesn't matter how much experience you have and you will never get bored of it. Even IF the heros are op, a team capable of teamwork can take those down. Or a well landed rocket. That mostly does the job well enough.

The beauty of Dying Light is that there's always something happening. The slums and their surroundings aren't the most evocative of settings – although they can be strikingly beautiful – but they feel alive in a way that is rare in expansive glossy gamespaces. As you wander the streets and leap across the rooftops, you'll often hope to be distracted from whatever humdrum errand the dreary cast have set for you. The game never fails to deliver. Whether it's a lone zombie, stumbling through the streets like the lost member of an apocalyptic pub crawl, or a random gang of marauders armed to the teeth, there's always somebody to play with.
Fancy leading those marauders into a massive crowd of zombies? You can do that and then watch as all hell breaks loose. Perhaps you'd prefer to taunt your enemies from a rooftop, lobbing knives, throwing stars and molotovs from on high? Fair enough, but don't be surprised if they manage to find a way onto your perch. There might even be a nearby trap that you can remotely trigger, causing an explosion that brings every dead thing that can crawl or walk into the vicinity.
Dying Light is consistently entertaining. As soon as the overlong prologue is out of the way, the plot mostly takes a backseat and leaves you to speed off in whatever direction you choose. You could become a scavenger, sneaking through buildings to find junk that can be transformed into deadly weapons, or you might enjoy exploring the rooftops, and trying to gain access to the secluded and secure nooks and crannies of the world. If you're as amused by the satisfyingly solid melee combat as I am, you could spend an hour or two squishing skulls.
Each of those activities will help you to progress through one of the three skill trees – Agility, Power and Survival – and, as I did, you'll transform from a man capable of carrying sixteen large metal pipes in his pocket while leaping from one building to another, to a man capable of kicking zombies to mush while gleefully bouncing around the city like a deranged Zebedee. Did I mention that Dying Light is gloriously entertaining?
There's a catch. There's always a catch, and in this case you might be able to guess what it is. If you've ever played a game, or paid any attention to the kinds of games that people play, you'll probably be aware that Dying Light appears to have borrowed all of its bits from various places. It's Dead Island with a bit of Far Cry 3, plus some AssCreed parkour, and so on and so forth. Of course, at some level everything is an amalgamation of influences and borrowings, but Dying Light looks like a particularly obvious magpie, with a collection of shiny things plucked from elsewhere.
That does mean it's rarely surprising. Everything works as you probably expect it to but, on the whole, all of the parts work exceptionally well. There's no small amount of skill involved in the combination of all these elements. If I were to criticise the game for being derivative, I'd perhaps say that it feels more like craft than art, but it's certainly good, solid crafting.
I'll move onto the most original aspect – the day/night dynamic – in a few paragraphs, after covering the basics. Melee, which is the bulk of the combat, feels weighty and has some extremely effective hit locations. Thwack a zombie on the back of the legs and it'll buckle to the floor, where you can continue to pummel it, preferably aiming for the head, which will burst like a melon in a war. Strap a couple of batteries and a power cord to a weapon and it'll cause limbs to twitch as the corpse collapses. The violence is extreme and when I was splattering a shambler over a wall becomes just a little too amusing, I often had to remind myself that they're already dead. It's fine. I mean, I probably shouldn't find killing dead people quite as funny as I do, but it's definitely fine.
Physics have been improved since Dead Island and the use of vertical environments means you'll spend a lot of time pushing zombies off things. This is to be encouraged, as is climbing out of reach and then making a racket so that zombies on nearby rooftops decide they want to eat you and foolishly launch themselves into the air. I can honestly spend an hour just walking around and watching the way they interact with the world, confused and sometimes weirdly tragic.
All of that climbing and jumping is courtesy of the parkour system. It's – ahem – leaps and bounds above anything that AssCreed has ever offered. Ubi's series is fine if you want to drive up the side of a cathedral by pressing 'W' or pushing a stick forwards, but Dying Light's parkour is about precision. You'll need to target ledges to grab onto them, which means a lot of your ascents will be slow and thoughtful. Eventually you'll move fluidly from one foothold to the next, but it'll take time and mastery.
The physicality of your avatar's body is strong as well and while there are occasional oddities – most often, I grab a ledge a split second after seeming to have fallen past it – the sense of being present in the world rarely fades. Even though you're doing impossible things, your character never has the invincibility or biological get boosters of a superhero. Every action feels like it requires effort, even if climbing and jumping never seems to drain the stamina bar that a few pipeswings will diminish completely.
And then there's night time. A couple of missions in, I was ready to throw a tantrum about how the danger of the darkness had been wasted. It seems as if the switch to the city at night is going to be a scripted occurrence, for certain story missions only, but thankfully that's not the case. All the time that you're outside a safe zone – areas that can be unlocked by clearing of unlife as you explore – a timer is ticking down, and eventually you'll be warned that you only have a few minutes to get to safety. That can lead to mad scrambles and desperate mistakes. Nothing worse than being pinned down by a crowd of hungry corpses when you need to be two blocks away, tucked up in bed in a brightly lit compound.
At night, you see, the real monsters come out to play. Capable of beating you in a race and equal to your climbing skills, the Volatiles are Dying Light's true horrorshows. You can run from them, pressing 'B' to glance over your shoulder as they chase, but that's only advisable if there's a safe zone nearby. They'll catch you eventually. Instead, you should hide.
Night time is either a panicked chase or a stealth game. The Volatiles are marked on your map, vision cones and all, and it's possible to evade them as you make your way home. It's another borrowed element, I guess, but, like the rest, it's well executed. There are tricks that make the night less formidable but it takes a while to discover them. Until then, it's better to rest somewhere safe and wait until morning. Except, experience points are doubled at night, so there's a reward at the end of all that risk.
Dying Light is the Frankenstein's monster of AAA games, an undead craft project made up of scavenged parts. As with the monster, however, Techland's latest is more than a shambling, stitched up chimera. The movement and melee feel solid and convincing, and although the world isn't as varied as I might have liked, it's a fantastic playground for thousands of emergent scenes, from panicked horror to improvised farce.

Overall there are many large improvements in visual fidelity and gameplay, while some textures are lower resolution than the original and some effects are dumbed down such as the blue light in the tunnel. The voice acting for Artyom while of a better quality, does lack the atmospheric feel the original had. Plus the children now sound like old women.
Though even with the few issues, the graphical improvements and gameplay improvements that are there more than make up for it. Such as much better and more refined combat, better dynamic lighting, better textures in most areas, better physics engine, more areas and secrets to find, better A,I, much better performance than the original, and so on.
If you enjoy the original 2033 and felt it just needed more polish, then this is for you. If you have yet to experience 2033 and are curious about it, Redux is the best option for a first play. If you just couldn't run 2033 even on your powerful system and clamor for better optimisation, this is for you.
Another cool little feature as well, would be the option to change the playstyle. There's one option that has the more survival horror approach of the original and another that goes for a more action oriented game.
Overall a wonderful remake that did much more than just update visuals, but basically everything else to a much better state.
