DL reminds me of Fallout with bland characters, lack of charm, and boring writing. The game play though, is what carries this game. Fighting hordes of zombies is tons of fun when my character was strong enough and I'd unlocked some cool abilities. The game play and aesthetic of the game feel like a beefed up version of Dead Island. I've heard some people say it's the game that Dead Island should've been. Dying Light does feel like a mash-up between the newer Fallout games and Dead Island. The graphics are decent. Nothing too amazing, but good. The game takes some time to get going. The first few hours are the most difficult as your character has very limited abilities and can be constantly overwhelmed. I almost gave up and quit playing. As the character gets more abilities, exploring the environment is more fun. The parkour of the game is done very well. Certainly it takes some time to master, but it's really easy to understand. The day/night cycle was really intimidating for a long time. At night, much stronger monsters come out and almost instantly kill you. I was well into the game before I could mount a decent counter-offense to those super tough monsters. Even then, it was usually just a better idea to go back to a safe zone at night and continue questing at dawn. Navigation in the game is mostly intuitive. There's a map, but just kind of going in the right direction will get you where you need to go; even if sometimes I ended up blindly swan diving of the side of a cliff because I couldn't see what was ahead of me. That goes for both the parkour and the driving. I really liked The Following DLC. It's DLC done right. It's still the same game, but they change things around. Instead of the cramped parkour map to traverse, it's the opposite. It's a huge flat land that needs to be driven around in your dune buggy of zombie death. It's still the same essential game, though. I gotta point out, the Dying Light community is one of if not thee best around. Many times, people would join my game just to give me cool gear. Weapons that wouldn't degrade after two fights like the normal weapons tended to do.  More experienced people would show up to help me out. That was cool and a big thanks to all those in the Dying Light community. Dying Light is good, and if you're a fan of the zombie slaying, open-world rpg genre, then it's the game for you!

“Saints Row 4” is quite characteristic in the series of Saints Row in the sense that you start the game as top dog then become underdog then become top dog again. Also this game requires somewhat of an investment in the series because it contains characters and references from all the Saints Row games. You are the president, you are badass and you know it; movie star Nyteblade is your pal who wants to hang out with you. You get to solve either World Hunger or Cancer and you punch a guy for disagreeing with you. The restart happens when aliens take over and blow up the earth, giving you two worlds, the real world and the simulation world. The game’s tone is trying to make you, the player, feel as badass as you can and it does this through giving you super powers, and a character that acknowledges his own superiority over everyone else. The gameplay also follows the same theme, making you insanely powerful through outrageous weapons and powers, super speed and jump making transportation redundant, and mini-games that utilize them.
The gameplay not only references and parodies pervious Saints Row games, but also a lot of pop culture, some guys from Game Front did a cursory job compiling it here:
. To an effect, it works as a nod to pop culture but it also works to put the protagonist in a multitude of heroic situations, making your version of the protagonist (which may be yourself if you are have an ego) the hero of every game and movie. The gameplay has stayed relatively similar to the rest of the Saints Row series: third-person shooter, capture this point, notoriety, blow up♥♥♥♥♥♥ Professor Genki, and included a few new ones: hack stores, platforming, and battle arena (where you fight a notable character in a previous game), all designed to make your character more of a badass than already is.

Generally speaking, the gameplay is very easy, which further purports the idea of your character being awesome, but the game also tends to drop those powers every so often in order to make the game a bit more challenging. Unfortunately the game does not distinguish the game world upgrades with the real world, which means that the game world upgrades will apply to the real world guns and body, which doesn’t make sense and never gets explained. Also the mini-games become less difficult as you get more upgrades, which takes the challenge out of a challenge. Of course this all demeans the level of accomplishment you get in beating “Saints Row 4” and its mini-games.
In a more in depth look, there is a distinct difference between the real world and the game world, which gave me a message that I felt was uncharacteristic of Saints Row. Understand that in the game world, your character is super powerful and in the real world your character is not. If the protagonist is the extension of the player, then in making the real world protagonist lame, homeless, and weak, and the simulation protagonist super awesome; then in playing as the real protagonist who plays in the simulation is a statement in saying that video games is an escapism from your lame life. While plot in the simulation world is relevant to the real world plot, the most meaningful change in power is from when the protagonist leaves the simulation and beats alien leader Zinyak in real life, which again is a statement in saying that you should stop playing and really wake up to the real world.
Overall it’s a fun game. You blow stuff up, Terry Crews calls you “playa”, and you win.

I dive off of the roof and he dives after me, we both fire madly on the way down, I activate slow motion and finish him off, moments later slamming into the ground, dying instantly. This game is awesome, diving and sliding around madly shooting everyone haphazardly, not worrying about your death count, only your style. I've played plenty of RPGMaker titles released on steam. Some really good, others completely miserable. This one is neither, but it definitely isn't all that good. That as hardcore completionist I left the side-jobs just to rush the main plot should say enough. Sadly, it didn't really lead to a satisfactory conclusion regardless.
So let's sum up why this is one of the "bad" RPGMaker games:
* Absolutely the worst thing here is the attrocious level design. Narrow ugly unnatural looking mazes. I've never before seen a RPGMaker game with such horrid levels to navigate around and play with. Also the overland map was the most sloppy and amateurish I've seen so far.
* Bad combat. 70% of the game exists out of fighting 2 guys who die in 2 hits... with a part of 4. Then the end 20% there's 3 guys that die in 2 hits. Both extremely weak. The other 10% is bosses, which can be stunlocked with ease, making them rather easy hitdumps. Even the final boss. Who for some reason needed to have insta-kill attacks on each hit. So stun or die. Oh joy. Guy has a fairly insane hitpool too.
* Some really weird balancing. The wizard character does more damage with the standard attack than any of his spells. Infact, the higher leveled the spell and more mana it takes, the less damage it does. What?
* Bad plot and characters. You can see the "twist" from a galaxy away, there is no believability for characters ("I'll never join the rebellion!" "Please?" "Oh, I will join the rebellion, you're so convincing!". Just way too many forced things ingame to make you scratch  your head. For example the final boss had a big speech about not caring for you and not wanting to fight you etc... and then after the long monologue it goes "Oh, I'm going to kill you anyway"... HELLO? And that was more rule than exception.
* Some slacky polish which stands out like blue/red flags being important then seeing a whole enemy camp in your flag color immediately AFTER the whole color conversion (*sigh*), people standing on chairs, moonwalking mining, bartenders asking you for a drink and not selling anything. Overall, it felt sloppy.
But I guess it does have some good things going for it:
* Low price
* NO random enemies. Thank god. Running past most boring combat was very helpful too.
* Generally citizens updated their conversations based on your actions, aside from some exceptions which are probably due to the sloppy execution.

Braid was told to me by someone in a forum, being an overlooked game and all. So after a year, I finally tried it out when it went sale. And...
There's a lot to compliment about Braid, and I'll start with the art style.
It is magnificent. Wonderful hand painted-like backgrounds to 2D variations sprites of these hand painted-like objects in the game. Everything good about aesthetics, this game has.
Next is the plot. It is a story about a rather looking middle-aged man named Tim, that traverses different worlds from his house to find and rescue a "Princess". There are only a few noticeable characters, and, including Tim, are all very odd. The game offers a rather...no...very surreal plot, in a way that not everyone would understand, and probably it's intended best that way, for the people themselves to leave it to their imagination. I would like to talk about the ending, but I'll just spoil you guys. Which I would have to say, one of the most surreal endings I've seen yet.
Finally the game's mechanics. It is a puzzle-platformer. 'Nuff said, but is it a good one? Yes,
. The system is so
, that it contrasts your average platformers, and it provides a unique mechanic in every world. With that, it takes away the "redundancy" we see in most platformers.
The system's mechanics are divided into two: The
; and The
.
The Basic Mechanics is supposedly Tim's otherworldly powers, which is controlling Time, either reversing it, forwarding it, or stopping it, but Tim goes along with the Time's flow, he does not stop in one point when he controls it, unless he has Time Immunity. The World's Mechanics, is how the World's reacts to everything, including Tim. The variation will differ in every new world. An example would be, that in one world, as Tim moves forward, everything moves forward, but when he moves backwards, everything moves backwards, disregarding him controlling Time to reverse time. As in another world, everything just moves backwards.
The game has
. Whenever you die, you'll just be prompt to reverse time, so that you can prevent what killed you in the first place. The puzzles are literally two parts; the platforming puzzle, and the puzzle pieces you actually collect.
Does it have hints? No. The introduction to controls are rather a-blurred, that if you don't know how Braid works at first, you'd find that you can control time when you die. It's not a game for casuals...I would think that, but...the game has no deaths, as I've said.The platforming is brutally hard per se, but I'm pretty sure everyone with decent puzzle-platforming skills can manage it. So long they get used to the game's mechanics.
Lifespan is more or less 5 hours if you're a decent puzzle-platform gamer. As you would see in my game time, that will include the time I had breaks, like alt-tabs. But that excludes(for now) the "Hidden" stuff, that you people would know later on.
. Probably as people say, it is an overlooked game amongst others, but I would greatly recommend this to everyone who enjoys puzzles and platforming.

Let's just get this out of the way;
Yes, the game cheats.
Having been quite frustrated with the gameplay I decided to have an experiment: I saved a game at a point where I had a 50% chance to hit an enemy in front of me. I then tried to shoot him, and missed. I then reloaded the game to try the 50% shot again. And I failed again. After about 10 failed attempts at a 50%  chance of probability, I only have to ask "How do you fail 10 coin flips in a row?"
Now, just saving your game before every shot would be a very poor way to play. But if even that can't win a mission, there's something seriously wrong with the game.
The probability calculation in this game is meaningless. There is some form of calculation in play behind the game mechanics that actually determines success or failure. If you make a decision which isn't considered tactically sound by the game's predefined (and very poorly defined) standards, you will fail regardless of probability.
This game is not hard.
A hard game would have low probabilites that could be raised by careful tactical choices. This game has arbitrary chances that appear to be given to us to indicate only whether or not the developers WANT us to make specific decissions. If the devs want you to fail, you will. Period. This is not a difficult game, this is not even a tactical game. This is a game of repeitition; you must experiment with various tactics until you find the one the devs decided you must use to win.
I genuinely have little to complain about in the game itself. It's fanbase is loyal for a reason; the game has excellent presentation and a genuinely fun UI. I only ask that the devs remove the percentages given to players to indicate the possibiity of success-- or at least replace them with a far more meaningful (and honest) Yes or No indication.
If you can't make a game hard without cheating, then you're not making a good game. You may make a popular game, but it won't be a GOOD game.

I came in expecting the simplicity of Galcon Fusion, but got something in between Galcon Fusion and Sins of a Solar Empire (though closer to Galcon). This is partially the games fault, and partially my fault.
The first third of the tutorial (what I'm calling the incredibly short campaign/story mode) is nightmareishly painfully slow to get through at first, but gets much better about a third of the way through. They overly spell things out for you, while not explaining other things your become interested in out of bordom that they shouldn't be showing at all. I think a single page overview of all iconography and abilities (without going into strategy) would have been more ideal.
The difficulties don't seem right. There are 5 settings (we'll call 1 easiest). Difficulty 4 feels like 2.6. I have yet to try difficulty 5, but will with my next game. It could be perfect (until one improves), or could be too high of a jump from 4. We'll see. Multiplayer seems non-existant. I hope you can can set it before the game starts and not change it (other than limited pausing). But I can't test any of these things. Match reporting is a bit bare bones, but does exist for a handful of stats.
So it's not perfect. Nice piece, but lacks polish. General gameplay feel is fine. Could use space jumping to alters, map selection preview, line graphs stats, match time, and some other very minor things.
But this game and the other two mentioned in this review are all fun. All recommended.

This game drops you right into conflict: you wake up amnesiac, barefoot, naked, with a hungry wolf-thing in the adjacent room of a cryogenic facility.
The first second of the game is pretty much the last time you won't be desperately hungry, thirsty, hypothermic, exhausted, bleeding out, diseased, hunted down, or some gruesome mix of these things.
From there, the game revolves around challenging resource management as you explore a large hex-titled world looking for supplies and answers.
Do you leave behind the squirrel-trap or the cleaver?
Do you carry the sleeping bag or the rifle with 5 bullets?
Do you risk alerting the raiders nearby with a bonfire or do you let the cold weather grip you a bit tighter for another sleepless night?
Do you eat the rancid meat or do you risk a fist-fight with another looter to see if they have food?
Do you slowly drag their corpse to the woods to cook their flesh or do you press onwards into the fog of war?
Do you run to your next destination and get there in a day or do you silently sneak there and get there in three?
Until NEO Scavenger, I had no idea a turn-based hex-tiled game could compel such a convincing post-apocalyptic desperation.
My advice to you is to just jump in and hang in there until you've spent a couple hours. To be honest, I didn't even like the game at first until I'd suffered about ten deaths or so. Then I began to understand and get a glimpse of what the game had to offer. Like when I let a bandit limp away from a fight only for him to come back five turns later to kill me in my sleep with the cleaver I left behind at a salvage site a few tiles away.
It also sometimes feels like you aren't making any progress since it's so easy to die (permadeath), but soon you realize that you're surviving a little longer every attempt - 3 days, 5 days, 1 week, 2 weeks. And the game just gets better and better as you begin to master it. What used to seem like a basic combat system turns out to be a nuanced one. What used to seem like a pointless skill/ability becomes your favorite. etc.
My only complaint is that the UI is sometimes a bit tedious. For example, having to put down the sleeping bag every night and remember to pick it back up in the morning. Or doing the same 10-mouseclick dance with the crafting system to chop wood, light a fire, cook meat, and then eat the meat. But then again, you're usually so happy to find meat that 10 or so clicks is a small price to pay.
Also, due to the crafting system UI, it's tedious to answer the question: "What can I craft with the things I currently have in my inventory?" As I accumulate items, I often find myself flipping through my recipes to see if I can make anything useful, only to do it again in five turns to see if anything changed. The game would benefit from a quick-view of "Here are the items you can currently craft" with the ability to click those items to instantly make them.
However, the grid-based inventory management system is a fun minigame in itself. It really is addictive to answer questions like "Should I put the pistol with zero bullets in my pocket or should I fill my pocket with these gummy bears?" - Oh wait, your worn-out pants are going to disintegrate in about five turns, but you'll probably get hunted down by a mutant wolf before you have to deal with that.
Good luck!

So, my review is only recommending Metro 2033 Redux, and not Last Light Redux. For one, I don't own the Redux version of Last Light, and from what I've read so far I don't need to. I own the original Last Light, and minus a few AI changes, I've seen no changes that really justify buying a game so recent a second time.
That all being said, I can seriously recommend 2033 Redux. Having been a huge fan of the original 2033 (if you wander over to my game list, you'll see I have played 2033 multiple times over the course of years since it came out, testing it on different systems), I was happy to see that it was getting the improvements from Last Light, a game that I had previously played on PS3, and then bought on PC recently.
The new engine certainly breathes new life into 2033. Not only is the lighting cleaner (though in some spots I wouldn't say it looks better) and character models more varied with slightly more detail, but it also runs a lot better. This is the first time with 2033 that I could have 1080p, with max graphic settings AND max Physx settings on all at the same time, and NEVER drop below 60 FPS (fair warning though, I'm using a 780ti, 16 GB RAM, and an AMD 8350 to power all that). The game looks just as gorgeous as it always has, or as gorgeous as a post apocalypse settings taking place mostly in dark, damp tunnels and ruined indoor buildings can possibly look.
Gameplay changes are probably the most welcome though. Not only are the same controls and UI brought over from Last Light in its entirety, but AI is a lot better (making stealth sections THOUSANDS of times more tolerable), and gunplay is smoother. The best part is, you can have all that while still retaining the same original Metro 2033 difficulty, which I loved to begin with.
The majority of the story is exactly the same, with 90% of the same voice acting and audio files. The most jarring change is the children however...they sound...worse. You can tell this time around, they just brought some adult that had a slightly high pitched voice to redo the acting, and it just sounds so...awkward. I know a lot of people hated to original kids voice, but at least it actually sounded like a kid.
If you also owned the original Metro like I did, you also got a discount on the pre-order. I don't know if that will last into the actual release, so don't quote me on that.
Overall, Metro 2033 really enhanced the experience while also leaving the majority of what made the original great in the first place intact, and that's the mark of a truly great remastered game. I can't speak for Last Light Redux however.

Dying Light is a lot of fun. I enjoyed the long time I spend playing through it. The game took over 50 hours and there's still a lot of side quests I didn't bother with. The writing in the game and the characters were the worst part of the game. I didn't really care about anything that was going on plot-wise. DL reminds me of Fallout with bland characters, lack of charm, and boring writing. The game play though, is what carries this game. Fighting hordes of zombies is tons of fun when my character was strong enough and I'd unlocked some cool abilities. The game play and aesthetic of the game feel like a beefed up version of Dead Island. I've heard some people say it's the game that Dead Island should've been. Dying Light does feel like a mash-up between the newer Fallout games and Dead Island. The graphics are decent. Nothing too amazing, but good. The game takes some time to get going. The first few hours are the most difficult as your character has very limited abilities and can be constantly overwhelmed. I almost gave up and quit playing. As the character gets more abilities, exploring the environment is more fun. The parkour of the game is done very well. Certainly it takes some time to master, but it's really easy to understand. The day/night cycle was really intimidating for a long time. At night, much stronger monsters come out and almost instantly kill you. I was well into the game before I could mount a decent counter-offense to those super tough monsters. Even then, it was usually just a better idea to go back to a safe zone at night and continue questing at dawn. Navigation in the game is mostly intuitive. There's a map, but just kind of going in the right direction will get you where you need to go; even if sometimes I ended up blindly swan diving of the side of a cliff because I couldn't see what was ahead of me. That goes for both the parkour and the driving. I really liked The Following DLC. It's DLC done right. It's still the same game, but they change things around. Instead of the cramped parkour map to traverse, it's the opposite. It's a huge flat land that needs to be driven around in your dune buggy of zombie death. It's still the same essential game, though. I gotta point out, the Dying Light community is one of if not thee best around. Many times, people would join my game just to give me cool gear. Weapons that wouldn't degrade after two fights like the normal weapons tended to do.  More experienced people would show up to help me out. That was cool and a big thanks to all those in the Dying Light community. Dying Light is good, and if you're a fan of the zombie slaying, open-world rpg genre, then it's the game for you!

First of all, I'd like to start by saying that I am not one for reviewing games, but the 4th installment of the Saints Row franchise, in my opinion, definitely deserves to be given an excellent review.

The overall plot and gameplay of Saints Row IV is amazing. Unlike previous Saints Row games, this one emphasizes the feeling of even more freedom when exploring the simulation of Steelport, along with having the ability to use various superpowers which does make this game extra fun to play.

You might even have a special bond with the other characters in the game such as Kinzie Kenzington, Shaundi, Matt Miller, Johnny Gat, Pierce etc. I know I do. And that for me makes me feel like I personally know them all like they are my best friends in the whole world. This feeling is of nostalgia, which is a happy feeling, but also sad in a way because of the fact that the world and characters in this game cannot exist in the terrible reality we live, but only in my head can they be real.
Finally, playing this game makes me feel like living in space - no worries, no troubles, no anxieties, not even anything I fear would go wrong at all. Just exploring my own personal dreamscape and being reflective on all the best monents of my life. Once again, overall I'd like to say that Saints Row IV is "THE" perfect game and it deserves to be an Overwhelmingly Positive rated game.

-Those who do not mind losing more often than winning.
-Those who want spaceship combat to be tactical, not a flight-sim.
-Those who excel in managing risk-reward decisions.
-Those that wonder how Mass Effect would have been like as a tactical RPG.
My Favorite Pros:
-Alien races are simple, and classic.  Like old-school sci-fi.
-Strategy, timing, and preparation all count in combat.
-Can't get enough of that music.
-Even my losses can create fun stories to tell later.
My Annoyed-At Cons:
-Some runs simply do not give you enough resources.  Bad luck.
-Hard to practice against the last zone since it's easy to die before them.  Just keep playing.
-One of the unlockable ships is almost impossible without cheating.  You'll see what I mean.

Storm Of Spears RPG is a RPG game (duh) made in RPG Maker. Although there is a warning about inappropriate content, the only inappropriate thing in this game is the characters' lack of clothing (which can be seen in the screenshots). The game itself tells the story about a group of mercenaries which are trying to do a rebellion against a kingdom.
I'm not sure whether the music is from the default RPG Maker asset, but i do know that some of them are. They are used appropriately, however.
Again, i'm not really sure whether they are using default RPG Maker asset, but i do believe that most of them are using the default asset. The character portrait doesn't seem like using a default asset, although that maybe the reason why the character portrait seems to be different from the sprite, especially their height.
The mapping looks lazily done; most of them are placed inappropriately, especially the no-wall section in some dungeons, which looks more like a "pitfall". Even if there is a wall, the wall is like a few tiles away from the floor. The mapping is also using two tiles for a chair (which is not passable) which makes you have to circle around to go to the place that you want.
The battle screen's background is also off; I mean, in most of the backgrounds, the character looks like standing in an obstacle. While i'm at it, there is this odd line where the "xxx attacks" message lefts out after each attack.
Aside from the mappings, the graphic fits perfectly for low screen resolution. The game can be changed to full screen to make the graphic looks blurred.
The UI looks like a default one, although i have to complaint about the quest menu which will close the menu when you are pressing X instead of going to the main menu.
Lastly, the text placement seems to be off; sometimes, the sentence ends in the middle of the dialogue box, sometimes, it fits the dialogue box, and sometimes, the sentence looks cropped (due to the dialogue box's length).
I think i'll just be blunt with this. I don't understand the prologue at all. You are catching someone out of nowhere which turns out to be a leader of a rebels because you are a group of mercenaries hired by someone. After that, it showed that you are in a troublesome kingdom with an unfit ruler which you plan to overthrow.
The MC doesn't look have much resolve at first, although i don't really see any character development on her. She just looks like following the turns of events and somehow made her place at the end. There is also this outstandingly smart little brother which looks like a child to me. The party's background story are explained, although not in detail, and there is also no character development for them except on one side quest.
However, the story keeps on focusing on its main mission without being distracted on some other places. The story concludes greatly and all the events are flowing smoothly.
The first thing that i want to address is how my cursor is always staying behind the game and how i can't exit the game by clicking X (close) button in the game window.
The game starts after you choose one out of three difficulties, with casual being the easiest, normal, and hard. After that, the game will start until you can control your character. For those who are not used with RPG Maker games, there is a short text tutorial about the controls after that.
Although the game has different difficulties, i think that those are scaled weirdly. I only play casual difficulty and while the enemies can be hard to kill (take around 2-3 hits to kill one of them, although there are 3-4 enemies in a battle), the bosses are no different from normal enemies except for a more hp and a more damaging attack (except for the last boss which has a one hit kill skill). I can kill them in a few turns except for two enemies (the last boss and an optional boss, namely the Dark Lord because i fight them in low level at that time).
You'll start with a four person party of an attacker, a healer, a buffer (and a strong attacker), and a magic user. However, i have to say that the classes are unbalanced. The MC, being an attacker in the game, is way too strong compared to the magic user. There is this OP skill which slash the enemies thrice which will have a tremendous damage if she got her attack boosted (which is a piece of cake with the buffer's skill). The mage hardly can use any useful magic and can even deal a higher damage by attacking rather than doing a magic skill. There are also skills which will be learned after they reach a particular level. Note that the damage dealing skills can only be learned by the attacker and the mage.
The game keeps track of its quest in a log which can be accessed from the main menu. The quest differentiates between side quest and main quest with an icon. However, some of the quest has a wrong icon, while there is one quest which has no icon at all. However, the quest is very simple and easy to follow with the quest log.
This game has a few dungeons which is designed perfectly. I do enjoy getting lost in dungeons and this game really helps me fulfill that desire. I'm getting lost several times in the dungeon because of the big map. However, having a big map also means more monster. Luckily, there is no random encounter in the game and the enemy won't respawn unless you leave the area. The only downside is the last town, Ironhorn, which is so big that i keep on getting lost in there.
There are some weapon and armor seller in some towns, although you'll get the equipment from somewhere else most of the times. The equipments are also cheap (less than 100g) which make the items look way more expensive.
When you are almost finished the game, you'll receive a dragon mount. However, you have to go one tile below the dragon to ride it.
Pros:
- 3 difficulties to select from
- Easy to follow quest log
- Greatly designed dungeon
- No random encounter
Cons:
- Unbalanced class
- Lazily done mappings

Well designed game and a good story. I felt all ascpects were well designed, or well, almost all. Becuase while lore, rewards, plot, pacing and pretty much everythig else was well made and well delived, there were three issues:
First one is just a minor but annoying thing; when you click the hotkey for closing the game. The game closes. No warning, no autosave, nothing.
Second one is that the sprites did not match the detailed art very well, the most jarring exaple beeing a skinny blue eyed kid with the sprite of a brown eyed chubby man. This is probably even more minor for most people, but i found it mildly imersion breaking, and thus worse in my book than a mere interface issue like the first problem.
Third one would in many other cases have been dealbreaking. The combat and stat/equipment system was boring. Each new peice of main equipment was a linear upgrade to the previous one, the player party was internally inbalanced, the battles seemed impossible to not win without activly trying to lose, and some stats/items felt outright superfluous and impotent... With that said, I did enjoy the battles at times.
All in all a good game, and as long as you don't expect too much from the combat system, you'll have nice time, and might be pleasantly surpriced at times. It's not a top tier game, but I think most top tier games could learn much from its example non the less.

Hoard is an intense arcade game where your dragon must claw its way to the top of the treasure-heap. However, doing so requires the most from your reflexes, because games quickly descend into a landscape overflowing with flying arrows, defiant knights, and other hostile forces who want to ground your scaly avatar. And that's not including the other dragons (AI or otherwise) who want to be Top Dragon themselves.
If you don't have the time for an epic dungeon-crawl or hour-long matches of bulletslinging, consider Hoard for bite-sized chunks of princess-hoarding fun thickly infused with adrenaline-pumping projectile-avoiding.

This game is a great time. The trailers depict the feel of the game very well (albeit the gameplay in the trailers is a little ridiculous). No game is ever the same. I've played this game for 269 hours at the time of writing this and have not once been bored. That number is soon to increase and despite the existence of established metas there is always room for new ones to emerge (Trust me very few people know about this thing I like to do on defence at mountain base).
Most of the complaints I have seen about this game are regarding matchmaking times. My experience with this is that it depends heavily on your region and the time you are playing. Later on weekends there are many more matches. On average in NA there are usually between 15 and 20 people in the queue, and I usually only wait a maximum of 3 minutes. On weekends I have had matches occur almost immediately. New players sometimes take a bit longer to match up, since the game tries to match you with fair opponents, and certain regions are slower than others. Block N Load's facilitator servers are pretty nice however. As a player in NA, I can still achieve playable network speeds on EU servers consistently, so if your region has few players, try another nearby region (The last set of digits in the tiny white text at the bottom of the screen tells you how many players are in the matchmaking queue. It only works when you yourself are in the queue.).
The real downside to the game in my opinion is the somewhat cringeworthy character design and voice acting. Though nowhere as bad as Paladins (god that game's character design was awful), some of the design choices might seem a bit archaic or mildly offensive. In my opinion the game itself is enough fun on its own that I can overlook some of these design choices, and the actual aesthetic, art and sound quality is still very much professional. This game is a good example of a game that is fun enough to allow for some disagreement with design choices and still enjoy the experience, something I believe is an indication that the game is well worth consideration.
TL,DR:
Game is genuinely fun. Matchmaking issues do exist, but can be circumvented and aren't necessarily awful. Character design issues also exist, but game itself tends to be fun enough to be worth overlooking them. Good game. The more people get this the better the game gets too, so if you're interested at all, TRY IT!

By now you probably know about Metro, the Redux edition is on Last Light's more advanced Engine and the game gets a couple extra bells and whistles. If you're looking for a good excuse to play 2033 again, this is it, if you haven't played the game and it's piqued your interest and you're into games like the Stalker series (albeit the Metro games are linear), do yourself a favor and get the Redux edition.

A handful a levels in so far, and it looks great. Definitely looks like Metro Last Light, and I thought I was for a moment with the loading screen. Have noticed a few areas where they bridged levels together, and I definitely helps to keep the immersion, but seemless levels, such as in the Dead Space games, would have been even better. The ammo limit introduced in Last Light was kept, and helps stay with reality, all though I will miss running around with over a thousand rounds of assualt rifle ammo. Loading between levels was fairly quick, and in the short time I've played so far, I've already discovered several new areas, such as two shooting galleries in the early stations, where you can win MGR, and you have unlimited rounds, so use your MGRs. I also noted that throwing knives and grenades are much cheaper at stores then they were before.
They do need to fix a few things with a patches though, such as displaying the cost of buying and selling ammo at stores, but not how much ammo you are buying and selling. Also encoutered a few graphical glitches, but nothing major. Slightly dissapointed with lack of graphically options. They tied mostly everything into a 'Quality' slider, instead of giving you options such a texture sizes, Ambient Occlusion, shadow quality, etc. They also added a new option to the SSAA slider, '0.5', which causes the game to render at half of your screen resolution, and upscale. This seems like a bad thing, but it can help people who have lower end computers run the game.
To give you a sense of preformance, with everything maxed out, including the advanced PhysX, and with SSAA off, I run at around 80 frames in most areas. With SSAA set to 0.5, I run at around 130 frames. With SSAA set to 4, I run at 15. Beware 4x SSAA, unless you're running SLI. I have an i5-4670K overclocked to 4.0 Ghz, and an EVGA GTX 770 Superclocked with an ACX cooler. Check my profile for the rest of my hardware.

If you ever wanted to play a hobo simulator, this is it.  If you manage not to get RNG'd into the dirt some compelling storytelling awaits you, although you could always avoid it and just try to survive as long as possible.
PROS:
- Excellent atmosphere.
- Smart writing.  It's both verbose and short when it needs to be.
- Mod-friendly.
- Great for both short and long gameplay sessions.
- Visceral combat.  Ripping an arrow out of your arm ans stabbin a man to death with it has a certain appeal.
- Sensible crafting system and multiple skill combinations encourage different playstyles.
CONS:
- It's not winning any graphics awards.  Fortunately this doesn't draw away from the strength of the gameplay, but still...I could see someone not digging the look.
- The RNG God really holds power over this game.  It's hard not to feel like the whole world is against you when you can't find a pair of shoes and your shopping bag full of whiskey and twinkies rips open.  Which leads to my next point.
- The whole world is pretty much out to get you.  There are a couple of somehwat less hostile areas but for the most part everything in this game wants to kill you.  It's like Australia, except Michigan.
- Visceral combat.  It's pretty soul-crushing to finally find a backpack and a decent pair of shoes only to later discover that someone has beat your head in with a sauce pan while you were asleep.

The beauty of Dying Light is that there's always something happening. The slums and their surroundings aren't the most evocative of settings – although they can be strikingly beautiful – but they feel alive in a way that is rare in expansive glossy gamespaces. As you wander the streets and leap across the rooftops, you'll often hope to be distracted from whatever humdrum errand the dreary cast have set for you. The game never fails to deliver. Whether it's a lone zombie, stumbling through the streets like the lost member of an apocalyptic pub crawl, or a random gang of marauders armed to the teeth, there's always somebody to play with.
Fancy leading those marauders into a massive crowd of zombies? You can do that and then watch as all hell breaks loose. Perhaps you'd prefer to taunt your enemies from a rooftop, lobbing knives, throwing stars and molotovs from on high? Fair enough, but don't be surprised if they manage to find a way onto your perch. There might even be a nearby trap that you can remotely trigger, causing an explosion that brings every dead thing that can crawl or walk into the vicinity.
Dying Light is consistently entertaining. As soon as the overlong prologue is out of the way, the plot mostly takes a backseat and leaves you to speed off in whatever direction you choose. You could become a scavenger, sneaking through buildings to find junk that can be transformed into deadly weapons, or you might enjoy exploring the rooftops, and trying to gain access to the secluded and secure nooks and crannies of the world. If you're as amused by the satisfyingly solid melee combat as I am, you could spend an hour or two squishing skulls.
Each of those activities will help you to progress through one of the three skill trees – Agility, Power and Survival – and, as I did, you'll transform from a man capable of carrying sixteen large metal pipes in his pocket while leaping from one building to another, to a man capable of kicking zombies to mush while gleefully bouncing around the city like a deranged Zebedee. Did I mention that Dying Light is gloriously entertaining?
There's a catch. There's always a catch, and in this case you might be able to guess what it is. If you've ever played a game, or paid any attention to the kinds of games that people play, you'll probably be aware that Dying Light appears to have borrowed all of its bits from various places. It's Dead Island with a bit of Far Cry 3, plus some AssCreed parkour, and so on and so forth. Of course, at some level everything is an amalgamation of influences and borrowings, but Dying Light looks like a particularly obvious magpie, with a collection of shiny things plucked from elsewhere.
That does mean it's rarely surprising. Everything works as you probably expect it to but, on the whole, all of the parts work exceptionally well. There's no small amount of skill involved in the combination of all these elements. If I were to criticise the game for being derivative, I'd perhaps say that it feels more like craft than art, but it's certainly good, solid crafting.
I'll move onto the most original aspect – the day/night dynamic – in a few paragraphs, after covering the basics. Melee, which is the bulk of the combat, feels weighty and has some extremely effective hit locations. Thwack a zombie on the back of the legs and it'll buckle to the floor, where you can continue to pummel it, preferably aiming for the head, which will burst like a melon in a war. Strap a couple of batteries and a power cord to a weapon and it'll cause limbs to twitch as the corpse collapses. The violence is extreme and when I was splattering a shambler over a wall becomes just a little too amusing, I often had to remind myself that they're already dead. It's fine. I mean, I probably shouldn't find killing dead people quite as funny as I do, but it's definitely fine.
Physics have been improved since Dead Island and the use of vertical environments means you'll spend a lot of time pushing zombies off things. This is to be encouraged, as is climbing out of reach and then making a racket so that zombies on nearby rooftops decide they want to eat you and foolishly launch themselves into the air. I can honestly spend an hour just walking around and watching the way they interact with the world, confused and sometimes weirdly tragic.
All of that climbing and jumping is courtesy of the parkour system. It's – ahem – leaps and bounds above anything that AssCreed has ever offered. Ubi's series is fine if you want to drive up the side of a cathedral by pressing 'W' or pushing a stick forwards, but Dying Light's parkour is about precision. You'll need to target ledges to grab onto them, which means a lot of your ascents will be slow and thoughtful. Eventually you'll move fluidly from one foothold to the next, but it'll take time and mastery.
The physicality of your avatar's body is strong as well and while there are occasional oddities – most often, I grab a ledge a split second after seeming to have fallen past it – the sense of being present in the world rarely fades. Even though you're doing impossible things, your character never has the invincibility or biological get boosters of a superhero. Every action feels like it requires effort, even if climbing and jumping never seems to drain the stamina bar that a few pipeswings will diminish completely.
And then there's night time. A couple of missions in, I was ready to throw a tantrum about how the danger of the darkness had been wasted. It seems as if the switch to the city at night is going to be a scripted occurrence, for certain story missions only, but thankfully that's not the case. All the time that you're outside a safe zone – areas that can be unlocked by clearing of unlife as you explore – a timer is ticking down, and eventually you'll be warned that you only have a few minutes to get to safety. That can lead to mad scrambles and desperate mistakes. Nothing worse than being pinned down by a crowd of hungry corpses when you need to be two blocks away, tucked up in bed in a brightly lit compound.
At night, you see, the real monsters come out to play. Capable of beating you in a race and equal to your climbing skills, the Volatiles are Dying Light's true horrorshows. You can run from them, pressing 'B' to glance over your shoulder as they chase, but that's only advisable if there's a safe zone nearby. They'll catch you eventually. Instead, you should hide.
Night time is either a panicked chase or a stealth game. The Volatiles are marked on your map, vision cones and all, and it's possible to evade them as you make your way home. It's another borrowed element, I guess, but, like the rest, it's well executed. There are tricks that make the night less formidable but it takes a while to discover them. Until then, it's better to rest somewhere safe and wait until morning. Except, experience points are doubled at night, so there's a reward at the end of all that risk.
Dying Light is the Frankenstein's monster of AAA games, an undead craft project made up of scavenged parts. As with the monster, however, Techland's latest is more than a shambling, stitched up chimera. The movement and melee feel solid and convincing, and although the world isn't as varied as I might have liked, it's a fantastic playground for thousands of emergent scenes, from panicked horror to improvised farce.

Best played with a controller, Shank offers a fluid action-packed arcade beat-em-up in a nostalgic comic style. You play Shank, a skilled fighter who is able to pull awesome combinations using a wide array of arsenals, including dagger, uzi, katana, chains, grenade, shogun and chainsaw. While some combinations are rather boring, like using a chainsaw to mow down an opponent, some are definitely memorable, like shoving a grenade into the mouth of a thug, or pinning an enemy on the ground while sweeping the incoming enemies with uzi  in both directions.
The game may be short (3 to 4 hours max each run-through), but it is definitely a gem offering enriching action gameplay experience.

Prior to its release, a lot of the previews made the game look like a reskin or DLC for Saints Row 3. I held out hope that the devs were going to expand beyond expectations considering all the wacky aliens, superpowers, and ridiculous weapons they were adding. Instead what we got was essentially Saints Row 3.5: a big & stupid Michael Bay sequel that feels like a really long add-on to SR3.
SR 2 & 3 had some restraint and at least attempted to build up to their big action sequences. SR4 starts off with a bang and never stops in the worst way possible. The only thing that breaks up the action sequences are a few comedic moments and nostalgia pandering scenes but even these manage to go over-the-top. Seriously, who has played SR1 and why is so much of this game wasted on referencing it? Many of the rest breaks I took while playing this were just to detox from the Michael Bay-ness of everything; I love blowing up spaceships as much as everyone else, but there's a point in time where you just want to walk through the city and beat pedestrials with a giant♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Much of the game feels like you are forced to take the most explosive route possible through everything; I really wish there was an ability toggle button because simply bumping into pedestrians or vehicles while super sprinting will have the police shooting lasers at you for miles. The majority of this game feels like action for the sake of action with most of it feeling unrewarding and boring at times.
Adding to the rushed feeling of SR4, much of the game doesn't feel playtested. For example, Explosive Blast's chain reaction will kill whole flashpoints with a single fireball from any distance, while the Buff ability feels like a joke considering how late in the game you get it.  Weapons have plenty of issues too; some weapons are completely useless unless you are handed them for a mission (obligatory useless sniper rifle, Alien SMG, Dubstep Gun, etc.) while others slaughter everything unupgraded (Disintegrator, 'Merica, etc.). I found myself using garbage weapons or abilities just to complete in-game challenges because otherwise I would've just used Blast & the Thump Gun for everything.
The storyline feels really slapped together too. Why bother with more simulation exploits when you have a suit of giant power armor in the real world? Everytime something cool happens in the real world it feels like the game drops an arbitrary hurdle for you to overcome inside the simulation. The whole in-out-in-out just feels like padding and an excuse to turn off superpowers for missions, especially considering your Health upgrades carry over into the real world. I really would've enjoyed more time spent in the real world... Perhaps the first part of the game inside the simulation with all the ridiculous superpowers and the second half in the real world, fighting Zinyak on his own turf? Overall it just feels like a missed chance simply because the devs wanted to recycle as much as possible.
So is SR4 just extended DLC for SR3? Yes, but really, really long DLC. I feel like they stretched SR3's assets as far as they could go and whipped together some quick alien tech from recycled STAG parts. People might try to draw conclusions between this and GTA 3 vs. VC & SA, but those were completely new environments, characters, vehicles, and so forth. SR4 manages to even reuse 3's map despite Earth being destroyed (whoops spoilers!)!
Should you bother playing SR4? If you've played any of the previous games, you will find something familiar here. If you are new to the series, don't expect "GTA With Aliens" because this is the most bombastic Saints Row yet. I enjoyed this but it would be my least favorite Saints Row if SR2's PC port wasn't garbage. I recommend giving it a shot but 2 and 3 are clearly better games.

Double Action Boogaloo is a great third person shooter, where players leap and slide around in order to dodge enemy fire. Points are scored based on stunt points, earned by scoring kills mid leap, mid slide, dodging grenades, headshots and more.  There are a number of weapons to choose from, but few playable characters to choose from.
This game features a slow-motion gimmick, where you earn seconds on a slow-mo clock that, when activated, slows time around you (moreso for your opponents) to make aiming easy. There are several maps and you will quickly find areas on these maps that you will want to control in order to dish out the most damage. Protip: da_cocaine's garage entrance ramp.
This game is exclusively multiplayer, but does support bots. I would recommend it to everyone because its fun, and not because I need more people to play this game so I have more opponents to make ragequit.

Review as of 7/22/2017
Pros:
-Ark like survival with a medevil/fantasy twist.
-Epic base building and crafting.
-Engrams learned after you level up in certain areas by actually playing the game.
-Familar game play for ark veterans.
Cons:
-Too many bugs to be currently enjoyable. Just released in alpha early release so I understand this.
-Steep difficulty curve. If you step 100 feet outside the starting area there is a good chance you will be attacked by something you have 0 chance of defeating.
-Fighting monsters is litterally impossible for the first 1-3 hours of the game. You can't hope to kill anything until you can craft ranged weapons, preferably a bow/arrows. Do not buy if you want to create a melee character. You will spend 3 minutes trying to kill a low level sheep with a sword.
-Building is a bit wonky. Hard to place ceilings, foundations place too far into the ground letting grass show through, ect.
Currently Bugs that I have Seen.
-Sky glitch where it looks like you are at a rave. Hurts the eyes.
-Gathering with axe and pick randomly goes from whatever you have it set to to less than x1 making it impossible to progress.
-Glitch with the collect 100 gold quest where you can't complete it and it won't give you a new one until you reach lvl 8, and will then come back at lvl 15.
-Random spots where you get stuck and can't move. I don't mean you fall in a hole, you just start to levitate. Other spots where you should be able to walk up a hill, but it won't let you.
Conclusion: Fun and cool idea for a game. If you want to play something that works, hold off on purchasing for a few months, or at least until they get some of these starting bugs worked out.

Fun and addictive no-frills, casual RTS.
Simple controls, graphics and maps makes for easy navigation and play. You can attack enemies planets and/or defend your own, invade and capture new ones, or lay waste to them in order to hinder your enemies' progress.
However all is not perfect. Everything is nail-bitingly slow paced, from ship building and repairing to resource mining. There is way too much room for improvement, and sometimes it almost feels like the project was abandoned after the very basics were finished, just so it could be marketed.
Traveling between planets can be quite frustrating as once you set your path you cannot retreat half-way through: you have to reach the original destination first, meaning that sometimes you're forced to engage in battles you didn't intend to.
Also, there are no ship or colony upgrades. You cannot make your fleet more powerful, nor can you speed up production, repairing and mining, for example.
When playing solo, the AI can be pretty dumb, often favouring siege over invasion, meaning that you'll end up with a whole lot of destroyed planets long before you have the chance to reach them.
Even with all the negatives, I think it's still worth a shot, but not if you're planing to pay the Steam price of course (*cough* indie bundle websites *cough*).
And last... it's got cards, so if you can get it for a few cents then the cards should pay for most of it.

Metro 2033 is a survival horror game released in 2010, based off of the novel of the same name. It was well received by critics, and a sequel was released a few years later. Metro Last Light brought an improved engine, as well as many optimisations. The goal of Metro Redux is to graphically improve Metro 2033 while giving the gameplay enhancements provided by 2033's sequel. I say that Redux does it's job very well.
Everything has been changed in Redux; 4A has rebuilt 2033 from the ground up in the newest version of the 4A engine, and it shows. The intro videos and main menu screens have been redone, and the graphics options are the same as Last Light. It is also worth noting that the new engine brings the optimisations that Last Light had, so Metro Redux will run well and still look beautiful on old-ish or mid-tier rigs (I can run almost all settings on max, including PhysX, on 1 GTX 770).
When starting the game for the first time, you are given the option to choose your play style. Spartan gives you the action filled style that Last Light has, while still maintaining the basic survival horror feel. Survival stays true to 2033 in that ammo is limited, and stealth and ammo conservation are vital. Both modes can also be combined with Ranger, which limits the HUD - this makes the player more observant, while increasing difficulty and immersion. Note that there is no "Easy" mode, at least from what I have seen. I chose to play on Spartan Normal (action-feel, while keeping the HUD). All modes include the more forgiving stealth gameplay from Last Light, so stealth is a bit easier and more realistic.
The story remains the same, but there are improvements over the original, besides the graphics. Notes are in the world, which expand the story further. I found myself exploring areas looking for notes. The music has been improved, although it is a bit loud for my taste (this can probably be changed in a menu). The sound design is good, but I feel it could have been improved. YMMV, however.
To close, I wholeheartedly recommend Metro 2033 Redux to people who enjoy FPS games with tight controls and excellent mechanics. Although there are minor issues (some bad sound design, lack of an Easy mode), the graphics, optimisations, and added gameplay make this an easy recommendation over the original. If you are new to the Metro games, be sure to check out Last Light Redux.

I'd start by saying that Grimind is by no means a bad or a terrible game. It's a somewhat interesting indie title, which is clearly not done with a massive amount of money, and I tried not to raise my expectations too high. And I didn't. But it still wasn't that good, and towards the end I just wanted it to end already. And that's not a good sign.
Grimind is supposedly a puzzle platformer, and there are plenty of puzzles indeed. Some are really good, but some are based more on the 'platformer' thingy and the game, meaning that it depends more on you're timing and pressing the right key at the right time, rather than you're puzzle-solving skills. The controls of Grimind were basically alright but not 100% fluid, and this fact together with some level-design decisions made me often get to a point of feeling nervous and irritated as I simply couldn't get through a certain section of the game, again and again and again... Until it stopped being and fun.
I could forgive this, though, but unfortunately there wasn't much to keep me intrigued and motivated to actually want to finish this game, aside for a slight curiosity about how the story would end, and my terrible tendency to finish whatever game I play even if I don't enjoy it.
So, I did finish the game, and unfortunately I didn't reach any satisfying conclusion to the game. Found out the I missed one secret and that finding all the secrets in the game would grant me an additional ending.
Went to look for that missing secret, made it to the ending again, and got an even less satisfying conclusion.
Grimind presents you questions and wanderings throughout the entire game but leaves you with no answers, no real conclusion, no real story.
So, unfortunately, awkward story + awkward gameplay equals not such a good experience.
And that's a shame, because Grimind does show potential, there were some entertaining moments, the game had a brilliant sound design which fit the creepy atmosphere, the graphics are very simple and yet captivating, dark and gloomy and yet colorful.
This indie title does have some good features and could be really enjoyable if it only wasn't getting so tedious as the game progresses. It is rather short though, so you could probably get it on a massive sale if you really like this type of things.

You wake up to the sound of freezing rain on makeshift tarp shelter. You take a quick look through your gear making sure nothing has been stolen in the night. Shoving the pieces of your shelter into your pack and throwing your hide cloak around your shoulders you take off through the pouring rain.
You rummage through a few houses not finding much, these where the first places to get scavenger after everything went to ****. As you exit the last house on the street tearing an old tee shirt into rags, suddenly hearing a loud clatter you throw yourself to the ground and watch as a large figure resembling Werewolf from old story's lumbers past. It passes by and you release a breath you didn't know you where holding in. Unslinging the rifle from your shoulder you top off the magazine, fighting a dog man today is not something you wish to happen.

A few days later you stand atop a hill scanning the area with half a binocular you keep slung around your neck searching for any movement while munching on a handful of berries. After several hours you see the flash a blue sash moving out of the tree line, a blue frog preacher not friendly and normally carrying somewhat valuable objects you will have no remorse from ending this ones life. Moving closer as to not waste your valuable ammunition you line up a shot from your rifle. With a loud accompanying crack the figure drops to the ground motionless. as you get close the man jumps to his feet and sprints back into the tree line, Swear under your breath you give chase into the dense forest.
He couldnt have gotten far you think to yourself examining the blood trail. The trees seem to press closer on you and your draw a small revolver from your cargo pants pocket, your rifle would be ineffective at these close ranges. The blue sash makes it easy to find the lifeless body after a few minutes. Your so focous on looting the corpse you almost don't hear the rustle of foliage, you grab your pistol from where it lay beside the body and scan the woods searching for the source of the sound. A single shot whipes by your head and you throw yourself behind a log still searching for your attacker. You take a deep breath staying here is suicide, you lung forward from behind the log in a full on sprint. Stumbling over the overgrown roots of the trees you feel relieved as you see the light streaming for the edge of the forest. In all fairness you almost make it before the second shot rings out catching you in the leg. Gritting your teeth against the pain you fire blindly behind you as you break out into the field. You leap into the tall grass silently thanking what ever god stays about for the concealment. The third shot hits you in the back going through your lung, you cough blood flying from your mouth and then the fourth and final shot the only you don't hear finally ends your pain.
Neo Scavenger is a post apocalyptic survival simulator. You must contend with food, water, the cold, the weight of your equipment, wild beasts and other people in your struggle to simply stay alive. Neo scavenger also adds in sides mission and a story although i must admit i have no lived long enough to complete any of them. Also random events can happen while moving about the hexagonal landscape ranging from slave auctions to abandon camps. Combat is turn based and visceral in its descriptions, enough to make you slightly uncomfortable with each killing blow. A skill is also in place allowing you to change your play style with each life keeping the game fresh. There can be quite a lot of reading in parts however its is done very very well, each line adds more to the atmosphere and does a good job of giving a visual of the surrounding area.
This is a brutal unforgiving game Death comes quickly to the unknowing and the unprepared. Its not everyone's game by far taking up a niche role in giving a somewhat realistic survival game, probably the closest ive found to a proper simulator.
I give NeoScavenger an 8.5/10
Menus can be rather clunky at times and starting off as a new player can be rather brutal but once you grown acclimated to the environment it becomes a rather masochistic joy to play. Just be wary of purchasing and watch some footage and play to free demo to see if you think you would enjoy the game.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a great strategy game, and also my favorite game of all time. It's like many other games: easy to learn, hard to master. There is so much nuance to this game that you won't see at first. As it starts to unfold, you realize just how clever it is.
There are two games in one here: The strategy game, and the tactical game. In the strategy game, you build your base, research new tech to use on missions, shoot down UFOs, and generally make all the big decisions. In the tactical game, you take a squad of up to 6 soldiers to a battle site. This is where you must use military style tactics against the alien aggressors. Knowing where to take cover, and how to flank the enemy, for example.
It will seem difficult and unfair at first, and quite frankly, it often is! This is a game where drama unfolds. Watching soldiers die is normal, and my soldier memorial wall can sometimes be quite large. It's not like a lot of modern games where you can expect a high success rate for merely showing up. Failure is mandatory, and it becomes acceptable once you understand that.
You also need to keep your tech flowing, as it makes a significant impact. Moving from ballistic guns to laser guns makes a shockingly massive difference, and so forth. Watching your tech jump in these leaps and bounds is very satisfying.
Now this paragraph is just for fans of the old XCOM (and I mean from the 90s). You should like it, so long as you appreciate it as its own game. It feels like the old XCOM, but certain things are very different. You have up to 5 inventory slots: armor, main gun, sidearm (or rocket launcher), and two miscellaneous. That's it. Most ammo is assumed to be endless, instead of being a carryable item. On the other hand, soldiers with rockets can only fire one rocket per mission, and that's it. (To be fair, rockets are REALLY useful). You don't load up your pants pockets like you did in the old days. Action points are gone. Now you simply do two things: Move and perform an action. An action like firing a gun, throwing a grenade, or moving a second time. I have heard complaints about this new direction, but for whatever I miss from the old game, I am quite happy to see action points phased out. I was a skeptic at first, too. You also don't get all sorts of firing options for your guns. Usually just "aim and shoot", unless you're using a special ability. I'm fine with this, as well. Again, it is its own game with its own vibe, but it does carry a lot of things that make you say "Yeah, that's XCOM alright."
I recommend this to game strategy fans, XCOM fans, even people who don't typically play strategy games. I'm one of them! For the record, I mostly play Enemy Within, as it is the same as Enemy Unknown, but with more content. Both are great!

Dying Light is a lot of fun. I enjoyed the long time I spend playing through it. The game took over 50 hours and there's still a lot of side quests I didn't bother with. The writing in the game and the characters were the worst part of the game. I didn't really care about anything that was going on plot-wise. DL reminds me of Fallout with bland characters, lack of charm, and boring writing. The game play though, is what carries this game. Fighting hordes of zombies is tons of fun when my character was strong enough and I'd unlocked some cool abilities. The game play and aesthetic of the game feel like a beefed up version of Dead Island. I've heard some people say it's the game that Dead Island should've been. Dying Light does feel like a mash-up between the newer Fallout games and Dead Island. The graphics are decent. Nothing too amazing, but good. The game takes some time to get going. The first few hours are the most difficult as your character has very limited abilities and can be constantly overwhelmed. I almost gave up and quit playing. As the character gets more abilities, exploring the environment is more fun. The parkour of the game is done very well. Certainly it takes some time to master, but it's really easy to understand. The day/night cycle was really intimidating for a long time. At night, much stronger monsters come out and almost instantly kill you. I was well into the game before I could mount a decent counter-offense to those super tough monsters. Even then, it was usually just a better idea to go back to a safe zone at night and continue questing at dawn. Navigation in the game is mostly intuitive. There's a map, but just kind of going in the right direction will get you where you need to go; even if sometimes I ended up blindly swan diving of the side of a cliff because I couldn't see what was ahead of me. That goes for both the parkour and the driving. I really liked The Following DLC. It's DLC done right. It's still the same game, but they change things around. Instead of the cramped parkour map to traverse, it's the opposite. It's a huge flat land that needs to be driven around in your dune buggy of zombie death. It's still the same essential game, though. I gotta point out, the Dying Light community is one of if not thee best around. Many times, people would join my game just to give me cool gear. Weapons that wouldn't degrade after two fights like the normal weapons tended to do.  More experienced people would show up to help me out. That was cool and a big thanks to all those in the Dying Light community. Dying Light is good, and if you're a fan of the zombie slaying, open-world rpg genre, then it's the game for you!

I don't write many reviews, but when a game has a feature that in my oppinion breaks the game. I need to write about it.
*The overview*
The game itself is quite good and fun, especially if you like to create your own sandbox and mess around and pretend to be some of the numerous civilizations. It "can" get quite dull or boring quite quickly, especially because some of the mechanics in the game are a little annoying.
*The complaints*
I absolutely hate some of the features and mechanics in this game. I will start with the one that made me write this review:
1) Roads have a maintenence cost. This seems logical on one hand, but combined with the fact that Automated Workers construct roads as a leisure past-time is utterly broken. You can either manually control the workers ( in a big empire it can be a hassle and take a way A LOT of unnecessary time ) or you can have them on automated, which is meant to save your time, but they will end up making roads to secluded and far fetched cities and allies.
This can get SUPER bad if you're playing with "teams" and your ally lives on same continent but far away from you... You workers will tirelessly build long roads to them (meanwhile also getting catched by barbarians).
To make it worse there is ABSOLUTELY NO WAY (that I know of) to get rid of said roads.
To make it worse there is no option to disable workers from building any roads at all. This alone cost me one game in which I dumped several hours, because if you have plenty of workers they build a long road VERY quickly.
I will add more negative points to this review at a later time, but currently this one REALLY ticked me off.

FTL, "Faster Than Light", a game where small decisions have BIG consequences.
I'll break this quick review into 3 parts; Graphics, Gameplay and Replay Value.
Graphics:
The graphics have a retro feel and are more than pleasant on the eye, brings back some nostalgia whilst maintaining a current age feel, 8/10.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is solid and forces you to explore, and in doing so, forces decisions upon you that could make or break the success of your mission. You are constantly thinking of what lays ahead and what you need/could do without. Balancing your power usage is hard enough without the threat of rebels and pirates. This is by far the most attractive thing about FTL, 9/10.
Replay Value:
Replay Value is solid but could do with a few new modes or missions to spice it up. Maybe being able to fit your own ship with anything available in the game from the start and see how long you survive pushing through sector after sector of hostile forces. Just something away from the current 1 mission campaign we currently have, 7/10.
Overall and doing some maths, I give FTL 24/30, an average score of 8/10.
A good game, which if picked up in the sales, will have you enjoying the warmhearted challenge that FTL provides, without breaking the bank at all.

Storm Of Spears is a RPGMaker created role-playing game with a very misleading title. There are other aspects of this game that may be misleading to players.
To start, the game's performance is below standards to play. Regardless of your system, the game will most likely stay at below 30FPS.  The game also runs an outdated version of RPGMaker (VXAce) instead of its current sucessor (MV). From the looks of it, SoS went through little time in development, so a simple switch to a better game creator version would have seriously improved its asthetics, performance and even resolution.
The design and visuals is simply inconsistent. The main character, Sura, has 3 different depictions of her; bust image, ingame sprite and trading card artwork. All 3 are very unrecognizable from each other. Also, the false and unrealistic breast sizes. This game has a "Nudity" tag and after completing the whole game, I recieved not a nipple. Nothing more than a clickbait tag. The story is decent, but mostly textbook. Also, there are many plot twists, expected and unexpected. A common trend to keep the story somewhat interesting. The battle system is stock. You have your 4 by the book retro RPG character lineup (Attacker, Stat Changer, White Magic, Black Magic). The sidequests are meaningless and the achievements are so simple to get. Just "play" through the main game.
Overall, Storm of Spears NEEDS a huge overhaul. Program update, custom asthetics, consistent character portraits and sprites, better story telling, alternate battle system beyond the stock, sidequests with high risk; high reward, and a name change.

I had an old review about the game, complaining about weird lags in the gameplay - I don't know what changed during the past one year, but the problems completely disappeared while I'm using the same computer. So, a normal review!
TLDR part: A crudely drawn, not too pretty platformer with really well-done physics and puzzles, with puzzle-oriented gameplay. Was featured in 14 bundles up to this point, the lowest price was 0.88€ - during a similar discount I really strongly recommend this unpolished gem.
This game is weird - it has simple looks, the character looks  no better word, weird, like a potato-hedgehog, the sounds are repeating and simplistic, but the game still works, for me in a really compelling way. The graphics are simple, but the physics behind it work pretty nicely - you need to throw items, activate machines, roll wheels, pull carts to solve puzzles. This is a puzzle platformer, and as each level takes around 8-10 minutes to complete, it's more centered around 1-2 puzzles a level, than platforming for a longer time than a puzzle ; also, trial and error elements are present as well because enemies can drop on you, or you take a wrong turn somewhere.
Each level has multiple checkpoints - I think the most time I needed to work to reach after my previous progress after dying was 2-3 minutes at max, so in this terms the game is well-balanced. Another strong positive aspect is the hidden little secrets on each level, usually something funny and unexpected.
For the biggest negatives of the game I would mention:
-The lack of proper animations and UI; while there is strong audio feedback on everything, it's hard to see if our character hold the rock or not, what way he's turning ; looking around is not really useful, but there's a part when you need to use the mouse / right stick to maneuver a little "ball" around a pretty hard environment - I repeatedly lost focus on the cursor because it has almost the same colour as the background. And with a controller, I'm pretty sure that that part would be troublesome with the controller.
-Basically the design of the game. It's a clear, focused background, with platforms, presented with silhouettes, and a LOT of back- and foreground. I found myself numerous times not sure if it's spike or grass, solid wall or foreground, and sometimes the puzzles are needlessly hard because it's simply hard to know what are you looking at it.
The happenings during level reflect the previous ones so there is at least some causation presented, but the game doesn't have a real, meaningful story - I don't feel like it's really missing. The game is more about going in a level, looking around, finding a physics-based contraption very likely haven't come across yet, make it work, go to the next level. And in my opinion, it works in a fantastic way, if you don't *want* to have a solid story.
I do can only recommend this game - despite the weird past I share with this game and headache it caused, I started it again with clean sheets and it proved to be a really, really pleasant surprise.
It's Battlefront. And it's great, even 11 years later! Just get it.

The art for the main characters is well drawn, although I did feel a little curious at the random blonde on the title screen that had nothing to do with the story whatsoever.  Fight mechanics are simple enough, with no random encounters, so any fighting done involves running into various mobs on the map.  I did find it disappointing that magical attacking never did the damage my mage could do with simple melee, which made the character feel kind of pointless.  I found the music to be somewhat forgettable, so I opted to listen to my own music as there was no need to hear the game.
For the most part, the game felt like a decent attempt at creating a short RPG with some quality from the SNES era, and did so well.  For it's normal $2 price, I'd recommended it without reservation, and even then with Steam's bundle discounts it can easily be bought for quite a bit less.
