XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a great strategy game, and also my favorite game of all time. It's like many other games: easy to learn, hard to master. There is so much nuance to this game that you won't see at first. As it starts to unfold, you realize just how clever it is.
There are two games in one here: The strategy game, and the tactical game. In the strategy game, you build your base, research new tech to use on missions, shoot down UFOs, and generally make all the big decisions. In the tactical game, you take a squad of up to 6 soldiers to a battle site. This is where you must use military style tactics against the alien aggressors. Knowing where to take cover, and how to flank the enemy, for example.
It will seem difficult and unfair at first, and quite frankly, it often is! This is a game where drama unfolds. Watching soldiers die is normal, and my soldier memorial wall can sometimes be quite large. It's not like a lot of modern games where you can expect a high success rate for merely showing up. Failure is mandatory, and it becomes acceptable once you understand that.
You also need to keep your tech flowing, as it makes a significant impact. Moving from ballistic guns to laser guns makes a shockingly massive difference, and so forth. Watching your tech jump in these leaps and bounds is very satisfying.
Now this paragraph is just for fans of the old XCOM (and I mean from the 90s). You should like it, so long as you appreciate it as its own game. It feels like the old XCOM, but certain things are very different. You have up to 5 inventory slots: armor, main gun, sidearm (or rocket launcher), and two miscellaneous. That's it. Most ammo is assumed to be endless, instead of being a carryable item. On the other hand, soldiers with rockets can only fire one rocket per mission, and that's it. (To be fair, rockets are REALLY useful). You don't load up your pants pockets like you did in the old days. Action points are gone. Now you simply do two things: Move and perform an action. An action like firing a gun, throwing a grenade, or moving a second time. I have heard complaints about this new direction, but for whatever I miss from the old game, I am quite happy to see action points phased out. I was a skeptic at first, too. You also don't get all sorts of firing options for your guns. Usually just "aim and shoot", unless you're using a special ability. I'm fine with this, as well. Again, it is its own game with its own vibe, but it does carry a lot of things that make you say "Yeah, that's XCOM alright."
I recommend this to game strategy fans, XCOM fans, even people who don't typically play strategy games. I'm one of them! For the record, I mostly play Enemy Within, as it is the same as Enemy Unknown, but with more content. Both are great!

The info:
In NEO Scavenger you will be fighting not only the vicious denizens of a post apocalyptic world; but nature itself.
Between the cold, hunger and baddies you will have a hard time surviving.
Finding something as simple as a potato chip bag seems like an accomplishment in this game as you will always be struggling to find ways to carry all the loot you find and and tools you need.
Every item in the game has a health and when that health runs out, it's gone forever and just like in real life if you find a old shopping bag it might have a hole or two in it so there is always the chance that loot you find will already be near useless.
Having to decide whether to go on with a sword that has 1% use left in it verses the completely fine stick just laying there will become a easy choice. But figuring out if the small pocket knife is better to take with you because it takes up less space or if it's worth losing that extra storage to a base ball bat is a much harder to decide.
Every choice in NEO Scavenger could mean regret or death in the next few turns or happiness and success.
Some things to note before buying:
If you like not being able to save your progress then this game is fore you. The only option you have is to 'save' game; which acquaints to going back to the start screen or quitting the game and being able to pick up where you left off however you soon realize it's not really saving anything the first time you die your save is gone. When you die you have to start over again with nothing . . .from the beginning. For me I really get depressed when I worked really hard to get what I got only to die because it was cold or because I drank some bad water.
The good:
Challenging
Tons of content to see
high replay value
The bad:
The random nature of  encounters and item generation is very unforgiving at times and often ends with your character being killed after only a few turns.
A limited (small) set of starting skills to choose from.

This is one of my favorite games of all time. If you liked Fallout 1 and 2, and you like survival and roguelike games, I think you'll love this. It's dark, creepy, atmospheric, insanely detailed and can be morbid beyond belief. Don't judge the screenshots - buy this game. Note: I played this off steam, that's why my game time is low. I probably hit triple digits in reality.
Had some of my most memorable gaming experiences with NEO Scavenger while it was in Alpha, and weirdly enough it wasn't even anything dramatic, just stalking deer and making jerky, exploring and braving the elements with my prized and carefully assembled "kit" of equipment, feeling like a badass survivor in a totally harsh and unforgiving world. In another playthrough, some truly weird♥♥♥♥♥♥went down in an abandoned insane assylum turned cultist haven: At the door, I gave up my prized kit in exchange for a hospital gown, got involved in some crazy masochistic, self-flagellating religious nonsense and cultist court intrigues, left on strange and uncertain terms, and then got shot outside the gates (left me absolutely speechless, like, WTF just happened?)
Quests go weird. Enemies can be unpredictable. Strange things can happen. Emergent gameplay up the whazoo.
This game offers so much all at once... The detail in it is enough to sattisfy your worst OCD compulsions, because this game has the most detailed inventory management of probably any game ever made (plastic bags that you can crumple up and put in pockets, pill boxes you can stock with individual pills, batteries that you can stock and charge with individual electric cells, etc.) It also has a really detailed and fairly simple to use crafting system, with absolutely tons of stuff. Just ridiculous amount of stuff, much more available through mods.
The atmosphere and tone is almost uniquely morbid. This is not necessary or recommended, but hypothetically you can kill someone with a sharpened stick, then carry their body to the woods, carve up the body into steaks and make canibal pemmican. That is outrageous, and disturbing, and just knowing the game lets you do that (though I think discourages it somehow), that in itself gives the game a uniquely dark tone (something about the graphic of the enemy's courpse, lying crumpled on its side, taking up your entire inventory and overburderning you, man that image got like burned in my mind I think).
There are randomly generated scripted events and RPG/Adventure type of quests, choices, storylines. And the writing is actually good, I would even say excellent. These are optional though, so you can kind of "sandbox" it if you want. Anyway, I've sunk weeks into this game and enjoyed it tremendously, back when it wasn't even complete.
Cons:
- None, really.
- After countless hours, combat can get a little repetetive.
- Of course, the interface is pretty clunky and strange in some respects, so while on the one hand I absolutely adore this game just as it is, I also hope that one day it gets some kind of over-haul or redesign/relaunch.
TL;DR: The game developer is a genius and this is clearly a labor of love. I buy very few games, but this is one I was almost giddy to pay for.

After 16 hours of giving this game a shot, I can say that I'm glad that I made the purchase. I see great potential for this game, because it brings out a lot of cool features that are not in other survival based games (A working market, towns with npcs, having an election system for someone to be king, etc.) This is just what I've seen so far, and I can imagine that there is going to be a lot more to the game once it gets closer to completion.
Some of the things that I like about the game are the different roles that you can go for and master. So far, I’ve noticed a ‘hunter’ spec, a ‘magician’ spec, and a ‘warrior’ spec. What I mean by that is, you have multiple avenues you can build into, and each of them have their own perks. On top of that there are multiple workbenches you can have for each spec (workbench for magic for example).  Another thing I like about the game is the taming mechanic. Shooting the potential tame with a hook arrow, and planting the other end of the arrow into the ground, to try and tire out the animal. One final thing is the beginning stages of an economy. Already there are markets that you can buy and sell items to npcs. This can definitely be built up on and there can be an actual working economy on servers, which I find amazing.
There are still a lot of things that need work. The loading screen for example. You can see when it reaches the end of the clip, because it momentarily shows a black screen before it starts to play the clip again. Another thing that needs work is the invisible walls on hills, where you stop dead in your tracks on a hill that looks like you will be able to go over it, but instead you get stopped by the invisible wall. One final example of what needs to be worked on is the npc’s in the towns. One of them in the elven kingdom has no clothes on, and his waist area is completely see through. But all of these problems that I mentioned are patchable, and I bet they will be patched fairly quickly.
All in all, I think that this is a very promising game with great potential. If you think of $1 an hour of gameplay for your purchase, then I’ll definitely be getting my money's worth out of it. If you do not want to play an early access game however, then I’d wait for it to come out of early access.

This game is a decidedly mixed bag.  On one hand, the story is very well told.  You can tell a lot of time and effort was put into it.  On the other hand, even for a RPGMaker game, it is technically unimpressive;  Sprites, music and sounds are stock RPGMaker assets, which cheapens the production values considerably.  The hand-drawn art is gorgeous, but all-too-often, it doesn't match the character's sprite it's supposed to represent.  A pretty guy with white hair as a portrait becomes a mustachioed guy with a huge chin as a sprite, for example.  Also, the art for the main characters doesn't change to express emotion, leaving for inappropriate smiling during sad moments.  It's a pity the effort that went into story and art apparently didn't reach the rest of the game.
Also, unless this is like your first RPG ever, do NOT play it on normal difficulty.  The game was so easy that the gameplay became rather tedious to get through in order to get to the story.  I'm not sure how well the harder difficulties scale it up, but the normal setting at least shows a decided lack of balance, unless "Normal" was a setting that was intended for casual players, in which case it should be named "Casual" or "Easy".
All and all, though... for the couple of bucks it goes for, it might be work a look, if only for its story and art.

Company of Heroes 2 continues to be a money grab and if it wasn't for the fact that as a heavy beta tester that I receive most of the content for free I wouldn't spend time other than to get the achievements. Since the last three major updates, the game still goes through massive ring around the nerf hammer which hits Axis forces more often than Allied forces which means if you were looking to play as Axis a lot, prepare to be dissapointed in most logical situations.
There is no historical balance or logic to the combat mechanics of the game and instead relies heavily on an RNG mechanic for "to hit" "damage dealt" "cover saves" and "armor saves" which means even if your unit is incapable of realistically damaging the target, chances are you still can and vice versa.
A great example of this is dedicated anti-tank units and self propelled guns taking multiple hits to destroy light vehicles, normally the same for all units regardless of vehicle class. IE: Jagdpanther Veterancy 5 can hit a light scout car and deal only 50% of its hp threshold in damage yet on a frontal armour penetration against a T-34/85 it can deal almost 60%. Logical? Not in the slightest.
If you play against the AI, it has access to all doctrines at the same time but does a very good job of hiding this unless you pay attention to the globals it uses. For example the Russian AI will almost always have access to Propaganda Artillery Strikes even if the Commander they use doesn't have access to it. When playing against the AI, it's recommended you use one of the "All Unit" mods which at least make the game somewhat fair and balanced.
When playing competitively, it's best to just do smaller player counts because most factions are not balanced on late tier games seen in 3v3s and 4v4s in which certain factions are punished heavily such as the USForces only having one premium doctrine that has a heavy tank compared to all the OKW and Heer having access to multiple heavy tanks regardless of doctrine.
Certain units are still bugged such as the crewing and recrewing of abandoned units on certain maps will result in the unit disappearing and being unable to be commanded, destroyed, or pulled out of combat. While rare, it's still in the game and it was a problem since beta two years ago. Tanks still can't aim on elevation which means if you want to really♥♥♥♥♥♥someone off, go up a hill and shoot down, 90% of all shots unless the player decides to manually control will go straight into the ground right in front of said vehicle.
Only buy this game when it is on sale for 60-80% off. If you are smart, don't buy any of the DLC unless it's 75% off or more. There is occasional free commanders at different times of the year so if you are patient, you can rack up some decent ones in addition to random drops. (Which don't even give you drops to your faction half the time.)

While the premise and concept of the game both were big selling points for this game, I cannot recommend it.
1. Nobody Plays Multiplayer - While there is a structure for having MP games, there is no one to play with online. The most people I have seen online at one time were three, including myself.
2.  AI Games are just bad - There is really no other way to say this, but in the two hours that I have played this game, it has only been against AI. These games typically amount to me pushing forward and finding the "battle-line" and then holding that until I can make enough units to move forward. Now one might think that to be the appropriate way to wage war in this setting, but the games eventually become a grind of fighting off waves of enemies that are too small to do any serious damage to your fleet and that just hurl themselves at you using no particular strategy. This is further more exasperated by the fact that the MP community is dead.

1. AI - FIX IT
2. Concept - While the concept is what drew me in at first, it soon became clear that it was a lot harder to execute than planned. In game, there are only 3 types of ships, Invading ships (for taking over planets), frigates (for fighting other starships), and the destroyers (they just destroy planets so enemies cannot use resouces). While only having three types of ships may fit the "simplistic" theme of the game, it is almost
simplistic, making the game boring because of the lack of variety.
Overall, I really wanted to like this game. I really thought that the concept was interesting and different, and at first glance, the developers have done a good job with the base game. But when looking at the greater picture, the boring mechanics, the grindy gameplay, the $hit AI, and the Empty MP, I simply can't recommend this.

Alright, look. I love the game. I do, really. It's awesome, it's fun, it's addictive, and honestly it could teach people a few things about surviving in such a situation that they can't depend on society anymore. Almost all the techniques in the game are solid survival techniques that could very well save your life in the real world. But after a series of deaths before I could even get enough supplies to make the journey east (which I understand is a roguelike feature, but bear with me.), I felt the need to write this review.
One word, ladies and gentlemen: Yezinka. There's only one of them in the game world, and it wanders the map until it encounters your player. When it does, it hovers around in the hexes around you, and waits for you to inevitably have to sleep. You can't kill it by jumping it during the day because it can manage to sprint somewhere around 12 paces per move, while you can manage at best 4. It's also very difficult to hit with ranged weaponry (never got to try melee). Now here's the lemon in the wound: When you go to sleep, it immediately beelines for you, and steals your eyes. You can do NOTHING about it. You get around two turns, which is enough to stand up and start to look for it, and suddenly your eyes are gone. You can't do anything to recover them unless you've happened to encounter this late in the game and are near the city, and have been hoarding enough cash for cybersurgery. I say you need to be near the city because the condition "No Eyes" seems to flag you and every single enemy creature on the map drops what they're doing and attempts to kill you. I made a valiant effort and managed to kill two bandits and a dog before I was just overwhelmed with going into a new battle every turn (every other turn very VERY occasionally). Maybe if I were given a chance to pack up the things I had and try to luck my way to the city and sell everything I had for a single eye, I wouldn't have such a problem with this. Maybe if I were allowed to live for a bit and get a balancing attribute after a few turns that mitigated the fact that I can't see anymore, that'd be fine too. But as it is, if luck allows this broken monstrosity to seek you out without being killed by other wild animals or lucky NPCs, you are screwed, and there's no preparation at all that you can attempt to save yourself. I cannot in good conscience recommend any game that has a chance of giving the player such an enormous middle finger. But if you can get past that and you think it's not something that will bother you, then buy this game. The Yezinka is an enormous infected zit on the face of an otherwise outstanding game.

As one of the first DOW games I've played, I can't help but compare it others I've had experience with in the RTS genre, and honestly, I don't regret buying it, but I did feel misled by the other reviews I read.
It's a good game, don't be mistaken. The units are great, the basic mechanics are good, and the amount of individual customization you can put into your units is where the game truly shines. However, the biggest issue with this is one that you can't help but notice, which is general responsiveness and map control.
When you scroll the map, the game will constantly get stuck thinking you want to keep doing it. It's very annoying when you suddenly want to change the direction you're scrolling (and considering the fast-paced nature of RTS's you will at some point). As for map control, the spacing your units will keep in multiple teams is both a blessing and a curse, as it allows you to cover more area, but if you ever get distracted and look away, singular squads may run off and get themselves killed while you're not looking. Large teams are also a problem, as they will constantly get stuck in narrow passes and fall behind when they may be needed to help in combat.
That said though, it's positives do far outweigh the negatives, as with some patience and management, the negatives can be accounted for to an extent. It's got good enough gameplay to keep you playing, a long enough campaign to make you feel satisfied (though tragically just for one of the many races). It feels cluncky and slow-paced compared to a more modern RTS, like Starcraft II, but it's still a fun game.

Quake Live updates the original Quake III with some changes like adding loadouts, which consist of a 'primary' and 'secondary' starting weapon. You can still pick up the many various weapons throughout the maps or off dead players, like usual, it just gives people some more opportunities to get started without waiting for a Rocket Launcher or your favorite weapon to start blasting some fools. At first it seems really scary, but I think this change quickens the pace and I definitely see it as for the better.
I can't comment too much on the new maps, if there are any? I assume there are. Because there are certainly maps I'm unfamiliar with. I dig most of 'em. A few kinda have a weird flow to it that I'm not really sure I find as fun as the others, but they're still pretty solid maps. I have not seen all of 'em.
Other changes:
-There's a new weapon, the Heavy Machine Gun. It's definitely stronger than that starting one. *shrug* I dunno seems alright, I don't use it at all.
-Damage numbers. I don't think these were in the original. It's been so long. But it's definitely useful seeing how much damage the AoE of that rocket did.
-The powerups have a visible cooldown so that everyone can more easily understand when Quad Damage is available or whatever. This definitely makes it easier for new players to understand when and where they are supposed to be. I totally dig this change, because I'd NEVER be familiar with the timing otherwise.
A couple complaints...
-You can't vote to change a map unless you pay for the ability to both vote and make your own server. I suppose I don't really see what else you could pay for so that they could get some cash off of this free-to-play version of Quake III Arena, but I'm not the biggest fan of the voting aspect.
-The other big issue is that, at least when I play (mid-day or at night) there are a whole lot of empty servers. The community is seemingly tight and I wish there were more servers with people playing in them because this has been the only first person shooter I've ever not got frustrated with. Community seems to be pretty alright, the ones that are there.
In the end, I recommend giving this a go if you love arena shooters or loved Quake III at the time and wanna relive the days where everything you did felt so good. I also want you to give it a go because I need to see some new blood in here. Or old blood. Quake is old. You are old. Play this old game. It's everything I want in a shooter and I was a child-baby when this game came out originally.

Excellent little RPG Maker game. Fully recommend it to anyone who wants something different for a change, a break from the AAA titles. I got right into it, sure the story telling is pretty cliche but they pulled it off quite well. There were very few bugs I ran into, to be expected that there'd be some. Nothing game breaking, most people won't even notice, all the ones I ran into were by accident. (like walking in areas you shouldn't be able to walk in). There was one zone that was really choppy for me (Bruske Mines, the Phantom area). I don't know why, but that was the only zone I had issues with.
As far as RPG Maker goes, this one has been the best I've tried so far. I got this as part of a bundle and it's certainly much better than some of the others that came with the bundle.
Idk if the developers read these reviews, if they do. I'd like to share some of my thoughts on this game and how it could have been even more enjoyable for me.
- I would have liked more playable characters, create your own party from the available hereos, or a job system allowing more styles of combat than just the default
- More monster variety, I don't mind a single race of monsters specific to an area (it makes sense that monsters would kill eachother off and only the strongest remain) but if area "A" is going to have only Ogres, for example, it could have many different types of Ogres, instead of just Ogre A, Ogre B, Ogre C every fight
- I thought the battle animations were a bit long, I didn't notice it at first but towards the end of the game my inner monologue was like "damn, another fight, cmon already"
- I liked the quest tracker system, keep that up, I wouldn't even have minded if it contained less detail and the player had to find areas themselves without the "head east" hints
- I loved that the zones weren't straight lines, and if you bothered to explore an area you were rewarded with treasure or sidequest. It was always worth your time. Keep that up.
- I found the difficulty quite a bit on the easy side, even the optional content wasn't challenging, at the very least a "JRPG" game should always have one optional quest thats like "wtf is with this difficulty!!"
- Offensive magic was not worth using, I would really suggest buffing that. My "mage" was doing roughly 3x more damage with his auto attacks than his strongest spell
Maybe it's just me, but I did not find 10+ hours of gameplay and then another 3+ hours of optional content as advertized. I talked to every NPC, did every side quest (except 1), killed every monster I saw, fully explored every zone in the game, read all the dialogue and as you can see, my total game time is just shy of 6 hours. Now I don't care that it's only 6 hours in total, it was a good 6 hours spent, don't get me wrong. I know I tend to do things quicker than others but I find it hard to believe that the average person would take twice as long to do everything the game has to offer.
All that aside, I had fun, and that's what it's about. Thank you for your time and effort into making this game. I will be following you and looking forward to your future games.

First off, this game is in early access, so it is not fair to evaluate or compare this game in relation to other, more established titles.  This review attempts to take an objective look at Dark and Light, with the understanding that it is still in Early Access. I will evaluate the game based on four factors:  Graphics, Content, Game Mechanics, and Potential using a 1-5 scale, where 1 is poor and 5 is best.
TL;DR summary:  Game is highly recommended with the understanding that it is in early access and there are bugs and some negative things with the game at this point.  Overall the game has very high potential and has something for just about everyone.
Graphics: overall rating 3. There are glitches, some odd colors reported, circles in the sky, etc. But once again, this game is in early access. Some of the odd things that have happened to me include odd positions after death, getting stuck inside of a rock (and I had to “trigger death” to get out of it), and odd color effects when certain graphics options are turned on.  Still, the game is not that bad, and it is playable, which is why I gave it a “3” at this stage.
Content: overall rating 3. This game has PvE and PvP. There are also (as of 21 July) dedicated PvE and PvP servers in place. The quest system that is in place is essentially a sort of tutorial that guides you through how to do things in the game.  The initial quest line is all about gathering certain types of resources and building your first set of stone tools. As you get higher in rank and advance, the quests are structured to open up other things that you can do in the game, such as build your own home, etc. The quests are still somewhat buggy in this stage – I am currently stuck on “sell resources to vendors” – which for some reason will not advance or recognize no matter how much I sell.  Also, the NPC sell model takes a bit of getting used to.  To sell to an NPC, you need to meet a threshold of what the NPC is looking for (i.e., 100 units of straw, etc.).  The game will not allow you to sell individual units of any resource, and at this time I have not seen the ability to resell your old tools, etc. Part of the problem with this is that the vendors have very low “buy” thresholds, so for example, a vendor may only buy three lots of 100 straw units each, and once that limit is reached, it won’t refresh for 24 hours game time. With several individuals all selling to NPCs, that threshold is reached almost 10 minutes after the refresh.  It can be frustrating.
Game Mechanics: overall rating 4. To advance in this game and gain “levels” you essentially “learn by doing.”  There are no classes – just a set of skills that everyone can advance in, and the way to advance is by interacting in the game environment.  For example, if you want to advance your fire magic level, mine sulfur from rocks, etc.  As you can levels in skill areas, spells and schematics open up for you to build – once again, with raw or processed resources (i.e., iron, etc).  The only drawback I see with this system is that with everyone having access to the same set of skills, eventually at the higher levels, you will reach a point of diminishing returns where everyone will be exactly the same.  I think that this can be avoided though – I am sure that the devs have already identified this issue and have a plan for the final, released version of the game.
Potential: overall rating 5. This game has great potential. I based that assessment on the fact that you have multiple options for end game content – you have the friction between the factions that can generate conflict; the PvE monsters, undead, etc, to battle and overcome; the creativity element with building structures; the environment interaction element – such as taming beasts, etc. Your vision and imagination of how you want to play your character is pretty much the most limiting factor.
Bottom line: good game with tons of potential.  Recommended.

"Played it for a short bit. There is virtually no lore on this game, nothing compelling at all. Half the game sounds are ported over from their Ark: Survival Evolved title. I said this after an hour or two into the game during it's initial launch. I stopped playing, heck I even demanded a refund. But after about a day I thought about it, I checked out Citadel projections and I decided my review was unfair and I didn't give it enough time. I went back and I did a serious play through. I have put in 300 hours into the game now. I have probably put more hours than most players currently in the game into the game.
I can honestly say that the developers have actively addressed and patched many of the blockers that origionally came up at launch. They are extremely responsive and the customer service team has been very strong thus far responding to my House (guilds) petitions/concerns. The world is immersive and the gameplay is dynamic. The melee is still a bit unreliable but it has come a very long way. Combat overall is getting quiet balanced as developers add more resistances to different types of mobs based on their percieved stregnth and lore. Additionally, there is much more utility and gearsets than Ark and other games which create an opportunity for diverse character development. There is also a skin system which hasn't been implemented yet that shows a lot of potential.
It's definitely a very early access game. It might have even been potentially released too early. I will however say that it's very playable, immersive, and addictive. The foundation is great and thus far the developers are on track to building it into a very solid long term experience. As I have put 300 hours into the game in my opinion I have already long since gotten my monies worth and would recommend the experience and journey to others. I put 3200 hours into ark and I would say this game brings in character diversity and more independance from tames that ark didn't have. My hope is that they incorporate more MMO elements such as skill trees and unique customization to continue to diversify styles of characters to traditional concepts such as melee classes, ranged weapon classes, and casters.

Storm of Spears has all the familiar elements of a good, thrilling classic RPG (including an evil empire to rise against, a strong-willed protagonist, and mercenaries with hearts of gold). I think this game has good intentions, but it falls short of true enjoyment due to an overall unfinished/unpolished feel to it. With a little more effort, Storm of Spears could be great, but for now I feel rather neutral about it.
I'm usually not too picky when it comes to design, but it is more than a bit confounding when the sprites in the game barely resemble the character art. The characters themselves could use more expression, considering the dialogue in game isn't horribly written by any means. But the impact of most of dialogue is lost once you see the character it is coming from always has the same grin or blank expression on their face no matter what. You can tell the creators put thought and care into the story, so I truly wish more of that thought and care would be shown in the art and design within the game.
Traversing the world map in the game was a tid bit boring, considering there were no random events or battles cropping up. You simply move from one place to the next. I also found myself getting lost quite easily in various areas (such as Daggeridge) due to the fact that most of the backgrounds were repetitive, without any unique markers to help me find my way around. This made quests rather frustrating, and this is also why I ultimately had to give up playing before reaching the end.
Now, on to what I enjoyed. At it's heart, Storm of Spears offers fun, straightforward gameplay. There are plenty of side quests to keep you busy, if you like. The story is fine, the dialogue is nicely written with at least some character development in there. The battles are quite easy, so you definitely can't get frustrated at the difficulty unless you want more of a challenge in your RPG's. I think Storm of Spears would be a good introduction into the genre for someone unfamiliar with them, or for anyone who wants to play a simple RPG without any overly complex elements to it.

Gameplay is straight forward, you’re constantly moving and holding the mouse button will make you fly up and if you let go of the button you descend down and if you end up at the bottom of the screen, you die. There’s stuff flying everywhere including birds, bees, ice cubes(what?), snow balls, comets, rocks etc. There’s boss fights too where a boos would appear and throw things at you and you have to dodge them. There are coins too which you can collect as well as some power pickups like a magnet which will collect coins even if you don’t go through them. The other power-up is a shield which makes you invulnerable for a short time and anything you touch will die.
Every time you start a game there’s a different theme every time. Some these include Egyptian theme, Space theme, Winter snowing theme etc. Other than that you can unlock new characters such as Santa pug, Sombrero wearing pug, a panda, a dragon, a hamster etc.
The sound in this game is so cute and especially the different themes’ music sound really relevant to their themes.
Conclusion: Cute game, cute music, addictive gameplay and only 99 cents (as of this review it’s 40% off and 59 cents), it’s a bargain. Even if you play 2 hours, it’s worth it.

Dying Light is possibly the best zombie game I have ever played. I love games like this
This game will have you sweating from your eyes, with the amount of sad stuff that happens in the story.
Anyways now to the actual review. This game has amazing mechanics. It's a free roam parkour open world game. Plus a lot of zombies. They are fun to fight in the beginning of the game and fun to drop kick off cliffs in the end of the game.
The leveling system in the game has 3 sections. Yes you can unlock every perk too.
Agility: All sorts of stuff that will change your ability to traverse the terrain around you, and kick more zombie♥♥♥♥♥
Power: Power gives you new abilities to use while fighting zombies and other enemies. You can learn to drop kick zombies off buildings. Like come on. That should be a game seller already. There are a lot of things to unlock and lots of ways to kill zombies.
Survival: This changes things like your ability to craft certain items, all the way to upgrading various things about your character's survival.
It takes a bit of time to get them all maxed out, and it is fun during it too.
This game has many easter eggs and lots of lore if you are the type of person that enjoys looking for side-lore.
The story is great. It's deep. Not only that, but it will leave you with suicidal thoughts, in tears, and possibly looking for a new way to handle the depression you just got diagnosed with.
The DLC for the game (specifically The Following) are great too. The Following continues the story of Kyle Crane, to help the people of Harran. It's a big open new map, lots of cool people to talk to, and. And. A buggy to drive around and hit zombies with.
The Bozak Horde is a DLC that will probably leave you with a smashed monitor and keyboard. It is fun, but it is also INCREDIBLY frustrating when you get to the last part of it with 3 lives and still lose. It's not what I thought it was gonna be when they announced it. It's a challenge arena. You have to do these challenges in a certain amount of time or else your leg blows up via leg bomb.
The CO-OP in this game also works quite well. It's just like playing alone, but you have friends walking around with you too. If you need to start a quest, they can TP to the quest starter if they want or they can run. But you can't just TP around for those of you wondering. It only allows it when you are trying to start a quest.
When you see that the game is made by the makers of Dead Island, you'd think this game might suck. But it doesn't. This game is by far one of the best game I have layed my hands on a keyboard and mouse for.
When you finish the game, you can restart it on Hard+, where everything is A LOT harder, so try to avoid zombies at the start.
The game overall is an amazing RPG with great mechanics, a leveling system and a great story. It's fun to play with friends, and it works with friends too. (4 Players) You never know the fun that lurks around the corner when you see your friend beside a gas can. Or playing soccer with a demolisher. This game has a large selection of weapons, and shops to buy from too, that get better with higher survivor rank. You also have a dynamic map that becomes not "dark" in the areas you explore.
If you have the money to spare, buy this game. I played it twice and it was better the second time. I didn't even finish everything. If not, wait for a sale. Even without a sale I'd say buy it.

Braid is a 2-D puzzle platform game where time control is the key game mechanic. There are a few places where quick reflexes are required, but for the most part solving the puzzles just requires figuring out the right sequence of actions. Most of the puzzles are intuitive yet difficult and require a lot of thought to solve. A few puzzles were so difficult that I had to consult a video walkthrough. The goal of the game is to collect puzzle pieces, and then assemble the puzzle on a canvas. The puzzles are artsy-fartsty paintings which are pretty decent, and it is trivial yet fun to put the puzzle together. There are also books in the game that contain pieces of a story. Just like the paintings, the developer is trying to get artsy-fartsy with this story as well. For me the story was too disjointed and "out there" for me, but this does not really detract from the game. The art and music for the game are very good. I played this game with a game controller on my PC, it is probably a bit harder to play in on a keyboard. Overall it is an excellent game that I can strongly recommend. If you like this game, you might like these 2-d puzzle games: Limbo, Vessel, The Swapper. You might also try 3-d puzzle games Portal, Portal 2, and Antichamber.

Dawn of War is a fantastic modern RTS that measures up very well against the greats in the genre like Starcraft and Age of Empires. It takes place in the Warhammer 40k universe but manages to appeal to players who aren't familiar with the tabletop or lore such as myself.
Dawn of War unlike most "older" rts games isn't focused on building or resource gathering. You gain resources automatically through capturing "strategic points" around the map and stealing them from other players. This encourages exploring the map and assaulting other players very quickly early on. Building is also done very early on so the majority of what you spend your time on is creating units and attacking players.
Combat in Dawn of War is done very well. Because there's very little micromanagement with resources and buildings you spend most of the game creating squads, upgrading those squads with different weapons and assaulting the enemy. Each of the 4 races are familiar but different enough so that you'll quickly pick out a favorite among them. Dawn of War's greatest asset is speed, games go by very quickly and you are always getting rewarded for the smallest of accomplishments like capturing strategic points. Which stack up greatly as the game goes on. There are also a lot of little details to the game like how Space Marine buildings are generated by being dropped from orbit.
The real unfortunate aspect about this release (The original Game of the Year edition) is it's arguably the one I'd recommend the least. It only contains four of the core races (Space Marines, Eldar, Chaos Space Marines and Orks) along with a fairly lackluster Blood Ravens campaign. I still do recommend getting it since it does introduce you to the mechanics of the game very well, and those races do port over to the multiplayer of the subsequent expansions. But by itself the Game of the Year edition isn't as impressive as Winter Assault or Dark Crusade.

I recently received this game for free from Free Games. It is an open-world RPGMaker-based game where the protagonist Sura and her companions hunt down a fugitive to obtain a bounty as members of the Night Swords mercenary band. The fugitive is captured and the bounty awarded to Sura. Sura's brother Lucas feels that his sister should free the land from the tyranny of Queen Lilliana and tries to get Sura to lead the rebellion against the Kingdom.
For an open-world RPG, this game is easy to finish, with an estimated playtime of 10 hours and doesn't require any grinding for experience levels or loot drops. The combat is very simple with every battle able to finish by using only normal attacks. Quest items, objects that can be interacted and entry locations are also highlighted clearly on the screen by appearing as glittering objects. All locations are small and easy to navigate, with no complex maze loops. All side-quests are short and easy to finish.
Graphics and soundtracks are decent, it would have been nice if the game allows the take screenshot button on Steam to work and mounting the dragon is more consistent as it can take a bit of walking around the dragon and pressing the interact button at each step just to be able to ride the dragon. Recommended when at discount.

Let's start with visuals.  The character portraits don't match the sprites on the screen, that goes for all the characters.  The main four characters have larger portraits that don't match the art style of the smaller portraits used for other characters and there is only one picture that is used for all dialogue.  This leads to jarring instances where the character is angry or sad but their profile picture is still grinning.
I also found that the game was very loud.  Even setting my headphones as low as they would go I had to go into the settings and lower the audio levels, however this doesn't apply to the title screen.  So when you stop and restart you get blown away by the title screen.

At first, I was not at all impressed with Company of Heroes 2. It was quite historically innacurate (Wermacht troops wearing full body camoflage? Come on!). Furthermore, it gave a relatively stereotypical portrayal of the Soviet Red Army. However, as I setteled into the gameplay, I found that this was a wonderful game. Combat is quick and satisfying, but with strategic depth and thinking. The addition of freezing to death really led to some frantic dashes to cover, experiences that can be unforgettable.
Huge explosions and massive advances gave me an exhilirating and often jaw dropping experience. The graphics are beautiful, but require a computer with an abnormally advanced graphics card. The sheer detail of the game bleeds quality and work, while permanent terrain deformation gives a sense of really being in a war. The Snow effects are wonderful, with realistic looking deformation. I would prefer to see a permanent corpse option to further sell the illusion, however.
The sound is amazing. From distant gunfire to close-ups of battle, the sound is both realistic (in my honest opinion) . Everything from the screaming soldiers to shells falling from the heavens are professionally done. Furthermore, the music is excellent. It truly sounds like Soviet music from the Second World War era, and enhances the battles.
It should be noted, however, that this game is not for the faint of heart. Soldiers are shot, dismembered, run over, and a whole slew of other violent deaths. Often, they are not immediately killed, but lie wounded, writhing and screaming in agony.  There is also some very coarse language and sexual innuendo ("Katyusha...the Germans call it Stalin's organ. NO! A music organ, idiot!", "No, I'm not defending German technical superiority, I'm stating the ♥♥♥♥ing obvious!", "My rifle, my knife, and my♥♥♥♥♥♥ I always come fully loaded.", etc.). Therefore, this game is not recommended for children, people with undeveloped moral compasses, or politicians. You have been warned.
Run through (out of 10):
Historically Innacurate: -1
Graphically Intense: +2
Excellent and Enjoyable Gameplay: +5
Fantastic Sound: +2
Total: 9

I really want to love this game ! And if I manage to play a few multiplayer games, I might be able to like it. I love how it looks simple, how it allows to play a multiplayer strategic game in less than an hou, how it allows the player to take its time. I do also really like the look of the game and its mecanism :
Few units with very distinct roles, feed lines that can be hijacked, simple fog of war and combat sytem giving its full value to scouting and sentries, simple but efficient planet upgrades, highest speed in systems you control... Really, that's plenty of clever and well thought minimalist mecanism.
However, when the developers states "Heavily focused at multiplayer", it does not mean that multiplayer is particularly weel done. Actually, many features are missing to correctly organise games and interract with your oponents.
No what it means, is that simple player, and more specifically the AI, is a joke.
First, the AI does not follow the same rules as the player : ships are produced at their headquarter. The ennemy does not even try to develop its economy, nor properly attack you. It knows how to produce ships in its factories, but rarely does so. While conquering an HQ, I noticed that it was filled with siege and invasion ships : enough to wipe out half of the map, and conquere the rest. But none of these ships had ever moved from there. Worse : the ennemy did not seem to have produced any fighter, which could have helped him, against my strike.
So, it really feels like the dev did not even try to implement any kind of AI, or that if they tried to do so, countless bugs severely crippled it down.
"Missions" might be more interresting, but they play like tower defense.
So my only hope to fully appreciate this game would be a proper AI update, a more efficient way to organize multiplayer games (taking in account player scarcity), or be lucky enough to have someone logging at the same time as me...
There is some great potential there. But the game needs more love !
Should I recommand it ? Well, if you are ready to wait for someone and play multiplayer yes. Otherwise, no. Or hopefully, not yet...

Before I start the review proper I just want to mention that it's
that the people part of this community that gave Goat Simulator overwhelming positive reviews and got Grass Simulator on Steam because they're stupid enough to be bribed with keys think they have any right to judge a game with barely a plot harshly. Really amusing.
Anyway, yes the plot is thin. Annoyingly so. I didn't get to see just what kind of creature the protagonist was nor why he was there and the ending was basically a downer of epic proportions similar to Hellraiser but from the start it was quite obvious this would be one of those "The journey is the story" games. Otherwise as far as gameplay goes I'm in love with it for similar reasons I was in love with Amnesia and Penumbra. The physics and world interactivity is awesome. So is the lighting (Those warm and cool color combinations look so damn pleasing to the eye).  I'm not really one that cares much for puzzles but in this case I just like seeing physics objects bounce around and there's plenty of that here. Kind of makes one wonder where the complaints are coming from since if I can manage to negotiate a puzzle in a game I'm pretty sure anyone else can.
The game is also technically interesting because of the engine the author wrote. It's a really simple one that just uses SDL, Bullet for the physics and TGA based sprites. I love it when people do stuff like this. So easy to just squeeze out a turd with Unity these days so it's extremely refreshing to see someone take a design and make it their own from the bottom up. This sort of thing is exactly what makes me remember the good times I had in my gamedev stints and makes me want to get back to it.

At first I was really torn wether to buy it or not because of some of the reviews but when I gave it a shot during a sale I got what I was expecting: A strategic game.
You are a fleet commander who gets orders to conquer this or that system or (in skirmish) exterminate every other player in your cluster.
Your capabilities are: Deploying forces, using infrastructure to maintain your fleet (build/repair new ships), destroying whole systems or conquering them for your own empire.
Be aware that every decision you make impacts the whole game: If you destroy a star system you will not be able to use it again.
Keep in mind that your empire can only support a finite amount of military infrastructure (see screenshot upper left corner), more military means more worlds to conquer.
With every battle won your ships gain rank and can enhance their firing rate!
If you are expecting something where you can micromanagement the ships, the planets, diplomacy --> don't get this game, buy (e.g.) Galactic Civ instead!

Ok guys this is going to be a long one. Bottom line if you've played warhammer 40k you already know this universe is insane. Secondly each dawn of wars campaigns don't shirk on difficulty to the point where from the word go you have to be moving. If you're wanting a game that will pamper you stop right now. This game is easy to learn and hard to master. There is an obvious lack of space combat but I can forgive that because of how massive the table top is.
Pros:
+ great openers
+ Squad reinforcement options give a smaller force a much more intimidating presence.
+ good balance appropriate for the races. Spacemarines are tough and versitile for instance.
+ Army cusotmization for skirmish games really gives a nice feel
+ focusing on whether to expand or turtle up gives a variety of options.
+ Punishing gameplay when mistakes are made. I've gone from crushing a chaos army to losing a skirmish fight because I elected to rebuild my forces.
+ Doesn't require a lot to work flawlessly on max settings.
+ AI skirmishes feel challenging on higher difficulties, forcing you to get better as a player.
+ Multiplayer versus AI or PVP can be fun and nothing is more satisfying than watching armies duke it out especially those opening shots.
+ Artillery
+ Resource management
+ place turrets anywhere
Cons:
This is the internet now I need to list the cons. Most are just adding to the fun of the game.
Serious con:
squad and vehicle cap are 20. That's 10 space marine squads (upwards of about 80-90 space marines) 2 tanks, an ultimate vehicle, an artillery piece and two light attack vehicles. Not a lot given some of the map sizes.
-AI difficulty ramping is BS. Easy AI doesn't attack you enough and standard rushes you right off the bat and can base wipe you early. Standard can even snowball the entire game. Still need to work to hard ai.
- Timed missions suck because they rush you and no one likes rushing. Besides ling rushes.
- its easier to ask a river to change course than stop an Ork Waaaagh! You don't know what fear is until you have 120 orks on your doorstep screaming Waaaaagh!
-Needing relics sucks as they're crucial to bringing out your ultimates.
-holding critical locations and strategic points sucks because its harder to hold them than taking them.
- pathing
--Tank pathing. That moment where you accidently box in your land raider. "Oops..."
- nearly impossible to turtle up realistically due to turret ineffective without crossing fields of fire.
- Stalemates Suck. Nothing is more nerve racking than not seeing your enemy for twenty minutes.
- artillery
Overall My wallet may scream bloody murder at me but no regrets. Buy this game and burn the heretics and let the grenades fly.

I wanted to wait to write this review until I had an appropriately preposterous amount of time spent playing this game. As many reviewers here and elsewhere will tell you, this game can easily consume your free time and more. Conservatively I can say I've played at least 50,000 turns in what I consider to my favorite game of all time.
Many will say that the game revolves around combat and that you will end up working toward Domination victories every playthrough. I disagree. The game offers multiple avenues for victory. Religion, Culture, and Diplomatic are a few to mention and they bring their own level of complexity and challenge. The mechanics from top to bottom feel fleshed out and worthy of your time to enjoy one of the best 4X games I have ever played.
Pros:
-Easy to get into, my 61 year old mother plays from time to time.
-Many Civs to play with unique attributes
-Sense of discovery in unlocking technologies
-Building your empire from nothing
Cons:
-The AI needs serious work and I believe they have done some, but not all of the updates needed.
-Did I mention the AI sucks? The difficulty level only increases the multipliers that the enemies civs get. It doesn't address their logic or ability.
-You will lose significant free time while playing this game.
Overall I'd say pick up the complete edition on sale and enjoy. Under$10 is a hell of a steal for a game like this.

Vote El Presidente... Or else!
Tropico is one of those games that make you appreciate the fact that smaller companies create so good games!
Well,the task in this game is quite simple, rule your island as the Dictator, El Presidente, keep the political relations with the other nations to a good level, provide food, work, housing and other important needs for your fellow followers, listen to some of your(at some points) terribly annoying advisors! And last, but not least- Lead TROPICO to the Glory.
Alright, this might not sound particularly interesting for many of you, I assume... sounds like yet another boring strategy game, right? Well... actually no. There is so much more to it than meets the eye, hidden in the small details that make this game unique:
-The set and atmosphere: You are on a tropical island, Earth's paradise, never before seen beauty. The perfect place to become a dictator! The islands are made so beautifully, it really sets you in the relaxing mood of the tropical culture, so to speak. It is just beautiful to look at, from any angle. The palm trees, the small animals, the buildings(some of which are hilarious), the cars(honestly, I love the design of the cars.. like come on.. who wouldnt drive a car like that in real life? I certainly would!!), and all other small details make up for a really sweet game.
-The soundtrack: Now, as I said before, the atmosphere is just amazing. But hold on there, buddy!! It gets even better when the music starts playing. You felt like you are on the island before the music started? Ha, just wait till the music starts, you don't feel like...YOU ARE on the island, right there, just by the Palace of El Prez, listening to his speech regarding the last elections, which he won with the stunning 96% of votes, of course... his opponent went missing after that, Penultimo gave him a ticket to go to a vacation you know... there's nothing more to that.
Beautiful soundtrack! They picked the music perfectly. It's one of the best out there for me personally. What better way to cheer yourself up than with some latino music, dances and songs!!!!!! Yaaaay!
-The gameplay: simple, yet a little harder to master! Build buildings, get more people on the island, pray not to run out of money- profit out of it.Thing is, you need a strong economy early on, otherwise you will quickly run out of money. Start building tourist spots and them pesky tourists will just pour and pour money in El Presidente's Swiss Bank Account- that is all he needs to know! Build better housing for your citizens, pay them more when you earn more money, make them happy, win the next elections!
Or just leave things as they are, gain a few rebels here and there, issue martial law, screw elections, survive an assassination attempt and keep ruling this beautiful nation that Tropico is! It is up to you! But beware, US ans USSR's ships are always seeking for that one moment to invade your country. El Prez must react fast! Quick, Penultimo, build that nuclear program.
All in all, this is a fantastic game if you want to spend some free time gaming and to chill after a rough day! It makes you have fun and be happy.
I have spent hundreds of hours on it on a non-steam version, and, believe me, every time i come back, I find something new. And this is what I cherish in Tropico!
I strongly recommend this game to everyone

Neo Scavenger is a brutal 2D survival game set in a supernatural apocalypse where you try survive the wasteland of everything that wants, can, and will kill you should they ever get their claws on you. Also permadeath is on. A shining example of gameplay over graphics.
Name: Neo Scavenger
Genre: Survival, Strategic Inventory Management
Personal score: I never knew masochism and sadism was an art form till today. Fun.
Neo Scavenger is a 2D survival game set in a hex based world where a devastation has happened to the world and well, apocalypse thing happen and you are a survivor of it. In first glance the innocent looking graphic and the non threatening looking trailer may throw you off on how brutal this game is but as people often say, 'you don't know hell till you been there' read on. Permadeath is on btw.
The main gist of Neo scavenger gameplay is well, scavenging old ruins of buildings and forest  to follow the trail of barebone story. Each hex has a protection value from beeing seen, comfort and how alert you can be when something goes near you. Each of this stats can be improved by items, shelter and other craftable. A low protection from the enviromental will make your character slowly freezes during the night and if their body temperature is already low enough they will die. A low alert level will cause your character to not wake up when threats are nearby and bandits/looter/stuff can kill you in your sleep and you will die. A low comfort will cause your character to fight less efficiently and you might suddenly fall asleep and you will die.
Adding to that, the map is hex form and you have a limited numbers of move during the day and far less during the night to move around, scavenge or perform one of the many in game action before needing to end your turn for the AI to move. On each hex you can scavenge supplies with city tiles having more supplies but comes at the increase risk of being discovered by bandits and obtaining injuries. Scavenging is extremely important in this game because it is your only way of getting randomized loots early game. Pretty much everything you need can be obtain by scavenging. Which might leads to a fight should you encounter bandits while on the move.
Fighting in Neo Scavenger is a game of chances and luck. A fully kited out bandit can still be defeated by you wielding nothing more than a rock but such a thing would of course take extreme luck due to the hidden diceroll system. Based on the perks you have chosen special attacks may not be available to you and only to the perk wielder. A few way fights can be resolve is through killing your opponent, dominating them and causing them to surrender or simply point your gun at them and watch them flee. Even an empty gun works occasionally to fool the AI seeing as in real life you would of course not attack the man with a gun even though its empty but you don't know that.
Should you get wounded in Neo Scavenger you will have to treat them to prevent the blood loss from draining too much and yes it regenerates slowly. Wound treatment has their own special menu where you apply splints, bandages and meds to your character. Left unchecked a large wound has the potential to end your playthrough instantly. Also water and berries you collected are often time poisones because the game isn't hard enough. This might cause disease that has a similar effect to a tired status or in worse case scenario cause a total system failure which leads to your death.
From all the materials you gathered from the scavenging you can use the crafting menu to create items. A wood with a sharp object will yield a spear that you can use to attack. Container with strings and stones will yield a noisemaker to increase the alert level of your campsite. Many other options exist for the player to find themselves.
The player character will also experience hunger and thirst which can be reduce by eating and drinking, failure to do so will lead to death. But as mentioned earlier, most of the water and food you find in the forest where the risks are low are poisonous and consuming them will lead to death.
Inventory management in Neo scavenger are quite realistic in terms of real life, your character has only 2 hands and thus can only hold 1 item in each hands without a bag. With a bag this frees up 1 hand for combat and allows more item to be carried but a bag is not your only means of carrying. Side pockets in pants, shirt and even a sledge can be found and use to help you carry more items which is especially important during end game where you often have to make far away expedition. Any item being held or use will eventually degrade before completely break down into nothing and in fact most of the things found in the wild are actually used goods and so they already have lowered durability. To beat the coldness of the night without a good shelter multiple cloths can be worn on top of each other to increase heat levels during the night and prevent freezing to death.
The day and night system is also quite important. During the day enemies can spot you from further away and the same holds true for you and the during the night the decreased line of sight cause your action points to be less that during the day.
As you traverse the deadly world of Neo Scavenger you might come across strange landmarks or building that will lead you to a random event. Success of survival and loot gain depends on the players perks chosen and dialog choices.
And lastly the perks. During character creation you can choose several perks with perk points limiting the amount. The best perks are usually the most expensive but to help player with that negative perks can also be chosen that frees up point for more positive perks.
Utilizing more ambient noises instead of spoken dialogs the world of neo scavenger is truly brought to life, The forest shakes and the ruined city exhibit an eerie feeling as the player explores it.
But well, good filler is better than no filler.
Everything is sprite based no exception. The characters are sprites, the menu utilizes sprites and even the backgrounds are sprites but like other sprites these are well done enough to pass the inspection. You can clearly tell what an item is at a glance which should be the most important thing in a survival game like this.
At least they do look pretty.

But the game definitely do not hold your hand at all from the moment you walk out of the facility till the next moment your guts spilled out from getting stabbed by an alcohol bottle. This game is intense. Fan of survival game should definitely get it.

TL;DR - good for a few hours, lacks the replay value that good strategy games should have.
Starts well as a really simple strategy game but quickly deteriorates into near-impossible missions that can only be completed if you divine the rules that they don't tell you. As if that wasn't enough, the same rules aren't applied consistently in later missions - it's a completely different game each time.
Add to that the fact that the AI plays by different rules to the player - if there are no shipyards or ships in an area then a player cannot summon more ships fom nowhere, but your opponent can. This really detracts from any strategies you might try to use and turns it into a simple resource management game. A really simple one - practically speaking, your only resource is time.
The thing I love about strategy games is that it's all down to the player and you can learn to do it better. This game deprives you of that fundamental feature.

This game is very fun, and incredicly frustrating. I cannot stress how easily you will die.
Killed by a dogman, 3 hours into the game (no weapons aside from fists to fight with).
Brought a knife to a gunfight thinking the enemy didn't have bullets (a rare and extremely expensive commodity).
Didn't have Botany skill, died from posionous foods (berries and mushrooms).
Got infections from having dirty rags on wounds.
Drank bad water.
Tripped in combat.
Random encounters.
The list is unending.
But through it all, this game is a lot of fun. After the 5th or 6th try, you start to get the hang of it (as long as you choose the same skills in the beginning). Get used to living off the land, by the way. Hoarding is good, but make sure you don't keep everything on you, you only have so much room.
Some good advice, you ask?
Botany makes for eating on the run, as well as making tea that helps boost your immune system (very important).
Ranged skill allows you to make bows/arrows, as well as slings (early game weapons), as well as use pistols, rifles, and shotguns more efficiently (more late game (as far as late game exists) weapons).
Always equip better durability gear.
ATN members are naturally friendly, and won't starts fights. They are, however, pretty strong, and will end them if you aren't similarly equipped, or ambushing them. (eaiest way to tell them from others is they have white faces, and mohawks)
Members of the Blue Frogs should be avoided, especially in melee combat. Just being near them gives you a chance of getting sick.
But most importantly...
Don't take off the Bronze Talisman...

In my many playthroughs since I have never been able to find another frying pan or torch, and things were even harder. Finding a lighter is so damn hard that I usually starve to death. Or if I just try waiting it out and eating mushrooms in forests, I end up dying of sickness. This isn't a game about surviving, it's a game about taking a while to die. 2 days is my usual record.
This game relies so incredibly heavily on luck that it just isn't fun. But survival is all about strategy, so this works out horribly. I've tried building a great shelter, but died of sickness. Tried never staying in one spot, but got mauled. There are only ways to lose and no ways to win. Also with the very small amount of recipes available, you'd think the game would give you hints on when you need just 1 more item to make something. Dragging the skills into the crafting table is just really monotonous. It should be doing this itself! It's the Minecraft crafting table all over again, with no user-friendliness.
And the skills, they were a selling point for me, but now that I've gotten to play it I only pick the same skills each time. They are just not at all balanced. This is what I'd expect from a game still in beta. I thought I'd be avoiding these huge flaws in a finished game. Incredibly dissapointing. I've tried other survival roguelikes and they were pretty bad too in there own ways.
Starting to wonder if this genre combo simply can never work.
UPDATE: Same day I post this, a wonderful person tells me about a free game in beta called Cataclysm: Dark Days Ahead. It's got more content than I can handle! And despite it's wonky controls, it has a very clear crafting system, and loads of methods for getting materials. It's also far more immersive with you actually exploring the areas yourself. Just hope you don't need graphics, because that's the game's only flaw. To play it like Neo Scavenger, just turn zombies off and NPCs on. And finally, when you die in it, you learn from it. You play better next time. Something I sadly can't say about Neo Scavenger, where it's difficulty is based on a dice roll.
Really in depth as compared to 2 and a much improved graphics engine.
Fun game, it's fast paced and action packed, with lots of gunfire and impressive moves.
A hidden gem, well worth the price on Steam.  I hope all my friends buy a copy so we can play together!!

There's a couple of things you should know about Crane before you get started. Despite supposedly not undertaking any parkour or general athletics since high school track, he absolutely LOVES climbing and can scale a 4 story building in 10 seconds, scamper up a lampost quicker than a squirrell, and jump from one rooftop to another, grabbing ledges and bracing against impacts which should break multiple bones in his body? Sounds superhuman, right? There's one problem: he absolutely always does what people tell him to do, even when he's clearly being had -  including following the directions of psychopathic, pantomine villains without any complaint. His tendency to not ask questions will get you into some real scrapes and as a player, might drive you mad.
Ultimately for me, it didn't matter too much. The vibrant heart of this game is the parkour, the bounties and challenges strewn across the beautifully crafted, fictional city of Harran (thanks to the writers by the way for setting this zombie story somewhere other than America for a change, by the way). The main story is important simply as a  reason to be there and to provide contextual immersion - but as a story I can't say it's anything to write home about. There are some real cliched caractures and scripts here, including the absurdly-evil Rais who will really drive you potty. The Following expansion takes you outside of the city and brings several key new facets to the game including the driveable Buggy, new challenges, weapons and enemies. The Following is a brilliant counterpart to the main game, but in both the story is average and the endings absolutely terrible. The key is that you are allowed to continue playing and exploring after you finish so you can almost ignore the endings.
This does occasionally produce plot contradictions, since it's possible, without rreferring to particular spoilers, to encounter characters in side quests despite the fact that they may have died as part of the main quest, This is strange, but necessary in allowing you to pursue the rest of the game regardless of completing the main game.
The survival and crafting elements of this game are fun and rewarding, and levelling up is satisfying. At the beginning you will struggle to fight even a single zombie and may not find any weapon other than a broken wooden plank. Your best bet is to run. By the end of the game, you won't be scared of zombies at alal, except of course at night when the real challenge begins. You might find yourself, like me, forgetting about the main story and trying to 'complete' the maps by unlocking al safe houses, completing all challenges, and creating the best weapons.
If it were not for these elements, I believe the game would feel empty and unchallenging, since the main story as I say can seem cliched and irritating with the chief antagonist always somehow one step ahead of everything and taunting you all the time.
It's not a perfect game for this and other reasons. I would like to see the ability in future titles to change your home, and interact with home environments more - since in Dying Light all there is to do is sleep and shop in safezones. I would of course like to have more satisfying, better written game endings, and better integration betwen the following and vanilla game would have been ideal (You start the Following as a new game, albeit using an existing character, rather than  being able to travel freely between locations. )
Despite these flaws, Dying Light is an absorbing and fun addition to the zombie-survival genre, which thanks to its parkour and Bounty quest system, manages to not take itself too seriously. An 8/10 for me, and a must-buy if on sale.

Having been a user of blender since 2.3x all those years ago, I have had a long and very pleasent exsperience with this great bit of artistic goodness.
Here are some Facts:
1. Bleander is not just one tool that does just one aspect of 3D modeling and Content creation. There are many tools here in one package. From Simple 3D modeling like 3D Studios, to Organic Sculpting Like zBrush and 3DCoat. To some other very awesome features like Animation and the like. There is pleanty of all of it in this one program.
2. Blender come with a steep learning curve and if hard to get a handle on it all when one first gets started with the program. I have been using this program for years and to this very day I learn something new almost every time i open up this program and start to work. I am constantly learning and I do this sort of work as a freelance and as a hobby game designer.
3. Blender really shines when the user finds and installs one of the gap filling plugins that are out three. but there is a small bit of a warning here. Not all plugins are easy to find and they are not all listed in the same place. Worse yet, not all plugins are mantained and some are even broken after some version of blender or anther. However almost all plugins are written in Python Script and anyone with some Python coding chops can take that code, rework it and fix these plugins if there is a great enought need. Maybe even release them back into the wild community for a resurrection of sorts.
4. Blender is 100% open source and 100% Free now and as they say blender will remains free forever as long as some one is still out there working on that code. It is even possible to take the code and create such a highly modified version of the program that it becomes a shadow of it former self and becomes it whole seprate program entirely. I have often dreamed of making a Unity Blender Brance that allows for the user to make models for the Unity Game engine in a 1:1 ratio. but i don't code well so untill then i'll just keep using what tried and true.
5. Blender is not ment for just one thing. It's designed for many types of projects and as such it not always going to fit your needs 100% of the time. You as a user are going to have to figure out how to make it work or what you will need as in plugins of 3rd party software to make what you are trying to do work in some way shape or form. This is especially true in the realm of most older Game Engines and at time newer or very current ones at points.
6: Blender, lastly can be used some how to do almost anything your mind could want to do. You need only be presistent and patient at time or have a good plan of attack setup before hand. If you keep at the problem you will find the way to do what you need done. Just don't give up.

I enjoyed playing this game over the free weekend. I am an FPS kind of gamer but the DoW series looked quite mesmerizing so I said "Screw it, I'm bored and it's free!" I am NOT disappointed with my decision to give DoW1 & DoW2 (& their mostly successful standalone sequels, a chance because I became addicted and in love with the two (which caused me to oversleep and miss the sale on the last day :P )
Great series! Definitely learn from my mistakes everyone! Pick up DoW1 & DoW2 if you can afford both. If you can only choose one of the two here are some tips for choosing if you know nothing about them,
- DoW1 is what you would think of a strategy game, meaning you build an HQ, barracks, generators, etc and then dominate your opponent (with the exception of some missions based on command one squad and infiltrate the enemy's territory)
-The multiplayer was hardly alive, and I was unable to join a match the first and last attempt I made.
- DoW2's campaign is mostly command the Force Commander (the main character which you get to name) and 3 other squads and dominate the enemy orks, farseer, chaos, tyranid. Did I mention it is co op?
-That isn't the only great part of #2 though! It also has a co op survival game mode called "The Final Stand" where you and 2 others work together to survive and progress through the increasingly difficult waves of enemy A.I. You get to choose your race and also level up each individually, earning new abilities, armor, and weapons. This game mode is still partially alive with players.
So do yourself a favor and buy Dawn of War (1&2 - or at the least 2)  :)
Skeptical? Look up some gameplay, and reviews! Keep an open mind if you prefer FPS action games.

*The overview*
The game itself is quite good and fun, especially if you like to create your own sandbox and mess around and pretend to be some of the numerous civilizations. It "can" get quite dull or boring quite quickly, especially because some of the mechanics in the game are a little annoying.

I absolutely hate some of the features and mechanics in this game. I will start with the one that made me write this review:
1) Roads have a maintenence cost. This seems logical on one hand, but combined with the fact that Automated Workers construct roads as a leisure past-time is utterly broken. You can either manually control the workers ( in a big empire it can be a hassle and take a way A LOT of unnecessary time ) or you can have them on automated, which is meant to save your time, but they will end up making roads to secluded and far fetched cities and allies.

To make it worse there is no option to disable workers from building any roads at all. This alone cost me one game in which I dumped several hours, because if you have plenty of workers they build a long road VERY quickly.
I will add more negative points to this review at a later time, but currently this one REALLY ticked me off.
