There are quite a few things that are similar to ARK but also a lot that is unique and different. In this game the character customization is very nice, 3 factions but you can play with any body template, human, elf, dwarf and then customize them until you have a character that is unique, I like that there are fantasy skin colors, there are a limited number of hairstyles but for the first day of an EA it went pretty well. I was on a private server so there wasn't issues with spawn gankers and such as I have read about on these other reviews. Personally with survival games where you can build your own base, I would recommend getting into a private server.
So the nice thing about starting the game is the Character Creator and there is a tutorial that pops up and gives little 'fetch' quests to help you level up. As you level  you automatically know a certain set of skills and other's you can use your xp gained to level up a particular skill as you wish.
The game is only 30% finished at this point but again this is EA and I think a lot of things are going to get fleshed out over the next year so I don't feel it's fair to judge the game to be 'bad' based on a first day EA. The developers have added more servers and PVE servers for those people who are not interested. That's a good thing and shows the responsiveness of the developers.
So for survival games, ARK players will find it most easy to get started, Every thing decays pretty fast in your inventory so just be aware of that.
Were there bugs? Yes, mostly one involving getting into a closed server with the password screen causing an endless loading screen. The best advice for this was to copy paste the password then hit 'enter' and do not use the mouse to move around the screen.
I want to explore more, already I see people taming some interesting animals, and I have not even picked out a place for a building yet or explored much past the faction city safe area. Much more to learn!

Very reminiscent of the Playstation 2 game Tourist Trophy, this game takes you through a progression from a amatuer weekend warrior all the way through to a top level Moto GP contender.  The bike selection is very robust, covering just about every manufacturer in the world, and in some cases even different generational models.  It even covers electric powered bikes.  And of course every bike can be upgraded with real life name brand aftermarket parts.
The racetrack list is also robust and includes famous tracks like the Nurburgring (both GP and Nordschleife configurations), Monza, and Imola to name a few.
The physics are on par with other modern sim-like racers.  Graphics are acceptable, nothing to rave about but also nothing to complain about either.  A.I. also falls in this category, though at times it feels like their positioning and pacing is predetermined based on the players performance.  Keep in mind my experience with the A.I. is only on the mid to easy levels so far.  More experienced players might find the A.I. more acceptable in higher difficulty levels.
Overall I would recommend this to any motorcycle enthusiast or sim racing fan that's looking for a sight change of pace.
FAIR WARNING:
A CONTROLLER OR JOYSTICK IS A MUST WITH THIS GAME!!!  You can get by with mouse and keyboard, but you won't have a fun time.
Also if you do buy this, don't forget to download all of the free content packs from the store.  Don't worry about getting the paid DLC as that content usually mirrors identical bikes already included.

Just to start off here I LOVE THIS GAME!!! I have put so many hours into this game and had so many playthroughs yet the game never gets old. This game has a lot going for it. Firaxis decided to go with core ideas from UFO Defence and then streamlined them to make them easier and somewhat more forgiving. The story in the game is decent but can get stale during a second game but this is made up during the missions you play in game. As you play the game you grow attached to soldiers that stand out or are general bad asses. You start out seeing them as rookies and then attach to them so much you are literally crying when you see him getting shot right in the face by a sectopod beam before dying. Even if they aren't complete badasses you can still connect even if it is the soldier that manages to miss the 99% shot at point blank. In my opinion that in itself makes the games "story" different every playthrough. If you’re not lazy like me you could even read the incredibly well written flavour text that is honestly very interesting. On top of the flavour text the game gives off a very creepy atmosphere that overall makes up for the somewhat linear story and keeps you immersed in the game. The cover system in this game is extremely easy to learn and overall the games combat system is easy to get the hang of. The game’s tutorial is extremely helpful and gives you a good summary of what this game is about. The game is also interesting and fun when you are in your Xcom base. You are going to be mostly focusing on research because if you aren't researching new weapons and armor fast enough your soldiers are going to go into battle with huge disadvantages. But engineering is also important if you are playing on harder difficulties. The hardest decisions to make are what countries you want to help. Every month you are given "abductions." These are when you have 3 countries that need your help you have to choose 1 and then receive the reward that country gives. The countries that you don't help rise in panic and leave the Xcom Project (if too many countries leave you lose). The decisions are easy at first but later in the game the decisions get extremely hard and you'll have to really think about it. Overall this game is very entertaining. The only bad things that come to mind are the "Xcom Glitches" aka funny animations and corpse ragdolls that are funny looking but break immersion for some people, and the somewhat dated graphics that still hold up but are beginning to show their age. But other than that the game is extremely fun to anyone who plays.
Final Rating 9/10

XCOM: Enemy Unknown (EU) is in short, one of THE best games I've ever played, and was the best strategy game for me until XCOM 2. This game is a reboot of the old X-COM: UFO Defense game. If you've played that game and liked it, you probably will like this game, if you didn't like it, you'll probably like this game. This game in all honesty doesn't follow the older games that well in anything but the strategy. You will see lots of the old aliens but a lot has changed to make the game more streamlined. I would say this has improved the game tremendously. It allows new players to jump in easier and old vets to find fun in the game. This game is very easy to ease into if you are new to stratregy games. Featuring a tutorial mission and helpful dialog to steer you in the right path until you are ready to begin. The game is fairly tough though so it will be challenging to some players but it doesn't take long to get into the swing of things. The game's strategy is some of the best I've seen from any game and on higher settings can be really tough if you aren't prepared. The game can be brutal but never unfair (well unless you miss 90% shots but that's XCOM baby!). All jokes aside, even with the occasional BS moment you can account for it usually. A favourite thing in this game for me is the upgrade system for your soldiers. Most of the choices made there are very tough and for most either choice could be good. On to some things that I don't like about the game. One is the graphics, while they look fine and get the job done, they can glitch or just look ugly sometimes. Next is what I like to call "XCOM glitches", which are littered in XCOM EU and XCOM 2. They consist of weird oddities that aren't realistic and may break immersion but I find them funny...Such as a dead sectoid's body break dancing across the map. That kind of weird crap. These are technically bad things but I find them part of XCOM's charm. The same goes with the 'That's XCOM baby!' moments I talked about earlier. The base customization is a bit lack-luster as well with the decisions to build this or that usually being straightforward, though this doesn't apply to the engineering projects which can be tough to choose which are priority. Lastly is the story and especially the ending which I won't spoil. But the game's story is basically nothing. However, I can commend it for the excellent flavour text regarding things that you research and about the different aliens. These provide a lot of depth into the background lore of the game. This kinda extends to the stories you create through your different soldiers. You always will remember that time when one support dodged 15 shots in one battle or when your heavy saved your squad with a well placed rocket. The soldier who hits every shot as a rookie and becomes a shotgun wielding assault, or the rookie who never hits anything but ends up a sniper. The real story of this game is told through your soldiers and not the game itself.
TL;DR Great game, XCOM glitches, "That's XCOM Baby!", bad story, great strategy
Final Rating: 9/10 Must Buy

Ah, X-COM. Few series can boast to be as long-running or as divisive as this one. The original game was known for its complex tactics, complicated mechanics, intensive micromanagment, and occasional silly moments; victory was possible through good tactics and a good equipment loadout. This one... is different.
Firaxis came around over a decade later and decided to reboot the franchise with a risky venture. They simplified or outright removed many mechanics in order to remove a lot of the tedium of the old games. Gone is the clunky micromanagment of checking everyone's ammo and equipment, and of individually moving each of your many soldiers step by step across the wide fields; now everyone gets one primary weapon, one pistol, one armor, one item, and one class that is randomly assigned despite you already having half of your roster filled with Heavies. You also have to move each soldier only on the paths recommended by the computer, which often says that it counts as dashing to walk through that open door to enter good cover three spaces away but you're free to run through three buildings to shimmy up a pipe and take low cover on the opposite side of the map. Aiming is also handled by this same computer that says you can not shoot at the enemy around the corner, but it is free to get a flanking shot on that same character without moving. Remember slowly expanding to have multiple bases so that you could cover every continent and have multiple strike teams out at once? Now you get one base and one Skyranger to try and cover the entire globe while panic builds in the countries you're no longer able to cover! Fun!
Whenever new gimmicks were added on for this reboot, they were often done just to punish old tactics. Did you want to rush in aggressively and take out the enemies before they could do anything? Too bad, mate! Each group of enemies gets a free movement period when first discovered to take great cover against your soldier who just used half of their turn! Did you want to sit back and snipe? Woe to the long-range fighter, as many enemies now possess teleportation, unerring poison spit, invisibility, enough health to take full bursts from your entire squad, and insane movement rates in order to dissuade the sniper. How about using explosives to take out cover or large groups of enemies? Well, actually, just like the old X-COM games that still busts most of the loot you wanted, so that's still the same. There's an enemy type and an accompanying ability to punish anything you might try that would be seen as "intelligent tactics", and you're only allowed to carry one countering item per person; that's presuming you psychically knew to bring those items along beforehand for that specific enemy hazard and did not mind giving up a different loadout for your team. Really, the only way to win with minimum casualties is to always have known in advance exactly what all will be waiting for you in the next randomized mission and gear up specifically for it. Fair!
The plot? It's actually better than the original, but not by much. Oh, but don't worry too much about it! The sequel totally retcons everything you were meant to accomplish in this game anyways, so any progress you make against the stacked RNG just to get to that next story objective is entirely meaningless. F***!
If you want to get maximum possible enjoyment from this game, then wait for it to go on sale and play it on any difficulty lower than "Classic" so that the RNG isn't quite as broken; it will not fix any of the inherent system flaws or bugs, but at least your soldiers will not arbitrarily miss an enemy that is only one tile away... assuming they're allowed to target it in the first place.

[EDIT: Final Game]
Now that the final game is out, I can't change my verdict.
It's far too buggy for release still.
The earlier problems I mentioned are still largely not fixed.   Largest complaints:  Weapons/tools wear FAR, FAR too quickly.   Animals are quite happy to approach your fire... which should not be the case.
I respawned with my view turned 90 degrees (like I was laying down).
I see no use for the tent.  I was hoping that health would restore faster, but I don't think it does.
I've not seen past the first age, and as with my last spawn the loot bag with my inventory didn't appear, I lost everything.  What a terrible drag that is.
Still a red thumb.
[finish edit]
The price of $12.99 is too high for the game in its current state, but for early access it shows promise.  If this were a $6 early access game, I would have given it a thumbs up.  There are FAR, FAR better games, in playable states, for less.
The game has two modes, standard and advanced.  I don't know anything about the advanced mode, but have written the developer to ask.  All comments relate to the standard mode.
First, the good -
The crafting system is straight forward. Took a few minutes to figure it out. I like the crafting mode where a template can be placed (for a shelter, for example), and you can add materials over time to finish it.  That's a great game mechanic that I've appreciated in other games, and I'm glad to see it here.
The environment looks pretty good.  Day nitght cycles, rain...   I saw only forrest... but I assume there are other biomes out there.
An arrow points toward your spawn point... so you can't get lost (given the lack of terrain features... it would be easy to get lost without it)
The not-so-good -
- First... animals should not approach the camp when a fire is burning.
- Tool/weapon wear needs significant tuning.
Clubs should almost never wear... wood or stone.  It's silly to craft five clubs just to be sure you have enough when you go hunting.   The spears should wear... but not nearly as fast as they do.  I'd say *at least* twice as long.
- I never saw any fruit or other forms of food besides wild boar.  Bears and wolves seem to only give hide.  (I did see an elk, but did not have a kill).  Forraging sure is needed.
- I built a Tee-Pee, but it vanished after I returned from a hunt.  The rains had started... did it melt in the rain or something?  That shouldn't happen.
- The spear should be useable in water to catch fish... but currently no weapons can be used, even if you only wade into the water.
- Loot bags seem to simply disappear on their own...  so there appears to be no way in the game to safely store the things you collect... pretty frustrating.
- Hunger sets in too fast given the scarcity of food.  If forage was available this might not be an issue.
- I lost my current game by starting an advanced game... and there are no "save game" provisions.  It seems to save your current game, and nothing more.  There should at least be saves for the advanced and standard games, so that you don't lose one when trying another.
Nothing wrong with the game that can't easily be fixed.  As long as the devs keep at it... it could turn into something great.

It's fairly obvious that the Payday franchise - and especially the "First World Bank" heist - was heavily "inspired" by the early scenes of The Dark Knight, in which The Joker and his dispensible lackeys rob a bank in spectacular fashion. Add in some other well-known heist/crime movies from over the years, such as Heat and The Taking of Pelham 123, and you have the franchise's main influences covered, story-wise. So is this short "web series", loosely based on the games, as good as the films I've just mentioned?
No, of course not. And nor did I expect it to be. Not least of all 'cause it clearly doesn't have the budget.
I do, however, expect these episodes to be good by the standards of low-budget filmmaking. Unfortunately...they're not. Everything which makes the games work - including a complete lack of characters with anything resembling a defensible morality - just doesn't work here. Our bank robbers are made out to be self-styled Robin Hoods, when anybody who's played the games knows they're just ruthless cop-killers. MASS cop-killers. Like, you pretty much kill every foot soldier in the city every time you play a map.
The eloquent solution of this series to this small ethical problem? "Cover fire". The bank robbers just spray numerous bullets in the DIRECTION of the cops and security guards, but rarely seem to hit one. So instead of the unrealistically tolerated body count spree of the games - in which you can somehow negotiate for your arrested buddy's freedom even after he's turned at least a hundred cops' wives into widows - we have an equally unrealistic depiction of big-time crime that barely hurts a fly, and only rips off "evil" big banks who steal from the "little guy". Gimme a ♥♥♥♥in' break.
The video games work 'cause THEY'RE VIDEO GAMES. This doesn't work 'cause IT'S A SERIES OF SHORT FILMS. The same logic and excuses simply don't apply. Good games don't NEED to be realistic or morally deep. Good movies and TV shows do. On top of all this, the "action" is just plain lame...clearly not a good thing in an "action" series.
A fourteen-year-old boy's weak-arsed wank fantasy, at best. Michael Bay would presumably be proud. "One thing is certain: it's got Steam, it's growing, and it's ready to launch." Seriously, EAT MY ♥♥♥♥ING BUTT-NUGGETS, YOU SHAMELESSLY CRASS♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
Oh, and for the record, the above review is mostly based on the first two episodes, which actually manage to concentrate on the antics of our four favourite bank robbers. After that, the storylines become more divergent, and the episodes only get WORSE.
Verdict: 3.5/10.

Never let it be said that you need a tripple A studio, an army of designers, developers and artists, and boundless resources to make a game that's challenging and fun.
Neo Scavenger is a breath of nostalgic air, harping games like Wasteland and Fallout, but with the new hardcore survival-style normally only found in modern titles like Rust.
Just a dash of RPG elements, an elloquent crafting system and an intense focus on resource management (though "scrabbling" might be the better word) the world of NS is a brutal one.
Combat is surprisingly deep considering it takes place almost entirely through text, and often results in a desperate brawl. You'll never be too well equipped, as even the best gear can't save you from some of the nasties out there.
Planning, tactics and luck will see you through though!
That being said, it's not perfect. There's a few terrible bugs, save games can be lost, and the nature of RNG can sometimes leave the player in unfortunate or outright unfair situations. Balance and tweaking post release will likely fix this.
But if you've missed games that punish you, or just have masochistic tendancies then this is the game for you.

It's one of the most satisfying games I've ever played. It's also one of the most unique and creatively written and designed I've ever played. The time manipulation just gets better and better...but the story is what sticks with you.

It's challenging - you may want to get some hints - but passing a challenge in Braid is more rewarding than similar achievements in most games, because you have to really dig deep and think about what the time travel gimmicks do to your plan. It's punishing in some areas but passing a level requires real problem solving and not flukey things like lucky runs or 'stumbling' upon the answer. You pass these levels by truly figuring them out, and that's a great quality for a game to have.
If you like puzzles, solid art design, enchanting music, and a really inventive and captivating story, please join Tim his special quest. A+ game, folks.

Braid is a very well executed puzzle-platformer. For some reason I was put off by the somewhat "childish" style of the game for a while before giving the game a chance. I'm glad I did eventually give it a try. All the puzzles are very well planned, and I didn't run into any bugs, which has been annoying me in some other games, because I couldn't be certain whether I just hadn't found the right way of solving the puzzle, or the game mechanics were glitching. Also, not once did I accidentally exploit any bug to cheat, which just proves that all the puzzles are meant to solve as they are, and my job was to find that answer.
The character and the surroundings respond well to controls. The music is suitable for the atmosphere, and it's mellow enough to prevent it from becoming repetitive. The artistic style is very nice after I got into it. Everything is just so pleasant to look at. The game also has an interesting message which is carried through the story. Overally, if you like puzzle or platformer games, there is zero reason not to play this one.

As with many Indie games, I find Braid is the type which requires you to fail in order to see the path you must take.  You can either opt to sit at a puzzle for what seems like an inordinate amount of time, mentally going through what course of action you'd take (which is difficult, as with the bidirectional nature of time flow in the game) or you can "do as you go", which ultimately ends up in repeated failures in a short amount of time (one of THE worst peeves I have).
I don't have much time with Braid, but that's simply because I could not tolerate that game mechanic being the crux of the game's success in my eyes.

Another stunning masterpiece from Milestone...
CONS:
GRAPHICS
Range from poor to bad. Legit looks 10 years old. Even running reshade and downsampling from 4k its meh at best.
Also has an issue with random flickering / flashing on the screen.
The bikes look ok. Id say they look like there was an effort for accuracy, but then the textures got rushed and they ended up looking like sample models from a 3d cad program.
The tracks look like they have been ripped from Gran Turismo 4 or Project Gotham Racing 4, as in OLD.
Trees look bad, road textures are very simple, and some of the buildings have texture work straight out of doom 95.
SOUND
If you have managed to never hear a motorcycle running in your life, then you might not have an issue.
Anyone else will notice how♥♥♥♥♥♥the bikes sound, either with 2 strokes sounding like 4 strokes, or the sound just being
completely off. The cbrr racebike sounds like someone has messed with a recording of a cat and called it a day.
BUGS / ISSUES
I could not get this to run in fullscreen. Despite the fact that the launcher had windowed mode turned off.
After about 45 minutes of looking for fixes and messing with .ini files, I ended up using a program called Borderless Windowed to force the game to fill my screen.
You have to use the keyboard for the compulsory first race before you can change the control settings.
The game does not automatically detect a controller.
The default gameplay setup includes AUTOMATIC BRAKING. I cannot fathom why a racing game would default to the computer braking for you.
PROS:
Once you have setup your controller and turned off all the unnecessary assists, the riding is probably the best I have experienced in a game. This is the closest to bike riding I've felt being sat infront of a monitor.
I will say however that when you compare the riding experience here to the driving experience I get with my g27 in dirt rally / assetto corsa, we are still a way away from a great realistic motorcycle racing game.
Overall Id say if you are REALLY into bikes and this is on sale, then you will probably have some fun.
But there is no way that this game can justify full price. Id go as far as to say that Milestone games should come out on release at about 20 bucks.
Lets all join hands and pray that the steam workshop can bring this game closer to what it should have been.

Great local co-op game. You are chefs and cook meals as the guests order them.
The idea is simple, the rules and mechanics are easy to learn. You use three buttons and an analog stick  - anyone can get going in ten minutes or less. Pick things up, use items and dash to move faster!
Cooking is easy - pick up some some meat and mince it on the cutting board, put it on a pan, then in a bun, put on a plate and serve. Maybe add some sliced tomateos or salad to the customers liking. Don't forget to do the dishes!
That does'nt mean the game is easy tho - it's both very challenging and rewarding, but it tests your ability to cooperate and coordinate instead of your dexterity or reflexes. The kitches have bad layouts, forcing you to run around wasting time, unless your buddies help you out. If you don't coordinate your actions, you'll keep bumping into eachother and won't get much done! Add some stress caused by the time pressure of impatient customers and you've got a recipe for some gripping gameplay right there!
The game is absolutely beatuifully designed, makes you have so much fun with so little in there. Wholeheartedly recommend if you've got some friends to play with in local co-op!

I received Tropico 4 for free from a Humble Bundle promotion.
Tropico 4 is a city building game, a genre not usually my forte, but it's similar to other ones that I've played like Simcity and the Anno (Year #) series. You decide what buildings to make, and your people will semi-automatically fill their roles to become your laborers, craftsmen, police officers, priests, and whatever else you need on your Caribbean island during the Cold War years (1960 onward).
Once you get the hang of things, you may begin to find that building a city from the ground up is extremely easy. Your people will demand certain amenities, but these demands are given to you on an almanac you may access at any time. Are people homeless? Build some apartments. Is a demand for healthcare, religion, or entertainment being unmet? Put down a clinic, church, or cabaret, and the problem will solve itself in time. If all needs are met, it's time to make some money with exports or tourism.
Throughout the 20-mission campaign (in which you almost always start with the same set of basic buildings and end up populating a small fraction of the island), you are presented with different obstacles... but you can build your city nearly the exact same way every time. One island supposedly has a crime problem, but you'll only need to put down a police station earlier than you otherwise might. One island has a rebel problem, so you'll need more military buildings earlier. The problems are thrown at you one island at a time, and only a small tweak is needed to keep things running smoothly.
Despite the wide variety of buildings, many of them either have little or identical effects. Farms growing cash crops, mines, industries, and tourism all make you money behind the scenes. All you need to do is analyze what your available assets are, and place buildings for the one that'll get the most return on investment. Your citizens handle the nitty-gritty of transporting and exporting the goods.
There's a wide swath of entertainment buildings, but unless you are going for tourism or trying to build a giant, deliriously happy island, most of them are not useful. Cabarets provide good entertainment for all Tropican citizens, and don't require electricity. Unless you are swimming in money (and you will be after a while), there's no need for pubs, restaurants, casinos, or roller coasters.
Your island has different factions like Communists or Capitalists whom you must please if you want them to vote for you in the periodic elections, but it's fairly easy to keep all of them happy. Even if you are in danger of losing an election, there are many ways to steal it at the last second, like signing edicts that people like, upping everyone's pay, bribing faction leaders, or just rigging the election. The same goes for foreign powers. In all my time playing so far, I've gotten China annoyed enough to embargo me once. That's all.
I'm going to say that I don't recommend this game, but with the stipulation that if you like city building games with an easygoing pace and low level of difficulty, you may like this anyway. If you're new to city building games or gaming in general, it might be a good starting point before tackling something less forgiving. But if you're looking for a challenge, look elsewhere.

After playing this game for 20 hours I feel like I'm ready to write a review. I'm a bike guy IRL, I ride my suzuki pretty much everyday and, even though I of course don't push to the limits, I kind of know how motorcycle physics work to a certain degree.

Not even the sound, which most people dislike, has managed to make me disappointed. In terms of physics it's pretty decent, you lose traction in the rear wheel if you give it throttle too fast, you can lock the wheel if you use too much front brake in a turn, big bikes wheelie if you are not careful with the power (that's why I would recommend use the right stick as the throttle/front brake rather than the triggers if you are using a controller which, btw, you should) and so on.
If I had to look for a flaw I would say AI, Other riders are a bit too agressive and they might take you down, but to be fair and sometimes do that too.
So yeah, it's a pretty good game if you like bikes, there are tons of bikes, enough tracks and good driving physics. You might enjoy it if you are a hardcore simmer or a racing games fan.

Dying Light: The Following - EE Is an amazing game which incorporates fast parkour-like movement and a brutal & bloody combat system. The game itself has an amazing story, fantastic graphics, and fun mechanics. As is probbably already obvious, this is a game which takes place in a "zombie universe" where the fictional city of "Harran" has been overrun and quarantined from the rest of the world. You are Kyle Crane, a GRE (Global Relief Effort) operative and it is up to you to do something about it.
Pros:
-Amazing Graphics
-Fun movement & combat system
-Interesting & immersive story
-Decent amount of stuff to do ingame (sidequests challenges etc)
-Co-op is pretty cool if you're into that kind of thing (I still finished most of it solo)
-The Following DLC adds more mechanics and an additional map and campaign, which are amazing!
-High FPS 90% of the game (50~60) with a medium specced setup. (And medium settings)
Cons:
- Some of the challenges really are not any fun at all, however if you're a completionist you'll find yourself performing many stressfull challenges.
-Only The Following is a worthy DLC, the rest just seems worse quality. Especially the (imo) lacking in fun, Bozak Horde DLC
PS: If you pick up or just have picked up Dying Light, dont forget to google "Dying Light Weapon Dockets" which is a nice way to get a few extra's ingame (while still possible, most codes have expired) And if you have an android or apple phone don't forget the companion app which apparently can in the end help you scavenge for King upgrades (legendary mods) if you level up your runners in the app.
Good night, and good luck survivors!

This is a wonderful game.  It is unforgivingly difficult, but very satisfying when you weather the storm and stabilize.
It allows many viable builds which will vary your play style significantly, although you will always play as a desperate scavenger.  Learning the survival systems and how to manage each is fun and engaging.  And it always feels wonderful when you discover the tools you need to make it another few days be it the means to make fire, clothes to stay warm, something to boil water in, or a large bag/sled to haul your stuff.
Although it seems unfair at times (such as when you are killed in your sleep without a chance to act) the real choice you made came earlier when you did (or were not able to) make a safe camp with noise traps.
I have one major gripe with the game is that the story elements, while immersive, tend to be too deadly, either ending your run prematurely, forcing you into a trial and error state to learn the proper choices, or spoiling the story by looking up the solution on the wiki.  While the rest of the game is fair but difficult, and revolves around the choices/play style of that run, these only involve foreknowledge of what is coming up and the time it took to prepare for it.
Even so, it remains one of the best indie games I've ever played.

So, after waiting for the reboot of this game for years, it has finally come. I'm not super positive or overly negative on the game, as I understand that it is in early access and will have more than enough room for development.
So, upon entering the game for the first time - character creation ultimately annoys me. The character AI moves around while I'm trying to see the changes I've made. Instead of the drastic movements, let the player move around the character in order to see their own changes instead of the AI moving like it's dancing topless in a club.
When spawning for the first time, the first thing I noticed was the lack of safezones even within a town. The floor was littered with dead bodies (not unconcious) and everyone had been looted of all their gear. The town guards did nothing to those who were killing people within spawn and it turns out you can kill said guards and shopkeepers (as I noticed when I went to go trade something and there was no NPC)
Once stepping outside spawn, it's like a madhouse. Random leveled mobs with no indication of how much health they may have left when you hit them, big ghastly skeletons that agro from far away, great winged beasts and gryphons that chase you all around the map and giant panthers (cats?) that can take a level one player out in one go. The fact of being killed more times than leveling up one level was insane.
I believe there should be safezones installed, and at least in the level one area - mobs that are in the 1-20 range. Getting chased by a level 84 wyvryn was not my cup of tea.
Allies/friends are a a great need in the game, so it seems. While chopping down trees near a house, had an entire group chase me down, throwing fireballs at my♥♥♥♥♥ Found a place to finally build my house - but wait! apparently a whole group had claimed the area and were killing anyone on site. Heck, even exploring was a massive task as either monsters were trying to kill you or players were. I prefered monsters chasing me over players however, players don't give up.
I can see certain spots where you need to farm materials being a problem. Especially near nodes. Looooots of pvp in the near future. Perhaps releasing a few PVE maps would be nice.
All in all, I do like the game. There are things that can be fixed to improve gameplay and player response. I do recommend the game, however; buy it when early access is over.

I waited until I finished the game for the first time to make a review, so here goes:
By far my favorite modern ARPG.
Diablo 3 had that honor until this game, because until this point I really liked a casual ARPG like D3.
No huge focus on specific builds, the art style was awesome, and the lore had been otherwise pretty built up.
It all came together for me, but this game is just miles ahead in everything except engine.
I'm suprised it took so long for my friend to convince to get this game for $7; it's worth way more than that.
The gameplay is your standard ARPG, like any other out there. You have your starting class, you have your skill trees (called Masteries), and you have your progression trees (called Devotions). You level up, put points into stuff you want to use, you left click everything, and you use abilities to kill as well as you can. Grim Dawn has a spin though.
At about level 10 you can select your Dual Mastery, meaning you can pick a
to use throughout the game. Want to be a Necromancer Arcanist who can spawn skeletons and shoot death rays? Want to be a plague Occultist Warrior literally possessed by an evil god? All of these and more are possible, and the build replayability is astoundingly large. This is the first ARPG I've beaten and actually
to keep playing.
Difficulty-wise, basic Normal mode is nothing to write home about. It
about casual ARPG difficulty, perhaps easier than D3 normal at points, so it's recommended to play on Veteran mode for your first playthrough. This buffs enemies, increases EXP reward, spawns higher quality loot, and spawns much more unique bosses and rare enemy packs. Even then however, if you are a seasoned ARPG player, the bosses, even the end boss can be trivial. I played through my first playthrough with two of my friends, all the way to the final boss and it was an absolute joke for us, even though the game is supposed to be harder for more players. I have heard however that the higher difficulties are no laughing matter and cannot wait to move on to a harder mode.
Graphically the game is fairly OK looking, when you're zoomed out at least. The game has an incredibly pleasing gritty dark eldtritch-esque atmosphere that immediately reminded me of the likes of Bloodborne. It's the kind of artstyle that just hits a certain coziness to cool ratio that feels like it fits perfectly. Abilities are always cool looking and manage to be very colorful and badass. Lighting is decent at points, as it has dynamic lighting, but the whole game otherwise screams "we made this on an updated Titan Quest engine" which really shows.
The engine of this game is a marvel, and also a bit of a joke. It supports dozens upon dozens of enemies on screen at once, full 3D rotation for countless different perspectives, and massive detailed and intertwined levels, and manages to run like mud and crash more than a teenage driver. It's not even a matter of the type of PC you have, I own a more than capable PC and so do my friends; it's just an old engine they tried to stuff DirectX 11 into, but the DirectX 11 render they used manages to cut your FPS in half compared to DX9. Especially in the expansion. If the FPS wasn't slogging, it would be multiplayer bugs such as freezing/slowdown while someone is joining, random crashes upon entering a new room, or a character just plain frozen in place serverside while clientside they are still right next to us invisble and still able to do damage and progress. The engine has it's quirks for sure, but it still definitely has a nice feel to it.
Sound design-wise it's actually really good. Weapons are sound meaty, attacks have the right punch, abilities sound cool, and you can hear enemies scuttle all around you in a decently high quality. The ambience is actually pretty top notch and sometimes pretty creepy; every area sounds unique and can sometimes catch you by suprise with distant whispering in one of your ears.
Music in this game is just awesome. It's the kind of nice warm dark tavern music you'd expect to hear from Diablo 2, and it all sounds pretty unique. The music in the base game does tend to repeat a lot across some areas, so there's no much diversity in the tracks, but they are all generally really well done and memorable. The expansion areas expand the music quite a lot though, and there it's also very high quality.
At the end of day, after many side-quests, returning to town to vendor trash, and even min-maxing my gear and redoing my build, the base game (4 Acts) ran me about 30 hours on Veteran Normal mode. I didn't rush, I found as many Devotion shrines as I could, and we generally tried to completely discover and play through the entirety of every level we came across.
This game has an amazing amount of content, huge replayability, and is just a ton of fun to grind through.
On a scale, it sits somewhere between Diablo 3 and PoE. Harder than D3,  and not as complex as PoE, it hits a perfect happy medium.
I'm gonna give this game a solid 9/10, subtracting a point for engine quirks and some disappointing end of Act boss fights on Normal.
Pick this game up on sale or buy it for full price, you wont be disappointed, and the expac alone adds about 50% more content.

Due to my love for racing games, hardcore and lo-fi sims ("simcade") in particular, I've had my eye on this game for a while. Having played previous Milestone titles, such as SBK 09 / 2011 / 12 Generations and MotoGP 13, I gave the demo of Ride 1 a try back when it was first released... and was swiftly disappointed. The handling just felt off and the game generally seemed to suffer from its share of technical issues and limitations.
A lot of time has passed, however, and when Ride 2 and most of its DLCs went on sale, I thought to myself: If there's no demo, why not give it a spin and just get a refund if its not to my liking? (Something I generally don't do - I usually stick with my choice of purchasing a game.) And here I am, almost 40 hours of play time later!
Even though I found the game's way of throwing itself at me upon first start less than perfect (i.e. forcing me to race a moderately powerful bike against the AI without letting me configure controls, difficulty and other things first), it nevertheless managed to provide a pleasant surprise within these first few kilometers on two wheels.
First and foremost, the precision of the controls (using a 360 controller) is absolutely spot-on. While I found the bike controls in SBK 12 Generations (my favorite out of the series) far too twitchy, and the MotoGP series in generally far too floaty and spongy, I finally found myself at peace with the bike handling in Ride 2. Precision is key to being fast in racing, and the bikes in this game do exactly what you want them to - unless you can't handle some overpowered superbike (Kawasaki Ninja H2R, I'm looking at you!), of course.
Performance on my machine (see below for specs) is great; I'm getting a rock-solid 60 FPS at maximum settings/1080p, and that's with a little bit of visual improvement using Reshade and Nvidia Profile Inspector.
In case you are wondering: The graphics, while generally clean and decent, could be a little more crisp in my opinion; hence I am using Reshade to add a tiny bit of sharpening and Nvidia Profile Inspector to force higher Anisotropic Filtering (the game does not seem to offer an adjustable setting, and the vanilla setting is awful IMHO).
Another issue that some will find quickly with this game is the lack of configurable field of view. After a while I found myself craving for a smaller field of view in order to improve racing in a tight pack as well as provide a better sense of scale, distance and speed; a lack of such an option as well as a lack of proper modding support makes it next to impossible to achieve it. As far as I understand, the community has been asking for an FOV slider since Ride 1 and did so again when Ride 2 was released, but ultimately fell on short ears with the developers.
On the sound side of things, my main issues are the perceived lack of raw power in engine sounds, as well as the missing wind sounds (especially noticeable in helmet camera, which is pretty much all I ever use). The music tracks in menu and during race are decent, though; a little catchy and pulse-driving, but not so obtrusive as to get on your nerves.
These bits of nitpicking aside, the technical side of things is otherwise fine as far as I can tell. The loading times, even when installed on a regular HDD, are only a few seconds for each race. On the downside, navigating through the menus could be a little bit faster - but that's criticism on a high level, really.
So how's gameplay? Good, actually. The game has several AI difficulty levels to choose from, as well as various settings for realism and driving aids. There's even a - very practical - rewind function, which can be helpful to analyze crashes in order to learn what mistakes were made and correct them. Traction control is also configurable during a race, and always starts off at "low". (Other options are off, medium, high and full.) Riding aids aside, the different AI levels should allow most people to enjoy tight battles against computer-controlled opponents in most races; although their situational awareness is... not very situational. Or aware.
That being said, the different single player game modes provide plenty of variety, especially combined with 30 fictional and real tracks and a huge load of bikes (~200 with paid and free DLCs, I think). Another reason to come back to this game on a daily basis are daily and weekly challenges, both of which allow you to earn tokens; these can be used to unlock permanent bonuses (i.e. "more money earned in time trial") or hire better AI riders for your team.
"But how realistic is it?", I hear you asking. Let me put it like this: Ride 2 is, from a physical point of view, as realistic as it should be. Racing simulations on 4 wheels can get away with more complex behavior since gaming wheels and FFB have become sophisticated enough to quickly and precisely convey lots of information about your vehicle to you, the driver. Motorcycle simulations don't have the luxury of widely available and affordable controllers made specifically for this purpose; gamepads - and their force feedback - are simply much less sophisticated (and less precise, too).
I am aware of a mod that aims to bring the physics in Ride 2 closer to real life, and I have tried it. Though I see the point and applaud the creator for their endeavor, I ultimately think the mod is not ideal for the enjoyment of the game because it is in no way balanced against the AI, time trials or other things in the game - as well as the previously mentioned lack of proper FFB. (The most FFB I get with my 360 controller is a little rumble during shifting - sometimes.)
It is also worth mentioning that, while somewhat limited, setting up your bike before a race is also available. And while it certainly is possible to race (and win) even with a standard setup, I
recommend changing at least some basic settings (i.e. ride height & gearing) for most bike & track combinations. It isn't too complicated, either.
Without a doubt, Ride 2 is a very good racing game. Moreover, it is probably the best motorcycle game I have played so far - in no small parts due to its precise controls. It's not perfect and its surely not ultra-realistic, but it
credible and authentic. There is a wide selection of beautiful, fast and exotic motorcycles that should make your heart leap for joy if one still beats in your chest; each and every one of them feels satisfying to tune and race. Most importantly, though, Ride 2 is addictive, bloody good fun on two virtual wheels.

A decent tabletop to video game conversion. Age of Empires II attempted to use in-game dialogue to simulate real time discussions and events between people in RTS games, but Dawn of War manages to make it even more believeable with the closer camera and the more dynamic movements of the models. The story is riveting, suspensful and startling towards the end. Anyone who enjoys a futuristic crusade and a struggle between good and evil should certainly follow this chronicle.
The add-on system of weapons, unit commanders and special attacks enhance the game play in a variety of ways. A menagerie of units is available to not only the Imperium, but the Orks and the Forces of Choas. The map design is very good and the structures are both impressive and fearsome sights. The voice over work is very theatrical and the cut scenes strongly resemble stage set pieces at times. The up close battles are especially well done. Swords, axes and electronic melee weapons all combine to spectacular effect. Dawn of War serves as proof that visualizing a table top game and taking time to develop solid game mechanics and credible army units can pay off.

I was pleasantly surprised by how all-round good this game is. Unlike so many AAA console ports nothing about it really felt "consolized" or dumbed down. Controls are great and even with almost all buildings being climbable there's none of the janky animations or buggy traversal mechanics that infest most of Ubisoft's parkour-games.
Weapon handling is excellent as well, most weapons have a brutal and heavy feel to them which is another thing a lot of games get wrong. I would have loved for firearms to be a bit more fleshed out though, with some variation instead of just the two 'generic handgun' and 'm4 lookalike' weapons we have now. I get that they want the game to primarily be a melee experience, but a few more handguns, perhaps even basic firearms you craft yourself would add a lot. Speaking of that, the bow that's available through DLC kinda makes early gameplay too easy. It has 10x the damage of any early melee weapon and with it you can engage huge hoards of zombies without breaking a sweat. Aiming the thing is too damn easy and they should have given the thing less damage or at least made it a lot harder to craft.
The graphics are some of the best I've seen in an open-world game. Textures generally look great, and characters and weapons look fantastic. The game however does rely heavily on "cinematic" filters, with some pretty intense chromatic abberation and grain going on, all of these can be turned off however. Little graphical details like how palm-leaves move in the wind and the lightting effects during dusk and dawn really add to the immersion. The only thing that seemed 'meh' graphically were the open water effects; physics-based tesselated water for Dying Light 2 pls...
Sound is another thing they got right. You get to hear some truly horrifying things, especially at night. Big props to the people responsible for the engrossing and well-acted cutscenes as well, you really get invested in the characters and story after a while.
There's a video editor, so that's good...

Fun ol' zombie slaying time.
As somebody who was one of those kids that would play Zombie Apocalypse around the neighborhood with friends, this game has exactly the coop experience I would have wanted as a kid. The way the multiplayer is done is excellent IMO. (You should disable players being able to invade your game though if you aren't in to that kind of thing, and just want to progress the story.)
The weapon upgrading is a big feature in the game. The parkour feels good. (Better than what I've played of Mirrors Edge IMO, but if somebody disagreed I wouldn't argue.) Even though the game doesn't have a focus on guns, what few guns there are in the game are fun to use.
The gameplay can change tones quite a bit. The three that I've found, are that during the day, it has a zombie-slayer feel. During the night, it feels like open world survival horror. When you're in a mission with people shooting at you, there aren't any zombies around, and you get a gun, it has a straight up FPS feel. All three of these types of gameplay blend really well for me.
The game runs really well for me, and I have a kind of old GPU (Radeon HD 7750. I really need an upgrade.)
If story matters to you, there's only a bit I can say. I haven't completed the game but I'm very far in to the main quest. It has a solid story. Nothing ground breaking, just a very satisfying story so far. If you like Far Cry 3 and 4 antagonists, you might dig one of the baddies in this game as well.
I prefer to play single player, but of all the zombie co-op games I've played, this one is my favorite, beating the Zombie Army Trilogy, Left 4 Dead 1 and 2, and Resident Evil 5.

A "game" with no gameplay elements.
Every aspect of the game is completely random and simply beyond your control. No skill or tactics to employ, just plain old luck determines whether you'll live each day. Combine this with permadeath, and you find yourself stuck replaying the same day over and over again, having about as much fun as Bill Murray did when caught in the same loop.
I'm being serious, you can fall, cut yourself, and die of blood loss just from *walking* if that's how the dice roll (advancing in combat carries the chance to trip and fall). Whether or not you find shoes and clothes in time to keep warm and not die from hypothermia, pure luck. Whether you wake up in time to defend yourself before an enemy kills you in your sleep, pure luck. Whether you can actually get to sleep because it's random whether or not you'll find a sleeping bag and it rains constantly... again, luck. Whether your very first fire started in a burnt out office building because you are hiding from the rain with nothing but a hospital gown and a large stick attracts an entire pack of feral dogs who you literally have zero chance against... need I go on?
There's just no meaningful interaction. All of your equipment wears out shockingly fast and it's a crapshoot whether you'll find a replacement. At times it feels like a miracle during an encounter just to close the gap to an enemy without tripping over yourself and falling to the ground before you can poke 'em with your spear. Start a fire to keep warm and attract an enemy you aren't ready to deal with. Lay low and hide, die of hypothermia. Damned if you do and damned if you don't. Either option is viable based solely on luck. You're not playing a game so much as just watching the unluckiest man on Earth die over and over again.
There is no character progression. You know how to make everything right away. Just put all of your swag into the crafting table and whatever can be made is instantly available. However good you are at fighting and surviving from the moment you wake up is as good as you're ever gonna be. All of your equipment has a ridiculously short lifespan. So even if you find a really good anything, don't get attached. Even crowbars wear out... CROWBARS! Solid bars of pure steel... wear out.  Seriously?
There's just no feeling of accomplishment. None. If you manage to survive for a week, it's not because you did anything right, you just got lucky. A first playthrough can net you shoes, cargo pants, a hoodie, a multitool, and a saucepan after 12 hours of scavenging. A second playthrough can net you a cut arm, 200 pebbles, a handful of poison berries, and 3 shards of glass after 12 hours of scavenging. The player is reduced to the role of spectator of the very short and uninteresting life of some guy named Phillip.
Without engagement, without meaningful choices to make, without progression, there's just no game here.

It is completely free with no microtransactions.
With that in mind I think any flaws the game has is mostly forgivable. I mean seriously it would have to be really♥♥♥♥♥♥to hate right?
So what is it about?
You do a variety of rolls, wall flips, and slides to take out the other players in a quick and hard to hit fashion.  Unfortunatly this looks more like everyone is just mindlessly sliding but they are still VERY hard to hit if they do it right.
There is so many ways to play but staying completely still is usually a horrific idea. Keep moving and dodging and people will have a tough time. Getting cornered can usually get you killed.
Weapons are varied but they all seem to be overpowered if used right. I can't argue that it is not balanced because they ALL seem to be powerful if used correctly.(Shotgun users camp doors, Macdaddy users slide in and go for the head, Akimbo users try to be precise, and everyone trys to make the best use of their guns to win)
Maps was not always my cup of tea but a really good map was one with city towers. You could jump from building to building and barely make it. Making for intense gameplay. A lot of times you could nearly fall to your death.
So overall I think this is a good game. It is free, good, and really deserves your attention.

You may think that the rocket launcher would be the game killer in these kinds of games but it actually has pretty weak splash damage (direct shots are killers though). Some maps are gothic some are futuristic. Also there is matchmaking so you will always be challenged if you hit play now rather than pick from a server (which is why you will have beginners luck since it still is trying to determine your skill). A big con is that you have to make an account (it uses Steam Cloud so why not use Steam username).

Got the game gifted to me so figured i'd give it a shot. Before I realized it, 8 hours had flown by and I am in love with this game. The story so far is interesting and the game mechanics (scavenging, crafting, parkour and combat) are all very well implemented. Even on normal mode you can very quickly find yourself in a jam if you draw too much attention to yourself.
One minor thing that I found frustrating was in combat some enemies seem to have incredible health for no reason. I can kill one "biter" in 2-3 headshots while another "biter" takes 10 head shots and still tries to stand back up. So I think hitboxes can be a little funky at times but its no problem unless you did something stupid like get cornered by a mob while scavenging a building and gotta fight your way out the door.
I dont know if fighting living humans later in the game gets easier but when you are low level and dont have a gun and steady ammo supply, they are a major pain. They block far more of your attacks than you can ever hope to block, kicking them staggers them at best 50% of time since they have balls of steel and they kill you in 4-6 hits while you can pound away on their steel skulls with the same weapons they have and you might as well be swinging a soggy pancake. Maybe there is a trick to melee fights early on but I definately havent figured it out.
Ive progressed far enough now I have the exploding zombies shuffling around now and those are annoying. When hit they blow up instant killing you if you are withing 3m. Many times I have come running around a corner and panic swung my weapon to stagger the "suddenly too close" zombie only to blow myself up because it was a bloater and my swing reflex is faster than my visual recognition. I cant speak for the other difficulty modes but in normal you just lose some expierience and spawn back at one of your safe houses and have to run back so I mostly laugh when I die from one of my stupid moments.
I found this game truly very fun and varied. I love open world games where I can chose how and when I do things. I have not done coop, I have only run around on my own. I did play Dead Island which is similar to this and while I thought it was okay, this game is so much better. If you have the money and like open world survival games then I definately recommend you give this a try.

This one however, is particularly interesting since it tells the tale of the legal battles between Activision and Infinity Ward, how they came to form Respawn, and how the prolonged legal entanglements affected the early stages of development. It's a really fascinating look at the intra-office strife they struggled through as well as some interesting pre-alpha/test footage of the game in various stages of development.
If you like Titanfall (which I have really really enjoyed) or are just interested in the history behind Infinity Ward/Respawn, I'd highly recommend it.

The Gold Edition of Dawn of War was one of the first M-rated games I bought as a teenager, and I always had fond memories of it because it catered to my personal favorite combat strategy: turtling. Nine years later, those feelings are still going strong.
For the uninitiated, turtling is the notion of erecting a stiff defensive perimeter, absorbing enemy attacks while establishing one's own economy, then lashing out with the full fury of one's tech tree and crushing the enemy in a swift show of force. Dawn of War's most effective strategy is what I like to call "Turbo Turtle" because of its resource mechanics. Unlike most games which require players to harvest resources from the game world in something of a parallel operation to the military stuff, the two mix together in the form of requisition, gained automatically from capturing various points around the map. This system keeps the game moving because no resource infrastructure is required to build infantry units. Just take a squad or two, capture some points, and you're off and rolling. These points can even have fortifications built on them, keepinig enemies at bay long enough for a force away from the flashpoint to react and engage and allowing the player to hold large swathes of territory (and resources) without desperately trying to get every detail just so to prevent exploits in the defense. (The other resource, power, is produced entirely within the tech tree with bonus areas available on most maps, meaning any shortage is usually self-created.) This keeps the game moving at a reasonable pace and prevents players from turtling for 20-30 minutes while advancing to the next tech level like one might in other RTS titles. This simplified approach keeps the focus on combat and battle tactics rather than letting resource gathering linger in the back of the player's mind.
The game also doesn't have players building infantry units piecemeal; instead, infantry come in squads which can be expanded and outfitted with heavy weaponry. The Space Marines - the sole faction the player uses in the campaign - have such powerful infantry that most early missions and even skirmish games can be won with 4-5 decked out squads of their mainline infantry, and the squad as the base unit can result in infantry combat on a massive scale at the climax of a battle. Five full squads of Space Marines puts 45 units under the player's control; mainline infantry for the other races churns out even more individuals, and it's all commanded at the squad level, so, again, no micromanagement.
The visuals were quite good for the time, although they haven't held up very well in the nine years since the game's original release. The upside to this is a lack of lag or chug on most modern PCs, even when the battles reach their most frenzied. There are fewer positives to be found with the story (quite dull and rather predictable) and the sound design (the voice acting is downright painful at times), but playing an RTS for the story is like eating a cheeseburger for the pickles; it's nice to have the extra flavor, but it's not really why you bought the burger.
Relic hit a home run with this game. Not only did they capture the essence of Warhammer 40,000 and its lore, they also made it something players new to 40k will be interested in and enjoy without getting bogged down in trying to bring 40k's rules to a video game, something other GW-inspired titles (read: Blood Bowl) could stand to learn from. Fun is the most important element of any game, and Dawn of War provides plenty of it. For the Emprah!

I don't normally recommend games that I have no intention of finishing, but this one has enough depth and originality that I'll make an exception for it.  If an unforgiving TBS game that features old-school second-person narration*, puts you in the role of an amnesiac cryonics patient who wakes up in a hostile post-apocalyptic world, and forces you to realistically manage every aspect of your well-being with meager supplies sounds like something you'd enjoy, I can safely say you won't be disappointed.  It exceeded my expectations, which were admittedly low, in part because of the uncreative title (but ultimately, it just wasn't my cup of tea).  The one thing I think needs an overhaul is the combat.  It feels tedious and, in contrast with the rest of the game, unrealistic.  It feels unrealistic when my adversaries are fellow human scavengers but never say anything before or while attacking me, and it feels unrealistic when, after beating a guy so badly that the game describes him as being in severe pain, coughing up blood, suffering from a concussion, and blacking out, he nonetheless refuses to surrender and continues trying to kill me.  Still, that's only a problem because this is a game that focuses on realistic survival simulation rather than combat, making it a relatively small complaint.
*It does not, however, stick to second-person, and instead frequently refers to the player literally as "player", which is annoying and breaks immersion, but now I'm just nitpicking.

This is easily one of the most creative and original games that I've ever played.  I loved the soundtrack. Jonathan Blow's decision to license the music--music written by composers for the sake of the art, not because they needed another track for a level--was excellent. The writing and story were superb! I can't say strongly enough how much I enjoyed the story (though to get the full story, you have to get the stars and getting the stars without looking up how is near impossible). The game mechanics were fun, consistent, and well thought out.
The puzzle design is by far the stand out feature here. Of course there's the "respect for the player's time" and "no filler" points that they make (and fulfill), but for me the excellence of the puzzle design is that each puzzle has a definite, "low impedance" answer (or answers, could be more than one, but each of them definite as I'll explain). Each solution is singular within the mechanics of the game, without introducing artificial limitations that contradict the rest of the game. There's no randomly twiddling with stuff until you slip past. While some games have some puzzles with no clear reason why the solution works, in Braid, discovering "why" the solution works comes first, and is the only real requirement to solving the puzzles.
If you've never played Braid, I envy the experience you have waiting.

Amazingly deep ARPG. The amount of choice you have in terms of combining classes, skills (and skill modifiers), devotions, items (and item modifiers) is just insane. This can be a little daunting when you are first starting out, but the game is friendly enough that you can just start playing and learn the game through experience. In addition, the game does not lock you into a certain way to build your character - you can respec all choices (although at some cost).
As is common for its genre, there is certainly grinding in this game, but it is not too much and overall quite enjoyable. There are various ways to grind, including going to bosses which are always in the same place, taking repeatable quests, and/or fight specific factions. The game is enjoyable both for people who prefer having a very rich end-game, as those who simply enjoy the process of levelling different characters.
Note that you do need quite a powerful computer to be able to run this smoothly at high/max settings. It's one of the very few downsides of this game. Secondly, don't forget that this game is moddable and there is a large variety of mods out there which add new classess, items, regions, or even new gameplay modes.

Ah Quake my good old friend. Where ave you been for so long?! What have you been doing?
Seriously I only discovered Steam had QuakeLive yesterday, and when I downloaded it it felt like a good old pal or brother was coming back home from the arctic or something. Welcome home you old dog you!
I have not played this game since 1999, but have fond memories of firing this up on the LAN at work, creating impossible killer bots via the console, so all my coworkers could bludge the rest of Friday evening away fragging eachother. I think I still have the old cdrom somewhere in the basement.
It's basically Quake3 Arena baby!! With a lot of things added to it, and best of all I love that it is free to play! Prepare yourself for how we old people used to play fps 16 years ago! No fancy killstreak awards, no boosting stats, no camping, no 360 noscope kills, no cheating and no nonsense! To play Quake3 (Especially Quake1) you have to have some skills, because you will get fragged... a LOT. So much in fact you will most probably ragequit. But the point of the game is not to die in a fit of rage! It is real competitive fps gaming. The only goal is to try to be 1st (when doing DM or TDM). The goal of this game is to blow off steam after a hard days work. The mission is to frag as many ppl as possible.
Of course CTF and other modes are also available, but they are just as fast paced as the others.
Tips for playing? Constantly watch your surroundings in complete paranoia. Also I like it how you can now loadout which weapon you start with. My tip is to start with a RAILGUN. It is by far the most difficult weapon to use in Quake3. You need to be spot on to be able to hit a target. But just keep using it to improve your aim, then the rest of the weapons will be a breeze. Also make sure you ALWAYS go for the in game powerups like armor, big health, the battlesuit and especially QuadDamageeeeee!! (You will hear that coming out of your speaker: Quaddamaageee!!!!!). People will be fighting over it, so be the first to get it haha.
Other than that, have lotsa fun, make new friends and enjoy this
timeless classic fps from the days of the old Pentiums. ;)

The Gold Edition of Dawn of War was one of the first M-rated games I bought as a teenager, and I always had fond memories of it because it catered to my personal favorite combat strategy: turtling. Nine years later, those feelings are still going strong.
For the uninitiated, turtling is the notion of erecting a stiff defensive perimeter, absorbing enemy attacks while establishing one's own economy, then lashing out with the full fury of one's tech tree and crushing the enemy in a swift show of force. Dawn of War's most effective strategy is what I like to call "Turbo Turtle" because of its resource mechanics. Unlike most games which require players to harvest resources from the game world in something of a parallel operation to the military stuff, the two mix together in the form of requisition, gained automatically from capturing various points around the map. This system keeps the game moving because no resource infrastructure is required to build infantry units. Just take a squad or two, capture some points, and you're off and rolling. These points can even have fortifications built on them, keepinig enemies at bay long enough for a force away from the flashpoint to react and engage and allowing the player to hold large swathes of territory (and resources) without desperately trying to get every detail just so to prevent exploits in the defense. (The other resource, power, is produced entirely within the tech tree with bonus areas available on most maps, meaning any shortage is usually self-created.) This keeps the game moving at a reasonable pace and prevents players from turtling for 20-30 minutes while advancing to the next tech level like one might in other RTS titles. This simplified approach keeps the focus on combat and battle tactics rather than letting resource gathering linger in the back of the player's mind.
The game also doesn't have players building infantry units piecemeal; instead, infantry come in squads which can be expanded and outfitted with heavy weaponry. The Space Marines - the sole faction the player uses in the campaign - have such powerful infantry that most early missions and even skirmish games can be won with 4-5 decked out squads of their mainline infantry, and the squad as the base unit can result in infantry combat on a massive scale at the climax of a battle. Five full squads of Space Marines puts 45 units under the player's control; mainline infantry for the other races churns out even more individuals, and it's all commanded at the squad level, so, again, no micromanagement.
The visuals were quite good for the time, although they haven't held up very well in the nine years since the game's original release. The upside to this is a lack of lag or chug on most modern PCs, even when the battles reach their most frenzied. There are fewer positives to be found with the story (quite dull and rather predictable) and the sound design (the voice acting is downright painful at times), but playing an RTS for the story is like eating a cheeseburger for the pickles; it's nice to have the extra flavor, but it's not really why you bought the burger.
Relic hit a home run with this game. Not only did they capture the essence of Warhammer 40,000 and its lore, they also made it something players new to 40k will be interested in and enjoy without getting bogged down in trying to bring 40k's rules to a video game, something other GW-inspired titles (read: Blood Bowl) could stand to learn from. Fun is the most important element of any game, and Dawn of War provides plenty of it. For the Emprah!

I was pleasantly surprised by how all-round good this game is. Unlike so many AAA console ports nothing about it really felt "consolized" or dumbed down. Controls are great and even with almost all buildings being climbable there's none of the janky animations or buggy traversal mechanics that infest most of Ubisoft's parkour-games.
Weapon handling is excellent as well, most weapons have a brutal and heavy feel to them which is another thing a lot of games get wrong. I would have loved for firearms to be a bit more fleshed out though, with some variation instead of just the two 'generic handgun' and 'm4 lookalike' weapons we have now. I get that they want the game to primarily be a melee experience, but a few more handguns, perhaps even basic firearms you craft yourself would add a lot. Speaking of that, the bow that's available through DLC kinda makes early gameplay too easy. It has 10x the damage of any early melee weapon and with it you can engage huge hoards of zombies without breaking a sweat. Aiming the thing is too damn easy and they should have given the thing less damage or at least made it a lot harder to craft.
The graphics are some of the best I've seen in an open-world game. Textures generally look great, and characters and weapons look fantastic. The game however does rely heavily on "cinematic" filters, with some pretty intense chromatic abberation and grain going on, all of these can be turned off however. Little graphical details like how palm-leaves move in the wind and the lightting effects during dusk and dawn really add to the immersion. The only thing that seemed 'meh' graphically were the open water effects; physics-based tesselated water for Dying Light 2 pls...
Sound is another thing they got right. You get to hear some truly horrifying things, especially at night. Big props to the people responsible for the engrossing and well-acted cutscenes as well, you really get invested in the characters and story after a while.

Got the game gifted to me so figured i'd give it a shot. Before I realized it, 8 hours had flown by and I am in love with this game. The story so far is interesting and the game mechanics (scavenging, crafting, parkour and combat) are all very well implemented. Even on normal mode you can very quickly find yourself in a jam if you draw too much attention to yourself.
One minor thing that I found frustrating was in combat some enemies seem to have incredible health for no reason. I can kill one "biter" in 2-3 headshots while another "biter" takes 10 head shots and still tries to stand back up. So I think hitboxes can be a little funky at times but its no problem unless you did something stupid like get cornered by a mob while scavenging a building and gotta fight your way out the door.
I dont know if fighting living humans later in the game gets easier but when you are low level and dont have a gun and steady ammo supply, they are a major pain. They block far more of your attacks than you can ever hope to block, kicking them staggers them at best 50% of time since they have balls of steel and they kill you in 4-6 hits while you can pound away on their steel skulls with the same weapons they have and you might as well be swinging a soggy pancake. Maybe there is a trick to melee fights early on but I definately havent figured it out.
Ive progressed far enough now I have the exploding zombies shuffling around now and those are annoying. When hit they blow up instant killing you if you are withing 3m. Many times I have come running around a corner and panic swung my weapon to stagger the "suddenly too close" zombie only to blow myself up because it was a bloater and my swing reflex is faster than my visual recognition. I cant speak for the other difficulty modes but in normal you just lose some expierience and spawn back at one of your safe houses and have to run back so I mostly laugh when I die from one of my stupid moments.
I found this game truly very fun and varied. I love open world games where I can chose how and when I do things. I have not done coop, I have only run around on my own. I did play Dead Island which is similar to this and while I thought it was okay, this game is so much better. If you have the money and like open world survival games then I definately recommend you give this a try.

Fun ol' zombie slaying time.
As somebody who was one of those kids that would play Zombie Apocalypse around the neighborhood with friends, this game has exactly the coop experience I would have wanted as a kid. The way the multiplayer is done is excellent IMO. (You should disable players being able to invade your game though if you aren't in to that kind of thing, and just want to progress the story.)
The weapon upgrading is a big feature in the game. The parkour feels good. (Better than what I've played of Mirrors Edge IMO, but if somebody disagreed I wouldn't argue.) Even though the game doesn't have a focus on guns, what few guns there are in the game are fun to use.
The gameplay can change tones quite a bit. The three that I've found, are that during the day, it has a zombie-slayer feel. During the night, it feels like open world survival horror. When you're in a mission with people shooting at you, there aren't any zombies around, and you get a gun, it has a straight up FPS feel. All three of these types of gameplay blend really well for me.
The game runs really well for me, and I have a kind of old GPU (Radeon HD 7750. I really need an upgrade.)
If story matters to you, there's only a bit I can say. I haven't completed the game but I'm very far in to the main quest. It has a solid story. Nothing ground breaking, just a very satisfying story so far. If you like Far Cry 3 and 4 antagonists, you might dig one of the baddies in this game as well.
I prefer to play single player, but of all the zombie co-op games I've played, this one is my favorite, beating the Zombie Army Trilogy, Left 4 Dead 1 and 2, and Resident Evil 5.
