While Battlefront II's graphics may not have aged well, the gameplay itself is still just as fun as that one day eight years ago when I finally popped it in and gave it a shot.
PROS
+Great gameplay mechanics
+Epic maps showing some of the most famous battles from Star Wars (including Geonosis, Kashyyk, Coruscant, Hoth, and Endor)
+Space battles! (which can be won by both dogfighting and boarding actions!)
+(Non-canon) Story-driven campaign where you play as the 501st Legion.
+Generic campaign system for galactic conquest!
+Heroes, each of whom has a different playstyle (for the most part).
+Vehicles!
+Class-driven spawning system familiar to anyone who played pre-Bad Company Battlefield.
+Each faction has two unique "special" units, from Jet Troopers to Wookies to Destroyer Droids to Dark Troopers.
+Original score from the movies!
+Additional "Hero Assault" mode where everyone is a Hero, allowing for such fights as Darth Maul vs Han Solo, or Jango Fett vs. Luke Skywalker.
+You can command NPC troops, a trait gone from most modern FPSs.
+Mods!
+Doesn't have EA's name on it!
CONS:
-Graphics are showing their age.
-Some of the voice actors are bad "sounds-like"s
-Balance issues in some various matches.
-Minor complaint, but there's no options to customize teams aside from Clone Wars/Galactic Civil War. So no fighting Droids or Clones as the Empire (except for two seperate campaign missions).
-No Space Heroes.
Overall an excellent game. It deserved a sequel/reboot infinitely better than that half-serious game EA offered (2015).
EDIT: Also better than that pay-to-win ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t EA thinks would make for a reasonable game (2017).

A great introduction to the Warhammer 40k universe. If you're like me you stumbled upon this by friends that either played the tabletop game, were into the lore or played this. As an RTS it is quite an entertaining one to play as you have your campagin of course which is really good as you play as a Space Marine chapter known as the Blood Ravens. It's even got a decent story to go with it since it takes place on a slowly chaotic planet filled with Orks, Eldar and Chaos Space Marines. I sort of wished the campaign was a little more varied in how you only play as Space Marines but it's still a rather competent campaign at that.
The game has lots of units to play as and often the game is territorial based meaning that you you have to keep moving and taking over relics and strategic points to get the resources you need to win the battle. It's a pretty good incentive instead of the usual building a huge army and steamrolling everything (not that steamrolling is fun but) it's refreshing to see a change in the RTS formula. When you're done with your campaign you have your skirmish modes where you play  against the AI with four factions to choose from (Space Marines, Chaos Space Marines, Eldar and Orks) and online mode where you play with friends and randoms which is quite nice and fun to play. Lastly you have your army painter which let's you customize your faction's armor and logo colour. It's cool but a little limited though not a lot of RTS games lets you do that.
Good campaign, fun skirmishes and online play makes Dawn of War a worthy RTS to have in your collection. It's over 10 years old and as a recent newbie to the series it is still rather fun to pick up and play. I give it an 8/10.

This game brings back all the magic of the original while still being new and fresh for newer generations of gamers who might not even know there was an entire series that pre-dates this game. Turn based combat is streamlined into 2 actions as opposed to the original's potentially frustrating action points and the seemingly arbitrary cost of actions always leaving you with leftover points. The only area I'd say that is streamlined too much is aerial dogfights with ufo's, which were admittedly fairly simple in the original X-COM.
I actually prefer the assortment of random maps versus the fully random generated maps of the original with occasionally nonsense layouts where your pilot decided to land his ship in the middle of a warzone amidst aliens armed with explosives who can mind-control your units, who have even more explosives. Now there's always a tactical approach that can be taken, and adapted to based on the situation, because while the map might be the same, the enemies may not be.
The game is easy enough to pick up, with ample tutorials and direction on what new buildings or items do, so much so that veteran's of the series might feel the first few cutscenes drag. The pace is otherwise spectacular and replayability is high with a number of difficulty mutators that unlock once you beat the game.
Overall I highly recommend this game to anyone looking for fast pace tactical gameplay and good "bang for your buck" replayability.

X-Com: Enemy Unknown is a great tactical turn based strategy game where you fight off an alien invasion.
It has some flaws:
There are a number of visual problems when the game cuts to show the shots you and the aliens fire at each other. It is a very common occurence that is distracting. Additionally, I don't think the in-game tutorial covers all that should be covered, most notably, fog of war and whether you will be in line of sight of enemies or not. Also, success in the campaign is mostly determined by your performance in the first 2-3 months (about 8-12 missions). If you make it through those first few months, the game will lose a lot of it's challenge, even on the higher difficulties. And finally, the multiplayer is a waste of time.
Now for the great:
As you begin to figure the game out, it becomes incredibly satasifying. Although you can get angry at missing a 90% shot, you will improve drastically as you begin to figure out how to manage risk so that you can always create an advantage against the aliens. There are a lot of meaningful choices to be made in between campaign missions that have drastic consequences that follow, whether it is choosing to prioritize a delayed reward in upgrading your headquarters base, or an immediate reward of equipping your squad with advanced weapons. The choice to aid one country will mean another country may not support funds for your campaign.
Overall, XCOM is a challenging and satisfying game that I would recommend to anyone looking for a turn based strategy game to get absorbed into.

The problem with motorbike games versus car games is the lack of a suitable peripheral.  Car games have a very sophisticated range of wheels and pedals to choose from and this greatly adds to the immersion factor for the gamer.  So for us bike fans we cannot even get close to the quality of simulation that car fans can.
Any PC gamer that has tried a bike game over the years will have experienced the frustration of keyboard or joystick "riding".   No matter the potential of the game, it was always limited by the player input device.   The general advice surrounding Ride 2 is get an XBox Controller for Windows.  For the PC player this is a new experience and does take some time to get used to.  But if you are interested in Ride 2 and are a PC player I would strongly recommend it.   Make use of the easier settings in the game and build into it.
The graphics on Ride 2 are satisfactory for a contemporary game.  Plenty of options to find your playing level to keep frustration levels at bay early in your playing experience.  The fun factor is the big compensator for any other deficiencies you may perceive in the game.   Early in your Ride 2 game time it may seem a bit too arcadey but as you get more competent with the controls the game delivers a more satisfying "riding" experience.
At some stage would love to see a peripheral that mimics a bike's controls - to some degree.  Maybe one that attaches to a steering wheel and has a twist throttle and levers - existing pedals could substitute for gear and rear brake.  But in the meantime it looks like the XBox Controller is the standard.
Overall, Ride 2 is worth a punt if you are into bikes, but get an XBox controller if you do not have one.

I don't really understand the negative reviews by people who haven't spent any time in the game. It has promise. I enjoy the magical elements, as well as being able to choose different classes to play, as well as the character customization (absolutely NOTHING like Ark). I spent 7 hours last evening in it, and once I joined a server with gather rates boosted by a bit, it was what I expected in most survival genre games.
However, where it falls short is its use for VOIP. There was a distinct lack of directional sound, or indication to know who was speaking. In a crowded town setting, all I heard was ten voices all around me, having no idea if one of them was speaking to me or not. For use in roleplay settings, that is a definite requirement.
Overall, I'm enjoying it on first day and encourage others to make up their minds themselves. If you like survival and magic, encourage you to dig deeper by watching gameplay videos or giving it a try, rather than the review bombing going on here.

You (a random guy) wake up from a cryogenic sleep chamber, and have no recollection of anything. Not even who you are. Your goal is to make it to "The Glow" or Detroit Mega City as you may learn to call it both. Your goal is to make it here, exploring along the way, better equipping yourself with the task of finding out who you are.
This is how I would imagine a post-apocalyptic Detroit happening.
Constantly being bombarded by the ruthless Dogmen, and Bad Muthas, a Detroit street gang of brutal, thuggish cannibals who will NOT hesitate to attack you on sight. Also strangers and looters equipped with scoped hunting rifles, and Detroit Mega City Guards with rifles, shotguns, and full SWAT-type gear ready to exterminate you.
You will be excited as ever to just find a pair of old plastic shopping bags and a shard of glass or a broken bottle to arm yourself with. Every little space in your inventory counts, so space management is almost as important to your survival as dealing with combat scenarios with a cool, calm, level head.
You will need to scavenge for loot while maintaining low visibility, otherwise if you think you're tough enough you can brazenly move into an abandoned building, scavenge it loudly and roughly, and hope someone or something doesn't hear or see you.
The choices you make for every little situation in this game need to be approached with clear thinking, and taking into account repercussions of your actions is seriously encouraged for this experience.
You will have random encounters within the story line and others along your travels.
You may succomb to diseases from exposure to sick people, bad weather (hypothermia and pneumonia), food poisoning, and even BREATHING toxic fumes over time.
You will wake up to people stealing your supplies and food or attempting to bash your skull in with a stone. Then be forced to make the decision to flee in complete terror, sneak up on the thief in the dark and take them by surprise, or just stand up from your sleep and attack them in a raging fury.
If you can get past the clunky UI and lack of animation or intimate graphical control, this game is a dirty gem just waiting to be appreciated by the next "arachaeologist" who finds it. I never pictured myself enjoying a game that's 60% text-based, but I quickly fell in love with this game. Here, you can learn quickly from past mistakes and keep pushing forward. If you ever thought it was hard to survive in other "survival" games, this is
more unforgiving but also more rewarding to experience. True-to-life combat system that allows your simplest mistakes to be exploted by your enemy, possibly resulting in your death or serious injury.
9.5/10
Even if you hate text-based games, or games with hexes (I certainly did), you may find yourself immersed and deeply invested into this game. I
recommend this for anyone who appreciates post-apocalyptic roleplaying games and/or heavy survival. Even at full retail price this is a worthwhile purchase. The game has a few flaws, but all are so minor and outweighed greatly by what
there is in the game that you quickly forget they exist or have trouble noticing them to begin with. Very reminiscent of the first game of the Fallout series, more so than the second, but this game has its own unique flavour.

10 years ago...
This game had captured the majority of my childhood. First time I got my hands onto this game, almost everyday was powering on my PS2 just to play this classic either solo or with my bros. Massive land-based battles, space battles, hero mode, campaign, and galactic conquest ate up most of my free time. There was no doubt that this was the best Star Wars game ever made, and if not one of the best games I had ever played.
3 years ago...
A new Battlefront game for the next gen was officially announced. Finally! I could look forward to re-living my childhood, but with some new twists. As more gameplay trailers were released as time went on, my hype kept building up, awaiting to be satisfied on the day of release.
2 months ago...
I finally got my hands on the new Battlefront. I powered up my PS4 in excitement, hands held firmly on the controller, expecting to satisfy all the built up hype that was stored for 3 years, and entirely focused on what I expected to bring back happy memories. As I pressed start on the title screen, the first thing I was supposed to do was to create an EA account. After 5-10 minutes of restless anticipation, I finally started playing singleplayer. Indeed, I had quite a blast on singleplayer, but there was still loads of hype that needed to be satisfied. That's when I started playing all the modes on multiplayer. Overall, I had an enjoyable experience on this next gen Battlefront, but unfortunately, all the built up hype still wasn't quite satisfied. In fact, this EA remake of the beloved Battlefront I grew up with didn't live up to all the childhood memories that I had been expecting to re-live.
Today...
Since my good old PS2 had been out of commission for over 2 years, I decided to bring back my childhood (Which EA Battelfront failed to do) by downloading the original masterpiece from Steam. To this day, it still holds it's title as the best Star Wars game ever made.
I couldn't recommend this game enough to any Star Wars fan alike, let alone to any gamer in general. If you grew up with this game and are wanting to bring back pleasant memeories, put it in your Steam library now! If you still haven't played this masterpiece yet, please don't hesitate to give it a shot, especially while it's on sale.

Secondly, the game is TOO brutal.  I get that it's a roguelike and roguelikes are supposed to be tough, but there's a lot of things that, quite frankly, are full of♥♥♥♥♥♥
I once stabbed a guy with a long, pointed tree branch made into a spear.  According to the game text, I viciously stabbed his upper stomach, and according to the in-game status text, he was bleeding heavily, in shock, and on the ground.  Somehow he managed to knock me out in one punch, steal my spear and backpack, and run away before I woke up, got an infection and died.
Several times I've started a brand new game just to not find any early game drops and freeze to death within a minute.  No hyperbole, I died within a single minute of starting a new game thanks to the RNG.  Other times I'll be walking around the game world and suddenly I've got diiarhea and I'm vomiting and my stomach hurts and I'm dead.
Don't get me wrong, this game is loads of fun to play and you should definitely give it a try if you like roguelikes and randomly-generated game worlds, but there's a lot of things that make me scream and swear at the game when I really shouldn't be.
Overall, I would indeed recommend this game.  7.8/10

It's tough for an ARPG to carve out its own path under the monstrous ever-present shadow of the Diablo series, and even moreso right now with the free-to-play Path of Exile doing extremely well, but Grim Dawn manages just fine.
The graphics are alright.  It's not as pretty as Path of Exile, but I'll wager it's because you can actually rotate the camera 360 degrees.  So many ARPGs will NOT let you do that.  I do feel inclined to complain about its slightly antiquated look, but mostly it's the fact that the majority of the skills in the game are just plain boring as ♥♥♥♥ to look at, with the exception of a couple of classes.
Most of the central plotline conversations are well voice-acted.  There's some great atmosphere here, but curiously enough the music is utterly forgettable garbage.  It almost doesn't exist, managing only an undead croak now and then.  It didn't bother me a whole lot because I listened to some dark music for my necromancer anyhow, but it's just bizarre to have such a stark contrast between the quality of the music and everything else in the game.
But nevermind the frills, how does it PLAY?  You know, what follows SHOULD be a rant of someone who plays ARPGs obsessively, who beats the game and then takes the character to a new difficulty, repeating ad infinitum, perhaps even having one of those hardcore league characters that stays dead after the first orgy of eldritch horrors.  But that's not me.  I love building characters, but I rarely go through an ARPG twice.  That means it's really got one shot to impress me, to show me the loot ratios, the difficulty curve, how the maps are generated, which fights are bull****, things of that nature.
For the most part, this game impresses me.  You pick a class at level 2, and then a second class at level 10.  There are no uniquely synergistic skills to be had, but because the three character stats have to do with gear instead of skills, you can pretty much build whatever you want with 220 (?) skill points.  There's also a constellation system with a monstrous 434 nodes you can choose from with up to 50 Devotion points across all the difficulty levels.  That's a lot of tweaking!
I'd have to say the maps are pretty standard ARPG fare in my experience, though I did have a nagging feeling that many areas were entirely too large.  I never did figure out how long it takes to reset an area, but I know for sure that they do once you restart the game.  This means that as you're traveling across the maps to unlock the fast-travel rift portals, if you run short on time or simply want to go do something else, you're going to be slogging through the managerie of fiends once again when you come back.  This can make for longer gaming sessions than you intended if you want to be thorough about clearing each zone at least one time before triggering the next portal.
The grinding impresses me, which is to say I didn't do it.  Although I completely cleared every area I went through, I was only a few levels behind the current mobs by the end of the game, and was pretty well-geared to boot.  That means that the game combined with the expansion is 50 hours of straight-up questing and one-time clears.  It's a big fat juicy steak that doesn't waste your time with a lot of crappy drops or grinding just to get through it.
Oh and one more thing.  You may be wondering if the expansion is really worth it.  As a cheapo, I can tell you I don't regret paying 15 bucks for it.  It may have the best rendition of a Necromancer that I've seen in an ARPG thus far (I know nothing about the Inquisitor class).  I do feel inclined to point out that like every pet class I've played in the genre, pets don't seem to understand♥♥♥♥♥♥about holding the threat, but this is really only a problem in the last several hours of the game when you hit Malmouth.  The expansion also adds somewhere between 15 - 25 hours, depending who you ask, so if you really want to soak it in, the expansion doubles the size of the game.

I love Blender. I've been using it for about 5 years, and I'm probably one of four people in the world that uses its game engine. This is an incredibly powerful tool for developers, modelers, animators, and even artists.
But I don't think you should use it as a professional.
It's totally♥♥♥♥♥backwards in terms of usability. It's got a crazy interface that goes against every industry standard. If you want to get a job as a modeler, animator, or game developer, Blender is a bad tool to start with. I wish I had known that when I started with it, because I'm so deep in Blender now that I find it too much of a waste of time to go and learn proper tools like Maya or Unity.

Two days into my first successful venture into NEO Scavneger, I've resorted to cannibalism. It's not like I really had to - I was taking a nap in a small city when a stranger woke me up. I was♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I took his soul away with a crowbar and noticed that I'm a bit hungry. Checked it - yes, not surprising - I can use a shard on the corpse and scavenge myself some tasty human meat. Two hexes later in the woods, I've made myself a nice BBQ and I'm feasting on that human.
As I chew on what was just two hexes ago my rival in an unfair fight, I am suddenly overcome with  disgust. I could have just left the corpse there, and move on to hunt a squirrel or pick some non-poisonous berries. Yet I chose to eat that person. And before doing that I looted him of his hoodie which was in a better condition.
But karma got to me quick. I was quickly poisoned in some mysterious way and then something wielding a 12-Gauge Shotgun blew me to bits, all my progress and looting down the drain.
NEO Scavenger can be really daunting at first; you'll die a lot. But once you pick it up - it's hard to put it down. It's a wonderful selfishness simulator that is fun and engaging, built on a fantastic crafting system which brings out the curious child in you. The "old" graphics do not deter from the enjoyment, quite the opposite – they only make it eerier and more atmospheric. The soundtrack is great too and generally it feels like a lot of thought was given to the game.
I haven't delved into the lore of the game yet but there are newspapers lying around with bits of info and it seems that there's a bigger story which unfolds as you manage to survive and stay alive. Unfortunately that's not as easy as it sounds, not at all; you can also go great strides (even without turning into a cannibal) and then get blown away by a shotgun or catch a disease. This could hinder the experience for some players who focus on storylines and want to complete the game – take to heart that this will be
. This game is hardcore as it gets and it doesn't hold your hand at all.
The best advice is to watch let's plays etc and if you do pick up the game, try it for yourself before picking up a guide. You WILL pick up a guide ultimately but try to experience it without any aid at all. It'll produce unique experiences in which you'll end up dead (in your hospital gown usually).
Overall this is worth much more than its price tag, a very refreshing entry to the world of roguelike which does it very very right - a sort of improved UnReal World with frightening creatures and a darker theme.
If you don't mind something a bit pretentious, pick this up.  The parallels to a classic Mario game alone make it worth your time.

It feels like I've still just scratched the surface but it has been a pretty unique survival roguelike experience that introduces a mix of new mechanics that work together quite well.
+ character attributes: it's not like a typical roguelike where you have you basic generic stats and grind xp. You pick out traits to help define your character (melee, ranged, mechanic, athletic, strong etc) and can pick weaknesses as well which let you get more points on good traits as a tradeoff and allow you to try to balance unique builds. These attributes influence completely what sort of actions you'll have available to you, how you handle conflicts, crafting, trying to find shelter, heat, food and so on. They define and influence your decisions way beyond the normal str,int,con type character building.
+ crafting : there is quite a complex crafting system in place that is entirely based on resources available and the traits you picked. If you find just the right ingredients in the early game to make a decent weapon or clothes you'll have a much easier time, otherwise you'll want to avoid conflicts and scavange more.
+(mostly) combat : deciding whether to fight, and how to fight is very important here.. not because you fight all the time but because the stakes are high and a few bad streaks could see you left bleeding in a field far from your shelter. I like this change to slightly more realistic combat. There's no visible health bar, it's all about waiting till you get a chance to strike, wounding your opponent, and then kicking while they are down. Not particularly heroic but if you make a mistake that leaves you vulnerable and they get a hit in, they'll do the same to you. It comes down primarily to trying to get in range for your weapon, stay out of range from theirs, and defend yourself until you have an opportunity. For example, if you have a melee weapon you can try to rush them but you risk falling on your butt at which point you'd be an open target, or you can advance normally but they'll be able to back away.
- combat balance: My con with this is that your weapons make all the difference and with the random nature and limited weapon types, you can either be useless in combat or feel like there was no risk. In my first play through I believe I hit a guy with a pocket knife like 20 times until he ran away after punching me and then I bled to death. In my second playthrough I tied a knife to a stick to make a spear, with a range of 3 is the longest melee weapon. And then proceeded to kill everyone that didn't have a gun without a scratch because they couldn't get near me without getting stabbed. And those with guns I could sneak on fairly easy and then once I hit them they were too wounded to fight back. It went from combat being impossible to being 'meh'.

Everyone seems to think Braid is just another 2d puzzle platformer with artful visuals and cryptic narrative, and they are right. However there is a reason I put this on my favorite games ever category and leagues ahead of say limbo. One, it is hard. I like hard. I like it when a puzzle game stumps me to the point where I have to come back weeks or months later. Some of the puzzles in Braid are so well crafted that you will feel like a goddamn prodigy everytime you complete them. So yea if you are an idiot don't play this because you don't have what it takes. The atmosphere brough about from the lush oil paint styled visuals and the simple but rich plucking string tracks is hard to really pin. I guess I would liken it to reading a damn good book and the feeling you get while reading your favorite part. As for the story, you don't HAVE to get it to still enjoy and appreciate this game. Which is good because the story is so cryptic, Franz Kafka would approve. Still if you are smart enough to beat the game you probably have enough understanding of the world and literature to read what is really being conveyed and let me just say when you realize just what the message is, so many other aspects of the game just become that much more impressive in how artfully crafted they were. Also the ending earns a spot in my "favorite sequences in gaming" list as well as favorite endings. If you are the kind of hippie that can see games as art but also are looking for well backed gameplay featuring intelligent design and challenging puzzles, well then here you go.

Best to get this on sale, and the value game pack isn't bad, since it helps out a lot in game! I promise myself not to dump any more money into this game like I did with Vindictus. However, I do find this game to be more asthetically pleasing vs the Nexon MMO. First and foremost, a LOT of thought was put into this game and so far, after a couple days of playing, I'm enjoying what I see.
- Music, constantly changing with whatever you're doing, which is nice.
- Physics! Feels immersive to mess with almost anything.
- Climbing up walls, balancing on a pole and even bumping into people... attention to detail is amazing!
- No limit to customization!
- Free stuff from events and attendance!
- Your character sweats and gets wet after taking a dip! Omg!
- The environment and open world concept is something I'm very attracted to when it comes to an MMO.
- Balanced when leveling up. You don't feel like leveling is too easy or too difficult.
- Combat system is amazing and very diverse. I don't have to mash keys or figure out which button to assign a skill or trying to keep track of everything, since combos are easier to execute.
- Crafting system. So much to do and make!
- Mounts early on, even without the value pack.
- Different styled armor and weapons even early on.
- You're not stuck with an ugly inner armor.
The only problems I have with this game so far is the storage system and the fact that money does weigh you down. I'm not so much worried with inventory slots, and organizing it to prevent myself from being overencumbered. I'm usually not one to review a game and not recommend it. Overcooked is a strange one; it starts out amazing... I was playing with my girlfriend as a co-op experience and the first section of the game is amazing. It presents a good challenge, and simple mechanics that all come together to make a fun game.
The part I enjoyed, and what I feel they should have emphasised for difficulty is the cooking. Burgers require various toppings and orders are varied; fish and chip plates vary as well as numerous types of soup. When orders are coming quick, and you're trying to keep ontop of chopping veggies/meats, cooking, washing dishes and taking out orders on time... this is where the game excels. They needed to just do levels with more variety and combinations of food to increase the difficulty; but instead they decided to keep the food relatively simple and focus on one or two items per level and make the level difficult to navigate.
The game goes downhill when tables start moving, you're on moving trucks, conveyor belts and various other things that don't let partners work as a team - but it decides for you what you'll be doing in each level. This went too far for me when one of the levels was pitch black and you are using flashlights to navigate a confusing kitchen area. This isn't fun. What was fun; was the hectic nature of quick ordering, cooking food, and trying to get your order out on time. They needed to introduce different food types on normal kitchen environments to increase difficulty. So basically; give me a level where I need to do fish & chips, burgers, soups, steak & fries, salads etc etc... that would be a lot to keep ontop of but in a good way.
It's a simple game that was over complicated in a bad way. They increase difficulty in the wrong way and went away from what was fun about the game. I really wish I could recommend the game. If it's on sale for a cheaper price and you are fine to play just the first few hours where the gameplay is strong; that's the best part of the whole thing. As it is; I've quit on the dark level and just found that it isn't fun anymore.

Before I begin, I have played Company of Heroes 1 for a very very long time. As a matter of fact, I've played it since it released. I definitely consider it one of the finest RTS games ever made and probably one of the most sophisticated games as well.
Enter COH2. How to possibly top the finest RTS ever? Initially I felt disappointed in COH2. I felt not enough had changed or that most changes were purely cosmetic. As such, after beating the solid campaign and after a few Theater of War missions, I pretty much stopped playing.
I came back to this game a few months ago and, with an open mind and fresh approach, I found one of the most remarkable RTS games ever made. Some might call this an overstatement, but having played RTS games since I was 5 and having gone through all the classics from Age of Empires, Age of Mythology, Rise of Nations, etc. , I can safely say that this is an outstanding RTS game. So let's finally get to the why.
The campaign, as I said, is solid. It starts off a bit slow, but gives some pretty exciting challenges as it progresses. Story is good with decent character development and overall explanations, but don't expect story driven RPG quality. A lot of people have talked about the negative portrayal of the Soviet Union as a bad thing or have even called this game pro-Nazi. Those accusations are largely baseless. Yes, the game isn't shy to portray war in all its brutality and isn't afraid to criticize waste of life, but overall it makes a pretty good point that the men who fight aren't responsible for political decisions. The story successfully portrays the conflict as a brutal and relentless struggle.
So, what do you do after the campaign? First of all, there is a set of missions called Theater of War which are actually very enjoyable. At first I didn't think I'd find them that fun, but each presents a challenge. I particularly recommend the Case Blue mission pack for its single player challenges. If you have a friend who plays, these will take a good chunk of your time to complete and you'll have fun doing it. The best pack overall is Victory at Stalingrad with some thrilling solo missions and really cool coop missions.
This is where I get to multiplayer. I really really recommend Western Front Armies along with the base game. With a roster of 4 unique armies, multiplayer is a thrill to get into, alone or with friends. This is where the game truly shines because all the possibilities and combinations come into place and it's incredibly satisfying to execute a plan with a friend. Compared to COH1, this game is slightly faster paced and usually you have less units. At first this might seem a step backwards, but quite the contrary, it prevents too much camping and keeps you on your toes at all times. The addition of winter weather is actually quite exciting because things like blizzards can be well exploited by clever players using light vehicles to harass enemy positions whilst they're unable to respond with abilities or their vehicles due to reduced line of sight. Likewise, frozen maps have crossings everywhere in form of ice, which can be very advantageous in flanking, but if your tank is caught on ice, there's a good chance he will sink. It's an element of the game which really demands that the player adapts to the new possibilities.
Finally, the reason I would recommend this game to a COH1 player is because though they will feel at home, it will be a refurbished home with new additions. If you're not a COH player, I would still recommend this game because it's a game which pushes the RTS genre forward, unlike a lot of big RTS games that are stuck in the past (khm Starcraft 2) and offers virtually endless amounts of exploring and learning. I hope this review was helpful in making a decision!

If you're a motorcycle fan, buy this.
It builds on all the good things about Ride 1 and fixes the major issue from the first game... team races. It was so obnoxious that you had no control over your teammates skill level. Nothing was more annoying in that game than getting gold in every race, (which was my goal for that game) but getting stuck with bronze or silver in team races because your counterpart wouldn't place above last place. It didn't hurt your career completion, but it was sure as hell annoying if you were trying to 100% the game.
If you're looking for a motorcycle game with the customization of gear and bike tuning like in Forza/ Grand Turismo for cars, this is as close as you're getting. And it's on point.
If you enjoyed Ride 1 but felt it wasn't deep enough and got to be a grind fest, Ride 2 changes that.
It has your standard races, championships, track days, time trials, team events, and special events. But it doesn't feel stale. The various bike classes, races mixed with the challenges, customizing of your bikes, motorcycle characeristics, and online races keep it fun.
The level of difficulty is up to you. You can make it play like you're on a rail and can't brake too hard or throttle too hard. Or you can make it feel like you're playing DIrt Rally with every single assist turned off and the difficulty cranked up, giving you an equally challenging/ frustrating experience. In first gear and crack the throttle to 100%? You'll get kicked off. Gas it too soon coming out of an apex? You and your bike will go flying. Pass on the inside of a corner with too much speed then go into a slide off the track on the last lap? Have fun restarting.
The performance ratings for parts and bikes the game uses is not perfect and there is still so much to build on. But being as this series is doing something new, that's to be expected. I would love to see more brands offered for parts with some more performance variations. Maybe just offer an EJK for a slip on/full exhaust. Or allow the ability to tune the ECU so you can use the same parts/bikes in various racing classes.
Well worth the sale price in the current Steam Winter sale and still worth the full price after it's over. This can easily be a 70+ hour game not even including online races.
I love the feeling of customizing the bike I own IRL with parts I can't afford yet and ripping around a track I dream of riding.

Overall very impressed with Dying Light.  I waited for it to be on sale as it had good to mediocre reviews by critics at it's release.  Honestly, I had a great time exploring the world of Harran and killing tons of zombies and it was worth it even at full price.
+Graphics - not the best of the year but it's not bad either and it runs smooth at 60 FPS on my 1070 at resolutions right below 4k
+World - Harran and the country side are full of fun areas to explore.
+Enemies - Zombies feel unstoppable, taking 10 hits with a melee weapon.  Human enemies are tough, parry your attacks, and can kill you fast with guns
+/-Weapons- weapons are great but they are mostly single handed melee weapons.  Most feel underpowered but it makes killing the zombies that much more satisfying.  Not a lot of variety in the guns.  Some new guns in The Following but they're not much of an improvement from the guns from the main areas.
+/-Story - didn't really care.  The main story was ok/good for a AAA games, the Following was worse.
+/-Crafting - kind of annoying but necessary.  Wish their were better special weapons to craft.
-Side Quests - Hardly ever did them or feel the need to.
-Night time - I mostly just died instantly.  No real reason to have it be so hard at night as it wasn't really ever used in the story outside of some side quests.
I didn't play coop, I prefer single player but on the first day I had the game a person seamlessly joined my game before I disconnected him.
Overall it's a great buy.  I tried Dead Island (also by Techland) and didn't get into it.  I was instantly hooked on Dying Light but was ready for it to be done at the end.  I'm excited to see what Techland makes next as this game was  blast.

Crossroad Mysteries: The Broken Deal is a hidden object game that has some good things going for it, but suffers from frustrating difficulty settings that hold it back.  This is one situation in which no achievements was a godsend.  I don't think I could've managed a no-hint/nightmare difficulty playthrough without tearing my hair out.
First, for the good.  The artwork is gorgeous and encapsulates all that I love of "beauty in decay."  I do so enjoy exploring deserted and crumbling structures.  However, in order to appreciate its full beauty you need to play in windowed mode, as the original screen resolution is clearly lower than the 1920×1200 standard.  This has the unfortunate side effect of making some of the items difficult to see, but 75% of the reason I play these games is for the artwork, so I had to do what I had to do to fully enjoy it. Atmosphere and music is also good with ambient themes and interesting sound effects that amplify the ominous surroundings. The voice acting was decent too, definitely better than a lot of other HOGs I've played.
As for the story, it's campy and overly dramatic, and feels like they tried hard to be dark and gritty, but maybe a little too hard.  There are a lot of religious references that may be a turn off for some people, so if you find churches and demons to be off-putting you may want to pass on this one.  At least the written text is fluent, as a lot of HOGs coming to Steam these days tend to have some questionable translations.
Unfortunately, the difficulty is where things really stumbled for me.  The way each is set up I felt like none were geared for how I play.  Hard or Nightmare is what I'd normally run since there's usually no highlighting of active areas, but the tooltips are completely disabled on both of these difficulties leaving the rate at which hints/skips renew as the only difference between the two.  And let me tell you, no tooltips in a HOG is the most frustrating experience ever.  You're just clicking around on random things, and when a window does pop open there's no decription of what that thing is or any other clue to steer you in the right direction.  It's just jostle it around a bit, then go back to fumbling in the dark again. So it was back to Easy/Normal for me, which both highlight active areas even though Normal isn't supposed to.  I either played on super hard or super easy, and I was not at all happy with either option.
The hidden object scenes on all difficulties were frustrating too.  As is standard in most HOGs, there are several items that need to be assembled and/or activated in some way before you can clear them, but the items you need to pick up and use on another do not highlight when you mouse over them, so you have to randomly click on everything to find the one thing you can actually use.  Yeah, not a fan of that setup at all.  Hints are also limited and are sprinkled around the areas as hidden items, but I've seen this done in other HOGs and actually like how it forces you to manage your hint usage instead of spamming it every time the button lights up.  Most of the puzzles were pretty unique, the difficulty of which is rather steep too.  Had I not already been frustrated with the game, I'd probably have tried harder at them rather than skipping every other.
I really wanted to give this game a recommendation because I feel it had potential, but I simply cannot encourage others to play it when my experience was so miserable.  Perhaps if you're one for super hard or super easy HOGs you might find some enjoyment in it, but for the price I can't say it's worth it.  If you ravenously consume HOGs and are intent on grabbing it, though, wait for a sale or bundle.
On a final note...Arial typeset is the most generically low quality font you can use in a game, period.  Not only does it look positively garish against the intricately painted backgrounds and UI, but makes the game look cheaply made.  Please, for the love of all that's holy, do not use Arial in your games. Thank you. Good day.

Everyone seems to think Braid is just another 2d puzzle platformer with artful visuals and cryptic narrative, and they are right. However there is a reason I put this on my favorite games ever category and leagues ahead of say limbo. One, it is hard. I like hard. I like it when a puzzle game stumps me to the point where I have to come back weeks or months later. Some of the puzzles in Braid are so well crafted that you will feel like a goddamn prodigy everytime you complete them. So yea if you are an idiot don't play this because you don't have what it takes. The atmosphere brough about from the lush oil paint styled visuals and the simple but rich plucking string tracks is hard to really pin. I guess I would liken it to reading a damn good book and the feeling you get while reading your favorite part. As for the story, you don't HAVE to get it to still enjoy and appreciate this game. Which is good because the story is so cryptic, Franz Kafka would approve. Still if you are smart enough to beat the game you probably have enough understanding of the world and literature to read what is really being conveyed and let me just say when you realize just what the message is, so many other aspects of the game just become that much more impressive in how artfully crafted they were. Also the ending earns a spot in my "favorite sequences in gaming" list as well as favorite endings. If you are the kind of hippie that can see games as art but also are looking for well backed gameplay featuring intelligent design and challenging puzzles, well then here you go.

Pros:
+Interesting story.
+Good voice overs.
+Beautiful graphics.
+Fast travel map.
+Variation of minigames.
+Good music.
+Amazing journal.
Cons:
-No Steam achievements for now (The developers plans to add them later)
The game length was average, around 5 hours and it technically has two endings. I encourage you to read everything because it is really important. I really enjoyed everything about this game and recommend it to all the HOGs lovers!

The time twisting, puzzle platformer is brilliantly made, fantastically designed but a killer on the brain. The introduction to the game drip feeds you the information you are required to complete it, and its all down to you to apply the knowledge you have been given.
Now this is where opinions will divide; I enjoyed the challenge and that inspired me to push on. You could argue this game is actually really boring, I would disagree, but essentially it is advanced jumping with time elements. The story is strong, the character is great, albeit eccentrically odd, and the mechanics are near flawless. If you are a naysayer, play this in chunks and it'll win you round.
I think compared to other indie titles this game is perfectly priced at £5 - £10. If you don't enjoy the art style, then anything below that and you have got a steal and its worth a shot.

Alright, so you wake up in some abandoned medical research facility, some sort of creature is pounding at the door ahead of you, using your affinity for mechanics, you lock the door and prevent it from getting in. Going outside, you notice its cold, so you scavenge a near by town for clothes, but its too late, you freeze to death.
So one more try. Again, you wake up an abandoned medical facility with a monster pounding at your door. This time, you chose to excell in strength, so you decide to fight this thing head on. You take a few scratches, but otherwise you beat. Using your trapping abilities, you managed to make a cloak out of its fur, keeping you warm for the forseeable future. Right on! so you start scavenging, you come across some food, a butchers knife, so shoes. You are doing pretty good! Buuuuut remember those scratches from before? You never treated them and they got infected, so you die. Again.
Third times a charm, no? So you start again. You kill the monster, you make a cloak, this time you manage to find some clean rags to cover your wounds and carry on. You scavenge, find a nice ole' shotgun to keep you safe, but you come across a stranger, you don't know much about this person so you ease your way up, you threaten them and they try to run so you blow them away. They start crawling, and you decide to finish them off and loot whats left of the innocent guys corpse. You get a little tired, so you rest in the woods when something wakes you up in the middle of the night. Its a feral dog, and oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ youre out of ammo. You decide to stick to beating the thing with the but of your gun, but its no luck. One too many bites means its game over.
Incase you can't tell, you will die a lot in neoscavenger. Like...a lot a lot. The game makes no attempt to hold your hand, and that will inevitably turn some people off, while others will find this a refreshing change of pace. Neo is a tough game for sure, and the survival aspects are fantastic. Of course you have to eat, sleep, drink etc etc but you also have to make sure you don't freeze to death, make sure your wounds are tended to and don't get infected, make sure you have shoes so you don't get blisters on your feet, try and make some interesting moral choices along the way (Do you help the mother and her child escape from the cannibals? How about watching people fight to death in an arena for scraps of food?)
All in all, I think Neo Scavenger is one of the gems of 2014. I didn't even know about it until searching through steams library. I think if you're a fan of the survival genre and want something that's tactical with a lot of options and a nice change of pace in terms of story other than your typical "Oh my god! Zombies!" schtick, I recommend you check it out.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

President Evil is a game that attempts to shove two completely unrelated satirical themes in to one giant abomination. On one hand, it's a Resident Evil parody. On the other hand, it makes fun of Donald Trump. Put them together, and what do you have? A completely unpolished title that seems impossible to beat. You run around, collecting letter cards and Statue of Liberty souvenirs, all while attempting to find your next objective.
You'll start the game off in a small shack surrounded by political propaganda. You might pick up some of the letter cards and the golden Statue of Liberty if you give a care enough to do so. You'll then open the door and follow the clearly cut trail in the woods to your first destination, and upon arriving there you may start thinking "That was pretty easy, this will be a piece of cake" while the long, badly translated dialogue plays out. You may even notice the blue dot on the mini-map in the upper right hand corner and start following it. Little did you know that the forest is riddled with death traps that can barely be seen, killer walls that mark the boundaries of the map, and mountains that are scalable by simply jumping up their completely vertical incline.
You'll continue to run around, die, restart, climb sections that would be impossible in other games, and attempt in vain to find your next destination; which is a shack in the woods. There are many shacks in the woods, but you need to find a certain one. You may even hit the ESC key to pause, bringing you to the sudden revelation that you have a cell phone in the game with a flashlight. You finally make use of that flashlight, which helps you to see the death traps a little clearer. If you're lucky, you might even find your way to your second destination. That's where President Evil really gets fun.
You see, President Evil has no rules. It has no understandable mechanics (other than run and move). It has no tutorial. Upon arriving at the second area, you'll need to find a jerrycan; all I can say here is good freakin' luck. I ended up finding it, only to be immediately killed by some spirit that comes out of nowhere. The marker on the map that shows where the jerrycan should be, does not lead you directly to said object; oh no, that would make sense. You'll find it laying up against a tree instead. You might even be able to outsmart the evil spirit that comes to kill you by running back to the truck that needs said gasoline. Guess what? You'll be told that you still need a key and a battery, and the spirit will swoop down and destroy you.
And there is where I ended my "adventure" with President Evil; the haphazardly thrown together piece of junk that it is. In fact, that's where most people end their time with the game, if they get that far. I've only managed to find one gameplay video on YouTube, and the guy couldn't find the jerrycan so he rage quit. To be fair, the store page does make it clear that President Evil is a bad game, but that's no excuse for it being so abhorrently unpolished; some of the letter cards aren't even able to be picked up. Do yourself a favor and steer as far clear from this one as possible.

Dawn Of War is one of the best RTS games I've ever seen and is definitely worth the purchase and all of it's dlcs, at the time of writing they were all on sale for a combined price lower than 10 dollars, that is an absolute steal. In short, Dawn Of War is an RTS that contains:
- 9 Incredibly unique factions ranging from the undead/robotic necron, who do not require requisitions but need to build massive amounts of power to sustain themselves to the legendary Warhammer Space Marines, the super soldiers who define the series with their powerful leadership units and decent unit composition making impossible fights slightly more possible (Though the expansions are needed for 5 of them, by default you get Orks, Chaos Marines, Space Marines, and Eldar though they are pretty unique and can in themselves offer hundreds of hours of gameplay).
-Interesting game modes such as the standard destroy the enemy's base ranging to hold various points for a set amount of time or even just slay the enemy commander before yours falls. Plus, you can set more than one victory parameter for maximum gameplay and strategic influence.
-Expansions that change the singleplayer experience (Soulstorm and Dark Crusade) to a map takeover in which all of the game's factions wage war and fight numerous matches attacking and defending territory with troops they earned throughout the campaign and even their fation specific commander his/herself.
In the end, it is an amazing game well worth your time, though I do suggest getting the expansions as they make the already great game even better.

Grim Dawn is a hack and slash action RPG with the likes of Diablo III but most noticably Titan Quest. It is built on the same engine as Titan Quest.
Pros:
- A varitey of gameplay types can be achieved thanks to a range of Masteries and the Dual-Class system where you can select two Masteries, one at level 2 and the other at level 10.
- A beautiful, dark and vast world to explore which is filled with varieties of enemy types and bosses.
- A well made faction system which unlocks more features and enemy types as you kill mobs and do bounties.
- Lots of unique item models to give you a badass look.
- A devotion points system to make gameplay even more attractive and exciting.\
- A good crafting system.
Cons:
- You can ruin a characters build if not cautious enough in investing points.
- No customization at character creation.
- Dull story with boring characters and limited voice acting.
- Limited number of story choices.
Overall, this is a very good game and well worth the money. A must buy for RPG fans.
Final Verdict: 9/10

Extremely well polished game, with great gameplay and a very good story.
- Genuinely terrifying. Being caught out at night is a nerve wracking experience, as is the recently infected zombies in the day who show up when you make noise from firing a gun or falling through a roof. Has a lot of similarities to ARK, which if you are following both games, you may or may not realize that Snail USA is a parent company for Wildcard. So it makes sense that they are using assets in DnL. So the "ARK clone" / "ARK ripoff" negative reviews can be ignored in my opinion.
So far I've played to level 13, and it's what I expected. A magic / fantasy sandbox. Having played ARK has helped with some basic things that neither game really ever tell you. Like using a pick axe vs. axe on rocks or trees, and the different resources you get when you swap out. Using a key to access things vs. having to hold E, etc.
Overall the game looks good, but I think they held back some settings because it seems like it's not quite what it could be. I suspect that it would not be horrible frame rates with full Epic settings. Likely we'll see this improve as development continues.
The level system / skill level system I'm not particularly excited about, feels like a double grind in some cases. Not horribly so, but enough that I'm testing a tweak of XP gain on my server. The problem is, you have levels which give you stat points. And skills have requirements before they can be unlocked. One of those requirements is certain level caps. It's not terrible, but I think it feels a bit too grindy.
Overall, if you liked ARK and you are looking for a fantasy/magic game, I think this will be it, though like ARK when it first released in EA, this has a way to go. I'd say it's a bit ahead of the ARK curve, but it's got a lot of room to grow.
If you're on the fence, my recommendation, with any EA game, is to watch the store page for update news. If a dev is continuously pumping out updates, improving the game, then it's likely a safe bet.
Also, I figure all my games values at time played vs purchase price. 8 hours for 25 bucks means about $4 an hour cost to play, so far. And I'll be putting in another 10+ hours over the weekend most likely.

Everybody makes mistakes. After all to err is human, but what if we revisit our past, fix the problems we create and come out the better for them? This is the crux of Braid, a game that at it's core, is about someone who has done something very bad and is now doing everything in their power to wind back the clock and make amends. Eloquently penned and highly symbolic it tells a story with a deliberate purpose, the details of which have been picked and scrutinized over. It's meant to be open ended, to inspire discussion, and ultimately to make you sit and ponder the outcome, which speaking purely from my own perspective caught me entirely off guard and was cause enough for me to pause and step away from it to contemplate what it all meant.
Built around the narrative (or perhaps the other way around) are the puzzles which again deal with the manipulation of time. At first it's simply a way out of the inevitable mishaps you get into, but as you progress they evolve into much more elaborate and inventive conundrums, continually changing up the rules while keeping the framework intact. Again and again I was astounded by the simple elegant way everything fit together, much like the jigsaw pieces you collect, each part feeling necessary and fleshed out. This goes a long way in keeping the puzzles challenging and absorbing, and although it is a short experience developer Jonathan Blow makes smart use of his time and doesn't waste yours with filler or sections that fall flat from poor execution.
The rich pastel backdrops that blend effortlessly with the stunningly animated sprites, create a scene that looks like a watercolor painting in motion. It's absolutely beautiful and perfectly matches the tone of the narrative, further complemented by the soundtrack which flows alongside it in time, seemingly telling its own story in the process. It's an artistic masterpiece that captivated and enchanted me the moment I laid eyes upon it, and the organic pacing kept me wholly engrossed throughout.
If you only play one puzzle-platformer in your time, Braid would be very close to the top of my list. It personifies the genre better than almost anything that came before it or after, and did so before the genre was anywhere near as prolific as it is today. If for some reason the story doesn't grab you the brilliant puzzle designs will, and those that look deeper be duly rewarded with what has been placed beneath the surface. I savored my time with it and am now, like our protagonist, wishing I could go back and relive it over again.

I like turn-based games.  I like survival games.  I like rogue-like games.  So a turn-based, rogue-like survival game?  Sign me up!  Except not for this turn-based, rogue-like survival game please.
IMHO rogue-like games like FTL and Don't Starve succeed because they're a streamlined experience, which makes "dying part of the fun".  Starting a new game is always exciting and you're confident you can learn from your past mistakes so you'll survive longer this time 'round.
This is where NEO falls short.  The dev had a vision and built the game to match that vision.  But if his vision of a post-apocalyptic wasteland does not align with your vision of a post-apocalyptic wasteland, prepare to encounter all sorts of frustratingly illogical, immersion-breaking events.
People call FTL brutally hard and overly random, but I "get it" - it makes sense to me when I play.  I can learn from past mistakes and play better.  NEO makes no sense to me.  The game design decisions are just weird, the interface is clunky, the graphics are grotesque.  Dying for no clear reason, when things seem to be going swimmingly right up until you die, *may* be realistic (?) in the dev's world, but not mine.
You get the same kind of all-of-a-sudden deaths in Don't Starve but it's always clear that "I shouldn't have attacked that Pig Man just for kicks" or "I shouldn't have tried to chop that last tree before lighting my campfire" or "I should have abandoned my hunt for gold and hunted berries instead, so I wouldn't starve".
Playing NEO is like being put in a straight-jacket designed by the dev.  "Play my way or not at all".  Okay dude - IF your way makes logical sense and there's a clear progression from A-to-B-to-C-to-You Died.   Going A-to-R-to-D-to-You Died does not help me live longer next time!
So "I shouldn't scavenge that random house the way I've scavenged every other house so far, because I should have known the roof was going to cave in"?  or "I shouldn't have tried to run away from that particular encounter because I should have known I would trip, fall on my♥♥♥♥♥and not be able to stand up again even though I'm healthy, rested and well-fed"?  How do I avoid either of those situations next time around?  That's two of the dozens of deaths that will leave you scratching your head going "REALLY?!?".
Forumites will tell you, take this skill, that skill and the other skill and you'll never die.  Okay, but what if I *don't want* to take those three specific skills.  What if I want to build the character *I want to play*?  In that case, prepare for many, many, many frustrating deaths because you're not playing his game the way the Dev wants you to.
I don't get some of these other reviews:  "Dogman killed me while I slept despite the fact that I put down multiple noise traps, Thumb's Up 10/10."  WTF?  Is that a joke?  It's not helpful.  "Stabbed a guy three times then kicked him in the head when he was down.  He was hurt, bleeding out and on the edge of unconsciousness but he got up, landed one lucky punch and I was immediately unconscious, Thumb's Up 10/10".
Troll reviews like that are turning this Reviews tab into a joke.

So far a really amazing game. It has far exceeded my expectations. After playing a lot of Tera i thought that i would hardly find any other MMORPGs as good as that one but i've managed to find the best there is out there so far. I don't have much hours in the game yet so there are still a looooot of things i don't know about but so far so good.
The graphics are stunning. The sound effects are well made. And the gameplay is amazing too.
The skill mechanics are really unique it definetly isn't one of those everyday MMORPGs where you're just spamming all the buttons. For each skill to activate you need to press a specific combination of the buttons on your keyboard and/or on your mouse. At the beginning it is a bit hard to get used to and memorize all the different combinations (because there are a lot to remember) but once you get used to it then you'll have an amazing time just using your skills in battles.
There are also some other elements to the game which can be found in a lot of other games but it actually differs a lot in this one. However i only know as much about these as i have heard as i have yet to experience these for myself. These include: fishing, sailing, gardening, mounts, pets, forming trading routes with NPCs and a lot of other stuff which i probably haven't even heard of.
In the end this is a super amazing MMORPG and i'm not afraid to declare that this might be the best one so far. It can be fun alone too but it is absolutely way more fun if you play with your friends.

Overall(8/10): Crate's Grim Dawn in an isometric Action RPG set in fictional location of Cairn.
Gameplay(9/10): 6(or 8 with Expansion) masteries and the ability to mix and match will get your altoholicism flowing. With Attribute points, skill points and Devotion points, there is plenty to customize and drill down with your character. Tons of gear, including legendary's and set pieces will keep you killing hoping for that drop.
Graphics(7/10): Decent graphics, most gear pieces affect how your character looks, plus there is an Illusion master who can make any piece of gear look like your favorite, for a price. On High/Ulta with most settings, stuck at about 48-60 fps, except when tons of lightning or pets on screen, then it dips down to about 35.
Story(8.5/10): Invaders and Old Gods, possession, brutality. Game has a good story, and the time spent on Lore(if you're willing to read/look) is pretty damn amazing.
Sound(7/10): Music/effects are done well enough. Truth be told, I tend to play this game with sound very low and have tv/movie going at the same time.
Controls(8/10): kb/m controls are sublime. I suppose standard but never had any issue with them in any game. Controller however leaves a lot to be desired. Supposedly this game is going to Xbox One, and as someone who has attempted to play the game with an X1 controller, they have a lot of work to do.
DLC(9/10): Ashes of Malmouth. A full expansion adding a 5th and 6th act, as well as 2 addtional masteries and tons more gear. The Crucible. A horde-type arena mode seperate from the main campaign. Makes farming for gear at higher level easier, but requires you to perfect your class to do the higher difficulties. Also has an illusion pack that most people(including myself) bought for the sole purpose of supporting the devs.
Summary: Amazing ARPG that puts Diablo 3, Viktor Vran and Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing(among others) to shame. The community over at
is thoughful and very helpful, will be able to assist both new and experienced player alike.

Overall very impressed with Dying Light.  I waited for it to be on sale as it had good to mediocre reviews by critics at it's release.  Honestly, I had a great time exploring the world of Harran and killing tons of zombies and it was worth it even at full price.
+Graphics - not the best of the year but it's not bad either and it runs smooth at 60 FPS on my 1070 at resolutions right below 4k
+World - Harran and the country side are full of fun areas to explore.
+Enemies - Zombies feel unstoppable, taking 10 hits with a melee weapon.  Human enemies are tough, parry your attacks, and can kill you fast with guns
+/-Weapons- weapons are great but they are mostly single handed melee weapons.  Most feel underpowered but it makes killing the zombies that much more satisfying.  Not a lot of variety in the guns.  Some new guns in The Following but they're not much of an improvement from the guns from the main areas.
+/-Story - didn't really care.  The main story was ok/good for a AAA games, the Following was worse.
+/-Crafting - kind of annoying but necessary.  Wish their were better special weapons to craft.
-Side Quests - Hardly ever did them or feel the need to.
-Night time - I mostly just died instantly.  No real reason to have it be so hard at night as it wasn't really ever used in the story outside of some side quests.
I didn't play coop, I prefer single player but on the first day I had the game a person seamlessly joined my game before I disconnected him.
Overall it's a great buy.  I tried Dead Island (also by Techland) and didn't get into it.  I was instantly hooked on Dying Light but was ready for it to be done at the end.  I'm excited to see what Techland makes next as this game was  blast.

Joking aside, Blender is very powerfull software for modeling and animating, and it is free.
Blender have three mode you can play with,
first mode is internal render, mostly used for light animation or game object modeling.
second mode is game engine. Yes, blender can used to create a game, but it's not powerful enough to build game with this one. I recomend you to use other engine for create a game rather using Blender Game Engine.
third mode is cycles render if you want to use it for realistic atmosphere for your scene.
And you know what, it has a motion capture system! How awesome it is!
Blender is harder to master than using other 3d modeling software and it's more time consuming than similiar software to create a same model. The supported vga for rendering is very few, so if you doesn't have vga on the list the only way to do rendering is with your cpu. The documentation is hard to understand so the best way to learn is watching other people tutorial or time lapse. But the result can be more powerful than other software if you try hard enough. And there are so much plugins that you can use to make model creation be easier. So if you still doesn't have money, using this software will not hurt.
So there is it, I very recomend this software since there are no other free modeling software which very powerful like blender. So try it if you want to create model and animation yourself, with a hard work you will not regret it. ;)

Civilization V is one of the first games I owned on Steam, after purchasing for sale in physical, CD form. This was one the first strategy games I had ever played so I was unprepared for understanding the mechanics of strategy games in general. Luckily Civilization V is a classic example of "Easy to Learn, hard to Master" so the mechanics and controls were not that hard to learn from a new player to the genre, such as myself at the time.
Civilization V gets almost everything right. Soundtrack is great, mechanics are satisfying and rewards you on multiple pathways on running your empire (Domination, Culture, Science and Diplomacy). Graphics are great, and even stand still very well in today's standards (and is arguably better looking than its newer cousin, Civilization VI). The only real viable critism I have with this game that I have is that the AI is questionably dumb and stupid at times which can be annoying and immersion breaking.
I consider this the best in the series, and a classic game in the Turn-Based Strategy genre. A must buy for veterans of the series and strategy and newcomers alike. 9.4/10
Extra Notes on Downloadable Content:
DLC that is worthy of purchasing I'd recommend is really only Brave New World and Gods and Kings, as these add mechanics, new civilizations, scenarios and maps. The other DLC can be skipped without missing out on much.

DnL portrays itself in its trailer as an ambitious project, trying to make itself the ESO we always wanted with epic quests, crafting, different styles of combat that are all viable, epci enemies, beautiful worlds, and to top it all off you can even make your own houses.
This games trailer does not come even close to portraying what this game really is, which is exactly the reason this game is going to get a negative review. This is not some amazing RPG survival game with crafting. It is ARK: Survival Evolved reskinned and with a more restrictive crafting system. Allow me to explain; in this game you have skill trees. To be able to make certain objects, you need a certain skill level in a particular skill. This may not seem to be too bad of a system, except it harshly restricts what you can create. It isn't like only some specialized objects need a certain level to be crafted. EVERYTHING NEEDS A CERTAIN LEVEL TO BE CRAFTED. Even a basic bedroll needs a certain level in a specialized skill that you will not get even after completing the tutorial which can take up to an hour to complete. You will not be able to start making a house either.
I understand this game is still only 30% done, but if this insanely restrictive crafting system is going to exist in the main game, I cannot in good conscience say you should play it. Don't get me wrong, some restrictions in a crafting system are fine. But its not OK when every ♥♥♥♥ing object in the game requires a skill level that can sometimes take a very long time to level up just once.
Now onto the combat where this game dissappointed me the most. There is a reason why you don't see melee combat in the trailer- it's because it is terrible. Only about two animations for swinging a sword which is your only viable melee weapon currently, and even then its not like you can specially control it. You can't block or use light or heavy attacks. All you get to do is just hold down the button. There are, as far as I can see so far, no real weapon sets either. You can't even just have a classic sword and shield, or two handed greatsword or axe. Just a basic sword and thats it. Even then, melee is unviable in every way. Magic and long range weapons like spears or bows are a far better choice than melee weapons, making melee completely useless except in last resort. And probably the worst offense of this game is that every creautre, and I do mean every, is a ♥♥♥♥ing damage sponge. You can hack away at a sheep for a good 5 minutes with your sword and nothing happens. None of your weapons feel like they have any weight to them.
In conclusion, and TL;DR- this game is not an RPG. It is ARK reskinned and with a more restrictive crafting system.
I would play this game if these issues are addressed and the combat is made far better than it is now.

Dying Light was a blast to play with a friend, and I'm sure even more fun if you have a full party of four. There are a lot of quests and tons of blueprints to pick up for customization. The environments scream "CLIMB ON ME" and they totally let you! The first time you get out on your own and fight some zombies it feels almost overwhelming because you end up having zombros coming at you from all angles like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ film gone wrong. It took about 35 hours for game completion with only a handful of extra things to do. The graphics were incredible and I really have to give it to the devs. The environments were spot on everwhere you go.
Now for the not so pretty aspects. Some abilites were near useless, especially the wall run. For the love of God and all that is holy DO NOT GET THE WALL RUN!!! Some other abilites became obsolete when we got guns which is another complaint. The guns kinda ruined the magic of the game. I know they were an eventuality, but it took a lot of the challenge out of the fights. Other than the guns, there are a few unlocks and abilites that take away from the "survival soul" of the game but that's kinda up to personal preference. I'd say the most agravating failure in this game is their menus. When you sell an item or transfer an item your inventory scrolls all the way to the top which means if you have a lot of stuff stored then you have to scroll ALL THE WAY BACK DOWN. This is nonsense.
Pros:
- AMAZING graphics, seriously beautiful.
- Parkour is spot on. The flow of movement in this game is unrivaled
- Lots of weapon upgrades (many you won't use, but still...)
- 40+ hours of gameplay if you do all side quests and DLC
- Zombies fall apart depending on where you hit them
- TRAVEL BAGS!!! (It's what happens when you kill so many zombies in one spot and move via picking up bags)
Cons:
- Boring unrelateable characters
- Menus are atrocious
- Wall Run ability sucks fat kok
- Not a terribly engaging story. I never felt invested.
Definitly pick this game up if you have friends to play with. I got it on sale 60% off and it was totally worth it. I'm not sure if I would have paid full price, but if this is your jame, and you got friends to play with. GET IT! :)

1. It's challenging. A game without challenge is pointless. When you first start playing, you will get yourself killed multiple times, in a variety of different ways. This will keep happening unless you engage your brain, and use the tools available to survive. Permadeath means that you can't afford to make mistakes, which makes the game much more intense, and progression is much more fulfilling. I wouldn't have it any other way. 10/10
2. Gameplay. This game is a sandbox turn-based rogue-likeish RPG. Some may not like this sort of game, but I've played many games of this sort, and it's the best of the lot. Most of these sorts of games over-complicate everything, and gameplay suffers as a result. This is not the case for Neo-Scavanger! The sandbox element is the cherry on top - do whatever the hell you want to do. Perfect! :D 10/10
2. Focus is on gameplay and NOT on graphics etc. Too many games these days look nice, but in reality they have no replayability or depth. Neo-Scavanger is the opposite - the graphics and UI allow you to play the game, they are not there to be pretty . It's graphics and art are still great though, proper old-school stuff. Also, there is the added benefit that ANY computer will be able to run this game. It's built in flash, so if your PC can handle some random online flash game, it can handle Neo-Scavanger no problem. 10/10
3. Depth. This game is deep! I have been playing for a few days now, and I have barely scratched the surface. I've just about got the point where I can reliably survive in the wilds, and have yet to actually explore the world. The game is mysterious, it's hard to know what the game will throw at me as I continue to play, and I love that feeling in a game. 10/10
4.Lore and story. I like anything to do with post-apocalytic settings etc, who doesn't? I havn't really played enough to comment on this aspect of the game, but from what I've played so far the writing and story is top-notch. 10/10
5. Thoughtful developers who listen. Having read a few dev posts, it is obvious that they care about this game. They are very open to suggestions and discussion. 10/10
6. Mods. I haven't researched the mods much, but I know that they do indeed exist. Always great to have that option!
Summary: 11/10. Buy this game now! Even if you normally don't like this sort of game, give it a go! It's cheap ;)
