This game is an excellent example of post-apocolyptic, open world Survival games. It combines elements of survival, combat strategy, crafting, perma-death, inventory management, rpg, and a real sense of danger just lurking around every hex -- mostly in that order, I'd say. It's also turn-based rogue-like with the map changing slightly each time you begin a new journey. Do not let the modest graphics fool you -- they will be the least of your concerns, I assure you.
The combat system is actually rather realistic! Based on the character ablities and flaws you choose from the beginning, the combat system allows you to pick from quite a few options such as Charging your opponent, Headbutting, Tackling them to the ground, franticly retreating, sneaking, taking cover, sneaking behind cover, Offer to Talk, Melee combat, kick while down, shooting a ranged weapon -- too many to name, here. Choose wisely, or face the consequenses. I really enjoy the combat aspect of this game, but I imagine there are lots of players who would perhaps prefer stealth over Strength, and trade-based ablilities such as Botanist or Hacking over Athletisism. You can choose from flaws (Examples: bad metabolism, fatiques faster) as well, which allow you pick another ability or two to boost your luck. And it is almost always luck.
I'm currently playing a character with the traits Strong, Melee, Athletic, Botany, and for my flaw -Metabolism.
I have no idea who I am, but I appear to be a hulking, savage vegetarian. It's been 14 days, and I've killed at least 24 people -- I'm losing count, and can no longer remember any of their faces. I've been alerting many opportunists while  scavenging with a pickaxe and a lighter, but in turn, I've killed most all of those who couldn't escape. I'm hunting. Am I even human, anymore? At least I haven't resorted to cannibalism... yet.. and I'm sick with infection somehow. I found a couple of white pills, but without any knowledge of what they are, I fear the result. I've made a temporary home in a high-rise for at least 4 days now, only venturing outside to eat berries and mushrooms, and to gather water while I wait out whatever has me sick. Hopefully, I can make it through just one more night.....

TLDR:  A good turn based survival game with neat setting and mechanics.
NEO Scavenger is a turn-based survival game whose difficulty I'd call 'tough but fair' once you get the  hang of the mechanics.  You play as Philip Kindred, a man who has lost most of his memories after being rudely awakened from his cryogenic-sleep pod in the near future.  The game is set in post-apocalyptic Michigan, with a mix of supernatural/horror and sci-fi elements.  Overall it reminds me of Fallout 1 and 2 in terms of tone and atmosphere.
Something you should definitely be aware of before buying: Permadeath!  There is only one save slot in NEO Scavenger and when you die the game deletes the savegame, forcing you to start over.  However you can get around this fairly simply by manually backing up your savegame files after you save, so even players who don't like permadeath should still be able to enjoy NEO Scavenger if they save often and remember to back up those save files.  (I believe there is also a mod that adds multiple save slots, or that automatically backs up your save game, or something like that.  I never tried it out myself, so I can't comment on it.)
NEO Scavenger is a text heavy game, and there is no narrator or voice acting.  Talking with friendly NPCs and fighting hostile ones both involve plenty of text.  Not that the game doesn't have a good UI too, but the lore and details of the game are all conveyed through text.
Speaking of which, the story of the game is told rather subtly, which I like but some people might not.  You'll have to search for clues to who you are and what's going on in the world.  Talking to NPCs, investigating strange locations, even simply finding and reading ancient newspaper article could tell you something important about the world of NEO Scavenger.  My point is you are going to have to really explore the game to uncover the plot.
There is an end to the story after which you cannot keep playing, but the game is pretty clear that going to that area is a fairly big deal and you are never forced to do so.
One of my favorite ways NEO Scavenger tells you about the world (and lets you tell the game what sort of person 'your' Philip Kindred is) is through random events.  These events will pop up occasionally as you explore the map, present you with a situation/problem, and a number of choices to deal with said situation/problem.  They're a bit like a single-page Choose-Your-Own-Adventure games.  Though sometimes a bad choice can get you eaten, so keep what I said about backing up your saves in mind if you dislike permadeath.  I've found several dozen of them so far and the choices and their outcomes are generally very satisfying.  There was one that actually let me ask for more information before deciding whether to help a slightly suspicious person, which is something I've often lamented a lack of in other games.
There's also a small modding scene, despite the lack of Steam Workshop support (flash and steam don't work well together apparently).  Check out the forums of the Blue Bottle Games website or Nexus mods for those.
Finally, I just want to mention that the actual total hours I've played this game are at least twice of what Steam says it is.  This is because I bought the game through the developers website and generally play the version I downloaded there.  Speaking of which. if you do decide you want to buy the full game, you can get NEO Scavenger DRM free on Good Old Games, or directly through the Blue Bottle Games website.

Absolutely love the concept behind Poker Night at the Inventory!  Admittedly, I had no idea who Max and Strong Bad were before playing this game, but the idea of having a mashup of characters and people from the video game industry, sitting around "after hours" and playing poker together, is still solid. And listening to their comments and conversations is often quite hilarious.
That being said, the whole thing does get stale after a while.  Eventually you hear all they have to say, it's not amusing anymore and all very repetitive.  Even the poker gameplay itself isn't all that great, because the AI isn't very bright or challenging.  Once you get a basic understanding about their tells and how they react to certain bets, etc, they are super-easy to manipulate.
Overall, Poker Night at the Inventory is a fun and silly time-waster, and I recommend it for the laughs (and the TF2 items if you care).  Beyond that it's rather disappointing from a poker perspective, so if that's what you are looking for then move along.  (I likely would have only put in around 15-20 hours total, if not for the Straight Flush achievement that took a ridiculous amount of time to get...)

Most versatile open source all-in-one 3D animation, 3D sculpting, game creation, video editing, compositing suite I've ever use.
This software is all you need for multimedia or 3D creation, if you manage to get a grip on the unusual interface. But once you understand the interface, Blender have the fastest workflow compared to most other 3D software out there.
Also bear in mind that most of Blender commands are keyboard shortcut only, and you HAVE to memorize them. Otherwise you'll be left clueless on what to do, since not all the commands are presented as icons in the UI. In-depth tutorials will be needed even if you've touched other 3D softwares before.
Despite the mind-boggling features it have that will even compete with Autodesk Maya, like most of other open source softwares, Blender have lack of optimization.
It'll start crawling when your scene have become complex, whereas on other commercial softwares the same scene won't be much of a problem.
But nevertheless, if you're doing a one-man-army project, a student or a freelancer, Blender is a winner. And in most case, Blender is enough, unless you're running a studio as big as Industrial Light and Magic.

Extremely well polished game, with great gameplay and a very good story.
- Genuinely terrifying. Being caught out at night is a nerve wracking experience, as is the recently infected zombies in the day who show up when you make noise from firing a gun or falling through a roof. I'm not proud of this but at one point in the game I just hid in a utility room in the car tunnel until night was over :(
- Incredible survival horror. The experience is like living an episode of The Walking Dead, you will scrounge for scraps of food, nails, cigarettes - anything which you can flip or use to stay alive. Oh, and the sound of your watch alarm going off at sundown - horrifying!
- Parkour system - I'm generally not a fan of parkour games, and its more climbing and leaping than fantastic flips and wall runs, but in this game you will be so terrified of the terrors on the ground that you will happily jump from roof to roof just to stay safe.
- Compelling story - I had seen some criticism of the story in reviews and it can be a little formulaic, but the  voice acting and gritty realism really made this an engrossing game.

The only complaint that I had from playing the game is that it's not upfront about what is important (satellites) and what isn't, but that might be a design decision. There are, infamously, those face-palming RNG disasters which will cause you to miss a 95% shot from 5 feet away. So, even if you're playing perfectly, luck still weighs in a lot on the outcome of a mission. That is kind of annoying, personally. But, I've played games that had even more punishing RNGs (cough morrowind/insurgency cough) and enjoyed them, so this isn't too bad. Combat tactics, when done correctly, are slow paced which isn't terribly engaging. I found myself playing for maybe a mission or two and then putting the game away for a few days, only to pick it up again later. In the 8 months or so I've had this game, it hasn't left my harddrive.

Welcome back, Commander.
XCOM Enemy Unknown is one of the most intense yet satisfying games I have ever played. It is challenging to manage your base, resources and also ensure that you leave the battlefield with all your soldiers intact.
Story: The story starts off in 2015, when a global alien invasion begins. As a result, a group of countries unite to form XCOM (Extraterrestrial Combat Unit) to combat the alien foes as well a defend the Earth from the their onslaught. I thought the story was pretty interesting as you get to unravel the secrets behind the aliens and slowly learn why they have attacked. There is a mystical aura around the story which I found fascinating although the ending felt a little abrupt for my tastes.
Graphics: Firaxis Games have opted for a cartoony look to the game rather than realistic and I think it works to the game's favour. Each of the soldiers look like a figurine while the aliens are well designed and have an interesting look to them. On the highest graphical settings, XCOM looks beautiful. All the particle effects from the laser beams, environmental things such as fires and general atmosphere of the maps are rendered to a great quality and really helps in keeping you immersed in the game.
Sound: The soundtrack for XCOM is phenomenal. It is both epic yet haunting, with drums creating a sense of excitement while the electric sounds used make the game feel eerie and a little disturbing. The voice actors for the main characters do a decent job at providing personality although they do feel cheesy at times, while the alien sounds are terrific. The screeches they emit upon death sound disturbing and terrifying.
Gameplay: Although XCOM is a turn-based game, I had alot more fun playing it than most action games. The reason being is that each decision you make has drastic effects on which countries you can save, how much resources you have as well as determine whether or not a character survives in battle. There is so much tension especially on the battlefield, as sometimes the enemy pops out of nowhere to ambush your troops and send them to the graveyard. Since characters permanently die, it is crucial to make careful decisions on where to move them, when to fire and when to retreat. This creates for exhilirating gameplay each and everytime you enter the battlefield.
Overall, XCOM: Enemy Unknown is an amazing game. Whether or not you are a fan of turn-based games, give this game a try. I think you will be pleasantly surprised.

DnL looks like ARK, though it is not ARK. It plays similar, but you will notice the different within the first hour. If you are interested, or has been following this, then you should give it a try within 2 hrs limit.
Those, who enjoy ARK, may not enjoy playing DnL. I personally interested in DnL more than ARK . Though from what I have see so far, there are some questionable design choices, which might be a result from taking things from ARK, but at the same time, trying to be different from ARK.
One of them that I notice right from start is the progression, where the game is trying to be opened-sandbox with adventure-rpg system in place. However, the linear crafting system are put behind the leveling of your skills/ranks, which is okay for the time being. Though if it continues this way, DnL will become a grinding game on a linear path to unlock stronger/better things to play with instead of the sandbox freedom. I don't think that the crafting recipes should be tied to the leveling, but instead should be learnt/upgraded from different sources, and have skills/ranks increases the efficiency instead. This is up to the team though if they can figure out the right formula for DnL.
I can't say anything more than what I have seen in the first hour, but imo, I am not impressed, maybe with some updates, it will be better.
I can run the game with my average PC on high-epic settings with acceptable drops (~40), and few lag-spikes on Solo. got 1 CTD when opening the menu in likes 50 mins.
It is a refunded for now, but I will keep my eye along the development road.

This is another flawed port from Tecmo Koei and Square Enix. I could never get the game to run at a solid 60 FPS. It didn't matter what the settings were, it could be all Low or all High, but I would always get a FPS that bounced around between 54-58 with constant stuttering. It make the experience pretty poor.
After investigating a bit and seeing many others with the issue, I found that one of the fixes for it was to have a Youtube video in the background paused. Sure enough that worked, and I got Silky smooth 60FPS locked solid. But only if the video was maximized in the background, because I would alt-tab back to the video and minimize the browser, and go back to the game and the stutter would be present again until I maximized the video. Launching the game in Big Picture mode also seemed to fix it. Wierd stuff though.
I wish Tecmo Koei and Square Enix would get their♥♥♥♥♥♥together. I mean, the game seemed like it would end up being pretty fun, and I loved the character designs, but I can't recommend it when it has issues like the one I encountered. I'll probably be submitting a refund request here.

Double Action Boogaloo is a third person shooter and runs on the Source engine. The concept sounds pretty cool, shooting bad guys while playing in an action movie. And it is fun... for 5 minutes.
The problem is the game gives zero ♥♥♥♥s about balance. The shotgun is easily the best and most OP weapon to use. The rifles are or semi-auto or have massive recoil on full auto. So you'll end up running around with a shotgun, just like everyone else.
Another problem is the approach the developers took. Let me explain.
By pressing different keys (duh) you can preform different kinds of stunts, whether it be a slide, roll, etc etc. This sounds fun and entertaining, which it is. But they seem to have made the game depend mostly on the stunts: the better stunts you have/make, the more points/score you get. So you'll end up with a bunch of jerks flying through churches with shotguns.
All in all, I think the point system is a stupid idea, but thats just my personal opinion.
If you want or are looking for an action movie type game I cannot recommend this game. However, feel free to check out Action Quake 2 or even Action Half Life (2). They have a completely different approach and focus more on actual fun gameplay, whilst maintaining the feel of playing in an action movie.
TL;DR: If you're looking for a fun deathmatch game then this game is probably not for you.

Like the first Ride, this is one of the best Motorcycle games I've played since Tourist Trophy on the PS2.  It is as difficult as you want it to be with scaling that rewards you for turning assists off (much like Forza).  It's arcady enough to where anyone can pick it up, and with just enough sim aspects to keep you on your toes if you wish.  Race and bike variety is great.  Small displacement 2-stroke sport bikes, dual sports, top heavy naked bikes, supersports, touring bikes, classics, etc.  The PP (performance points I assume) system is new to this title.  Reminds me a bit of Grand Turismo's way of measuring overall performace.  Many people do not like it but it keeps the races interesting by having PP limits on events so you can't just max out the tuning on an eligible bike and smoke the AI competition on every race, which was a bit of an issue for me in the first Ride.  Tuning and customization options are practically the same as the first title, with just a bit extra.  The bike selection and tracks are great and much improved from the previous title.  It has a very accurate Nordschleife which combined with excellent controls always makes for a great racing title.  I recommend both Ride and Ride 2, but so far Ride 2 is the definitive title in the series thus far.

Hey guys, let me start off by saying while I do not recommend this game, it really isn't the worst game ever. When playing games like this, I like completing the quests, getting cool gear, making my person look as amazing as possible, and exploring a tonnnn to try out new things. If you're like me, you'll probably be irritated by the same things I was. Let's dive in, shall we?
PROS:
**Unique Combat: Lots of combos, options, some classes have both ranged and melee options. If you value the combat in MMOs, you'll like the combat here.
**LOTS TO DO: Really there is so much you can do in this game, what disappoints is the lack of explanation for this (I'll go into detail later).
**Character Customization: It was legit. Think Sims 4 meets MMO style customization. You can do so much to your character's appearance.
**Auto Walk: It's glorious because the world is so large. You navigate to a quest or area and press T and your character will walk themselves there no problem. Get up, go make some coffee, go pee - and they're doing all that tedious work for you.
Okay, so the CONS:
**Little Explanation: Now I'm not saying I need vast amounts of details on who, what, when, where, how. Part of the game is exploring, right? But when I have to Google regularly because I have no idea what things are for or how to do something or how to find something - we have a problem. I mean there's so much to do in this game and they don't even touch on half of it or why it's important or how to get started. Why include so many things to do if you don't touch base on it?????
**NO FAST TRAVEL: The map is freaking huge. HUGE. And there are no fast travel options. Yes, auto-walk is legit but it's like having commericials on your Hulu account. It's pointless, just watch TV instead if you want commercials, k?
**Combat System: It's really cool and all but there are so many combos (and some of the skills are poorly explained) that, let's face it, most people aren't going to use or remember 90% of those skills. I need my hotkeys back pls.
**Armor: It hardly changes in appearance as you get higher level gear. Woooah it added an armor plate where there wasn't one before. Much wow. Seriously, if you wanna look cool or even just different from others of your class, prepare to drop some $$$$$$.
**Inventory: They have slots AND WEIGHT LIMITATIONS. Like WHAT?!?!? Having both is redundant. YOUR CURRENCY ALSO HAS WEIGHT. Just WHY? Either I want my slots or I want my weight limit but I will not be limited by both O:<
To conclude, with how I play MMOs - this game just wasn't a fit for me. Play Tera if it seems like you value what I do in an MMO. It's free, and has been #1 for ages in its genre.

DQHII is one thing above all else: fun. It's clear that when the devs set out to make this game, that was their full intention; as well as keeping with the thematic, and aesthetic touches that the Dragon Quest series is known and popularized for.
This game avoids becoming just another "Warriors-esque masher" by implementing charm, beautiful opimization, well implemented and executed graphics, series loyalty, and an empathetic and well scaled difficulty system. It's a joy to play - it posesses both a well directed and nicely nuanced story (one with a twist or two for those who seek it) and characters that far more than simply amorphous blobs of j-art - they possess all the character, spunk and vividness of an actual, dedicated character.

The graphics in this game are amazing. This is exactly what you should ask for when you want a anime esque series to come to life on your screen. It perfectly scales what are classical 2D characters from DQ and sticks them in a vivid, rich and storybook type world. It does this while not taxing either your GPU or CPU - people claim there is all sort of things that affect performance jam-packed into this client - but I didn't feel it. My GPU and CPU were never over 50%. If you experience issues, run a 10 hour youtube video behind the windowed client on your screen, and it can help keep frames consistent.
I personally hardly experienced this issue - and optimization is pretty well implemented. Ultrawide would have been appreciated, but I realize I'm in the minority there as far as screens. Everything ran smoothly, 60FPS, all things maxed, and this game truly felt both "next-gen" and "last-gen"; when I say last gen I really mean that in a classical, nostalgic sense.

Sound is impeccable. Classic DQ themes? Got that. Fitting music that never gets boring or tiring? Got that. Immersive boss music that gives a sense of levity while deftly juxtaposing desperation? Got that. This music displays an innocence and a classical touch that really suits the game and does exceptionally well.
The schema for this game is well implemented, and I highly recommend using a controller. I took a few seconds to dabble with keyboard controls, but honestly this is a console port and should be treated as such. It's functionality with the X1 controller is flawless. Movement in this game can be a bit slow - so it's best that you focus on timing, and getting your attacks to hit in the weak points of the bosses. You slow down when you fight as opposed to your regular movement, so be wary of this - but your control of your character is tight and right, and you will quickly reach a state of "flow" as you switch between characters.
Ultimately, this game is a "Warriors" type slasher with a great deal of charm and zest. It takes that formula and owns it, implementing it right into a very beautifully built world. Just like Warriors games you can collect a cavalcade of weapons, from war fans to punchy fists~, abacus to greatsword. A great touch is that you can switch your main character to a plethora of classes, really helping the high paced action. You can easily switch between charas to get yourself into the action as another if the main characters skills don't quite scratch your respective itch.
The main joy in this game is in the combat system. Your fighting is fluid and well coordinated, and your animations look exquistly fluid as you roll, dodge, block and slash through waves of recognizable DQ monsters. There are quests to go along with the story - none which are super crazy except for ONE WHICH SHALL GO UNNAMED - haha. The difficulty of this game is for those both unintiated novice and erudite game grinder - you can finish the story in about 30-35 hours, but there are over 150 hours of content (grindey content, but if you love the game like I do, worthwhile content) for those who are deeply engrossed in the game and love a great grind.
A downside is I wish there was more people online to play with. It'd help me polish up achievements faster, but its not a big loss. The AI in this game is pretty sharp, and your ability to switch charas and skills is a big assist to having a great time.
Get this game on sale and add it to your library. Really get into it and enjoy it, because it calls back to an age where gaming was about aesthetic and taste. It wears a "Warriors" face, but truly it possesses a 1996 Heart, made of golden nostalgia and "before the meme" humor. This game has really given me so much joy, and I have no problem recommending it at a slightly reduced cost. This is a game that if you have friends to play with your joy will multiply, and alone you will soak in a truly worthwhile run.
Add me as a friend if you want multiplayer help, I'd be glad to be at your side.
Enjoy the game, and I hope my review helped~~

Instead of creating your army one unit at a time, you can now create an entire squad of a specific unit and have it fight as a whole. It moved the focus from resource gathering to strategic point captures, freeing up your focus from managing gatheres to managing your army.
The single player campaign, unfortunately, only follows the Space Marine storyline, so it seems quite short. However, you can still play with the other races in either multiplayer or skirmishes.

I love Overcooked - it's one of the best couch co-op games I've played! I've showed it to many people, and I can say that even people that have never touched a controller in their life can learn it quickly, thanks to a well designed tutorial, and have fun.
The controls are simple, move around, interact, and pick things up. However it is the teamwork and streamlining of tasks that is the best part of this game. Every level has a different kitchen layout, and you'll get a queue of tasks (food orders). For example, say you'll be making burgers this time, which requires: picking up ingredients, chopping vegetables and meat, cooking the patties, assembling complete burgers, and dish washing. The grill could be on one side of the level, with the cutting board and ingredients on another. You'll have to plan with your teammates who will take which task, and what method to transport the raw and cooked ingredients, in order to not take too long and♥♥♥♥♥♥off the customers!
I beat the entire campaign + all DLC with one other friend, while I've played most levels a 2nd time with 2~4 people. The levels are pretty well balanced for different group numbers, with a small portion of levels that seem to be more balanced towards 4 or 2 people, usually due to size. For example there was a huge map that would have worked better for 4 people due to its sheer size, whereas some small kitchens get cramped with more than 2 people. This is only an issue if you want to get 3 stars on everything - I've found all maps are beatable with any group, allowing for level progression.
"Hey! Grab the soup, grab the soup, it's going to burn!!"
"Crap, just one sec - oh no the counter is moving, I can't get over there!!"
"We have no plates!!"
"Oh shoot I'm doing it NOW!" (Countdown timer almost at 0, run over the length of the level and grab the soup, rush to the delivery...)
"YESS!!!"
I heartily recommend this game for the strategy and cooperation involved, as well as good times with friends!
I have an Xbox wireless dongle for PC, 4 wireless Xbox controllers, and have Overcooked on my laptop and desktop. When I'm at friends' places, I bring the laptop and hook it up to their TV. When I'm at home I just use my desktop or laptop in the living room. This is truly a portable game if you have the wireless dongle and controllers - everything fits into an average school backpack.

I've played this game a little and here is what I will comment on:
1. It's basically a FTP + Microtransactions ... but for $5-10, it's still a no brainer in my opinion. It's still pretty fun even if you do not spend another cent. But if you decide to play ongoing, I do recommend a little investing in a few pets, weight increase and increased bag storage. It makes a huge improvement in playability. All the rest of the cosmetics are for those who want to look "rich" in attire or in residence ... you know, color coordinated, fancy designs etc
2. It reminds me a great deal of what I would envision Ultima Online 2 to look and play like had it ever happened (I played UO for about 6-years).
3. I DO NOT recommend you buy this on STEAM at this point because of two things:
First, Lots of AFK activites built into the game (like fishing and processing) which can run for many hours unattended, I literaly am logged in 24/7 while only actively playing for maybe 8-hrs at a time, and the game has "hours played" milestone rewards ... so until STEAM allows multiple games at the same time... it realy suxxorz to have to shut it down to play other STEAM games.
Second, When I bought it, it said "Steam Trophies" ... but they didn't work for most people and have since been removed... who knows if they will return.
4. The crafting and gear enchanting is pretty unique. You use NPCs in shops you own to craft gear and craftables. Some of these you will/can use, while some you will just sell in faraway places for good profits. The game actually gives every player rewards daily that can be claimed, and there is almost always an event going on that provides neat things and RNG chances at some of the best gear in the game.
Enchanting is what the player is responsible for... it's guaranteed to succeed at low levels but at HIGH levels… it's RNG that rivals games in Vegas for "odds" and chance vs reward (extremely addicting for some people). Only the most dedicated of players even has a chance to enchant gear to the highest levels.
5. Graphics in the game are stunning ... the world is big... no HUGE! There are a bunch of massive cities, and dozens of smaller towns, farms, and hamlets scattered everywhere.
6. There is PVE and PvP (PvP enabled for all players at lvl 50, but advancing is elective). Guild vs Guild is the bulk of the regular PvP as top Guilds compete for control of all regions of the world (control = income from taxes and trade). There is also dedicated PvP on servers that are labeled as such.
7. If I was to pick one thing I would personally wish for in this game, it would be that I could play my other STEAM Games while letting BDO run on another PC on the same account.
I really like this game, and have invested perhaps $100 in my over 4000+ hrs played … worth!

The main problem with NEO Scavenger is, sadly, the scavenging. While there's a decent bit of good writing to be found,  you'll probably never discover it unless you edit the game files or get incredibly lucky with your scavenging rewards, as health, weariness and thirst tick down with absurd speeds, areas get tapped out of resources in no-time(meaning that setting up a camp, which is necessary unless you get ridiculously lucky finding backpacks, etc. is useless) and all your items decay with ridiculous rapidity, too.
You'll never really get to actually PLAY the game, is the thing, you'll be stuck doing nothing but grinding berries, cured meat and boiled water(which you can only get if you're lucky enough to find a saucepan), and then when you finally get enough of it to start moving somewhere... your backpack falls apart and you have to leave it all behind.
But, okay, let's say you're good at management and overcome that hurdle. Then you may find one of the twenty or so locations you can interact with beyond scavenging(in a map of thousands of hexes, and only a few of them look any different from the surrounding generic town hexes)... and whatever you do roughly has a 50% chance of instakilling you or losing you all your carried stuff.
So now, good luck, you can do all your grinding again! Hope you're lucky enough to find a saucepan early on this time around, too, or you may as well just restart.
The combat also boasts a lot of choices to make, but it boils down to either: Have a ranged weapon, keep distance, shoot shoot shoot, or have melee weapon, close distance, beat beat beat. A few of the other options might occasionally be tempting if the game gave any indication of how likely they were to succeed or not(say, percentages or odds or something) rather than just vaguely suggesting a "high" or "low" chance(what's high? 50+%? 75+%? 95+%?).
Long story short: Needs more obvious mechanics, needs less busywork to pad out playtime, needs to make consequences of choices more predictable/obvious OR it needs some sort of save function. It feels like someone played FTL and A Dark Room and wanted to copy them without understanding them.

Overall awesome game that I'd reccomend, I've had it for over a week at the time of writing this and after sinking nearly 100 hours it has just been such a great and enjoyable experience.
What I enjoy:
-Graphics are absolutely incredible, makes the game very immersive.
-Combat is very engaging and actaully require some learning and skill.
-Freedom in what you do whether that be questing, life skilling, grinding, etc, you're not limited in terms of progression and you can choose your own path.
-Open World with no teleportation, if you can see it in most cases you can go there. This adds to the immersiveness making it very entertaining just to ride around the world and explore.
-A ton of depth in literally everything: knowledge, every life skill, items, etc. Lots to learn and explore and it'll definitely not bore you anytime soon.
What I disliked:
-Thing's suddenly appear like bushes or leaves when running around which is a bit annoying but it's no way game breaking.
-No autolooting feature, this is probably my biggest complaint. The only way to have auto loot is to own pets which cost around 9$ per pet in the pearl shop, although you can purchase one off the market for 8 mil. they sell out increadibly quickly making it very difficult to obtain one when in reality you need at least 3 to pick up items efficiently. As the game is not free to play I'd expect basic features to be included in the package like auto looting but that's not the case. A bit annoying but the game is definitely still playable.
Overall I still have a lot to experience in the game but so far it has been very fun and I'd definitely reccomend the game to anyone, espicially people who can spend a bit more than the base price in order to fully enjoy the game.

Generally speaking I know within the first 10 min. whether or not I am going to like a game, and I like this game.
Sure, there are unavoidable PVP elements for now, but that makes things exciting. I am sure later in the game when you actually have things worth killing you for in your pack, that there will be plenty of far off places to hide *fellow hermits rejoice*
While there isn't much instruction about how things are intended to go down at first, that is because the game is pretty straight forward. Also, the user interface design is nice and clean; I respect that they didn't cheese it up by trying to go all overboard with themed skins like some games do.
As far as the whole controversial performance thing goes, make sure you're choosing one of the many servers available to you with the lowest ping possible and that you have a connection that is not comparable to dial-up... Also, keep in mind that if you have a potato for a computer it isn't going to run this game well. I am sure they'll work on optimization, but for now, if you're currently operating on a potato you're SOL.
I run the game just fine with the following specs (on Epic setting)
• Motherboard: ASUS Z170 PRO GAMING LGA 1151
• Processor: Intel Core i7-6700K Skylake Quad-Core 4.0GHz
• Video Card: ASUS GeForce GTX 1060 6GB ROG STRIX OC
• Ram: CORSAIR Vengeance DDR4 16GB
• Hard Drive: Intel SSD 600p Series
With that said, for me, there is no difference in performance between medium (default) and epic, and visually speaking the game just appears slightly more defined, but overall about the same, which indicates that they're likely working on it/or it something they have to finish. Also, another crazy thing to mention is the lighting/shadows - they're kind of wonky looking.
My only real gripe about gameplay so far is how crazy fast your hunger meter dips, and how very little berries and apples will go towards filling the hole, but eh, I'm sure there is better food later, and berries are easy enough to obtain; just go punch some grass.
Also, the game's wilderness areas are beautiful, and I can't wait to see what the devs are going to do in the future, as the game has a lot of potentials. It's that perfect spot in-between Life is Feudal and The Black Death. I think I've finally found the right survival game for me (PS: I didn't like Ark, so maybe that's why...I hear a lot of comparisons, but this game isn't like Ark other than the fact that both are survival games imo.)

First off, even though I would not recommend this game... it does look like a lot of fun if you are in a situation where you could play 2-4 players on a TV and is probably the only way you'd actually want to play it. Maybe two players at the computer, but only if you both have controllers.
The game in general seems fun, but it is not a very good single player game. If you want to use the keyboard, the buttons make it not enjoyable at all and there is no ability to rebind them. This seems like a very basic feature and there is no excuse to not have this option in the game.
Also, it is only local co-op/multiplayer. Even games in the 90s let you play with other people through the internet. There is really no reason to make a non single player game, especially on the PC only let you play locally. You might be able to get around this with Hamachi to simulate a LAN environment accross the internet, but again a game this new should not need this even if it does work.
In short, do not get this game if you want to use the keyboard, or if you want to play single player, or if you want to play with friends who aren't sitting next to you.

I usually don't take my time to write a review of games, but felt like this one needed the support it can get. I have to say, all these negative reviews are beyond stupid, most of them haven't even played it for more than 2 hours or gotten out of the spawn area, yet feel like they can judge the entire game..
The thing about this game is, so far from my experience, the further you get, the more fun it gets, you'll be able to do more, craft more, shoot a bunch of cool magic, explore more, there's a ton to explore, trust me, and the scenery is actually quite nice with Epic settings (You may require a bit of a heavy PC in order to play with Epic for now, game needs a bit of tweaking here.).
What these negative reviews seem to forget, is that this is an Early Access game.. You know what that means? It's not done yet.. They put it out earlier so that people can play it, help test it and leave feedback on what needs changing.. Some of them are complaining that it's similar to ARK, in ways, yeah it can seem similar, but I played ARK a bit myself but couldn't get myself to enjoy it, where this, I actually enjoy. (Few tiny details, this game, Dark and Light, was in development already back in 2005, but production ceased after the development team had some legal issues. The game was recently picked up by Snail Games, and development has resumed. They bought license to use ARK assets.)
Some of the complains are that the game gets stuck on the loading screen, yes, happened to me too on the first run, took forever to load in, waited like 5 minutes, so I just closed the game, opened it up again, and the issue never occured again.. Easy fix.
Also if PvP games aren't your thing, you may not like this yet, as all servers are full hardcore PvP, I'm sure that some no-PvP servers will come in later, but for now, if you don't like PvP, don't buy it yet.
I do need to give a small warning to people looking to buy this though:
The beginner quests are horrible, I can admit that, they don't offer any tips on how to complete them, just tells you to "Gather this and that", where you'll end up having to ask the chat for advice on how to complete the different quests, as there is no advice or any quidance from these quests, so the beginning of the game will feel a bit ugh, but once you get out of the city, that's where the game gets really fun.
I thought the biggest threat of this game was the players looking to kill you and take your loot.. But man was I wrong, I was fighting a unicorn, no issue, it was a bit dark so couldn't see very far, suddenly I had some goblins come and attack me, I found out that their attacks actually will knock you unconcious after a few hits.. I got away for a bit, but ended up having 10 of them surround me, they knocked me fully unconcious and one of them decided to steal all my items, all my tools, food, gold, materials for crafting, etc. Once they had taken all my items, they decided to leave me and just walk away, I honestly couldn't stop laughing, was so surprised, never expected to be robbed of all my items by a couple of tiny goblins. (You can kill them and get your items back, so fear not.)
Either way, the game is actually a lot more fun than what these reviews are showing, the issue is just that they never got outside the city I assume, given that most of them only have like an hour in-game or so, Trust me, when you get outside the city and start to explore, you'll be amazed, the game does need some heavy tweaking, absolutely, I will not deny that, but I'm 100 % convinced that they'll fix the bugs and errors there are, as that's what Early Access is here for.
If you want a fully complete and polished game, this isn't for you yet.

Possibly the best survival game I've ever played. I was very hesitant to purchase this particular game after my experience with Don't Starve. Although I did enjoy the gameply of Don't Starve, I feel no need to come back to that game, because even with it's rogue-like elements, it feels like the same experience every time. This is something I feel NEO Scavenger did much better. The skill system has so many good choices, that no particular set feels like the "best" way to play the game. It simply comes down to which way you actually want to play your current playthrough.
The other thing NEO Scavenger did particularly well is entry to the game itself. Without limiting the player's choices, the developers found a way to keep the game simple enough at the start that you wouldn't get lost in the incredibly complex mechanics until you actually need to use the particular rules of the game. By starting you with noting to survive the cold weather, you're forced to learn how to utilize the scavenge mechanic, which is the most important decision of the game. If more games that were this complex had openings like this one, I feel more people could explore the depths of these incredible games.
Even though it's clearly done on a budget, the art of the game is very well chosen. I found it easy to destinguish between the different items that I scavenged, and I rarely felt confused by the sprites that were on screen.
Even though the story itself isn't the big draw to the game itself, it's very well written. I found myself genuinely caring about my character and even being sympathetic to some of the people i encountered. These characters were made so well that I genuinely found myself thinking if I really needed to kill the people I came across. Even though it's clearly "every man for himself", the difficulty of recovering from fights and the chance of my having to drop my cart and run made each encounter a very difficult choice.
This is quickly becoming one of my favorite titles that I found on steam.

The very best compliment I can give this game is that it copies aspects wholesale from vastly superior games.
It's Dead Island (same developers), emphasizing the parkour from Mirror's Edge. At day you're vaulting over endless hordes of weak, respawning zombies so numerous you may as well ignore them. At night your movement ends up being more subdued, lest you attract the attention of night-specific zombies primed to obliterate you in seconds. If you're detected the game shifts into a chase mode where you run or die not unlike Amnesia. Day or night it's almost always better to avoid combat with zombies.
Because your melee weapons suck horribly. You may take anywhere from one to twenty strikes to kill anything with a melee weapon. Until you get a gun (halfway into the game) you're better off not bothering to fight. By comparison, one single bullet to the head kills almost everything.
Occasionally your guns get stripped away and you're forced to fight with melee. It is fundamentally broken and does not work. Between random amounts of damage and enemies randomly dodging your attacks, melee combat is frustrating and almost completely futile.
Looting is just as futile. You'll get random items to sell for cash. Everything you can buy is HILARIOUSLY overpriced beyond useless. Crafting is boring, looting ingredients for crafting is boring, just give me the final product in the box for ♥♥♥♥s sakes and don't make me jump through menu hoops to get them. Other than a handful of molotvs and medkits I didn't craft ANYTHING. All of the unboxing was as useless as a monthly subscription to Lootcrate. Don't inundate me with dozens of useless weapons that are only slightly better. Just give me a gun in the beginning.
They had the ♥♥♥♥ing nerve to introduce enemies with guns by forcing you into an unescapable fight against five people, in which one of them had a gun and you were restricted to melee.
One against five is bad enough, but I'm not ♥♥♥♥ing Batman. I can't kill someone with a gun if I don't have one myself. At least let me fight one guy with a gun by himself so I can punch him uninterrupted and steal his weapon.
There are so many horrible problems with this game, and I haven't even touched on the fundamentally broken first person parkour. Jumping to small platforms didn't work in Turok two decades ago, and it doesn't work here and now. Give me third person if you want me to jump and platform or don't bother.
You can cheese all the difficult fps combat against humans by pressing q to see through walls. The only advantage they have is killing you almost instantly, almost balancing it out.
Several times I was being chased by a hoard, running through them since combat is so pointless. Trapped in a sewer tunnel, the devs coat my monitor in Vaseline to simulate the putrid filth. And it's a good thing I couldn't see because I smacked the lone zombie that I ran up into only for it to detonate instantly killing me
Good thing I couldn't see it for all the♥♥♥♥♥♥on my screen. Otherwise I would have stayed back and not beaned it on the head, killing myself. Thank God I was able to replay that entire section, I just ♥♥♥♥ing love redoing the already repetitive gameplay, said no one ever.
That spiteful "gotcha" moment by the developer is enough for me to slam this game with a big fat red thumbs down, but there's so many layers of♥♥♥♥♥♥on top of that recurring problem that I can't begin to understand how anyone could enjoy this game.
The writing is godawful nonsense with character motivations that are shallow to nonexistent. The handful of "plot twists" shoehorned in are so transparent I could see them from space.
Bonus: the final boss is a series of QTEs.

So, around the beginning of the year, I was on Steam when I heard that Saints Row IV was on sale. Now, I'm an avid Angry Joe watcher and I knew he had said that this was a game worth playing because of it being crazy, wild, and smart fun. So, after having a few friends agree with this sentiment, I decided that I should get it and try it out. Now, it's time to give my take on this game. So here goes...
Premise: Being a direct sequel to Saints Row: The Third, you are still playing "The Boss", but you have now gone from a celebrity thug on the streets of Steelport to becoming the president of the United States. But all of a sudden, aliens invade, take over the world, and capture you and your friends. Now it's up to you to save them and stop the alien menace.
Pros: OK, when Angry Joe said this game was fun, all I can say is that he MEANT it. I'd compare it to GTA if you added the wackiness of TEH INTERNETS, up to and including using a ♥♥♥♥♥ bat, use the aptly named Dubstep Gun that makes everything around it bounce around while you're killing baddies, and, in this game, use super powers. Among your powers you have super strength, speed, telekinesis, and more. The story is also really great, with you quickly becoming motivated to take down the Zin Empire and save your friends lives. Yet they don't feel generically evil either, with the leader, Zinyak, being a hilarious, upperclass ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who will operatically sing "Just a Friend" by Biz Markie, quote Shakespeare while kicking your ♥♥♥, and talks like a distinguished British gentleman at all times. The other characters on your team are also very likeable and funny, from the buttmonkey that is Pierce to the nerdy, kinky Kinzie and even Keith David (yes, THE Keith David). Plus, the game also has two player compatibility, which is always fun. Well, almost. I'll explain more later.
Cons: If you don't like the general craziness that I mentioned before, with the ♥♥♥♥♥ bats and such, you might not enjoy this game. In general, I feel it is a fairly accessible game if you don't mind or even enjoy it, but don't come in expecting a story like with GTA V. Also, one thing I find irritating with the Saints Row games in general is that with certain programs, like Yahoo IM or similar, you can actually get pulled out of the game while in the middle of it, which can cause some problems if you're in the middle of a fight or traveling around. And as a final note, one thing that makes me not as crazy about the two player compatibility is that when it's used it can sometimes feel like your fights end up one sided, with one person getting to take care of most of the stuff going on while the other scrambles to do anything. Maybe it's just my experience though.
Either way you look at it, SRIV is a very fun game, with lots of stuff to do from the actual game to DLC, plus just traveling around having crazy fun with superpowers and wild weapons. If you want a game that just feels like pure, unadulterated fun, this is definitely one you should take a look at.

Before I start this review, I play on the stand alone launcher.... Not on Steam.
This game in short is a combination of:
EVE Online: Takes a very long time to Learn/Train skills to an effective level, and a Huge map with no Server Restrictions. The game may have multiple servers, but you can hop between each server every 15minutes.
The Sims: Buy a house with in game currency, decorate it with in game or real life currency. Lots of Character Customization with "Fashionable Outfits" that overwrites your current gear. Pick a "Job" and master it to make money.
Dynasty Warriors/Dark Souls Franchise: Lots of high speed action against groups of mobs, insanely grindy after lv55, lots and lots of dodging/rolling/evading.
And ill toss in a dash of Minecraft because you can spend days cutting trees, harvesting plants, mining, etc... just to build new gear, furniture, and boats. Luckily you can hire workers to do most of this for you, but you still have to manually do some of it.
Ive been playin for about 3months now and it took me this long to finally learn a good amount so I could write a decent review on it. If you try to compare this game to other traditional MMOs like WoW or SWTOR... dont lol BDO is more of a Social MMO in my eyes. I havent done PvP at all yet in the game, mainly because I spend all my time training horses or fishing/cooking to make money.
At the time of this review, I havent even gone over lv56 in over a month now. If im not Training Horses, Fishing, Harvesting, im just chillin in my house and customizing it... or hanging out in big towns chatting it up with random people.
I recommend this game because you can never be bored in it, always something to do, always something to work towards. My only issue with the game is the complete RNG when upgrading your items. If you try to upgrade your items yourself, not only could you cause perma durability loss towards them and have to get the same weapon to smash them together to repair it... you could lose the item completely. When you have a weapon that costs 9mil silver, and lose so much durabilty that you need 8 more of those weapons to repair it... it could drive you nuts and might force you to rage quit.
Which is why I just "Farm" out the in game currency and buy the best gear I can from the Auction House. Also, I used to hate this fact with the game, but now I dont mind it at all... You can Auto-Fish AFK or Auto Travel while AFK. Like EVE Onlines Autopilot. Final note, anything thats on the Cash Shop, can be bought on the Auction House from other players. If you do the quests in the game they give you tons of Inventory Slots and Weight Boosts, so you dont even need to buy them in game from the cash shop. No Monthly Fee... not bad at all for a game thats only $4.99-$9.99 depending on sales.

I don't usually write reviews, for any games, but I couldn't help it when my hands felt ticklish by reading another player's review.
I understand it when people say: "It's up to each person's tastes" and I have nothing to against that, obviously, though, when people misunderstands game mechanics and put up badly made up reviews, it triggers me.
Grim Dawn is in NO WAY a restrictive game, you can be and do pretty much whatever the damned hell you wish to do. The variety in skills and combos for your own build, that you can pick, is so VASTE it might even struck you and leave you as confused at the very first.
There's no way you'll be playing up to end game with only two skills in your skillbar, and if you do, well, I'm sorry to say you've been playing Grim Dawn in the wrong way and it might be time to start another character and put more thoughts into your skill and build choices. And even then, if you can't come up with a perfect build by yourself, the Grim Dawn community is so huge that I really doubt you'd be left without finding the build that suits you the most.
Gameplay is fluent, it's animated godly, IMHO. I mean we're speaking of a game that's trying to be a Diablo runner up, actually, trying to BEST Diablo itself.
It really isn't appreciated enough for the potential it actually has, even with the recent DLC, Grim Dawn lived up to all the expectations I've been having for it, ever since.
I've played through the game not once, but something close to 6 or 7 times and I rarely grow tired of it.
As I previously mentioned you have so many choices for your classes, be it the primary or the secondary one, that you'll rarely feel like you're stuck in making decisions. Devotions? What to pick? Easy, there's a dozen of choices. Read through them. Skills? Only two skills in your skillbar? Easy fixed, read better through skills description and make actual combos instead of picking up random skills. Attributes? Again, easy if you have any idea of what the three attributes classes mean at all.
Something I found funny was reading that people complained about having to spend point to level up: isn't that a common thing in games nowadays? You level up, you get skill points, you level the skills up.
In Grim Dawn, you could easily find many flaws, but the classes, skills and leveling system truly isn't one of them.

This is quite possibly the most well-thought-out game I've ever had the pleasure of experiencing. I can't speak from experience as to how accurate this game nails the zombie apocalypse because personally I have not been in one, but from the fact that I'm a zombie fanatic I can say this game is quite realistic when it comes to living in a wasteland.
You wake up in a cryogenic facility with something (You later find out it's one of the game's meany creatures, a Dogman) trying to break in. You select your skills and use them to your advantage to defeat the beast, and then you are sent into the massive and unforgiving world that is NEO: Scavenger.
This game absolutely nails scavenging. You search around for ages finding useless, irrelevant items such as string and broken glass bottles but that feeling of pure, unadulterated satisfaction when you find some of the more useful items such as a backpack or especially a crowbar, is amazing.
Don't get me wrong, this game is unforgiving. As you'll read down below, someone didn't feel like boiling the water they found, got cholera, and died. That's the kind of thing you have to expect on a daily basis from this game. I once forgot to set my noise trap and was murdered by a guy with a meat cleaver in my sleep. I had a shotgun and a noise trap, but it was in my backpack and I didn't feel like getting it out. Another time, I shot and killed a deer, took the meat, put it in my backpack and forgot to cure it, and proceeded to eat it a few hours later after it had spoiled. I got some sort of weird disease and died after hours of diahorrea and blood loss.
And while it's unforgiving, it's ultimately very satisfying to play. You find youself getting killed, cursing the game out, and then coming back a few hours later for seconds. And that one rare playthrough where you don't die a horrible, painful death, you just feel awesome. I have tons of screenshots I've taken of the various times when I've had a surplus of stuff.
Also the developer, Daniel, is always reaching out to his fans. I'm personally friends with him here on Steam because I wanted to ask a question, so I shot him a friend request and he responded.
If you are thinking about getting this game, get this game.
If you are not thinking about getting this game, get this game.
If you hate this game with a passion, get this game.
If you're going to propose to your SO, buy them this game and put it in a virtual box.

Okay aside from my hours played i have done a lot of research on this game. and to be honest i am extremely dissapointed. as "diverse" as this game claims to be the reality of it is very limited. first reason this heppens is because of the leveling machanic itself. you run around hack and slash and lvl up. then when you do level up you have to sacrafice points to "level" up. (yes you read that right) there are two leveling up features. your character level is set aside from your character level. which means your not able to put points into your skills. so this means that your characters skills are going to be very limited aside from skills items give you. and if you do not focus on 1-2 skills (when they allowed 8 skill slots to be used) it very limits your characters abilities. basically full abilities is considered "end Game". THEN and only then will you be allowed to actually start putting points into your secondary class. which they allow you to pick in the beginning of the game. but puting points into this class at any point in the game prior to "end game" isn't practical.
so basically in the meat of the game you are going to run arouund with nothing but two skills (unless your lucky enough to find good items that give you skills for your class) to even have a formidibal player on a veteran game (which to me is boring) then after you completed all the quests and gone through all the acts you finally have a character that MIGHT have a full skill bar. which to me doesn't give the promise of "diversity" they claim to have. not to mention classes skills restrict what type of weapon is used with that skill. so if you want to do anything else you won't even put points into your classess main top skills in the skill window.
final note is that this game is so overly complicated you end up getting restricted and unless you pay in game currency you can't respec. because in most cases you cannot go back on most skills sets. and with the devotion skill trees (that you build around your character) you can't take those back. so if you really want to do anything else. you have to build a whole new character.
overly complicated and overly restricted.

I'm not a big fan of JRPG's, but Dragon Warrior was my first RPG ever (I got it with my Nintendo Power subscription). I was feeling nostalgic and decided to give it a whirl. The game is action-oriented, with some light RPG elements (stats and classes). Its often compared to Dynasty Warriors, which I have never played- basically you run around a semi-open world and destroy mobs upon mobs of enemies. Combat is fun, kinetic, and anime-style over the top.
The game is packed with collectibles, crafting, and achievements. I quite like this feature, because there is a lot of grinding to be done, but you never feel like you're just mowing down enemies to get a few levels. You're always progressing towards some goal or reward. Its actually what I like most about this game- it never wastes your time. Even if you lose a battle, you keep all of your earned XP and gold, so while there is grinding, you don't have to repeat it even in the event of a mistake.
The world is fun to explore and theres some light Metroid elements (need certain characters to unlock areas). Theres a large cast of characters to choose from, and they all feel reasonably unique.
I didn't pay too much attention to the story, the slow pacing and extraneous dialogue is something I don't really like about anime/JRPGs in general, but thats just personal preference. Even skipping it, the game is a lot of fun.

its a hack n slash RPG based on an old classic: Dragon Quest (Dragon Warrior for U.S) which stars 2 characters which are changeable that are knights-in-training that has exchanged from Dunia to Harba, when ALL OF A SUDDEN the prince of Dunisia attacked Harba, breaking the thousand year prophecy. Its up to the 2 of them plus a few other characters they pick up along the way to figure out why the prince of Dunisia attacked, and more about the war.
PRO'S
~Beautiful graphics, not realistic, but more like 3D anime
~Its very smooth, I had almost no problems with lag (other than a billion things going on in one screen)
~almost everything is Open world except for story levels, and even then, some of them are EXTREMELY massive
~Theres lots of things to do in the open world, including find chests, find ingrediants, grind (although you probably wont need it), and get to hidden locations using your parties' powers
~Voice acting is good, both english and japanese
~You can change classes for your 2 main characters
~MULTIPLAYER (although it feels like nobody is ever online, I only found 2 other people in my 20 hour adventure from when I wrote this review)
CONS
~Theres little strategy to this game, mostly just mindless pressing buttons
~The game automatically expects you to have a controller, so you have to use the keyboard settings to know how to do what action, but its easy to master after maybe an hour or so
~The story feels too cliche.
(SPOILERS KINDA) After you save the realm, OOPS, THE REAL THREAT WAS UNDER YOUR NOSES THE ENTIRE TIME!
the quests are also poor, they're more or less "kill this thing with this one type of move" or "give me these ingredients"
~There is little variation to weaponry, I believe theres, like, 6 or so weapons for each class, which sounds okay, but then you realize that they're EXTREMELY expensive, like, 30K for 2 swords expensive. Not to mention, theres no armor except for reskins
OVERALL:

DQH2 has more story.  This can be good or bad, depending on your preference.  I found myself enjoying the admittedly simple storyline, and the option to skip cutscenes exists for those who don't.
DQH2 is more challenging.  In most other Warriors style games, powerful enemies are merely opposing generals.  Their movesets will be comparable to your own, meaning they will require a large stat advantage to make them challenging to fight due to the fact that a player will generally be superior to the AI in terms of skill.  In DQH2 Heroes, the powerful enemies are monsters with bodies and movesets that differ drastically from the heroes.  This, along with the fact that you are much more often pit against multiple powerful enemies than in other Warriors games, brings the difficulty in line with what one might expect from a traditional ARPG.  This leads into the next point...
DQH2 has more RPG style features:  levelling, buying equipment, side-quests, the ability to travel anywhere in the world you currently have access to rather than just the next battle.
Those who played the previous DQ games will appreciate the nostalgia appeal, as many of the playable fighters are heroes from previous games.  They also come with remixes of their original theme music from those games.
Battles with defeatable allies can be frustrating, as your allies will generally be far more helpless than in other Warriors style games.
Overall, this is an excellent game that will apeal to many more gamers than just Warriors fans.  Anyone who likes ARPGs will be able to enjoy DQH2.  I can recommed this one generally to anyone who wants a fun but challenging romp through hordes of monsters.

For those reading this review FTL is a great game. If you are a fan of real time strategy and space exploration, this is for you. It will make you happy. It will make you cry. Then it will make you lust for the eventual success of your ship and then destroy your hopes with a lucky laser blast from the enemy.
You will love your crew. You may even make little stories for them and give them cool names. Then as each of them get slaughtered by the shear evil and danger of space you will cry silent tears as you attempt to hold up your ship with the single surviving crew member you have left. But do not keep faith, as he or she too will go down with the ship. You will say that you will never forget the brave men and women who fought valiantly to save the Federation and then immediately toss them aside when you create a new game with a brand new ship to do the same insanely difficult task.
Sometimes you will get sidetracked by the small quests and hard decisions you will have to make, sacrificing essential resources that could have won you the game in the end. The Rebels may catch up to you and blow you into little chunks, dying in vain and no doubt increasing the effect of Kessler’s Syndrome over the planet you had orbited. But never fear, for the universe is too big to give any lick of care for your loss. But in the end you will still go back to the hanger to unlock new ships and toys to better assist you in your quest to beat the Rebel scum.
If you mod this game you will have even more fun, inevitably dying but getting cooler weapons, effects, and in the case of the "Captain's Edition" mod, a ton of more unique encounters and background stories that may or may not assist in the explosion of your ship.
In conclusion this is a great game. It may be 2D and pixilated but FTL definitely feeds adventure, strategy, and excitement to its players who will end up dying over and over to just to save the fleeting Federation.

Dawn of War is one of my favorite RTS games, even though I suck♥♥♥♥♥at them, Dawn of War is one I find myself picking up again and again to play. The game takes the setting in the Warhammer 40k universe and lets you control one of a few factions from the Warhammer lore to battle other players. In the end if you enjoy games like Company of Heroes, Starcraft, Warcraft, etc. then I would recommend this game. The gameplay is well done, pretty well balanced, and enjoyable to play with some friends or just to pass some times with. If you are a fan of the Warhammer 40k lore and setting than this game is great.

This is one of those artsy indie games. Also one of the first larger successes in the "public" indie scene.
The game itself it a platform puzzle game with elements or references from games like Mario and homages to several other "old school" NES games.
There also is a very interesting mechanic that is important to the core of the gameplay; Rewinding time.
This little feature will prove more important than a simple "save point"-feature in games such as Prince of Persia: SoT. In Braid certain elements are unchained from the time/space continuum - In other words, you can rewind time and unchained elements will stay put, or if you are holding them; Follow you back to where you were.
This entire process is used cleverly in the puzzles you are faced with.
Apart from the puzzles there is a very neat story tucked into the game(as with most artsy indie titles).
Without getting into too much detail on that part; It reminds me of a very well known "Save the captured Princess" scenario... With a twist.
I'm not going to spoil it and I'll leave it up to you to figure out the rest.
It's a short but great game - clocking at around 5-6 hours to beat it.
For what it is, it's well worth the time spent.

It's got a ton of issues, no doubt. I went into the game expecting them (and worse) so I'm not negatively surprised about how the first day of the Early Access came out. Personally, I enjoy the features of the game. I like the Medieval Fantasy setting with magic and mythical creatures more than the sci-fi and Dinosaurs from Ark. I also really enjoy the factions and NPC cities. A game with Realm vs Realm vs Realm warfare is always a good time!
Now, there are a ton of issues, like I said. This first hotfix *should* fix two of the most glaring issues: Mobs being incredibly hard to kill due to lag/combat related issues and gatherables not being very... gatherable due to server lag. This hotfix claims to fix both, so we'll see in about an hour.
There's also some tweaks that needs to be made. The bed roll needs to be unlocked much sooner. Waiting until level 10 for it, with the current skill/leveling rates on the Official servers, is brutal. Most people fail to realize they need to interact with NPCs to unlock more buying options that include foods that will make it so they no longer need to worry about sleep. Of course, sleep is free... if you can get a bed. Speaking of, on the server I played there seemed to be a bug where buildings in the NPC town were not rentable - one of the features I was looking forward to the most. I was also hoping for rentable beds in the Inns - which seems to be planned, but not yet implemented. Hopefully the server reset and hotfix will change that.
Base building is most definitely in the game and it's about what you would expect. It seems to be about the same as Ark, but could use more fleshing out which I guess will come with time. When combined with the House (guild) system, there is a very nice and powerful set of permissions. Using a House Seal makes anything within its range immune to raiding *unless* an opposing House decides to (literally) throw a war banner at your House. Within your House, you can set up multiple permission groups (aka Ranks) and fine-tune what they can and cannot do within your protected House areas. You can also set up alliances - which can be named! a nice fluff feature - with other Houses.
Then there's the NPCs. They mostly act as places to buy very basic goods and sell stuff for Gold Coins... on the surface. When you dig into it, they're a bit more advanced than that. Hopefully they'll continue to flesh them out. Most people don't realize you can Donate to the NPCs to unlock more advanced items, reduce prices, and have the vendor hold more of items. You're supposed to work with the rest of your faction to 'level up' the vendors via donations, but I haven't seen much of that yet. If you decide to play, join Knight 2 in the human faction as I've unlocked a fair amount by donating a lot of money to the Tavern Wench. With a small amount of gold you should never fear running out of focus or spiced meat because of my hard work. Do your part!
And speaking of working together with your faction, the Lord system is interesting. I've yet to see it in use but I've gleamed some information by looking at the billboard found outside taverns. If you reach level 20 and are the leader of a House, you are eligible to sign-up for the Lord vote. Once you sign up, other players can vote for you via the billboard. I guess if you get the most votes (not sure what the timeframe is...) you are given the Lord title. As Lord you get access to the castle, which appears to have some form of housing surrounding it? Not sure if or how it works, though. You can set up the rules/laws of the land, but how far those rules reach I don't know. Could be they only have any sort of effect within the city walls.
One thing I noticed during a tooltip in a loading screen is that you should be able to achieve higher ranks within your faction by contributing. I'm guessing the only real way to contribute right now is via donating, but so far I haven't unlocked anything to my knowledge. This brings up one of my biggest gripes about the game: Lack fo documentation. I have no idea what anything does or how to do anything, except what I've learned through little bits and pieces I've gathered from other players, or what I learn via trial and error. There needs to be a better, more in-depth tutorial or some sort of in-depth out-of-game documentation to help us figure things out.
So, do I suggest the game? Yes. So long as you meet three criteria: You liked the gameplay of Ark: Survival Evolved, Medieval Fantasy interests you, and you can comprehend what you might run into while playing an Early Access game.

We all have done something in life that we immediately wanted to take back. We said something rude or cruel in anger, we forgot to do something important, we end up doing something that shoots us in the foot. Braid is about fixing those mistakes as they happen, and what it means for us to be unable to do in real life.
That's not to say this game has a focus on story. Instead, the majority of your time will be spent on thoughtful platforming puzzles, with each ability affecting time in a different way. Puzzles can be fiendishly complex, but the majority can be completed with some patience without too much handwringing, and it's easy to be patient because the game is absolutely beautiful, using a paint asthetic to blur the lines between static art and actual level design, which is complicated by a short but beautiful soundtrack.
Braid isn't too long, taking at most the better part of an afternoon, but for someone who appreciates games as an art medium as much as entertainment, it's among the best Steam has to offer.

Gosh..
So this game.
This wonderful wonderful game.
I've been looking for a game similar to like, Diablo or Torchlight. Was recommended this by a dear friend. Eventually I picked it up, on sale. Then I noticed like, an expansion came out. Not a DLC, but what I see as an "expansion":
It's like picking up another chapter of a game... Classes, items, story, levels, area, exploration... It "expands" on the content already in the game... whereas a DLC to me -might- do that... but mostly DLC is presented in a bite size piece... and it's something that can be done easily without in most terms.
I didn't get to play the base game way back, or without the Ashes of Malmouth... I just shrugged and picked up the expansion after getting the same friend that recommended it to start playing, he picked it up... another friend too picked it up after seeing me play it so many days in a row.
My gosh. A few weeks into playing this... I already have five characters, plan on making more. Have played through the main campaign once fully, and nearly done with the story I think on Ashes of Malmouth as well? If not already completed. There's still so much more to go off to explore as well in the entire package.
This... This is the type of dungeon crawling sort of game I have wanted to play for so long. There's so many options, there's so many choices, there's so much to go exploring...
I suppose the only thing it -does- seem to be missing is a dungeon that is randomly generated or something... Some sort of roguelike area or campaign to adventure through and start fresh after deciding you've had enough? It is a static map I think... There's some features in the landscape that have made myself and friends question if there -are- a few variables that are randomized... but for what it's worth, I have made five characters as I said. I'd easily make more... and easily wouldn't mind exploring the same terrain that many more times. There's just so much that I feel like finding anything like lore or hidden stashes... It's just a wonderful experience. It's very rewarding in many, many ways.
Easily this is the game I'd recommend if you enjoyed such classics as Diablo, Torchlight, or heck... even any games from the Dark Alliance game engine days. You can use a 360 controller in this game and it feels like -that- with the controls. You can hotkey pretty much anything really fast, and the implementation for the controller feels really... thought out. Menus and things completely take on a new appearance, and there's even buttons lined out along the bottom in said menus to remind you of what button does what... -just- in case you forget.
Even the layout of the menus is optimized just for the controller input... When you use the keyboard or mouse? It'll correct itself to that format after like the game was only made for mouse and keyboard, too. It's amazing and I've never seen such a smooth implementation done as well as that.
Heck... this is how adventure hack and slash should have been made from the getgo, and I'm glad I finally not only picked this game up, but finally got around to playing it...

Company of Heroes 2 is a very unique game. The gameplay can vary from realitively easy to very challenging. How you approach a scenario can lead to either victory in a match or a compelete failure. The game allows infantry units to use a cover system. This ranges from light cover to heavy cover. If your guys are in heavy cover and your enemies are in no cover, you're more likely to win that engagement. You can also loot enemy bodies for special weapons they may of had, such as Flamethrowers, Bazookas, LMGs, etc. This can affect your units combat ablities in many ways. LMGs and HMGs (Light Machine Guns and Heavy Machine Guns) allow you to suppress your enemies forcing them to be pinned down where they are vunerable to Artillery or flanking. Heavier weapons like cannons such as Howtizers can be hijacked by killing their crews. Same goes for vehicles, although it's less likely they'll survive if you're using Bazookas. There is also a weather system in the game that can effect unit movement. Mud and deep snow will slow your units. Blizzards and deep snow may cause your units to freeze and possibly take casulties. The game is very rewarding and fun. I would recommend it for people who want a realistic strategy game. Not to mention the Campaign and Theater of War stories are interesting as well.
