NEO scavenger is, without a doubt, the best surprise I've got through Humble Bundle. What at first seemed a little interesting survival game turned out to be a massive and addictive experience, with the most detailed survival mechanics you've ever seen (except maybe Project Zomboid).
In NEO Scavenger, death is considered a sure thing, the question is how long you will last for. Survive the cold, survive the wounds. Survive the infection, survive the unboiled water you were forced to drink because you had no way to make a fire. Survive the blisters you got because you hadn't found boots yet, while a dogman chases you. Survive the poisoning you got eating unidentified mushrooms. And worst of all, survive the people (NPCs) who want what you've managed to gather.
The world has unique lore, setting a post-apocalyptic world with paranormal phenomenons happening left and right, but extremely well presented, gradually giving you the information, which is spread through conversations, pieces of newspapers and others.
The atmosphere is similar(ly angsty) to those of Dark Souls, or EVE online, but more personal and centered around the desperate situation your character wakes up into, like Spec Ops: The Line.
The combat is quite simple and brutal: He who connects the first hit usually wins. This enforces a visceral and all-or-nothing mindset, with no place for holding resources back, and a "shoot first, ask questions later" policy that makes you question your own acts as a player.
Both combat and map gameplay are turn-based, and reward thinking carefully about your next move, since the game works with permanent iron man mode (dying deletes the save file) to ensure that you're adequately kept on your toes.
Overall, this is the best survival game I've ever played, and definitely the best one-man-made game out there:
10/10

What do the characters symbolize? The Thief could very symbolize childhood innocence towards himself and his inner sexuality. His act of stealing money by pretending to be some one that he is not is actually a very deep symbolic description of those who have to hide themselves and their sexuality from the world, the actual act of stealing is his repressed side coming out in a violent and destructive manner, hurting others and society similar to how Foucault believes happens in the modern world (by calling his friend and bragging about it is his silent cry for help, similar as to how a man in depression will lash out, hoping that someone will save him, also ironically drawing distance from himself and others).
Now this is where the clip take a broad statement that I am having trouble figuring out. The punisher/executioner could very well be either a strong representation of society's view on sexuality or a representative figure of either sexual liberation or an actual shadow/other of the beneficial side of his sexuality, trying to show that his discovery of his sexuality would actually bring him happiness and not pain.
If we look at The Executioner aspect (the aspect that the man with the belt is a symbol of society) than we can see a great disgust with modern society's treatment of sexuality. The man, upon learning of The Thief's stealing caused by his repression, chooses to punishes The Thief instead of treating or caring for him for his "criminal reportable" offense. He toys with The Thief before he tells him of his punishment, similar as to how a man can be arrested and be kept detained before he goes to court. Meanwhile the clip points out an even more disgusting feature of The Executioner aspect: the entire time, he is shirtless.
What does this mean? The director points out that for The Thief's crimes, society itself is also guilty. Not only does The Executioner shirtlessness points out that in modern society that condemns sexuality, we also promote it blatantly in advertisements, porn, and almost every aspect of our lives, causing confusion and angst in today's youth. We can even go as far as saying that what the director means is that every person in society is in some sense not always in the social conformity, and that people will always have some sexual aspect of themselves that is not socially acceptable (as The Thief's nature points out, by trying to fit into a standard people will inevitable cause pain in both themselves and those around them).
Since as I mention the act of spanking is in itself a homoerotic action, than we can know that the symbolism here is that even the act of punishing someone for their sexuality brings up a somewhat devastating sexual act on the social norm--even in punishment we see traces of sexuality, which the social norm would say shouldn't be there. Here, the director makes a great humanistic expression that we can never fully repress our sexual nature, and that society should cast away its judgements and punishments about sexuality. Instead, embracing it in order to bring happiness and a more progressive society.
But if we look at The Punisher aspect (where the man with the belt is a sexual liberator), we see something entirely different. Upon hearing The Thief's bragging, he recognizes the repressed cry for help, and choose to punish The Thief to bring liberation. By bending The Thief over and committing the homoerotic act of whipping punishment, he shows through the hidden sexual nature of The Thief. Inevitable he would recognize the act as sexual and will compare the punishment experience with every aspect of his sexuality, gradually loosing himself up to the idea that sexuality would, instead of pain, bring happiness to him. He will in the end change his position that his sexuality will bring harm to himself to the (true) idea that it will bring only happiness to him.
Something to note is that in both cases of The Punisher/Executioner aspects is that The Man With The Belt calls his mother, who he first brings with a peaceful idea of sexual punishment but instead she suggests the more violent whipping. Anyone with a brain can figure out that this is a subversion of the Oedipus Complex, The Electra Complex. Where, the father figure being the Man With The Belt, and the mother being the mother. Here, the Mother is a figure with whom is associated with violence, and The Father being the one who the son commits the sexual act with. But since the spanking is the Mothers idea and yet the Father carries it out, what we have here is a subversion of the subversion: The Father and The Mother who are both separate, are also the same person. Since The Thief's sexuality is muddled, both his father and mother have become one person in his mind, both of them he wants to murder, and both of them he wants to have sex with.
Ultimately, since the subversion happens on more toward The Electra Complex instead of the Oedipus Complex, I would have to say that it is possible that the two men may perhaps have their sexuality leaning more on the Homosexual aspects than any straight aspects. Which is shocking, the director is implying that these by the books, straight as can be white dudes may be homosexuals! Of course I may be reaching, but what audacity would it take for a director to show two perfect straight men by our social standards, and then spit on the face of our preconceptions by showing they may actually be homosexuals! Again, I of course could be misreading and misinterpreting, since the blatant nature of their straightness is so almost painfully obvious, but as far as we know, they do show signs of homosexuality, but if they truly commit to that nature would require the viewing of the whole movie, or more intelligent film scholars in future generations.
I hope that today's and tomorrows generations can all see this clip and be reinvigorated by it. Perhaps one day we can stand by the light of our sexually invigorated sun, be bathed in its light, and take in this clips message as one of the most important statements that was ever made in our time.

Dawn of War is one of my favorite RTS games, even though I suck♥♥♥♥♥at them, Dawn of War is one I find myself picking up again and again to play. The game takes the setting in the Warhammer 40k universe and lets you control one of a few factions from the Warhammer lore to battle other players. The factions in this game are the Space Marines, Eldar, Orks, and Chaos Space Marines.
The game, and the series, has many pros; the game has base building, units in squads, vehicles, and pretty decent destruction effects. The aingle player is decent I think and is a good few hours of gameplay and then the multiplayer is like a lot of RTS games however it has resource points you take and hold on the map to keep a steady flow of resources to your side to build buildings and troops. The game offers a variety of modes players can wage battle in such as take and hold (which is taking critical points and holding them to win), annihalation (which is just killing the other side), and capture the flag and so on.
The only bad thing I think when it comes to this game is that it is an older game and a few computers have had issues running it but for the most part it seems to be able to run on the newer systems. If not then most fixes can be found online.
In the end if you enjoy games like Company of Heroes, Starcraft, Warcraft, etc. then I would recommend this game. The gameplay is well done, pretty well balanced, and enjoyable to play with some friends or just to pass some times with. If you are a fan of the Warhammer 40k lore and setting than this game is great.

The very best compliment I can give this game is that it copies aspects wholesale from vastly superior games.
It's Dead Island (same developers), emphasizing the parkour from Mirror's Edge. At day you're vaulting over endless hordes of weak, respawning zombies so numerous you may as well ignore them. At night your movement ends up being more subdued, lest you attract the attention of night-specific zombies primed to obliterate you in seconds. If you're detected the game shifts into a chase mode where you run or die not unlike Amnesia. Day or night it's almost always better to avoid combat with zombies.
Because your melee weapons suck horribly. You may take anywhere from one to twenty strikes to kill anything with a melee weapon. Until you get a gun (halfway into the game) you're better off not bothering to fight. By comparison, one single bullet to the head kills almost everything.
Occasionally your guns get stripped away and you're forced to fight with melee. It is fundamentally broken and does not work. Between random amounts of damage and enemies randomly dodging your attacks, melee combat is frustrating and almost completely futile.
Looting is just as futile. You'll get random items to sell for cash. Everything you can buy is HILARIOUSLY overpriced beyond useless. Crafting is boring, looting ingredients for crafting is boring, just give me the final product in the box for ♥♥♥♥s sakes and don't make me jump through menu hoops to get them. Other than a handful of molotvs and medkits I didn't craft ANYTHING. All of the unboxing was as useless as a monthly subscription to Lootcrate. Don't inundate me with dozens of useless weapons that are only slightly better. Just give me a gun in the beginning.
They had the ♥♥♥♥ing nerve to introduce enemies with guns by forcing you into an unescapable fight against five people, in which one of them had a gun and you were restricted to melee.
One against five is bad enough, but I'm not ♥♥♥♥ing Batman. I can't kill someone with a gun if I don't have one myself. At least let me fight one guy with a gun by himself so I can punch him uninterrupted and steal his weapon.
There are so many horrible problems with this game, and I haven't even touched on the fundamentally broken first person parkour. Jumping to small platforms didn't work in Turok two decades ago, and it doesn't work here and now. Give me third person if you want me to jump and platform or don't bother.
You can cheese all the difficult fps combat against humans by pressing q to see through walls. The only advantage they have is killing you almost instantly, almost balancing it out.
Several times I was being chased by a hoard, running through them since combat is so pointless. Trapped in a sewer tunnel, the devs coat my monitor in Vaseline to simulate the putrid filth. And it's a good thing I couldn't see because I smacked the lone zombie that I ran up into only for it to detonate instantly killing me
Good thing I couldn't see it for all the♥♥♥♥♥♥on my screen. Otherwise I would have stayed back and not beaned it on the head, killing myself. Thank God I was able to replay that entire section, I just ♥♥♥♥ing love redoing the already repetitive gameplay, said no one ever.
That spiteful "gotcha" moment by the developer is enough for me to slam this game with a big fat red thumbs down, but there's so many layers of♥♥♥♥♥♥on top of that recurring problem that I can't begin to understand how anyone could enjoy this game.
The writing is godawful nonsense with character motivations that are shallow to nonexistent. The handful of "plot twists" shoehorned in are so transparent I could see them from space.
Bonus: the final boss is a series of QTEs.

For those reading this review FTL is a great game. If you are a fan of real time strategy and space exploration, this is for you. It will make you happy. It will make you cry. Then it will make you lust for the eventual success of your ship and then destroy your hopes with a lucky laser blast from the enemy.
You will love your crew. You may even make little stories for them and give them cool names. Then as each of them get slaughtered by the shear evil and danger of space you will cry silent tears as you attempt to hold up your ship with the single surviving crew member you have left. But do not keep faith, as he or she too will go down with the ship. You will say that you will never forget the brave men and women who fought valiantly to save the Federation and then immediately toss them aside when you create a new game with a brand new ship to do the same insanely difficult task.
Sometimes you will get sidetracked by the small quests and hard decisions you will have to make, sacrificing essential resources that could have won you the game in the end. The Rebels may catch up to you and blow you into little chunks, dying in vain and no doubt increasing the effect of Kessler’s Syndrome over the planet you had orbited. But never fear, for the universe is too big to give any lick of care for your loss. But in the end you will still go back to the hanger to unlock new ships and toys to better assist you in your quest to beat the Rebel scum.
If you mod this game you will have even more fun, inevitably dying but getting cooler weapons, effects, and in the case of the "Captain's Edition" mod, a ton of more unique encounters and background stories that may or may not assist in the explosion of your ship.
In conclusion this is a great game. It may be 2D and pixilated but FTL definitely feeds adventure, strategy, and excitement to its players who will end up dying over and over to just to save the fleeting Federation.

In the game you're the captain of a ragtag space crew of misfits that hurls ineptly through the galaxy trying to fight off the rebel fleet. There are a ton of ways to play it, tons of choices, and each playthrough is completely random. All this leads to infinite playthrough possibilities from a relatively simple game. Is it going to be your favorite game of all time, probably not, but it's a great way to burn through some time when you've got a few minutes to slack off at lunch.
Also, it's fun to shoot out a ship's weapons, light it on fire, then watch their crew burn to a slow death.
Or you could continually shoot out their oxygen system and punch a hole in the hull so you can watch them slowly suffocate to death.
Although, it's much more likely you watch through tearful eyes as the enemies do the previous two things to you. Over and over again.
All things considered it's a great game.

- Graphics:
The game is beautiful, on EPIC settings, and I have read that switching to epic settings doesn't cost too much power because it's based on Unreal Engine 4, which a lot of reviews support. But, it does have issues with the resolution: I have set it to 3840x2160 and it's definitely not displayed this way. However, I read in a review that one has to pull the resolution scale slider all the way to the right, which might explain it. (Update: Indeed, pulling the resolution scale slider to the right works!)
In the character generation screen I had a bug where the feet were not displayed correctly, but everything else worked just fine. Also they were displayed correctly once ingame. (Update: This seems to have been fixed.)
- Loading times:
The FIRST loading on official servers takes very long, and with very long I mean very long, most likely due to the generation and (down)loading of data, but the loading times after that are relatively short. (Update: Indeed they are long aswell.) Don't know about inofficial servers though.
- Monsters:
There are sheeps with level 36 or level 9 in the starting region. Both of them can not be killed in a reasonable amount of time, this has to be scaled to a reasonable range. However, I have managed to kill one which had level 2 or so, so it's a matter of the level range for spawning such animals and not the animals themselves.
- Asians:
I'm not racist, but asians are flooding the european servers which totally affects the ingame atmossphere. However, besides that I can't say that they misbehaved or were attacking other players or so, so I just hope that they go to the asian region servers, or that more such servers get created. (Update: In the meantime this seems to be solved, they have reacted within one day and added several servers.)
- Sound:
The game has it's own soundtrack, although some elements have been copied from ARK. In the character creation menu I believe that there were two soundtracks that overlayed and didn't fit together, so maybe deactivate music while generating your character.
Besides those issues there are a lot of positive aspects aswell:
- Graphics:
Gosh, where do I start. The character generation allows a lot of options and is blending the changes in in a realistic manner. Also Elfs really look like Elfs :) Unfortunately some people don't take character creation serious and then run around with an obscure character, probably because they think it's funny.
The animations are beautiful aswell, not just copied from Ark and also feel realisitic with the character generated. What I dislike is that you can punch trees, although it takes a long time until even bushes break with "fisting", excuse the language.
The UI is NOT a simple Ark Clone, there are different aesthetics to it and it's also organized in a much better way and it doesn't feel techy or so. I had watched a video some months ago where the UI was simply an ARK clone, but that is not the case anymore.
Also you get advice from some mentor-like figure as part of the tutorial which I like and helps to immerse in the game from a fantasy standpoint.
- Gameplay:
The first two hours seem to be a bit grindy, most likely due to magic not being unlocked. However, once one has crafted a wand (staff), resource gathering seems much easier and faster.
Also, again, this is NOT an ARK clone. If you look at the amount of crafting possibilities and magic skills one can develop, I don't see how one can say that.
Additionally you can really level your character and allocate skillpoints to different attributes. Judging from the short time I played however, it seems that leveling takes a long time, so that's a negative but can easily be balanced out.
Having said that I'm kind of glad that it's not as fast as with ARK because this is supposed to be an RPG and leveling should definitely feel rewarding.
Please keep in mind that I will update this review, but for now this is what I feel.
Do I recommend the game? As an early access title: Definitely! It has enough content to be called a game. BUT:
This is an early access title, so bugs, even game-breaking once have to be expected. In this case I would advice to report the bugs to the devs and not write negative reviews based on an unsubstantiated first reaction. (Update: I haven't personally experienced game-breaking bugs so far.)
I really, really hope that people judge for themselves, and not just based on the first few minutes, this title deserves it. And also maybe, before giving a negative review, give the devs some time to adjust and patch the game.
Update: There are a lot of people who dislike Snail Games being the producer of the game. However, they managed to put out two patches, addressing several issues within one day. I'm not worried that they will let me, or anyone who purchases down. *thumbs up Snail Games*
Update 2: Some Survival tips:
Follow the tutorial, for berries and resources hit the bushes which are scattered around, for flowers hit them with your sword. That covers you staying alive.
To progress in the "Craft a Stone Axe" (or how it's called) you have to either gather a lot of materials from bushes, sell them at the merchant close to the spawning area which buys wood etc. and buy some stone axe from him. That way you can level up that skill much faster.
Alternatively I think you just have to gather more resources or hit some trees until they break, but the later takes a long time.
I hope that helps.

Braid is the game that deserves to be experienced. I have a good friend who complains that he hates when indie games seem pretenious. This one definitely is, it constantly reminds you that it's that sad vegan girl who loves pretending to know who Arthur Russell and The Dancing Cigarettes are while she eats quiche and carries around a ukelele that she can't play. Yes, this game can really feel that way at times, but you know what? It deserves to present itself that way because it does deserve to be treated differently.
The music and art style are all excellent as are the controls, mechanics and controlling time. Even the puzzles can be damn good. Not the puzzle picture you make for each world of course, but figuring out how to get those puzzle pieces in the first place (as well as a certain other collectible). But the biggest draw here is the story. There is what you can gather from the surface (some lovely prose and paintings) but there are more layers to the game. I will leave it up to you to figure everything out.
Braid can be just a relaxing platforming breeze of a game, but you really should take a look at the puzzle elements of the game and I mean that on every level. If you want to get the most out of this game, analyze the story and solve the puzzles on your own.

Nicknamed ''Hobo Simulator'' by some, this is THE game you have to play if you enjoy survival games. An unforgiving roguelike where you start with nothing and everything you scavenge is randomized, NEO Scavenger is played from a top-down perspective in a turn-based fashion. There is a story to go along with your desperate search for food, clothing and materials, and from what I saw, it's alright. However, nothing keeps you from simply playing as a wandering vagrant murdering people for their belongings.
This game does not hold you by the hand. You will die repeatedly while learning the mechanics, but it's one of those games in which ''losing is fun''. For 10 bucks, it's a great deal.
Some cons to take into consideration:
- EVERYTHING is turn-based, including combat, which can get very tedious when you have to select the same option over and over again to run after a fleeing target, attack someone, etc.
- Since scavenging is entirely randomized, it is entirely possible that you will find nothing to help you survive your first days, and die from exposure to cold/sickness/a blow to the head without really having the time to get into the game. This can be a huge turn-off for some.
- A few bugs here and there.

This game is very pretty and engaging and has a lot of activities to do, but it has a lot of grinding and repetetive aspects.  If you're willing to grind and actually learn how the economy and game mechanics work then you'll find a game that's worthwhile.  Otherwise, if you're offput by gender-locked classes, a lot of running, grinding and the high prices for outfits and costumes, then this probably isn't for you.
The main quests are usually very repetetive and you'll soon realize that they fall into a simple and repeating pattern.
First, you kill a small number of enemies, then kill some more attempting to collect their gear based on an RNG system that has you hoping the enemy you kill will drop the quest item you need.  After that, you will exterminate a large number of them and then summon the boss for that enemy race.
After that you move on to a different area with a different enemy and repeat.  Occasionally there is some variation, but that's the main outline.  Also, there is a lot of running in between quests and you will find yourself browsing memes while alt-tabbed in the meantime (I personally just play
).
The combat system is engaging and is more than just pressing a key to activate a special attack.  You need to momorize button combinations to pull off optimal combos, and it forces you to be actively involved.  This makes you feel like you are a skilled fighter and not just a button masher.
There are professions that you can invest time in such as fishing, farming, managing other people to work for you, and other fun jobs.  Those are usually decent income, and even more money can be made from the in-game economy and guild system.
The economy system is very complex and requires you to learn about nodes, guilds, taxes, investments, marketing, and property.  It takes some time to understand (I have no idea how it completely works still) and once you learn it you'll have mastered a good portion of the game.
There's player housing, crafting workshops, and other forms of residence that you can invest in in order to further your monetary ventures.
The armor in the game will change very little with different armor pieces and will have no personalization options excluding the ability to dye it, which will cause you to look towards the in-game Pearl Shop.
Outfiits tend to run from $5 USD to $30+ USD depending on if you purchase individual pieces or the whole set.  You don't have to purchase anything from the Pearl Shop however, and MOST of it is purely cosmetic.
I said MOST things are cosmetic because Pets can be purchased and can assist the player in looting and combat.  You can also purchase outfiits such as a fishing outfit that makes fishing better and a Ghillie Suit that literally hides your name, allowing you to sneak around.  You can purchase more inventory space as well.
Take this how you will, but personally I haven't had any problems with these in-game purchases since I've gotten along just fine without buying these.
The XIGNCODE3 is used and it was the only thing stopping me from buying this game at first.  However, if you're worried like I was, realize that if you have installed Blade and Soul before you probably have it already like I do.  Once I realized that, I went and bought this game because I had no problems with BnS.
However, this is just my case.  I don't think they'll ever change the anti-cheat, but realize that it's only scanning for cheats.
There's still a lot I didn't mention that this game has to offer, so if you're willing to give it a try, it's only $5-$10 USD depending on when you buy it.  You're not obligated to purchase anything more than the game, and anti-cheat has not given me any problems.  It is grindy though, so that's a personal thing for you.  Other than that, just know that this game is much, much more than a fighting game.

I think I hate this game. I think I honestly and truly hate this game. I really wanted to like it, I love the thought of being able to ride bikes from all my favorite manufacturers, but this game has made it a grueling and utterly dissatisfying experience.
I've rewritten this reveiw three times, but I think I finally know my problem with this game: it's arcadey enough to make the experience joyless. When I buy a racing game, like Asseto Corsa, I want to lose myself in the simple experience of driving. Just learning a car and seeing how it feels. In this game, unlocking vehicles is tied to money, which is tied to winning, which is tied to modding, which is tied again to money. Quite literally, this game's issue is "mo' money, mo' problems."
Racing becomes a chore because to get the bikes I want, I have to save money. To save money, I have to mod bikes to the absolute minimum, so I wind up running in races I'm outclassed in, furiously cheesing other motorcycles by cutting them off and blocking them so I can just barely succeed and get that much closer to what I actually want. A racing game is doing it wrong when the racing itself is an obstacle to fun.
Had this game just thrown up its arms and let you do whatever, like Asseto Corsa does, then it would have been a thousand times more fun. Had the game thrown out any semblence of realism and made the bikes balanced against each other (which they very grossly are not) then it would have been a thosuand times more fun. Unfortunately, simulation and arcade do nothing but get in each others' way, an experience only complicated by a load of poor technical choices like a bizzarely centered first person camera (in soviet russia, bike leans around you!), TCS that only feels like it slows you down, boring "straight upgrade" modding options, and suspension/gear choices that have no discernable effect on performance.
In short, an arcade simulator that attempts both and acheives neither. If you want to simulate, get Asseto Corsa. If you want to arcade, get Redout. If you want a frustrating haflway point between the two, get this.

I tenatively recommend this game to people seeking a multiplayer Real Time Strategy game with fast paced modern combat. By modern combat I mean combined arms manuevers involving supressing fire, artillery, and tank combat. The single player is complete garbage and is almost unplayable. If you're interested in this game, buy only one army at first and see if you like the online play. Because essentially that's all there is. Not that I'm complaining, the online play was the best part of COH1.
Beware this is kind of a pay-to-play game! Some players invest in "premium" commanders and will probably wipe the floor with you at some point. Thankfully, that doesn't happen often.
So why recommend it at all? Because it defies that boring RTS trope of economy and combat being seperate entities. Resource points are physical areas that automatically increase your economy, so taking and holding ground is a goal in and of itself. Also, the graphics are good and the sound is amazing. Tanks battles in particular are lovingly animated with burnt-out hulls, ammo explosions, indepdently damaged systems, and ricocheting shells.  Being something of a history nerd will make this game more enjoyable. But don't expect realism. Balance always takes precendence over realism in the patches.

Half-Life 2 is one of a kind game. When I first tried it already was 5 years old. One can write a lot of facts about this games pros and cons. Just one note would be that for me this game has some nostalgia, which mainly marks the gap between old games and modern ones. And this game falls on the later category. I have tried to play such games like Duke Nukem 3D and it felt too old for me, but this one still feels modern. As in general I don't like difficult games and always more attracted to casual games this might be the reason why I still like this game so much. Because of that I completely understand players who find this game to be bland, because from gameplay perspective (especialy after all sandbox addaptive AI trends) it is very shallow.

This is what Ride should have been. Like many people I wasn't happy with Milestone and their lack of updates to any of their MotoGP or Ride games, yet I was always stupid enough to buy the next one that came out, but they really hit the nail on the head with this one.
Pros:
-Game runs buttery smooth
-Improved physics (ragdoll)
-Bikes handle more realistic
-Improved A.I.
-Lots of new tracks
-First person view is much improved
Cons:
-Customization isnt as much of an upgrade from the first game (what about rear shocks, windscreens, rearsets, brake master cylinders, high compression pistons, ect...)
-New bike rating system isn't perfect (some bikes will have a lower rating after being modified but will be noticeably faster around the track)
-Would have like to have seen more bikes added
Overall this game is not a ton different than Ride but they've fixed almost all of the issues with the gameplay to make it a much more enjoyable experience. The new bike rating makes for much closer races. Opponents will not think twice about stuffing you going into a corner, they are much more aggressive with passing than before. If you're on the fence about buying this game I would give it a shot, no other motorcycle game comes close.

After playing the first game and enjoying it I decided to scoot on over to this game when I came across it on sale. I paid roughly about 30 dollars and jumped on in. First of all I have to say the game runs very smooth on my gaming labtop which surprised me. The characters are new and fresh also the story exists. The combat is fun more fun than I would say DQH1. Now the reason I say this is because of a few things.
You can now explore the lands a bit between the big missions which you are stuck in once you accept.
You can call in a buddy or random person once you start a story mission.
If you jump into someone elses game or they jump into yours you can select any of the past characters from DQH1.
You can only select those characters when you are helping someone online or doing an online mission with them.
My favorite part personally is now you can transform into the bigger summons. This is one of the best parts of the game that was added that is just a delight. I love becoming the stone golem and smashing big bosses down town. If you do play online as a helper though you can not summon or transform only help with your one character which kinda is lame. You also lose your summon coins if you go to a new part of the story ect which is alright I understand as if you were hording the mega summon coins it would be a cake walk of a game.
Now that I got some of the new cool features out of the game I need to talk about the delightful music. Its honestly great and makes the game keep going. Its colorful and does DQ justice in 3D, sometimes the characters 3D model looks better than their 2D art.  The voice acting is actually pretty good and you can choose between Japanese / English.
You can choose your class for your main character and level it up!
Now the bad parts of this game.
Some of the story missions are pretty dumb, like a 5 year old came up with the idea or something when it comes to some of the missions. The choices that are made you have no real options you just have to follow the story pretty much. If you are doing a story mission and some are really long and you die you have to restart from the very start of that story mission, mind you keep all your EXP so its not a total loss. Sometimes its worth it to lose just to grind a section for that EXP.
Overall this game is an upgrade in my eyes from the last game and I recommend it.

Blender is a professional, all in one, free, easy to use 3d software.
Blender allows you to model and sculpt 3d objects; rig, animate and texture them. Simulate physics.
While blender has many rivals in 3d development, it is one of the few that offers more than a single function well enough to be recommended for all. You can use Maya or 3dsmax for detailed modeling/ animation, Mudbox, and Zbrush for better sculpting and substance painting for better textures but blender offers great solutions for most of these and allows you to have a faster workflow while not sacrificing much quality.
It is a solid recommendation if you are looking for anything like this.

This game is a glorious beauty. When I first picked it up I had no idea what I was getting into, never having heard of WH40k outside of scant references in a few corners of the wider Geek/Nerd community. When I first picked it up and played the tutorial, I was a bit put off because I couldn't amass a large force of tanks (a la
and
). And
was melee combat still a thing??
I ended up putting it down to play other games until, feeling bored and wanting to procrastinate on studying for finals, I decided to pick it up again, this time approaching the game with the understanding that
. I decided to embrace the melee combat as a unique element of the WH40k universe.
I created my own army (which was surprisingly fun) and then went and did the campaign. As of writing this I have all but finished it, and I must say that this was surprisingly enjoyable. As someone who can intuitively predict the endings of most movies, I have to admit that during the first half or so of the game I was kept guessing about what would happen. Some of this is undoubtedly due to the fact that this is my first introduction to the WH40k universe (if you're familiar with the franchise you *might* guess what can/will happen next). It is probably one of the more enjoyable campaigns I've played now in awhile.
As an infantry combat game, the infantry battles, upgrades, and mechanics are engrossing and satisfying. Base building does have restrictions (you can only build within a radius of the stronghold or strategic points) but it balances the game nicely and is enjoyable.
Research is pretty interesting - you unlock new buildings and units by building new buildings and/or upgrading your stronghold/starter building. You can research upgrades for your units at specific buildings (eg, for the Space Marines at least, the armory will give you a research option which will increase the number of special weapons you can carry + gives you access to more weapons like rocket launchers). You can also upgrade you units in the field (eg, dreadnought can be upgraded with an assault cannon or twin laser cannon, predator can be upgraded with all manner of laser weapons, squads can be given a sergeant, etc.).
Edit: There are a few bugs, mostly related to saving a game in the middle of playing a campaign mission, etc. These can be overlooked though, they are relatively minor (eg, missing voice queue/background music, etc.). The biggest bug that annoys me is that the game
to forget to increase your infantry pop cap when you research the last upgrade. This can be worked with but it can be downright frustrating. Bug does not appear to affect the vehicle cap.
This game is fun. Even if you're not into War Hammer 40,000, this game is still worth playing. Play it, lest you be accused of HERESY!!

The space battles, abeit limited are very good and no star wars game since has made casual dogfighting as much fun as this. All in all, this game is a must buy if you are a star wars fan (like myself :3) Despite the missing multiplayer component, it is still great fun to play. This is a great game.

While this game does bear a lot of resemblance to Ark, I think it's better for it. It's an overall satisfying experience as far as survival games go. Despite its early stage, I've enjoyed it a lot playing with my brother. I'm just about level 20 and things are really starting to open up with metalworking and higher tier building coming in to play. There's a lot of room here for a very good game that, while similar to Ark, has plenty of room to grow into a unique variant of the same genre. The magic itself opens up a lot of very cool possibilities. Instead of holding a torch, you craft runes to give yourself an ambient light, runes to lighten your load, to heal you, etc. It frees your hands to fight or gather.
A slight word of caution: The initial load time is *very* long but after that it's quite stable and smooth. Haven't crashed in my first 13 hours and the frames can only get better. (Though still very playable as is, and higher end systems are getting great frames.)
I'd reccomend this if you liked Ark and want something different. Any fans of survival games will enjoy this, as will builders. It's not a groundbreaking build system, but it's still very nice.

*** Review in progress, will update this once I play this more***
Let me start with a disclaimer: I'm not a "fanboi" or "white knight" about this game. I learned about it like 48 hrs prior to the release, had never heard of it before. I read an article about it, liked what the devs had in mind and decided to give it a try. So it might turn out to be a disappointment, and I don't consider this to be something like the most innovative game ever. It basically seems like "Ark-inspired game set in a fantasy setting". It is amusing how so many people now say "Yuck, an Ark-clone", when a) it was pretty obvious from the start b) so many games are clones, and a lot of times, people don't mind or even applaud it, as in "Hey, look, a fun D3-clone with a better setting" or whatever.
Anyway - I like what I see so far, but you should always keep in mind that this is totally early EA, so I don't get why so many reviews complain about bad optimization or bugs.
Performance
There is a long loading screen at first (even though it was shorter than the one in Ark was when I first installed that game last December), but after that, the game ran smoothly.
Performance-wise, yes, it's obvious that the game is very early EA, and therefore not very optimized, yet it ran fine without stutters on my PC, which isn't exactly state of the art anymore (i7, 16 gigs of ram, GTX 960 with 4 GB RAM)
Gameplay
There is a tutorial which will guide you through the early stages. There are some bugs there, as in hints not being displayed correctly (to level a certain skill, you need to do certain activities, and those aren't always listed correctly). There are things missing, as in a way to sleep (couldn't find any NPCs renting rooms/beds to rest in etc.), but that is to be expected.
Gathering by magic is fun, and leveling skills by gathering/crafting is a nice touch. So you don't have to use points you earn to learn engrams (like in Ark), but level your skills by doing other things. Example - gathering wood or grass will help you raise several skills, which in turn unlocks recipes/engrams belonging to those skills automatically.
Looks
The graphics don't look as amazing as they do in the screenshots yet, but I expect that that, like many ingame-systems, will change during the development
Controls
Of course very similar to Ark. Hotbar with different slots. Drag tools into those slots, activate them to use them.
Bugs
No crashes at all. There are some things missing, and the most annoying bug right now is one tutorial quest I for some reason can't complete (have to sell goods to vendors to earn 100 G. I sold several piles of goods, earning thrice that amount, yet the quest won't complete). Haven't found a way to sleep yet, which means that my char will die occasionally until that is fixed, or requires me to eat piles of flowers. =)
In summary
It is day one of the EA. I did expect a game heavily inspired by Ark with some changes to the gameplay systems (vendors, gathering by magic, leveling skills) and a different setting. I do like what I see so far. I expect a ton of things to change, as they should for a game in development, so I will update my review and eventually post a final review once the game has been developed further and is out of EA.
If you expect a fully finished product, stay away from this. If you dislike Ark - this is very similar to it (think LOTRO, Rift and a ton of other MMOs compared to WOW), so it might not be the right game for you.
I am looking forward to seeing this get developed further, and will update the review accordingly

- I've had mixed success with it. I've now played it with 6ish different groups, and it has about a 50% batting average for whether it was a good experience or not.. It can get very intense, and one individual's small mistakes can doom everyones efforts. Some will not enjoy this.

- Bottom line: this game is a must own for any serious couch co-oper. Highly recommended.

This is a truly excellent game, and I'm glad to see it's getting some press, although not as much as it deserves.
I knew nothing about this game going in. I got it as part of a Humble Bundle and figured it was worth a try. I think I played it for about 5 hours straight that first time. It's probably the greatest random find I've had.
You have various perks and handicaps that you select to build your character, so you can choose to have excellent vision and mechanical skill but be a weak, feeble insomniac. After you create your character, you wake up in a hospital, with no idea what's going on and why the world has gone to hell around you. Immediately, you have to deal with a dogman who's charging down the hallway towards you. Your traits will affect how you can deal with it.
Afterwards, you venture into the outside world. It is bleak and largely empty. You'll set off, with nothing but the hospital gown on your back. You can forage for food and water, but you should really make sure that the food's fresh. Do you know what berries are poisonous? Can you trust that water? Explore a little further and you'll see some ruined buildings. Scavenge in them and you might find some actual clothes to keep you warm, maybe some preserved foodstuffs or a cell phone. Be careful, though, and try not to make too much noise.
You see someone on the horizon. You wonder whether they can explain what happened, but then you notice the rough spear that they're wielding. They charge at you, and you try to run. You can't get away fast enough, so you try to fight them off with a broken bottle you've picked up. You take the spear in the shoulder, and you stagger with the pain, but you get in an incredibly lucky thrust with the bottle and your opponent goes down. You shred some of your clothes and wrap the makeshift bandages around your wounds, but it's too late--infection has taken hold. In your last conscious moments you watch night fall, and you see a glow in the distance. It may be an illusion created by your feverish mind, but it almost looks like city lights...
Each playthrough is memorable in this game, even the ones where you freeze to death the first night. If you survive in this strange new world, you can find people and locations that will help you find out background about this world. There is a story here, but you have to go searching for it. Even if you don't find all the backstory, you still have a tale of desperate survival that's incredibly compelling. I heartily recommend the game to anyone who's interested in survival games.

Ultimately I can't recommend Ride 2, despite thinking that it has a lot of really good elements: pretty solid graphics, great bikes with excellent detail and it runs solidly on my machine. Generally speaking, I *like* the "simcade" style racing games, where traction and line and setting up corners properly are important elements, but I've just come off playing quite a bit of Forza Horizon 3, a game which has such a well-constructed loop of races, events and getting new vehicles that just moves you through the content at such a good pace--a game that feels great to just play--that Ride 2 is like hitting a brick wall of inaccessibility.
I'd actually managed to forget that I went through this with the original game when it came out. If you don't play moto GP games, even if you play other racing games, prepare to place dead last in every race even on very easy difficulty, and to do this for a very long time. Slowly you will chip away at the difficulty, and over a period of weeks you will eventually start winning races, cranking up the difficulty, and actually get to the point where the game is tense and engaging, but this is a weeks' long project. There is no gentle difficulty curve or onboarding to speak of. You are going to need to accept having a bad time for a very, very long time before you are going to be able to have any fun playing this game.
Assuming this turns out like the first one, there really is a fun game hiding in here, but it's the chipping; it's the long, tedious and unfulfilling process to get to the level of capability you will need to have to expose that game. It just kills me that once again they've made the decision to make this game basically unplayable by non-fans when all it really would have taken was the addition of easier difficulty modes that non-experts can play on, and massaging the reward curves for playing to make it just a little less of a grind to experience the game. Why throw all that hard work away on a great racing simulation by making such poor game design choices?
So as both an IRL game developer and motorcyclist I have to give this a thumbs down. SO close to greatness, but just hamstrung by making it so miserable for new players to pick up and play.

A solid Warriors entry that, like many of the recent spinoffs, brings things to the table that make it stand out from the mainline entries.
In this case, Dragon Quest Heroes 2 feels way more like a traditional RPG with how the game progresses (with the game's large sprawling overworld that you travel through in order to get where you need to go - and the game abandoning the typical Warriors "capture/hold fields" structure in lieu of more conventional objectives, such as "Kill this guy" or "go to this point in the map"), how the characters operate (magic users feel completely different to more physically-inclined characters), and how combat progresses (thanks to larger monsters having multiple tools in their arsenal, they can easily feel like mini-bosses in their own right, requiring you to patiently observe and react to their moves in order to beat them safely - there is also a monster medal system through which you can call upon the monsters you defeat like assists in a Marvel vs Capcom game).
Combat isn't really deep, but there's excellent variety in the movesets - an important thing for any Warriors game. That you run about in a party of 4, and can switch between characters mid-combat seamlessly, really helps keeps things feeling fresh as well. Party composition is of slight importance too, as you'll typically always want at least once character capable of healing your party (much like you would in an ordinary Dragon Quest game).
If you're a big fan of Dragon Quest and always wanted to know how it'd feel if it was more of a hack 'n slash, you'll enjoy this. If you're simply a fan of Warriors games, definitely give this a whirl as well.
If you're not really big on either, you probably won't like this game. But let me stress the "probably" part, as this really doesn't feel like your archetypical musou game to me.
Also, you don't have to be familiar with Dragon Quest in the slightest in order to play this. The story is completely self-contained and doesn't expect you to know any more about the characters from other games, or even dragon quest as a whole, than the main character does (that is to say - nothing).

In 41st Millennium there is only war...
Warhammer 40k: Dawn of War was RTS game from the universe developed by Relic.
Gameplay is large scale and epic with a mix between base building and managing units. There are two main resources: Power and requisition. Requisition is used to make buildings, units, upgrades. The same can also be said of power, which generates slower. To acquire these resources you need to capture points on the map and hold them. You can field a variety of units including infantry, land vehicles, heroes and super heavy unit. All units cost requisition to make. Upgrades are also available for purchase from buildings. You can upgrade squad with weapons or more members.
There are two modes to play with: Campaign and skirmish. Campaign follows Captain Gabriel Angelos of the Blood Ravens chapter of space marines as he faces off against the orc horde. Unlike the latter entries to the series, the campaign is set into levels.  Each level of the campaign starts you off with a few units. Your goal is to build a base and then an army to accomplish various objectives. Such objectives are split between primary and secondary ones and involve either destroying a specific building or enemy unit. Completing all primary objectives will win the level, while secondary ones are optional. Skirmish mode has you face off against up to 7 players/bots in game modes such as annihilation and victory point capture. There are a total of 4 races available to play as including Eldar, Space marines, Orcs and Chaos. The other expansion packs (ie Dark Crusade, Winter Assault, Soulstorm) will allow you to select more races to play as and against, should you acquire them.
Audio is excellent. The weapon sound effects feel as they should. Background music fits well with combat. Voice acting for campaign (as units) are well done.
If you are looking for a good RTS game with lots of action or you are interested in the 40K universe, this is where to start.

Coming from over 1700 hours on Ark, this game feels like a breath of fresh air from the staleness of Ark. The similarities aren't that egregious, its really just similar resources (wood, twine, straw to arks wood, fiber, thatch) and the same design concept of a survival game with tameable beasts. The major difference is in DNL you have NPCs with prebuilt towns, magic, and an actual skill type system.
In Ark, when you level up you get 1 skill point to spend in 1 of several stats, and then a number of "engram" points which are used to purchase plans to build everything in the game.
In DNL, when you level up you get 2 skill points, one for Health/Attack/Mana/Constitution, and then one for Stamina/Weight/etc (can't remember the last 2 off the top of my head). Plus the crafting tree is learned by doing, not by banking points. To learn how to make melee weapons you craft ones you already know, or you go out and harvest stone and that helps learn the next rank of melee weapons. There are numerous categories that are gated behind character level and then the crafting skill level. It's an interesting system that sort of borrows from 7 Days to Die in a way. I really enjoy it.
Now, the bad part is when I first logged on I tried to play online on one of the official servers. They only offered PVP servers, and I picked one that at the menu said was 0/70 with low latency for me (40ms). I load in and there are people everywhere (clearly not 0/70) and there was a 2-10 second delay from trying to gather a bush to actually getting the berries or whatever. It was bad. I tried this for about 30 minutes and gave up. A few hours later I came back and made a single player game and I got sucked in.
As far as performance goes, it was about as I expected from the first iteration of an early access title. On all epic settings I see about 30 fps pretty consistently with occasional drops to 25 on my rig (see below). A lengthy load in, even being on an SSD, but no load screens after that initial load. I expect over the course of early access there to be graphical improvements as well as performace optimization.
Rig:
i7-6700k 4.4ghz
16gb RAM @ 2.4ghz
EVGA GeForce 1070 8GB
500gb Samsung EVO SSD
2560x1440 gsync monitor
In the end, I planned to only spend about 2 hours on this and then wait and see what Citadel offers next week, but ended up going for 10 hours on the first day. No regrets.

This is a first impression about Ride 2 because I'm thinking of getting a refund. I'm not sure, so take it for what it is, a bit less than two hours into the game.
I have been patient with Milestone, even hopeful at times (silly me). I have played the last four motorcycle games they have made now and every time it is the same. I really try to like their games, and to be fair there is some entertainment to be had there, if you can swallow the anger, frustration and if you had any high hopes - your initial expectations. I don't know what the folks that are praising this game compares it to, given the fact that they somehow accept this. Well actually I think I do; they compare it to previous Milestone games, as there is pretty much no competition, and that would explain a lot.
Graphics are not worse than before. The mirrors actually seem to reflect what's behind them as opposed to only the sky or the ground as in Ride 1. Too bad you can't turn your head more than an inch to actually view the mirrors (depends on the bike), or the rest of the things going on beside you, and on top of that you are not being able to adjust the field of view (what were you thinking Milestone? I'd really like to know). Still not up to what you would expect from a game this generation. Low poly bikes, low res textures and shadows - the usual stuff with a bit more polish. Xbox 360/PS3 graphics. Again.
The helmet cam is, once again, a joke. This is really odd since there is a really nice one used during the replays. The one used there may be a bit too "busy" for gameplay but it features more realistic movement and a good sense of speed, two things not present during actual gameplay. Again, what were you thinking, Milestone? You have two first person cameras in the game in gameplay mode and both are pretty much the same exept one is just obscured by a totally unrealistic view of a helmet. I don't think any of the devs put on a helmet to see how it looks like. I just get sad during replays seeing what could have been there during the actual racing.
The sound is a bit better than before. It is still not very good though and the lack of wind noise ruins the immersion for anyone who actually knows what it's like to ride a bike. In fact, this game fails on almost every level to replicate the feeling to ride. Quite ironic given the name of the title.
Riding a bike in real life is an awesome feeling. You are out there in direct contact with the elements rather behind a shell in a car. The force and sound of the wind and weather fighting against your body and your bike while you, with the power of the engine and it's beautiful roar push through the air, victoriously. It's just awesome! This game makes it seem boring and that is a shame. It should be at least somewhat exciting even if you are on your first Scrambler or whatever the bike may be but it is just boring, even as you progress to faster bikes. They did include some really sweet café-like bikes, which I love, but they are just so boring to ride here so they are just eye candy at best, along with the other not superfast bikes. I understand that it is difficult to make slower vehicles exciting in games but with everything Milestone constantly does wrong it just ends up with below acceptable gameplay.
Maybe no one at Milestone is a biker and they just don't know better. Maybe they are an underfunded developer with good intentions. Maybe they are just bad developers. I don't know. I am however constantly let down as soon as I think they might learn and improve from previous mistakes. To enjoy this game I'd recommend getting it on a sale, without expecting too much.
I'm sure there is some fun to be had despite all this but so much here is so flawed I cannot recommend it at its asking price. It is a Milestone game in its purest form.
I'll update this review if I discover I'm wrong about something or if something else needs attention, if I decide not to request a refund that is.
*** Update ***
Multiplayer:
No option to communicate with others via text, not even in the multiplayer lobby. Connection loss has been very frequent for me. I don't know if it is because of netcode issues or just the host disconnecting (no dedicated servers) but it has ruined at least 50% of my races so far. If the host sucks att Nordschleife (3 laps minimum), don't expect to be able to finish the race. And there is no player list available in game so you're in the blind much of the time regarding player positions. I haven't had any issues with lag though.
Quick multiplayer update: The game has frozen on me multiple times now while hosting races, followed by a message some seconds later saying everyone has left the race, so there seems to be some serious issues with the network stability. And you lose points when you're disconnected. This bloody game, man...
Customization:
Basically the same as in Ride 1 and it still feels tacked on. There are for instance sometimes five, six or so chains to choose from on some bikes, looking exactly identical with identical effects on the bike. The ONLY difference being the name in the selection box. That says something about the ambitions they had with customization and how they try to hide it (not very good). Many times you can't even change the base color of the bike. Visual customization is a joke and a lot of opportunities are lost. Just imagine what they could have done with the café-bikes. The rest leaves a lot to be desired as well. Nothing new here.
As expected though, there are still some nice moments that contrasts all the negatives. It can be a really satisfying feeling when you nail a corner or a section. The replays are nice. Too bad you can't save them. I'm glad they included Nordschleife and Monza, two of my favourite tracks.
The actual handling of the bikes is pretty good. It's just so undramatic and calm as opposed to what it should be. If you are not racing on the faster bikes it can be compared to a casual ride on your mothers scooter.
In short; if you like Ride 1 you'll probably like this as well. Just don't expect any real evolution of any kind and don't be surprised to find most of the previous game's flaws still present in Ride 2.
If there were alternatives I wouldn't touch Milestone's products. Most of the hours I've put down with this game is just me being an achievement wh*re.

I am enjoying the heck out of this 'rogue-like' (I HATE that term. Who apart from myself and my aging buddies even played Rogue? Kids these days with their graphics and multi-cores!) space game.

To start: I used to add a much longer header to these reviews, but since it often made the reviews too long to submit, I've opted to leave it on my Backloggery.
Gameplay: One thing that's very difficult not to do when talking about any base-building RTS, let alone a military Sci-Fi RTS, is to not compare it to Starcraft, especially considering the influence that the Warhammer 40k world present in Starcraft. After all, there's a race of humans kinda like the Terrans, there's an alien race like the Protoss, and while not present in this game, there is a race similar to the Zerg. Also much like Starcraft, the gameplay is centered around building bases.
The differences come in, as you might expect, with the gameplay. While this is something of a personal taste, I really do quite like how resources are handled in this game. Your two basic resources are Requisition (kinda like Minerals) and Power (kinda like Vespene). You gain requisition from controlling Strategic Points on the map. It is also from these Strategic Points that you build your base, from which you can build in a radius that expands up to a certain point. Unlike Starcraft, you gain resources at a set rate per minute, which is slow enough to require you to think about what you wanna build, as opposed to spamming harvesters all day. Power is gained from building generators, and much like Requisition, is gained at a set rate per minute. There are also Slag Deposits on some maps, which you can capture and build a special generator on, allowing a bit more strategy with your expansion.
Units are produced in squads, and vehicles have their own unit cap outside of the squad unit cap. With some research, you can increase your squad cap to 20, and your vehicle cap to 10. While this doesn't sound like much, keep in mind that each squad can have up to ten people in it, reaching Starcraft's famous 200 unit limit very easily, and surpassing it with vehicle count. I do wish that your construction units didn't count as one squad, which can be especially obnoxious as there is no way of recalling your construction units other than sending them out to maybe punch the enemy's base or something.
While the game doesn't necessarily have as many units as Starcraft, the matter of unit composition is largely handled by equipment. Your basic squad can be outfitted with four different special weapons, of which each squad can have up to four specially equipped members. Another aspect to this game is its Morale system, in which you can use particularly gruesome attacks to break apart squads, leaving them easy for the pickings as well as discouraging some easy rushes from time to time.
The single player campaign is somewhat disappointing, as it only features the Space Marines. I'll talk more about the story later, but for now know that there aren't Eldar, Ork or Chaos Marine campaigns (Eldar being the kinda-Protoss race and Necron being the unlisted kinda-Zerg race). There are apparently campaigns in the expansions, but since I haven't played them yet, I can't speak for them.
Now, we come to the important question: how fun is the game? This was my first "legit" introduction to the Real-Time Strategy genre, and I gotta say; I picked a damn good game to start out with. The gameplay is very streamlined, there's usually a great bit of action going on at any one time, and the mechanics are simple enough on the surface while still having a good bit of depth to it for people to play for quite some time. If you're looking for an RTS to get someone's feet wet with, I can very easily recommend this one over Starcraft (although Starcraft may take a bit of weening into) for first timers to the genre. Simple on the surface, deep underneath, very streamlined and just overall a hell of a lot of fun to play. 9/10.
Story: Since the completion of this game, I've gone on and read some more of the Warhammer 40k lore, and I've gotta be honest; the campaign doesn't do the series justice. The content is kinda neat, and the Orks are still fun to watch bumble about, but for the Space Marines, this game doesn't do very good in showcasing just how grand their empire is. It feels kinda... fanfic-y, in a not so great way. They try to do some intrigue, but it just doesn't work, and the cliffhanger at the end is, to be quite frank, inexcusable. While the dialogue and writing in-game is good, the actual story itself just isn't good. At all. Disappointing. 6/10.
Graphics: Unfortunately, to get this game to run at 1080p I had to download some modded files, which may trigger anti-cheat protection if you happen to play multiplayer. Also, running these files breaks the HUD for the Space Marines (although strangely not for any of the other races). It's frustrating, and I really would expect Sega to get around to making 1080p available in-game without any modding required. Despite this, the game looks pretty good for a 2004 game. Unit design is pretty neat, most of the areas that you visit throughout the campaign look really cool, and of course, seeing an Ork mech tear a Space Marine in half is just plain awesome. I never suffered any frame drops, which is always nice for an older game, as older games around this generation like to depend entirely on your integrated graphics chip if you happen to have one, leaving your GPU idling uselessly. 4.5 for not having 1080p available by default, but the half point comes in because a mod is very easy to download and install.
Sound: The voice acting during the cutscenes isn't bad, but it's not exactly award winning work either. Voice acting in battle is pretty good, though, especially for the Orks (I may also have a bit of an Ork bias). The music is pretty excellent as well, and is definitely memorable. Paid $24 for this game and four days after purchasing the game I had almost 24 hours on it. $1 per hour of zombie killing mayhem is a deal I will take any day of the week. Bought this game for the co-op mode and was not disappointed at all.
For the base game:
Pros:
- Hordes of zombies mean you need to constantly be on the move.
- Nice variety of zombies
- Guns are super-powerful (as they should be)
- Unlock the ability to dropkick zombies
- Unlock a grappling hook (turns the game into Just Cause 2 with zombies)
- Some of the best co-op I have ever played
- Fun leveling up unlocks (see above)
- Night is spooky
Cons:
- Story starts out strong but starts to fall off about midway through the game.
- Could have had significantly more character development.
- Story is rather short. I highly recommend doing some side quests between story missions. I did about half of the side quest missions. If you just rush through the story you may find yourself lacking the gear or upgrades to fight tougher zombies.
Considering this game is from the same developers of Dead Island, this is a hands-down improvement and I am excited to see what Techland does in the future. This game addresses most, but not all, of the concerns/complaints of Dead Island and I'm confident that in the future Techland will learn from the smaller, but still present, mistakes in Dying Light.
All in all, I give the game 8.5/10

Company of Heroes 2...it's often best to say it's one of those game that people like, or don't like; There is no grey area from what I've seen in the reviews, but I have generally liked it.
Coh2 (At least vanilla.), is the sequel to the first (Duh) Company of Heroes, but instead of the Western European front, this one throws it towards the Eastern European front, with the Ostheer and the Red Army of the Soviet Union duke it out in mud or snow.
Gameplay is similar to first, basically a micro managing scenario, along with your standard tactics with the first game (Suppression, Vehicle Direction, Cover, ect.), while adding a few little quirks in this one, the first being the "True Sight" fog of war system, which provides more ideal places for ambushes and makes smoke more effective, instead of making every unit clairvoyant and can see something over where it realisticly shoudn't. Another one is the winter maps, particuarly the Easter Front ones, where Blizzards can rage and deep snow (There are mud and river fords in non-winter maps.), which can freeze your infantry to death.
There is also a recent expansion that gives you two new armies, basically the Western Front Germans, and the Americans, which now gives you four armies like the Original.
There is now a 5th new faction, the British, which still have their unique defense options from the first COH, but now have introduced mobile set for those who wished to us the Brits in more offensive options thant the first. (I swear they better add goddamn Duffy or else I'm gonna be mad I spent 10 bucks.)
Besides this, do get this game on sale instead of regular price, and make sure that if you are willing to shed some green on DLC, get them on sale as well. Besides this, I do like this game still, and is particualy fun to play with friends, randies are just nasty man.

This game.....I love this game to death. I've played countless hours on the ps2 version of this game, and now that i've had it for a while on pc...Its still as great as it used to be! This is THE star wars game (If you're looking for the infantry viewpoint) to play. Graphics and animation are par for the course (if not better) from the ps2 era of games. The sound design is wonderful, blasters and lightsabers sound the way they should. Though, the original cast didn't make a return to voice the hero/villians (Mark Hammil, Harrison Ford etc). The story is wonderful, the telling of the republics fall to the empire and retelling the story from episode 3 and the story arc ends at the battle of hoth. There is also galactic conquest, a board game type play style where the objective is to capture planets and establish a hold over the galaxy. Then comes the meat of this games replayable nature, instant action. This is the "free play" mode of the game, being able to play on every planet, with every game mode (Conquest, 2 and 1 flag ctf, hunt, and my favorite hero assault). The space battles, abeit limited are very good and no star wars game since has made casual dogfighting as much fun as this. All in all, this game is a must buy if you are a star wars fan (like myself :3) Despite the missing multiplayer component, it is still great fun to play. This is a great game.

Braid is an astonishing love letter to the medium of videogames.  It simultaneously resituates the Mario-style 2D platformer and challenges genre conventions with contemporary takes of common tropes like "dying" and "lives" and so on.
The art is gorgeous and vibrant, and the occasional personal background touch or oddly out-of-place applique lend an air of legitimacy to the title, preventing it from being a by-the-numbers tileset of levels.  The music is pulled from varying classically-trained artists and perfectly juxtaposes the peaceful, but engaging gameplay.
At its heart, the puzzle-platforming is brought to perfection, with mechanics that are devious as well as delightful.  You will use your brain.  You will hurt your brain.  And at the end of it all, you'll walk away from an adventure that will leave you in awe.

Although a large majority of my hours have come from afk fishing and things of that nature I still have spent some time playing BDO and here are my thoughts.
PROS
- large non instanced world.
- decent sized player base.
- large amount of classes (much variety).
- extensive trait/ability options.
- very thurough character customization.
- fairly noob friendly.
- offline progression (sort of)  the game allows you to do task like trading, fishing, walking, traveling, and farming while sending the game to the tray of your computer reducing the stress on your computer and allowing you to AFK.
- boob physics
- (this could be a con also) very grind heavy gear must be leveled up using stones and once the gear reaches a certain level it has a chance to fail or even break so this becomes some what frustrating but rewarding once you reach end game.
- ways to level without questing.
Now on to the cons
CONS
- gender locked classes.
- microtransaction shop, although not game changing can allow others to have more inventory slots or higher exp gane, however mostly cosmetic.
- (as I mentioned above) very grindy game.
- guild based this applies to solo players, very guild based.
- content become slightly repetative but there are many options of content so its not really a problem.

Too long; didn't read:
A fair improvement over Ride 1 and certainly a decent game in and of itself. A few issues, but decent track list and bike selection make up for it. Overall: 8/10
Gameplay:
Overall, not bad. Let down maybe by the lack of open maps (i.e: Not being able to use the dirt track on Franciacorta) and LONG auto-drives to the start line.
Graphics:
Great Motorcycle graphics - sharp and quite accurate. However, not so great track and out-of-track graphics (most notable around the Nurburgring)
Sounds:
Average music for the game (not necessarily a bad thing) and fairly decent Motorcycle sounds. Not too many complaints.
Physics and Camera:
Not bad all-round, however sometimes the P.O.V camera can be floaty which can be a little disorientating at times, but in all, not that bad. Handling is markedly different compared to Ride 1.
Selection:
Great bike selection, however, I think categories could be expanded (i.e: Classic-style Motorcycle). Tracks are great, however I would personally love to ride the Hayabusa around the Castelletto SuperMoto circuit.  Gear is a bit more than ni the old game, but generally much of the same. Chracter/Rider probably has less choice over Ride 1, but still isn't bad.
Overall: Not a bad game and definitely an improvement over Ride 1. I would personally recommend using some sort of cheat engine to get your money to maximum and buy all the bikes and just mess around at first few hours. Then have a go at the races.
Total rating: 8/10 - Improvement on the previous, but 1 or 2 areas could be improved further, but they are fairly minor areas.
