Ride 2 actually does improve on the 1st one in a lot of ways and makes it a much better game, so I'll go ahead and split this into sections so anyone debating the game due to price gets a good idea of what to expect.
Story/Campaign:
They've completely redone the campaign mode from the original game, and it now flows MUCH better and makes way more sense. The campaign is much like driveclub and the original game, but separate sections are added in to help newer players go along and learn to actually handle bikes and figure out correct racing lines before getting a literbike and smashing into every wall (Though you do get to enjoy that in the first race).
Upgrading bikes increases an arbitrary performance point value which are limited based on the event you're entering, so you actually have to watch what you do to your bike if you want to race. As far as it keeping you from becoming much faster than the competition, there's still room to improve there, as I used the NSR125 to gold every event in the first class.
Bike handling:
This is honestly the biggest part of the new game. Bikes handle MUCH better. They handle very realistic and it's much easier to control them as the game does give a bit of assistance with inputs from a gamepad for obvious reasons. As another review complained, bikes seem like they have too much grip in the rain, though this is due to the game limiting steering input (to lower lean angles) and smoothing out braking. Whether this is a bad thing is up to you. Motorcycles in the rain are very finicky and require smooth inputs, which are difficult to do with a gamepad, so I believe it's an elegant solution with a good outcome.
The supermotos are also extremely fun to race, and require an entirely different method of racing compared to street bikes. The selection of bikes included is about as big as the previous game, but the bikes themselves seem to be modeled much better and handle much more realistically than the twitchy hell that was RIDE.
Customization:
There's been a large amount of customization for bikes added, and many redundant menus were killed off from the original game (I'm looking at the wheel menu that took 10 minutes to get to the end of).
Everything has been streamlined, the race bike enhancements are a nice touch, and you can still customize a great deal on your bike. With this said, it's still a bit limited and very much like the old game, especially in terms of power modifications. I never had much of a problem with the old system save for the really long menus, but since those have been fixed I feel customization is at a very good point in this game.
AI:
The AI still leaves a bit to be desired thus far. They still seem to have trouble seeing the player and like to crash into you if you're in their way. However, it's improved by MILES since the first game.
The AI in the first race shows this, as they all followed good lines, and only the riders below 5th seemed to be braking too early into corners. At some point, I even ended up leaving 3rd place by 6 seconds and got in a battle for 1st with the AI, which led to me finishing in 1st by 0.029 seconds. In my experience, they've at least made the AI okay enough that you can play through the races with them and not get frustrated by AI crashing into you at every corner.
Graphics and audio:
The graphical enhancements do show through in-game, and I feel that it looks much better than the original. The Audio in-game has also been GREATLY improved, with bikes no longer sounding like hair dryers, but rather actual bikes. You still do need to ramp up the graphics settings in the menu to ger a proper looking game, but all-in-all this entire section of the game has been greatly enhanced and you'll most likely enjoy it.
Misc:
I'll just use this for other little problems I feel the game has:
Taking screenshots is a bit stupid at this point in time. You have to set the camera and wait for the menu to disappear so you can use steam's screenshot function, as it won't let you take a picture otherwise.
The race starts are still very abrupt, and if you're not ready as soon as the track loads in you're probably going to miss the start.
Loading times are still fairly long. They've been improved and load time gets cut in half after you've done the initial load, but it's still a good wait.

So I've played this a bit before release so you know... Playtime not entirely accurate.
I don't really have much to say or add but here goes:
It's a minimalist, roguelike, RPG that manages to be intruiging without any visual elements.
Obviously there are visuals and not just text, but they serve more to simplify the UI.
The UI is pretty great honestly and it's something a lot of these hardcore roguelikes just don't give a crap about, so it's a breath of fresh air to say the least.
I love the addition of the ambient soundeffects and the music. It livens up the experience quite a bit and makes it easier to immerse yourself.
To sum things up: it's immersive like a great text adventure. Lots of descriptive text and important decisions with the addition of much needed visuals and soundeffects.

The port is lazy and lacks standard features for a PC game, and for this reason I downvote it. In terms of gameplay, it adds and improves much needed RPG aspects to this sub branch of Warrior and DQ series. Most notable is the open world feature. The last DQH was based out of an airship and used a flat map to transport to maps with pre-set missions, this game adds a very light open world exploration element that greatly improves the formula. The 2 protagonists can now change classes and weapons, but cannot use all weapons, overall it is a step in the right direction. There is no basic appearance customization and only pre-made outfit changes are in place. Monster Medals are still in the game, and while useful, play a much smaller role, which takes the emphasis off tactics and increases the emphasis on combat, which certainly isn't an improvement, but goals and gameplay is a little more diverse. The different fighting styles are extremely simplistic for a warriors game, which is saying something, if it didn't have magic and monster medals spicing things up it would be incredibly boring.
On the whole, the port isn't the worst out there but it's definitely not something to be proud of, being lazy at best. The combat is fairly dull and repetitive and is dependent on gimmicks to keep from being a yawnfest. The RPG elements are very limited and minimal by normal standards, but are noticeably improved and barely manage to salvage the gameplay and keep it interesting. If the port wasn't lazy and halfassed missing a lot of basic features I would have given it a thumbs up, but the gameplay is barely in the positive as it is.

Paid $24 for this game and four days after purchasing the game I had almost 24 hours on it. $1 per hour of zombie killing mayhem is a deal I will take any day of the week. Bought this game for the co-op mode and was not disappointed at all.
For the base game:
Pros:
- Hordes of zombies mean you need to constantly be on the move.
- Nice variety of zombies

- Unlock the ability to dropkick zombies
- Unlock a grappling hook (turns the game into Just Cause 2 with zombies)
- Some of the best co-op I have ever played
- Fun leveling up unlocks (see above)
- Night is spooky
Cons:
- Story starts out strong but starts to fall off about midway through the game.
- Could have had significantly more character development.
- Story is rather short. I highly recommend doing some side quests between story missions. I did about half of the side quest missions. If you just rush through the story you may find yourself lacking the gear or upgrades to fight tougher zombies.
Considering this game is from the same developers of Dead Island, this is a hands-down improvement and I am excited to see what Techland does in the future. This game addresses most, but not all, of the concerns/complaints of Dead Island and I'm confident that in the future Techland will learn from the smaller, but still present, mistakes in Dying Light.
All in all, I give the game 8.5/10

Let's talk about why Relic would do good with a publisher like EA.
- They're constantly releasing useless patches for the neverending crashes and bugs that come with the game, if I had a dollar for everytime I got a "Bugsplat" error report (keep in mind, all my nvidia drivers are updated and I'm playing on an ASUS G750 series, so it's not my computer for any of the game's fanboys that will try trashing my hardware), I'd be able to pay people who actually know what they're doing to fix the game myself.
- Let's go over the huge imbalances (not only in the core factions, but the DLC factions as well) between tanks and infantry, and emplacements alike.
- Starting with the Wehrmacht, Relic has made up for their HORRIDLY squishy infantry with overpowered tanks (remember how in WWII the German infantry had better training than ANY OTHER nation as well as equipment?, Relic must've forgotten that part in their "we want this game to be as historically accurate as we can make it" chapter in their book entitled "what's a history book?" But we'll get to their tanks flaws in the next paragraph.
- The Russians I have nothing but hate for due to their overwhelming numbers, which IS historically accurate, but due to many patches their infantry are actually far more enduring than the German infantry, meaning if you're playing a match of Soviets versus Wehrmacht as the Axis, you're gonna wanna break your keyboard in the first 20 minutes...until you get tanks, then the one sidedness shifts, that's IF the Soviets haven't stockpiled an armada of AT guns (AT in the soviets case stands for "ALL TARGETS" because it murders everything in it's attack cone, which far exceeds that of any other unit in the game, including snipers believe it or not.). And then there's their Tank destroyers, which can also be used to annhilated anything in it's cone (which thanks to a toggle mode, is the same as an AT gun). Any variant of the T34 can take on a panzer one on one and come out on top (bulls***, their nickname even by their own troops was "the tincan"), and their heavy tanks can T-bag a Tiger (THE Tiger, THE TIGER TANK, GET'S SLAPPED BY RUSSIAN MACHINERY) As far as the Russians go, thanks to a million unnecessary patches, are easily the most frustrating faction to fight in the game.
- Now comes the reason I'm writing this review, the DLC, starting with the Western Front Armies.
- MURICA, if you were to send a paper mache tank into the battlefield, it'd have more success than this game's version of the legendary sherman, while historically wasn't the strongest tank on the field, it was certainly versatile and reliable, which this game fails to understand, instead we're given a tank that can barely hold its own against and Anti-Infantry Flakpanzer. The infantry I will admit are very adaptable if used correctly, so nothing bad to say there. So why am I complaining other than the fact that their tanks are in a word, useless? Because, I, like many people, pre-ordered the DLC  for 20 bones with high expectations, hoping we'd get 2 new factions with variety, but instead, we're given 3 commanders with each new faction, only to find out that there are far more that can be obtained through this new "drop" system, that should only exist in MMO's. I'll rage about that in a second.
- Oberkommando's, putting it simply on account of the fact that I've only used them a good 4-5 times because I find them...just boring. Starting with the fact that they have only about 2 different kinds of mobile infantry (3 depending on the commander you're using), then there's always the case that their AT emplacements can retreat (which defeats the purpose of the word "emplacement"), as if AT guns weren't overpowered enough, they can also occupy buildings (because apparantly something that shoots shells large enough, and with the force to penetrate tank armor, is perfectly fine just chilling in a fragile structure, yea that makes sense), they have a tank that shoots nukes, so there's no point in defending against them, and literally all of their units are high damaging armored units, making them MURICA's nightmare (despite them being the faction that came with them in a DLC bundle, talk about promoting imbalance)
- Finally, it comes down to why I started with the sentence "Let's talk about why Relic would do good with a publisher like EA." Because all of the DLC that people had to pay for before this s*** drop system they now imply, is now free so long as you just farm drops in game, (basically this STRATEGY game is now pay to play, pay to win). Even worse, not only did me and I don't even know how many people spend money on all the commander packs for nothing, but the new factions had additional commanders to start with that can only be obtained through drops (I didn't find this out until I recently got a commander for MURICA and literally flipped s*** thinking to myself "thanks Relic, for giving me a fourth commader for this faction that cost me $10"), and the only thing the people who pre-ordered this s*** DLC got were a few camo's and faceplates.
So here I am, a simple gamer with crushed dreams because he thought he was gonna get what he payed for, only to find that I dropped $20 for 6 new commanders, some s*** maps which are dwarved in creativity compared to the ones from the workshop (which are free), and 2 armies that either stand on the line of "Just good enough," or "Overpowered as s***." It's sad to think this pile of imbalanced, impartial s*** comes from the same developers who made the original CoH and Warhammer: DoW 2, yet I will shamefully continue to play this game, because I will hold on to the small hope that one day Relic will get their s*** together, patch the things that need to be patched, and eventually somewhere along the lines come out with a Dawn of War 3, instead of that s*** MMO they're coming out with. Thank you for listening Steam, alot of these words are just my opinion, you can take or leave them for what they are.

OK, First Impressions. Have only tried a few races and time trials but looks good so far. Big improvement over the original ride. Graphics are smooth and detailed with good lighting and appear quite realistic. I'm getting 60fps synced with everything maxed out except AA at 2560x1440 on a gtx980ti. Really good sensation of speed in the bike and helmet cams. The helmet cam is the one I use but I just wish there was a way turn off the helmet. Since you spend a lot of time tucked in, it would also be useful if the fairing windscreen wasn't so darkly tinted as it tends to obstruct your view. If you use the suggested line feature to get your legs it works very intuitively, not just coloured green through red, but the triangles stand as you approach a slow corner and lay down as you get toward the suggest speed. I haven't see any obvious pop-up, clipping or bike parts popping on and off that have sometimes appeared in previous Milestone releases. I'm not getting any framerate hitches or skips when going through corners either.
Bike handling is arcade even on Pro settings, so it's no MotoGP or SBK. It's quite enjoyable, the relaxed handling doesn't feel off or unrealistic, just very forgiving of throttle and braking. I would be wishing for something a bit less forgiving at pro settings but they're definitely aiming at a more casual level. If I there was anything I liked about the original Ride it was just collecting the bikes more so than upgrading and customising; so I would probably say the same here.
Haven't hit any trademark Milestone bugs, everything works rather smoothly. Remapped my controller without issues and haven't had any crashes or had to do any fiddling to get up and running.
I'm enjoying it but don't buy expecting a hardcore simulation. The game makes the original Ride completely redundant so if you buy consider it a total replacement. If you have a Steam Controller you're in luck; the game doesn't have native support but using the gyro as left stick with a bit of anti-deadzone works great and is a really immersive method of control.

I really enjoyed this game for much of the near 300 hours I played. It is very similar to the first two Diablo games.
I made the mistake of switching to Veteran mode near the end, because many opponents were becoming too easy to beat. However, one of the opponents I soon ran into was a "Nemesis", or super-monster. I was unable to continue past that, so never even tried the expansion packs. Most opponents were appropriate level throughout the game, though going back to earlier areas they didn't scale and were too easy.
There were some bugs. Once, an NPC gave me a reward of a sword when my inventory was full. It was dropped under the NPC and impossible to pick up. The bugs were generally minor annoyances.
There was no sense of when the endgame was near, so it came as a surprise and a bit of a letdown.
It was repetitive. I replayed the same areas many times fighting foes I'd already defeated to get more supplies found in those areas.
Overall, I'd say this game is worth playing if you get it on sale, and can deal with the things I've mentioned. I recommend not choosing a higher difficulty until you finish the game and expansions once. Even then, hope you don't run into a Nemesis monster in the way of a mission.

Updated review after playing 12+ hours:
Veredict: IF you like motorbikes, this is a MUST BUY. If you'd like to play a motorbike game closely resembling the Forza Motorsport series, this game is for you. If you're looking for the Assetto Corsa of motorbikes, then keep looking. This is an accesible, fun, informative and nicely detailed look into the world of motorbikes, not a sim racer.
PROs:
- Graphics are two notches better than on Ride 1. Better effects, reflections, and a more realistic tone to everything you see on screen. They could be better optimized, though, I am getting frequent frame drops.
- Control is vastly improved, especially in first person. It's now very fun to ride first person. The finer control is most noticeable when assists are off and the motorbike reacts to slides, changes in weight distribution, and the like.
- AI definetly is better/faster than Ride 1. When bikes are equal, you need to stay on your toes and the smallest mistake usually results in lost positions. On the other side, AI is very cautious and never risks deviating from the perfect driving line, so you can use that to your advantage. Sometimes you can see them fighting for positions or going to the ground, too.
- Loading times are definetly better, no more "having dinner while loading".
- The starter 125cc races are a blast. Sound is great on those tiny bikes, too.
- Each motorbike's description is very interesting to read. Seems more fleshed out than on Ride 1. Manufacturer's descriptions and history are also great for bike lovers.
- The new circuits are a blast.
- Supermotard is a nice addition. It takes some adaptation to ride those beasts, but it's quite fun.
CONs:
- First person needs more vibration to convey the feeling of high speed motorbiking.
- Some circuits are too flat. Nordschleife in particular, is bumpy as hell and it feels -almost- perfectly flat in Ride 2.
- Riding the cafe racers is a bit boring. Being highly tuned, hand made bikes, you should expect some less-than perfect handling or at least some differentiation from stock bikes, but that's not the case. The best thing about those bikes is their descriptions.
- Invitational events pay a little too much. After a couple of them you're able to buy any stock bike on the market, even after only a couple hours of play. I guess they're there so you can buy the super expensive superbikes.

After about 60 hours into the game, having one complete run through the normal difficulty I can safely post my review now I think.
This game is a must have if you are a fan of Action-RPGs, not only does it have an interesting story line, with much for yourself to find out lore-wise it also has extremely slick controls and a nice aesthetic (Which was recently reworked to look as stunning as it does now).
Pros;
-Classic exploration driven Action-RPG with casual loot everywhere you look whilst still providing a fun challenge on normal difficulty for first timers.
-Multi-class!* You can have two 'classes' at a time, to gain access to their respective skill-tree, each combination having their own class-name.
-Re-speccing skill points.
-Great story line, side-quests fleshing it out nicely by often providing places with lore notes/books.
-Choices matter! Be it a reputation gain/loss or how some NPCs will treat you.
-Rich characters.
-Smooth gameplay, you thought Titan Quest was smooth? Diablo 2? Diablo 3? Nothing compared to Grim Dawn. And with the recent gamepad update, can you now more easily play with a controller.
*You have about 6 masteries (Soldier, Demolitionist, Arcanist, Occultist, Shaman, Nightblade) and 2 DLC Masteries (Inquisitor and Necromancer) and you can combine any. I for example have a Sorceress (Arcanist/Demolitionist) and a Witchblade (Soldier/Occultist).
Cons:
-Strainous collector sidequests; Whilst giving a decent to great item that may aid your journey, the quests take too long and require restarts of the game. For example, you are asked to bring some cloth, around 8-10 I believe. They only drop from enemies in certain area's. Once you cleared the place, you'll be lucky to have found 2-3 if not the usual 0-1. I had to restart the game at least 5 times to be able to clear the area again to get enough cloths.
-Confusing builds; If you are a casual player, creating or reformatting your skills can be tough with all the combinations to consider, adapt gear, do the skills from either class compliment each other if you combine them this way. It's not a pick-up and play game. (Subjective)
-Repetitive enemy types. Certain area's hold a specific theme in terms of enemies, whilst giving the feel areas are dominated by a certain species, it does feel forced. The Grim Dawn was recent, how could they have grouped together on specific locations that quickly? Or why at all? I'm talking about the non-ethereal monsters, obviously. It boggles my mind somewhat and it does break the immersion in my opinion. Whilst in Titan's Quest it felt only natural, here it feels forced in my playthrough. The enemies on their own are varied nicely, gameplay wise this will not hinder your experience.
-Farming. In the sense, even some common materials listed as non-rare are even more rare than rare items. Chipped claws are used in a lot of things, yet these are so rare. Bristly fur on the other hand, also used in a lot of crafting things, is abundant.
Conclusion:
Give it a chance, it's still getting good updates from time to time. If you see this game on a sale don't hesitate.

Overall the game is quite fun and enjoyable and has its own style and pacing.
Graphics: They look a bit dated for a 2016 title but it's not trying to be a AAA game. You do get used to them and the art style actually becomes intriguing after a while. It reminds me a lot of Diablo 2.
Gameplay: Like most good ARPGs, Grim Dawn has some fun challenges of clearing trash mobs, champions and bosses. Unlike most modern ARPGs the quests are somewhat more interesting and evolved than simply going to Point A or Point B and clearing mobs of monsters. However, the monster killing does get somewhat repetitive after a while.
Sounds: Decent sounds. Dark and creepy and reminiscent of Diablo 1. The music can become a bit intense so I tend to toggle it on and off. It allows you to hear the ambient noises better.
Replay Value: The maps tend to suffer from Scooby Doo syndrome. You can run across a map and it all looks the same and seems impossibly large. Of course, games like the Diablo series and Path of Exile and other ARPGs have the same problem.
Fun: Fairly worthwhile with lots of classes and adding a secondary class probably means you could mess with combinations of the 8 classes for hundreds of hours. But I can't see me doing that on single player.
Rating: 7/10

Review SOLELY for The Following. Not the base game.
Having sunk some hours into it, I overall cannot justify getting this DLC unless your getting it at a steep discount. Much of the time spent has been grinding filler, rather than actual FUN. Driving from one end of the map to the other, spent the first hour looting every car I saw for car parts before realizing it really has no benefit whatsoever and then only stopping if there were 5-6 military vehicles parked. Okay, coin flip chance of stopping, I just drove past many because it wasn’t worth the effort to stop and loot them either.
The Pros:
- Crossbow is a nice weapon. Great for dealing with hordes of undead if you hop up somewhere with a vantage point. Yes, it's one shot at a time, but headshots instant kill most enemies. So if you need to loot that crate, it can be easier killing 50 zombies with silent headshots than trying to hack and slash your way through, or using guns/explosives and dealing with the constant waves of virals that follow. And you can always go recollect your ammunition while you loot the corpses.
- Guns and bullets. Bullets are like candy now. You will find them EVERYWHERE. So many military outposts. So many military zombies who have ammo when you loot them. Crates filled with military ammo resupplies which give 50% ammo to ALL gun types, behind only a medium lock. Generally multiple of these crates around when you find one. If you don’t mind shot gunning viral hordes that spawn for using the gun, you’ll never need a melee weapon again.
- The bosses are an awesome touch. They are GREAT enemies, satisfyingly difficult to kill and offer good rewards for doing so. Prepare to die multiple times, and use up your entire stock of bullets and explosives killing some of these guys. The small arena's they are in also prevent you from really using cheap exploits to injure them without getting hurt yourself. You gotta fight em fair for the most part.
- The story is interesting. Short, but hey, it's a DLC not a main storyline. It's intriguing enough to keep you interested, without dragging on unnecissarily. Your here to kill zombies, not figure out the inner workings of a cult, right?
- Volatile nests. Much like in the main game, the darkzones filled with volatiles are a blast to fight through. You really feel the pressure as the timer warns you how long till dawn arrives and your pretty much screwed. Loved clearing them out.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
The cons:
- Driving sucks. I hate this aspect of the game. The car handles like crap. And the map is so stupid giant that you really NEED that car, or you’re going to be trekking through 2 kilometers of empty farm land to reach your next objective. So if you wind up on the far side of town, you have to weigh whether it'll take longer to fight your way BACK to town, get your car, and drive around again, or just go to your next objective on foot.
The car seems to serve no purpose BUT to justify the maps size though. You can get upgrades for it: Better suspension, brakes, engine. You can get perks for it: Better armor, craft better upgrades, etc. But at the end of the day…it doesn’t offer anything. It’s literally a distraction to sink money into so you can get from A to B faster. The only times the car has helped me in any way other than “I gotta cross the whole map to get to this objective” was mowing down hordes of zombies in my bumper. But I only run INTO those hordes…in the massive expansive open farmland between A and B.  You need the car to get through the hordes, and the hordes only exist to have something to do to hide the fact that 70% of the map is empty space.
- Driving and volatiles sucks even MORE. If you’re driving at night and get volatiles chasing you, it is legitimately easier, no exaggeration, to get out of your car and lose the damned things on foot than try to outrun them. Because the instant you get in the car, every volatile instantly becomes the road runner with jetpack boots, and will match you at 80 miles an hour. The difference is, once again, the car SUCKS for driving. So speeding down crowded roads, hoping not to run into side streets that are blocked off but not marked on the minimap, or hit any debris or zombies that will slow you down makes it all but impossible to shake off the volatiles once they’re chasing you. Later on you can get upgrades to help with this: UV headlights, mine dropper, armor plating for your car, etc. But even with those, it’s faster to just hop out, throw a flare and wander off 100 feet while they wander aimlessly looking for you.
- Parkour is nonexistent. Again, massive massive map, lotta empty space. In the main game, I found my agility rapidly boosted past my power xp, just because I running, climbing, and flying kick enemies into spike walls every 50 paces. Out here, It’s now the reverse. There are so few reliable pitfalls, traps, spikes and environmental dangers that you have to hack and slash your way through every fight. And since so much of it is open farm land, your agility growth is gonna slow to a crawl. It’s a really weird choice to take a game that’s all about its parkour freedom of movement…and remove that core aspect from the game.
-  Crafting supplies are dramatically reduced. One thing I took for granted in the main game is just how much junk is lying around. I was never short on household supplies and chemicals for bombs, or string and alcohol for Molotov’s. Now the map is so empty, I have to purchase most crafting supplies at every trader I see, or slow to a crawl stopping at EVERY parked car on the road to open the trunk and hope to find something good. There’s not many apartment buildings and crates just randomly filled with junk laying around every 10 paces anymore. You really need to go grazing for it rather than just loot along the way to where you wanna go.
Overall: Get it on a particularly good steam sale. On the bare surface level, it’s more of the same dying light fun as always. But the driving and stuff drag it to such a CRAWL that you will spend more time just trying to drive around than actually doing something interesting. I cannot justify it at full price, at all. But if you get it for $5 on a steam sale, and go in with the knowledge that much of your time is going to be spent running and driving through empty places, it can be an alright add on. Just don’t expect loads of replay value.

I love this game, it's totally legit.  I think it definitely feels like a true RPG, it's just the battle system is Warriors-ish.  But it's got character leveling, skill buying, proficiency grinding, hunting for items, crafting, and so on.  I think it's awesome.  If I would call the game out on a couple of things it's the AI of both your party members and the enemies.
More specifically, the boss monsters seems to automatically target whomever the player is controlling the majority of the time.  It's kind of frustrating when you're trying to play a long range class or a support character.  There isn't any sort of aggro or hate system and, yeah, that blows.  Best to just stick with a class you can stay up close with and/or be very good at dodging.
Regarding your NPC party members, I've caught them snoozing on the job while you're fighting monsters.  They just stand around doing jack squat and, sometimes, the healers in the party don't heal you when you need it.  You have to get used to switching to the healer and healing the party yourself for some of the harder battles.
Besides those gripes, which can be major for some, I think the game is great.  Definitely worth the price I paid.  I've finished the main story and there's a ton of content still left to play.  I'll probably be at this for a while.

I.) The Basics
Dragon Quest Heroes™ II, or DQH2 for short, is a so-called Musou game, where you battle hordes of weak enemies with a few stronger enemies mixed in to make matters more interesting, as well as the occaisional boss fight. This all is presented in the universe of the JRPG franchise Dragon Quest with the graphical style of manga artist Akira Toriyama of Dragonball fame.
II.) DRM
The game is protected by Steam DRM with a layer of Denuvo anti-tamper.
III.) Graphics, Settings and Performance
The graphics in this game are colorful and capture the unique style of the DQ universe very well. For DQ series veterans all the monsters will be recognizable in an instant from the lowliest, smiling slime to the largest dragon. The effects, for the most part, share the colorful scheme, but can get in the way of situational awareness in heavy combat.
The settings are fairly limited. For one, only 16:9 resolutions seem to be supported. There is also no way to tweak AA or AF and many other comforts enjoyed in other PC titles are still missing.
The performance itself seems to have similar problems as on the first game, meaning achieving a stable frame rate seems to be nigh on impossible, as in certain scenes with complex lighting (e.g. Lavalands) dips in frame rate are a given.
IV.) Controls
The game is a port from consoles and plays, as such, best on a controller. However, contrary to most games developed by Koei Tecmos Omega Force, keyboard and mouse is also an option in this game. You only have the option of one key per keyboard command, however, you can double up on the mouse and at least five mouse buttons are recognized. Intriguingly, the mouse, contrary to many other Omega Force titles, can be used for moving the camera around, which is a plus.
V.) Music, Sound and Voice
The music by composer Koichi Sugiyama is orchestral in nature and has many of the staple pieces of the series. It flows well and is nice to listen to and lends to the charm of the game.
Sound effects for the most part are spot on and give a good aural feedback on what is happening in the game.
The game is not fully voiced, however where it is I prefer the Japanese voice actors. English is still acceptable, though.
VI.) Gameplay
DQH2 starts off with the selection of a male or a female character as the main character, however, the other will be playable throughout the game once character switching is learned. There is no difference between both sexes in this game. You will gain other characters from other parts of the main series DQ games throughout the story.
Every character has individual skills and new ones can be learned both through leveling up the characters themselves and spending skill points or by increasing the weapon proficiency in combat.
The fighting styles offered are diverse, though there are some characters/classes that are stronger than others.
The combat itself feels, at least if compared to games like Bayonetta, a bit clunky. You can dodge and block attacks, however, to do so you must not be in an attack or skill animation. Which means you need not only learn enemy attack patterns, but also your own attack cool downs if you want to avoid damage. A character with healing abilities should be part of the four man group because of that, as avoiding damage can be hard when an unexpected attack from off screen does happen. Other than that the combat system is fairly easy, granting long invulnerability periods on dodges and not being timing intensive on combos.
The AI of both your companions and the enemy is fairly simple and can cause bouts of violent attack as well as times of characters standing around and doing nothing. Micromanagement, at least when it comes to healing, is indicated.
VII.) Story
The story itself has few twists and starts of with an attack of Dunisian monster forces on the town of Harba, where the main characters of the story are currently visiting. It is a standard story of some great evil trying to awake and the heroes struggle to prevent that, with few memorable characters and truly emotional moments.
VIII.) Online
This game has online multiplayer, however, it is not a true co-op experience, as players can only opt to help out others in story missions, which they themselves had already completed previously or in a seperate dungeon mode. If you were looking to play through the game in true co-op that is sadly not possible.
IX.) Final Verdict
If I were to assign numbers to this game to rate it, it would be a 7/10. It might be enjoyable for both fans of Musou type games, as well as the DQ franchise, though for purist the action oriented might be too much. If you are in it for the story mode only, you will look at about 20-30 hours of gameplay. If you are an achievement hunter you might get as much as 180 hours out of this game, due to some grindy achievements.
All things said, I can recommend the game, but not to everyone. If you are looking for a more RPG style oriented Musou, this might be your game, if not, wait for a sale.

-Combat is enticing and nerveracking
-Very difficult, survival-esque rollercoaster.  You can't have it all - choose wisely.
Cons:
-May get repetitive.  This doesn't fully count as a downfall, but you'll typically run into the same crowds of aliens in similar circumstances and text dialogue, which makes total sense from a game design perspective.
-There are none.
I cannot say I have seen it all, for there is still dozens of more playthroughs to attempt, fail, repeat, and eventually succeed.

Ok this is my impression so far of the game. before I get started the first load takes an abnormally long time and I have noticed some minor gliches with the graphics, most center around the character creation but they dont seem to happen every time so its hit and miss.
In terms of performance I can run a dedicated server off my pc and join that same server with a steady framerate. Pc wise I'm running a geforce gtx titan x, 16 gb of ram and an i7, if your using something less than that don't expect to play on the highest settings, which you will really want to do, as the lower settings are not all that impressive graphically. reminds me most of ESO in terms of visuals if I had to compare it to something. (I have noticed some reviews from people with better pc builds than mine who couldn't get it running well at all, mostly with 1070's and 1080's makes me wonder if the pascal arctitecture is reacting badly to this game)
In terms of gameplay, you are looking at fairly standard survival game fair for the most part, harvest materials, forage for food, hunt and tame creatures or deadlier monsters. However way that craftables come to you is a little different than how it usually works. The various craftable items and spells are aquired through gaining experiance in that area. for example if you want to learn about light magic you can craft the sigils you need for casting light magic or go all voldemort and hunt down unicorns for light exp, progressing to stronger spells in that chain, there are several types of magic to use so where you start is up to you and what interests you most.

Addressing the elephant in the room, yes the game is more than similar to Ark in the survival aspects if you don't like Ark you more than likely wont like this game. Between the two games the key differences are:
-the 3rd person only camera
-dodge roles and back jumps to use in combat makes melee fights more viable than most survival games
-the addition of magic as a key game mechanic from simple spells to help survival to more advanced magic
-npc towns with vendors and currency note:(vendors only buy bulk items, and what they want to buy seems to change) ---donating gold you have earned to your faction vendors will change the goods that they have and will earn you titles in your faction
-the character creation is more indepth, 3 races to choose from and enough sliders that you can get your character to look more or less how you want them to, I would like to see a few more options for customization but its fine for right now.
In the end I would recommend this game to those that enjoy survival games, a more mythical environment and want to see a different approach with some more choices as to what your building towards. as with any early access title if you are not prepared to face glitches and problems during the ongoing development better to wait this out, or buy and try, if you really don't like it you can get a refund.
ps: as I have been playing on a passworded server of my own creation for friends and myself I have not encountered the player killing community that is no doubt present, if you play online survival games you know how toxic they all are,human nature at its best. so team up with friends or be prepared to have a bad time on official servers, or host your own like me and pve with just the people you want.

Well, i bought this game when it was still in development, and i've to admit that I didn't play this much for the time it's been in my mind.
It's the legit child of TItan Quest, but in a way more mature world.
PRO :
- Story :a bit used and over-used but I still enjoyed to follow it, and to do each and every quest that i could find.
- Mechanics : The same skills system used in TItan Quest, well I can't really explain it, it's better to see it to fully understand how does it work; but in a few lines : you choose a first class that use specific charecteristics and you obtain a skill-tree, in wich you have to spend point to progress, up to 50. This allow you to unlock spell and spell amelioration more an more powerful. At level 6, you can have a second class/specialization that allow you to mix two differents class. Thus, you have an impression of huge freedom but it"s double edge, if you mess up too much you end up with a character that is kinda... weak. But you'll have the opportunity to re-alocate points, but you won't be able to change classes.
- Gameplay : it's not as nervous as Diablo 3 where you run / jump / dash / teleport everywhere, but the rhythm is really enjoyable. The game is really nice as you can farm factions' reputation, and thanks to a DLC you could challenge another game-mod which is survival like, you have to confront successiv waves of monsters, stronger and stronger, then you can reclaims a rewards or try to take on the upper level ! Enjoyable !
- Graphics : Well it did aged, it's still really nice but can't be compared to today's game.
CONS :
-The  interface, that I don't really apreciate. I find it quite messy but it's my personnal opinion.
-The difficulty is quite the same as usual : you finish the game in normal mode, then have to restart for the next level of difficulty. I know that most of a-rpg game use this mechanics, but it can be quite boring.
- If you plan to play this game, it's always nice to try to check some informations about the build in order to not screw up your skills. Because you'll always be able to build as you want it's always effecive as you start the game, but in the end-game you'll have a hard time.
Well i totally recommend this game, must have !

Cons:
- Some 'random number generator' frustrations because of the way 'chance to hit' plays a big role in the game.  At 75% chance to hit, you can count on missing multiple times every couple of battles, which usually results in a teammate dying.  (And even though the game is kind of designed to let characters die now and again, it's actually such a big penalty that you do NOT want it to happen).  Even at max, 95% chance to hit, you'll get the occasional 2 or 3 in-a-row miss that drives you crazy.  Save often so you can quit and reload when someone dies.
- It's possible to ruin the game for yourself early on through the base management (the Sim City-ish bit).  I can't remember what it was, exactly, but one thing you can invest in results in the aliens levelling up.  Invest too much too early, and you'll be facing deadly aliens while you're still at low levels with no cash.  At that point it is literally impossible to win.  Definitely look up a couple of FAQs before you start, so you can avoid this.
Pros:
- Absolutely, utterly, everything else.
- The storyline is brilliant.  Intrigue, conspiracy, side-stories that tie in well with the main story, and gameplay and character and facility development that is heavily tied into the storyline.
- I was really surprised that the sci-fi alien attack setting was really well done.  Enough human development and intrigue focus that it didn't feel overly 'Star Trek-ky' or anything.
- Base and facility development isn't my kind of thing, but it was actually quite enjoyable in this case - more about levelling up aspects of your team than really micro managing everything Sim City style.  There was one thing related to how you level things up to avoid (see above), but otherwise it seemed secondary to the actual missions and battles.
- A good amount of variety amongst the types of soldiers you can get, with such different abilities that you really utilise them in different ways.  This really plays up the strategy aspect, as you decide which combinations of soldier types to use each battle.
- Having soldiers get injured, so they can't join missions for a while, is a great idea.  It forces you to play with combinations you might avoid otherwise, which adds extra variety and depth to the game.
- The abilities... and then the super duper awesome abilities that you won't believe you get later!  (Hint: If you read any FAQs, don't trust them when they say you need to focus on one set of the two super sets of options that come available.  You can afford to invest in both, and it's MUCH more fun to have both).
- Quite a good range of mission types and alien types keep the variety going.
- Other stuff that I can't remember or can't tell you for spoiler reasons.
The cons are pretty big, but you can avoid one if you read up on it a little and reduce the other by getting into regular saving habits.  I did both, and I honestly think XCOM is the best game I've played in years and years.  There are some other great games (like Divinity: Original Sin) that come close, but this edged them out because... it is simply THAT cool.

Spacejacked really breaks the formula of the Tower Defense Genre.
As someone who has played TDs since Warcraft 3 custom map days of Wintermaul TD, I was excited.  The more I played the more I didn't feel like I was playing a Tower Defense.
The best aspect of Tower Defense games is the freedom of build.
Spacejacked only lets you build in designated spots, with only 3 towers.
The "fast-pace" gameplay is overdone.  Not only can your hero serve as a turret, removing the passive element of traditional TDs, you need to sell & build towers constantly as you never have enough resources.
I commend the developers for mixing up the genre.  I just can't recommend the game at a $10 pricetag. I would recommend the game Dungeon Defenders for TD fans wanting a "fast-paced" TD experience.

It reminds me a lot of Super Crate Box with tower defense mechanics. You are in control of a space dude with a blaster. The blaster has a recharge, it can only shoot for so long before going to a real slow semi-auto function. To aid you in destroying the intruding monsters on your ship, you have access to metal which can be used to construct defenses. What are you protecting? A core that controls your ship....when it's gone....you are gone. There is three rooms to defend and if one core goes they all go.
Defenses come in three flavors.
This does damage while slowing your enemies. It is quite useful when it comes to aliens who move at a sprint or to just slow a crowd. It's the only defense that hits more than one target.

Blender is a free open source 3D modeling, texturing, and animating tool.

Blender originates from a Dutch Animation studio known as “NeoGeo”, in 1995 Ton Roosendaal rewrote NeoGeo's 3d software into what we now know as “Blender”. Naturally, Blender has greatly changed since it's rewrite in 1995, however, those who use Blender have Ton Roosendaal to thank for this excellent open source 3D Program.
Reference: Blender (2009) History of Blender. URL:
For 3D graphic designers, there are quite a few different software choices out there. After getting out of college, I was a full fledged AutoDesk 3ds Max user, with a tiny bit of experience with AutoDesk's Maya, and Mudbox.
Unfortunately I wasn't working in my career field where my job provided my 3d modeling software for me
. Ultimately this makes practicing 3d very difficult because my student license's all expired a few months after graduation.
Thus started my quest for finding a 3d open source program that I could use; for those who don't know “Open Source” Software is software that can be freely used, changed, and shared. But it is only distributed under licenses that comply with the Open Source Definition. I suggest checking out
for more information on open source software!

There are far too many outstanding features on Blender to highlight in my review, there are customization that will make blender more user friendly, depending on the 3d modeling medium you were trained in.
You will probably need to look up a tutorial to learn where everything is, but Blender lets you model objects, from faces, edges and down to the vertices, apply modifiers, texture, animate, by using key frames, and much more.
No steam achievements in this review. However there are real life applications for getting good at blender, your models could actually be used in video games.
Blender is a free open source 3D program, you can download Blender on steam, on at their website... again, completely free.
I can't help but sing the praises of Blender, most of the greatest details that will make or break a 3d software program will be in high end work flows, since Blender can actually have addons that makes it's potential dynamic and limited only to hardware.
On that note, there is one consideration before you dive into blender: Hardware. 3D software eats up RAM and graphics like the most state of the art video games. You need a gaming rig to model professional looking work.
Blender even works on lower-end computers, but it can and will crash if you push it too hard. If you find your computer having difficulty, you shouldn't try to work with blender while Steam is active.
I recommend Blender for anyone who's interested in becoming a 3D artist, or those whom are looking for a cheaper way to practice their 3D art, design for video games, movies, and much more.

Compared to the other games I've talked about so far this one's a bit obscure, and seems to have gone under the radar. I was fortunate enough to be gifted it during the Summer Sale, and I'd say it being overlooked is a shame, because it's quite a good title, especially for the developer's first game as it seems to be.
Spacejacked manages to be even more low-key than Orcs Must Die in its environments. As the name implies, it takes place entirely on a single spaceship with four rooms, only three of which will actually be attacked. You also have much less towers than usual in this kind of game, at only three: a gun that shoots rapidly in a straight line, a high damage, slower laser, and an area of effect one that slows enemies down a bit. A bit mundane, but the real trick is in the layout of the rooms. Enemies will spawn at the top before working their way down to the room's core, and some complicate matters by crawling along the ceiling to take detours. Thing is, your player character can do the same thing, by manipulating gravity. This lets you build towers on both the floor and ceiling, which can drastically alter how good your defense is. You also come equipped with a blaster, which as another reviewer put it, is strong enough to matter but isn't too powerful, and can only fire for so long before it has to recharge.
You'll need every advantage you can get, as despite the game's cutesy look it becomes brutal pretty fast, with any of the rooms spelling a game over if it goes down. Your defenses persist throughout the campaign, but it's good about pressing you despite that, and selling turrets (which gives you all of what you paid back) is sometimes a necessity. Each level is one day, which so far contains three waves, meaning that losing doesn't set you back too much though, which is nice. I'm not sure how long the main campaign will be, but besides it there's an endless mode and a lot of challenge levels if you're still looking for more. It seems designed for more arcade fun than a sheer amount of content, which is certainly a valid focus to have.
Lastly, I also like the game's sense of humor; it's not hugely in your face, but it definitely doesn't take itself very seriously. One touch I liked is in the first challenge mission, which takes away your gun. Instead of just doing nothing when you hit the button, your spaceman points his finger and goes 'pew pew!' Hard not to recommend a game that does that.

Ok this is my impression so far of the game. before I get started the first load takes an abnormally long time and I have noticed some minor gliches with the graphics, most center around the character creation but they dont seem to happen every time so its hit and miss.
In terms of performance I can run a dedicated server off my pc and join that same server with a steady framerate. Pc wise I'm running a geforce gtx titan x, 16 gb of ram and an i7, if your using something less than that don't expect to play on the highest settings, which you will really want to do, as the lower settings are not all that impressive graphically. reminds me most of ESO in terms of visuals if I had to compare it to something. (I have noticed some reviews from people with better pc builds than mine who couldn't get it running well at all, mostly with 1070's and 1080's makes me wonder if the pascal arctitecture is reacting badly to this game)
In terms of gameplay, you are looking at fairly standard survival game fair for the most part, harvest materials, forage for food, hunt and tame creatures or deadlier monsters. However way that craftables come to you is a little different than how it usually works. The various craftable items and spells are aquired through gaining experiance in that area. for example if you want to learn about light magic you can craft the sigils you need for casting light magic or go all voldemort and hunt down unicorns for light exp, progressing to stronger spells in that chain, there are several types of magic to use so where you start is up to you and what interests you most.

Addressing the elephant in the room, yes the game is more than similar to Ark in the survival aspects if you don't like Ark you more than likely wont like this game. Between the two games the key differences are:
-the 3rd person only camera
-dodge roles and back jumps to use in combat makes melee fights more viable than most survival games
-the addition of magic as a key game mechanic from simple spells to help survival to more advanced magic
-npc towns with vendors and currency note:(vendors only buy bulk items, and what they want to buy seems to change) ---donating gold you have earned to your faction vendors will change the goods that they have and will earn you titles in your faction
-the character creation is more indepth, 3 races to choose from and enough sliders that you can get your character to look more or less how you want them to, I would like to see a few more options for customization but its fine for right now.
In the end I would recommend this game to those that enjoy survival games, a more mythical environment and want to see a different approach with some more choices as to what your building towards. as with any early access title if you are not prepared to face glitches and problems during the ongoing development better to wait this out, or buy and try, if you really don't like it you can get a refund.
ps: as I have been playing on a passworded server of my own creation for friends and myself I have not encountered the player killing community that is no doubt present, if you play online survival games you know how toxic they all are,human nature at its best. so team up with friends or be prepared to have a bad time on official servers, or host your own like me and pve with just the people you want.

You know, I originally rated this game positive and cited some pretty fun encounters and experiences I had. Unfortunately those experiences were the exceptions and I was lucky to have had what was essentially a perfect early run at the game. However, after much more time spent in the game I can give a far more accurate review that I really didn't expect to give.
TL;DR Game is not enjoyable, not worth asking price.
As of August 9th 2017, my number of hours is fairly high, borderline no-life status, for someone playing this game.
In those hours, a fair percent of it spent in the obnoxiously long loading screen, I have yet to hit a resource and gather it with the first or even second hit in the best of circumstances, I have yet to utilize melee combat effectively due to the in ability to register hits on others, I have not been able to build a decent base due to innumerable bugs and bad design choices, I have spent insane amounts of time taming animals with such broken AI that they are virtually just fast-walking storage containers, Some times a tamed animal that I was able to actually use would just get stuck on an invisible broken piece of terrain forcing me to manually screenshot and write an email to the devs in order to report the map bug..... I could ramble on forever on the absolute insane amount of bugs, glitches, and poor design decisions that make up this game.
I was one of the first to tame a frost dragon(broken AI), activate dark alters(doesn't work), become a lord(does nothing "yet"), use NPC's(broken), obtain rare mounts(9+ hour tames), and really fully experience the game on a vanilla official server(game client doesn't sync with server so nothing registers).
I held out and went through the hell of dealing with all the bugs and nonsense in hopes that the devs would steadily make patches, fixes, and finish content. So far, out of several minor and major patches only three things have been added/changed: A giant death scythe with cool particle effects for a melee system that does not work, increased light levels at night so that it is completely pointless why the hell is it called "DARK and light" anymore, and they added full stat bars to animals so you can see exactly their hp levels and stamina totally breaking immersion.
I even dealt with the fact that you're required to sleep as a regular survival mechanic but you can't actually sleep until level 10 which takes about an hour plus to reach, 40mins for quick people.
The patches claimed to fix a lot of things but didn't actually. Claimed to allow NPC's to respawn, most players have never seen the them still. Claimed to fix melee and gathering hit detection, feels worse.
I seriously could ramble and ramble about the short comings and failures this game stacks up but I feel a point is being made here.
This game continues the tradition of vaporware early access, claiming to have so much and then the moment the game is in your hands spilling the truth in the most indirect way possible.

Fast paced tower defense plus 2D run'n'gun that pushes all the right buttons.  Awesome retro simplicity in gameplay (run, jump, shoot, build one of three towers) with plenty of modern features (upgrades and extra challenges galore) along with an intentionally silly story make this game utterly scrumptious.
You know those crazy dreams where a bunch of random pieces from your life / movies / video games get smushed together in a ridiculous fashion that somehow make a weird kind of perfect sense?  Well, imagine a dream where Megaman lost his job and decided to instead pursue his secret wish of becoming a spaceship handyman, only to be sucked into an 80's sci-fi movie plot where aliens were invading the ship and only his newfound turret-building skills and rusty blasting action could save the day.  This is Spacejacked in a nutshell, and it is glorious.
Spacejacked's innovative take on the usually stagnant tower defense genre seems almost ridiculous on paper (retro-arcade 2D tower defense? Reeeally?)... but somehow, it just *works*.
You control a Mega-Man-esque engineer named Dave, blasting away at waves of various enemies while your turrets provide an abundance of heavy fire support.   However, instead of one simple tower defense layout to maintain, you have *multiple* areas of a space ship to defend, with enemy waves attacking one or more areas at a time as they try to reach the ship's core.  In the few seconds between waves, you must frantically warp between rooms to tear down turrets (which refunds their entire cost) and build up new ones in the room(s) that are about to be under attack.
Simply put, I adore this game.  The gameplay is fast and fun, and the frenetic action is interspersed with a quirky story that meshes well with the underlying retro-sci-fi vibe.   While Tower Defense isn't everyone's cup of tea, the beauty of Spacejacked is that it turns the usual layout-planning concept into a strategic-action-arcade mashup that anyone can enjoy.  Spacejacked is the perfect example of an Indie title done right, and I highly recommend giving this delightful game a shot.

When I first saw this game, I thought it would barely have enough content to keep me entertained for a couple of hours. Well, I'm glad I was proved wrong.
How can I even start to describe this game? "A super fast-paced arcade tower-defense" it's a good start but it doesn't cut it.
This game makes most tower-defense look easy by comparison:
- You have to manage to defend your spaceship's cores located in different rooms from getting destroyed. This means, you have to fend off hordes of enemies in several separate rooms, basically at the same time, with limited resources (metal). Since you barely gain any metal from the monsters/ aliens you kill, most of the time you'll be running from room to room destroying your own turrets to get metal to build or upgrade turrets in another room and then repeating this process until all rooms are secured.
- To complicate things further, you can only build a few turrets in each room and those must be built in predetermined spaces (i.e., there are specific spots to build them).
The character itself is very easy to control. He can either walk on the ground or in the ceilings. And did I mention that he wields a blaster that looks like a chicken as a weapon? It has limited fire time (cooldown time) though.
To help you gather metal, there's also a bullet hell mini-game, in which you control a pod and try to destroy ships and other objects for as long as possible, while trying to collect metal. If you touch another object, your pod is destroyed and you are back on HQ (hopefully, w/ more metal). You can only play this mini-game once a day.
The
is funny and entertaining but it also takes time to complete, especially if you are after the achievement "Perfectionist" like me.
Besides Story Mode, there's also "Challenge Mode" (which contains several challenges to be perfectly completed) and "Endless Mode". Both a lot harder than the first.
The
is very fitting for this arcade game and the
is what you can expect from a retro game (not that it's a bad thing).

Coh2 Main:
I loved the first COH, and with its add-ons it became a fully featured and diverse game allowing for multiple stratagems to solve problems and such a wide array of units and teams that you never got bored.
Coh2 however started life in a vastly reduced state, while it would be silly to assume a game would emerge fully matured and formed with balanced sides and add-on packs like the first it still felt very lacking , the single player story was for the most part engaging but on occasion seemed to jump randomly to missions that didn't make much sense. The graphics don't look all that much better than the first but they are nothing to be scoffed at , explosions fly into the air with impressive fireballs and the sound equally reflects the visceral nature of combat.  After playing the game at a friend's house I waited to purchase the game until it was on sale as it offered much less than the "long in the tooth" coh1 for me , but it gave me a good experience over all despite its difficulties.
A point should be made here about micro transactions , a system so flawed by its overbearing nature that it ruined my multiplayer experience,  to remove skins/faceplates/commander then sell them back to us at a cost might not seem so bad until you're in a multiplayer game and get rolled over by someone with a bought commander using abilities you can only dream about.  with the latest add-on it seems they have all but disappeared but just the very concept of allowing the system to go live knowing how much it would cripple some users worries me. I'm quite happy to have some cosmetic features like skins and faceplates etc being able to be bought as they are for looks not actual game play , if we have bought a game we would like to get to play with all the toys not have you cut them out and charge extra for them.
Coh2 DLC:
Case blue, southern fronts , victory is Stalingrad.  Well would you like a slap in the face with some added disappointment? As I've said before I got the game on sale and so added the DLC thinking along the lines of COH1 expecting a new storyline , units and an expansion to the game, especially as normally they were £7 , what I was greeted with was almost an unlock with maps , in the theatre of war part of the game (individual missions) you only get 1941 to begin with limiting you use of units you may have just used when playing the single player , but there was no 1942 +   until the DLC added some new missions in future time periods and allowed you to use those units, missions ranged from bland to annoying with odd one standing out as fun but if I had paid full price for all of them I would be bitterly disappointed in what I had just paid for, to recreate all of the DLC simply make a custom game limit your choices of units and pretend you have an objective tada done.
Western Fronts:
A much needed addition to company of heroes 2 to start approaching the brilliance of the first game but sadly all the new sides don't come with any single player missions or campaigns , that being said Coh2 multiplayer despite some issues is a refreshing change to previous multiplayer experiences in that the players are for the most part friendly , supportive and good fun to play with.
Overall if you added everything available to this game as it stands (7.7.14) It will be a good game to play but still not as engaging or as featured as the first, if you've played coh1 to death get this and imagine it as a very large expansion pack, if you're considering which to go for first ... buy coh1 and its add-ons its far more bang for your buck.

I know that sounds like a lot of petty ranting. Dragon Quest Heroes 2 isn't a bad game by any stretch, but it isn't really that spectacular either.
I say if you're able to pick it up on sale, and you're interested in Dynasty Warriors style gameplay, go for it. If you're not a fan of Dynasty Warriors and you're interested from an RPG/Adventure standpoint, or even as a fan of Dragon Quest, you might not be into this. You sure as heck won't be into it if you don't like anime-inspired dialogue, fetch-quests, and shallow stories.

Ignore any reviews of this game written before March 2014, as it has radically changed since then.  In March Relic overhauled infantry mechanics, made light armor more viable, and generally made the game worlds better.  Up until that point I preferred the original game, but now returning to CoH 1 has lost its appeal - this game is better.  Just as tactical, faster paced, and even with the new US faction, not nearly as blobby.
Since March Relic improved balance to the point where it's pretty solid, though there are some minor issues.  Even the new WF factions are pretty balanced, which shocked me because normally whenever Relic adds a new faction to their games it breaks everything.  This time, though, they got it just about right.  They're still working on it, however, so waiting a bit might be wise if you want a more refined experience.
The "Pay 2 Win" complaint about the DLC commanders had its merit months ago, but at this point Elite Troops and Soviet Industry have been tuned down, and the most used commanders are ones in the base game.  They've also added a system that randomly gives you commanders and other stuff  slow rate, something like one item for three hours of playing, so at this point you can get everything in the game just by playing it.

Dawn of War is one of the first "real" Warhammer 40k RTS games to ever hit PC´s.
You get to follow Gabriel Angelos as he uncovers a major plot in the Tartarus campaign, this is the first game in a long series of Warhammer 40k games that was created by Relic while they where still owned by THQ, also the very first game where we got to see the Blood Ravens as they where created purely as a "PC Game" chapter.
Story wise the game is as good as you can do with an RTS, you get a deep sense of where Gabriel Angelos comes from and what his goals are as you get deeper and deeper into the game the story changes and there are some major plot twists all the time.
Graphic wise Dawn Of War is an old game and that is visible, however SEGA (now owners of Relic) keeps supporting the game and recently even released a patch to deal with some of the issues that had been around for awhile, this is despite the fact the game came out in 2004 which makes it over 10 years old now.
Gameplay wise DoW is very straightforward, you build bases and kill stuff as any other RTS, however the way that Relic gave us the Warhammer universe with the Dawn of War series is amazing, you get a deep feeling for your chapter and your enemies, you get some great story and a great experience as you go through the missions one by one.
Even now the multiplayer is very much alive and working very well, you get to pick between Space Marines, Orks, Elder or Chaos Space Marines which gives you a great chance for some epic battles, Relic even included the option to paint your own army and use it online.
All in all a great game for old RTS fans and even more so if you are into the Warhammer 40.000 Universe.

Preface: I did not play the original Dragon Quest Heroes, but I have played every other Dragon Quest/Warrior game to date - including my personal favorites: the Monsters subseries. This review is for the PS4 and PC.
Story: If you've ever played a Dragon Quest/Warrior game before, you should know what to expect from this entry's story. Archetypical heroes kill heaps of monsters in their quest to vanquish evil and save the world. The real variation between the quality of the storylines in this series comes from the dialogue and voice acting. Dragon Quest Heroes 2 is light-hearted, not taking the plot or it's characters overly serious. The humor is really cheesy, but well-placed. The voice-acting is definitely some of the best I've come across in any game.
Gameplay: The combat system is real-time action, with single button skill execution for spells (which cost mana) and button combinations for weapon-based abilities (which cost no mana). You're typically fighting anywhere from 10-100 monsters at any given time, with the exception of boss fights.
Let's take a second to talk about the boss fights. Most bosses have such an enormous pool of health that, unless you 'Call for Help' (the multiplayer feature of DQH2 that allows you to bring in other players' characters to help out on story missions), they can easily take over ten minutes of tedious dodging and attacking to get through. Personally, I found it a little frustrating that I had to choose between a coma-inducing boss fight and calling in someone else's overleveled character to wreck the boss in 0.5 seconds.
Still, aside from the boss fights I found cutting my way through the hordes of monsters to be very fun and rewarding.
Item creation and customization in DQH2, while a nice thought, is a little too simple for my taste. It does offer a little extra fun as you try and max out your characters end-game, but creation and enhancement is very linear and doesn't offer much room for creativity.
Graphics: Do not expect DQH2 to leave you a slack-jawed, drooling hork. Visually, it's no masterpiece. But the polish, the details, and the animations are actually very pleasing. The DQH2 world and its inhabitants are very well-designed; everything down to lip movement for speech looks smooth and debugged.
Controls: Whether you're playing on PC or Console, I would highly recommend hooking up your controller. Controller commands were intuitive and responsive, while the PC keyboard controls will probably just have you panicking and mashing buttons randomly as you inevitably spiral towards the game over screen. This is purely preference, and you can always reassign your button bindings however you please.
OVERALL: I really enjoyed playing Dragon Quest Heroes II. I felt it was very much worth the $59.99 I paid for it, and I have already recommended it to many of my friends. It is a very simple, but very fun game for someone who, like me, enjoys Diablo-series monster density and action combined with many classic JRPG elements.
No-Context Rating: 8.5/10

So I've played the game for a bit and I can see the appeal BUT honestly the game has a few problems.
1. The game is poorly optimized: My laptop with nvidia 1070 can't handle it unless I lower the resolution scale and then everything doesn't look as sharp as I would like (Early access game problems)
2. This game doesn't really warrant a stand alone release: This game could EASILY be released as a paid DLC on ark with new creatures as assets along with the spells, level up systems and quests and STILL sell like crazy.
3. Graphics: Most of the fancy graphic effects in the game look REALLY bad even with everything maxed out (understandbly it IS early access)
4. The camera perspective: Locked to third person which I think is a mistake, should be more like ark where you can choose between the 2
5. Skill system: Level up system isn't as robust as it is in ark
6. Quests: Quests aren't as good or as interactive as a lot of MMORPG games out there for PC and I don't see why you'd settle for something between a good MMORPG or a good sandbox like Ark survival evolved.
7. The grind:  honestly it looks like an even bigger grind than Ark just to get to the level of riding a dragon
There are SOME good things
1. The concept is really cool
2. I like the magic effects that they tried to implement into the game.
3. Unique creatures
Honestly I think if some content creators in ark got together, they can make an entire ARK remake mod that would probably be better than this game in many regards, such as A) Ark is better optimized now B) Ark has a MOD system so that community can contribute and make their OWN fantasy game like the skyrim community or fallout has with their mods C) Keep the player base in 1 game! why make an entirely different game with the same game engine just different assets and restrictions when you can just purchase ark and possibly load the total conversion mod as I explained above!
I think ARK survival evolved is a way better game right now to invest in despite the higher price (wait for a steam sale). I'm not saying I have played this game for a long time, but I will say the first impression has left much to be desired and I rather go back to playing ark than continue griding in this game.

The good:

The bad:
* Pacing is really off. Feeding yourself off rabbits can take several in-game hours.
* You sometimes feel like you're playing a hobo.
* Sometimes too hard.
* Lack of real character development options.
* Unguided gameplay. You really have to dig deep to find the story and main quest.
That said, I still think this is a superb title.

I know they’re not generally the most sophisticated of games but there’s just something about tower defense games that keep me returning for more. I find the genre to be particularly enjoyable and addictive. They’re addictive because each level sets the bar just that little bit higher. Today Steamified is fortunate enough to feature a new tower defense game and one that has somewhat innovative gameplay. Spacejacked is the Steam debut of Rotten Mage a Singapore based indie developer.
First, what I thoroughly enjoyed about this one is just how fast it is and that not only do you get to build the actual towers to do your defending for you but you also get to shoot the big bad aliens as well. In that respect a similarity can be drawn to Fortified which we featured back on Valentines Day. However, unlike Fortified which draws its third-person shooter and graphical inspirations from the likes of Orcs Must Die! Spacejacked is a pixelized graphics game that appears to be more of a platformer-arena shooter. Another component that achieved satisfaction is the requirement of large doses of quick thinking strategy in order to be successful. The seemingly simplest choices that you make from the beginning of the game can make a significant impact later in the game. Resources carry over from day to day as do the defenses that you have already built. But be certain not to make too many of them because resources are scarce enough that the game can almost be considered a resource management game. You never stop and that is one of the really beautiful things about the game.
The only thing negative that I can see in the game thus far is that the level of difficulty can swing rather violently in both directions. At one point I was seemingly crushing the enemy and then without warning I was dead on the very next wave. There was seemingly nothing that I could do myself to save myself from this death. I didn’t think that I had overspent on my towers and I thought that I had utilized the correct ones. It was just that one wave was suddenly much harder than the one preceding it. Those who have finished the story mode have complained that the second half of the game is weaker than the first in regards to difficulty. This may be because the first half of the game teaches you exactly what defenses you need and you spend the rest of the game using your resources to upgrade and if necessary repair.
The dev team were intelligent in their design choices bringing the game to Steam with both trading cards and 22 Steam achievements. They also utilized the Steam Cloud and Steam Leaderboard systems. The game has full controller support.
If you’re looking for a new tower defense game with some innovative gameplay mechanics then Spacejacked will be right up your alley.
