Being a fan or tower defenses I was interested in trying out Spacejacked. After playing the game I have to say that I was pleasantly surprised by Spacejacked since it is unlike any other tower defense game that I have played before.
In most tower defense games you build up your defenses and sit back and see if your strategy worked. In Spacejacked you are always working. You are building defenses, tearing down defenses, and shooting aliens. Since you don't have enough resources in the game, you are forced to break down your defenses and move them to where the enemies are. The chaos of constantly building and moving your defenses could have become overwhelming but the game does such a good job handling it that you will quickly be building up new defenses and tearing them down to move to a new location. I found this mechanic a lot more enjoyable than I was expecting.
I only have two complaints about Spacejacked. First the difficulty is inconsistent. At times the game is too easy and other times the game is too hard. Around the half way point the game gets really hard and relies on you having the best tower setup. Then the second half of the game becomes quite easy. The other complaint is that the story mode is a little short. The game only has around 20 levels which should take 5-7 hours to complete. The game does include challenges (which are hard) and an endless mode. While you can have fun with these modes, if you usually aren't into these type of modes you probably won't get much more than 5-7 hours out of the game.
If you don't like tower defense games, Spacejacked probably won't change your mind. If the idea of an action tower defense game appeals to you though I think you will really enjoy Spacejacked.
Note: I received a review copy for the game from the developer. Other than receiving a review copy I received no other compensation from the developer.

I'm a huge RTS fan, but for whatever reason, I never picked this up until recently. I was introduced to the Warhammer 40,000 universe by way of the Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine third person shooter, which I greatly enjoyed. This universe has intrigued me since then, and I have tried to catch up with the more long-term fans of the franchise by reading up on the lore and such online. It's quite different from most fantasy; where magic and medieval type weaponry is common in fantasy, Warhammer has a refreshing spin on things, relying more on machinery and gunplay while keeping the magic and awe the fantasy genre offers to players. It also falls in the area of dystopian, which is by far my favorite genre of any entertainment, and it is interesting to have a protagonist in this game whose ideals and beliefs could be viewed as fanatical by our standards, but would be understandable in such a future where he serves beneath a totalitarian empire.
Moving on from the universe to the gameplay, Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War is an RTS that is unique in its approach to a genre that is tried and true. Whereas many RTS games focus on base building and annihilation, this game simplifies the base building and relies more on strategical points that you must capture for resource generation throughout the map. Each campaign or skirmish mission "gets going", so-to-speak, much more quickly than other RTS games. You spend less time buiding and more time moving your armies along the map. For those that find some in the genre to be slow moving in the beginning, Dawn of War brings a welcome change.
Something else that Dawn of War does well that not enough RTS games do (sometimes at all) is reinforcements and upgrades. Where some games have you upgrade units from their respective recruitment centers and it encompasses all units of the same type, Dawn of War gives you more choice in how you want them upgraded. You can build a group of Space Marines, add reinforcements (making an initial group of four into up to eight), add sergeants later on, commanders, etc. In addition, with upgrades you can have a few men within the group upgrade their weapons, and the selection of weapons is up to you. You can have four rocket launchers, two rocket launchers, one flamethrower, and a laser pistol, or any combination between. This gives the player an ability to build up a small army for one intention (rocket launchers are great at taking out vehicles and buildings, for example), while creating another for a different intention (sending a differently equipped army to fight infantry). Even within firefights, you can reinforce your army if you possess the resources, giving the player a second chance in battle when most RTS games give none.
Lastly, it should be noted that I am a single player only strategy player, so I buy games like this for the campaign and skirmishes. In saying that, this game's campaign is fantastic. While somewhat short (eleven missions and about 15 hours of gameplay; note that Steam did not track all of my game time), the story is quite good and involving, taking you across many different types of landscapes and introducing you to different races to fight against. The cutscenes are a bit stilted due to the game's age, and the voice acting (while over-dramatic at times) is fantastic. The missions are vast and varied, and the game never gets in the habit of annoying you with time limits (I hate timed missions in any game, personally). The missions were challenging without being impossible, and they were friendly to both players who like to rush and complete the missions, and players like me, who like to leisurely explore the whole map and take over all positions before deciding to fully vanquish my enemy. Skirmishes are available, offering a few dozen maps that you can choose to play on, giving you choices as to what colors your army wears to which races you fight against, along with a whole myriad of other choices to make to tweak your gameplay if you so choose.
In summary, Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War is a fantastic RTS title that makes me very happy I purchased the Master Collection of games, because I am looking forward to experiencing more of this interesting universe. I would recommend it to any fans of RTS, as well as those looking to get into the genre, as this game is extraordinarily user friendly and has a fantastic tutorial. If you are unsure, I urge you to try the demo. I played the demo some time before buying the game and loved what it offered, so it is a fair representation of the game. I can see myself adding this to a list of games I come back to every now and then, because it offers a truly unique strategy experience that stands apart from others. I went into this game with no expectations other than what I'd read through some of the reviews, and after beating it, I consider myself a fan.

Dawn of War is a timeless classic. I've played this game years ago but it seems it hasn't lost any of it's sweetness.
Here are some things that make Dawn of War different:
1.
The more strategic points you control and the better you fortify them, the more of the 'requisition' resource you get.
Investing into strategic point fortification, makes them harder to capture and after simple upgrade, they can shoot at your enemies. So you're basically building sentry turrets that mine resources for you.
2.
Most units operate as squads. You get a squad of 4 marines, and you can add to it (reinforce) untill you got 8 marines. With upgrades you can add a sergeant who has a skill to rally them and instantly restore Morale. If few of your marines die, you can just reinforce the squad, and they will appear at the squad position at the fraction of a cost of a new squad. This allows you to push forward after a battle with little delay without moving new forces from base to the frontlines.
3.
You can equip your squads with weapons effective against certain types of units, you can mix them up in one squad, or just have a dedicated squad for every type. This provides interesting choices and allows for more variety in your tactics.
4.
Having your units sit in a bomb crater, behind a wall or in the trees, makes them harder to hit and they also feel better (see Morale)
5.
Certain situations make units lose their composure and lower their effectiveness. Especially when they fight outnumbered, or against intimidating opponents or weapons (flamethrowers, snipers).
6.
You need to think about the space your forces are going to operate in. You wont fit 3 tanks and 4 squads of infantry into a narrow street, without totally compromising their ability to efficiently move and operate. They will get stuck, bump into each other and wont be able to all get to the front to shoot the enemy you encounter. Some people say it's a downside and speak about "bugged pathing". Pathing is ok, it's just that Space Marines have "Space" in there for a reason :>
If you fail to chose the path wide enough for your forces to move through comfortably, you're going to have to accept the fact they take much longer to get into position, and if they get attacked while the squad is not in tight formation, some of them will be in range to the enemy while others might not be.
It's Warhammer 40k.
In the Dark Grim Future there is only War. Space Marines aka "Adeptus Astartes" operate in chapters similar to battle-orders of old and live to fulfill the will of the God Emperor.
They routinely drop from orbit in droppods, a
Whole WH40k universe is full of awesomeness and I guarantee you wont regret getting into it.
Dawn of War has some of the best voice acting in videogaming of last decade.
Most buildings you build are dropped by your battle barge Litany of Fury from high orbit with a very loud "thump" when they impact (it's hard to call it landing).
Animations of a dreadnaught cherry picking an orc from enemy squad, breaking his back while setting him on fire and then tossing him in an arc over 2 tanks and a squad of infantry are priceless.
Blood is everywhere and in general you can set perment scaring and bodies, so your progress through the map can be marked with bodies of your enemies.
TL;DR:
Dawn of War is a game like no other, except it's successors in the Dawn of War series: Winter Assault, Dark Crusade, Soulstorm
Totally recommend to any and all fans of RTS games and/or WH40k universe.
If you think you could like this game, but would like something with a bit more replayability (Dawn of War only has Space Marine campaign and skirmish/multiplayer) take a look at Dark Crusade and Soulstorm, which are a source of endless entertainment with their conqeur-the-planet style of gameplay and 7 different races to choose from.
Also be advised, that it's an old game and it has problems with wide-screen resolutions which might or might not be fixed.
Myself I just played it in a 1280x1024 window. The same problem exists in Winter Assault, but Dark Crusade and Soulstorms are ok with any resolution in fullscreen.

I love JRPG's so I am used to the grinding but boy oh boy does this game take the grind to a whole new level! However for the main story grinding isn't really necessary. Gameplay wise, the combat mechanics of this game is at it's core a musou game with your standard combos from other musou titles. The game also gives you a way to equip abilities to extend your combat efficiency. Although the game has musou combat mechanics it is so far from being a musou game with boss mechanics and some pretty intense difficulty hikes. Having said that, I only failed one quest throughout the whole story and that only happened once so the difficulty isn't that intense.

The soundtrack as with all Dragon Quest games is absolutely great!
I would recommend this game to any Musou fan and any Dragon Quest fan. At the end of the day it is a Dragon Quest game. It is a very solid game and I am still enjoying it 60 hours in!

There seems to be a lot of bad blood aimed at this game due to its association with Wildcard and Ark. It certainly doesn't deserve a mostly negative rating though.
It is still pretty early build, but it's a solid start. Yes, there are bugs. No, it's not polished hence it is an early access game.
I've seen some pretty grievous abuses of the rating system, but this time it's blatantly obvious. The game needs work, the developers know that, it's an early access title for a reason.
That said, the game itself is exactly what it markets as being. A survival RPG with optional online play. Setting up a single player game or server resembles Ark closely, and some of the UI, gathering, and taming elements resemble Ark, but that is where the similarities end.
This game is a high fantasy survival game, with gathering, resource management, NPC towns, and a massive world. There is a lot of potential here, and while there are definitely some bugs to be ironed out, if any of those things sound like stuff you enjoy this game shows a lot of promise.
If you're not up for a bumpy start with bugs and potential performance issues then wait and let the game get a few patches in. However, if that doesn't bother you and you want to support the developers and dive in to a very cool idea then I definitely can recommend this game.

I'm not very far in game yet (just left the forest / graveyard), so if my feelings about this game change, I'll edit this review accordingly.
While I liked the first one, there were many small problems that kept me from loving it. It seems the developers have fixed most of these problems and more, which makes this a much better game.
You can play at >1080p, change the camera distance, many actions are greatly sped up, like upgrading accessories or buying and equipping items. There is an option to skip the coup-de-grace animations, after the very first one for each weapon type.
The graphics are the same, or at least not much improved. Since I like the art style, I have no problem with it.
Combat "flows" a bit better, compared to the first one. The addition of class switching (for both main characters), along with minor differences depending on your equipped weapon is a great way to keep the game fresh and interesting. You also get more than 3 or 4 spells with each character, which you can pick and choose from, and customize a bit.
The spells of your party members are also improved. Multiple characters have healing spells, so you're not locked into one specific character like the first one. Same with buffs and debuffs.
The story is more of the same so far, still typical JRPG / anime stuff, I'm not really a huge fan but it's unoffensive.
I haven't tried coop yet, so I can't comment on that.
If you liked the first one, you should definitely check this game out, since it's more of the same, just better.

The ai in this game seems to be more of a focus than Ark as well. Creatures seem to be more dynamic than they were in Ark. They do what you would generally expect of them. This game is one of those low-tech gems that you find yourself immersed in despite it's obvious difficulty and it's lack of flashy presentation. You experience the life of someone in a strange, while still somewhat familiar world and you are left to what you can find to survive among a population that is more aggressive than passive. Friends are in a short supply, as are the means to adequately defend yourself from both the enemies of the world and the elements of it, two threats the game pits against you that are only outweighed by the threat you pose to yourself and your body's basic needs for survival.
Can it look better? Probably. Does it need to look better? Absolutely not. Throw away what you think a game should look like and remember instead what a game should be, because that's what you'll find here. Certainly a selection for the determined as you will suffer inexplicable loss time and time again, but the constant struggle for survival make all of the moments of success you encounter, however many or few that you may find they be, all the more rewarding.

Oh my.... Where do I start?
I came to find this game thanks to ''James Recommends'' from Extra Credits. So I knew that, based on his review, this game was going to be good.
But... when I played it, I realized that my expectatives of ''Good'' were an utter underestimation. The game wasn't ''Good'', it was ''DAMN EPIC!!''.
For a game with less than 100MB of size, this game stands WAAAAAY HIGHER than many Million Dollars AAA titles when it comes to survival; not even Fallout:New Vegas or State of Decay can hold a candle to NS when it comes to TRUE SURVIVAL. Which, when combined with Rogue-like makes for a WHOLE NEW GAME every time you play it; one in which you can never know if you'll succeed or fail until either of them shows up (Like when I found the Crowbar, some Binoculars and a Sauce Pan on the first town and I thought I was winning, only to freeze to death because I never found any shoes or clothes).
Unlike in those games where you charge into a group of enemies with just a knife and an angry roar, knowing that if you die, you can just hit the Load Save button, in this game, you gotta think out real carefully each of your moves. Just as you would do if you were in the player's shoes (or bare feet). This makes the game feel extremely real and complex.
''Do you sneak up on that scavenger to kill him while he's asleep to steal his shoes and his gun? You already know that almost every gun you see lacks ammo, but what if this one's loaded? What if you trip on something and wake him up? You could end up losing all you've gathered so far, and there's a high chance you won't encounter most of that stuff again.''
That's the feeling you get. And that's not something I've been able to feel with any AAA titles.
Just a warning, tho; be prepared to die a thousand times, even right after the start. More than once I stepped into the first area just to be torn to shreds by a Feral Dog.
My only critics to this game are the following:
-Crafting Instructions are just too vague.
The crafting system's utterly complex, but the instructions and recipes are even worse. You can't just figure out what do they say or what do they require until you go read the wiki. Perhaps if the items had some sort of Status Screen that told you what properties do they have, it'd be much easier to do this, as just figuring it out can take THOUSANDS of tries.
-The Full Map is too hard to understand.
At simple glance it looks just like a 300% Zoom on a SNES-era Sprite. You can't even tell what's what and even those places that are marked, it's hard to make out WHERE is the mark, as all you see is a big word. (Dunno if the iSlab or Smarphone's GPS Apps make it look better. Never gotten any of those.). I know this must be hard to do with a randomized map, but right now, there's just no real purpose to use the Full Map other than locating the Glow.
-The Full Bottles' colors are confusing.
Whiskey are orange-colored when full of whiskey, but also when full of water. Same goes for the Corn-a-Colas which are yellow. This can lead to a lot of confusion at the time of picking up stuff or even drinking. More than once I've been carrying around whiskey bottles filled with both water and whiskey and I've accidentaly drank Whiskey because I thought it was water and got drunk, which often led to death. This issue can be easily fixed with a couple palette swaps, so I hope it's fixed by the time the game leaves Early Access.
-MOAR STUFF!
No, seriously, this game needs more stuff, it's already cool enough as it is, but it could be even cooler. The current Item Pool is just too small for such a neigh-infinite world of random possiblities, so it's a bit sad that, once you manage to get some clothes and shoes to stay alive, they're almost always THE SAME. (Your shoes, the Hoodie, three shirts, some Cargo Pants and a Backpack if you're lucky are what you always end up wearing.). A game this big should have at least twelve variants of every piece of cloth or shoes.
Aside from those, I have no other complains. This game has the markings of an Indie Masterpiece, and so far, it hasn't let me down. So I hope it has become even more of a Masterpiece by the time it leaves Early Access.

When they say fast-paced, they really meant FAST-PACED.
In Spacejacked you play as Dave, an engineer/technician charged with defending your spaceship against ALIEN SCUMS. It is not enough to just sit back, strategize your denfenses and plant your "towers" (in this case, turrets). You'd often find yourself jumping into the fray - blaster in hand - or the ship will soon be VERY quickly overrun.
The aforementioned blaster is powerful but will overheat if used continuously, so shrewd planning and resource management will be required to deal with the waves of attacks. The inclusion of a player controlled character sets it apart from most tower-defense games and makes everything much more exciting. You'd teleport from one part of the spaceship to another in order to deal with incoming enemies and when they start appearing in multiple areas at once you'd wish there were more of you.
The game starts out relatively easy (easy to me, since I've played the endless-mode demo) but soon climbs in difficulty. Just when you thought you had it all figured out a new type of enemy would appear to wreck havoc on your ship. It can be punishing at times and so far I've encountered a difficulty spike but thankfully the save system is well implented enough to prevent you from unnecessarily wasting time.
This is the sort of game where you'll die multiple times. But the reward and satisfaction in successfully defending against a particularly gruelling onslaught of enemies will be immense. Try out the demo if you have doubts. This is definitely a recommended buy for me.

Imagine Tetris, but each block is one square, and the square has one or more arrows on it. You cannot move the blocks around and drop them where you want like you can in Tetris. They just fall and mix things up. If it reaches the top, you lose, just like in Tetris. The game consists of clicking on a square, and a light pops out and goes up to three spaces away, lighting up any other blocks of the same color, following those blocks' arrows as well. If you light up three or more blocks, they each disappear, and the other blocks fall lower, Tetris style.
The problem is that sometimes you just can't find a match. Tetris is always engaging, even when it's moving slow, in my opinion. However, with Tidalis, there were periods of 60 seconds or so, where I was just staring, without 3 blocks that I could match, waiting on more to fall, and it could take a while. I believe you can speed it up, a bit, but I think the lack of things to do at times in this game is a fundamental flaw. I don't like Tetris better because of nostalgia. I will sell the original Super Mario Bros out to any game I think is better, and same with Tetris. However, Tidalis is not superior to Tetris, or even on the same playing field. It's kinda like rebooting a film when the original was great. Reboot something that is garbage and make it better.
Tidalis should have been a spin on a game that needed improvements; not on a fairly perfectly-designed game, at least in my opinion.

I started using Blender way back in the version 2.3 days. I still use it now. For such a relatively small program, it can do things so well.
The reason why it looks as if Blender is breaking standard conventions on user interfaces is because there were no conventions when it was made. It started its life as an in-house tool for a 3d graphics company, way back when commercial applications like 3dsmax weren't mainstream yet, so it invented its own control schemes.
The thing is, in its own little world, the controls make sense, and once you get used to them, your work gets done fast (it favored hotkeys a lot).
I use Blender for creating low-poly, realtime graphics (i.e. 3d models for video games) so I can't comment on how well it does graphics meant for movies.

I've read most of the negative reviews here and they have two recurring themes: either people are constantly crashing or the Multiplayer is not what they expected. First of all, I have not crashed yet in 8 (now 60) hours of playing. Not to say that their experience is irrelevant but crashes are extremely hard to pinpoint especially for PC players. Moreoever, there are what like 30-40 negative reviews complaining about crashes out of the 14,000 owners of this game (according to steamdb). That's .2 percent of the community.
Secondly, the Multiplayer. I haven't tried yet nor have I really cared to Multiplayer as soon as I loaded the game. Believe me, seeing multiplayer was a BIG reason why I bought the game but funny enough when I started to play I didn't care too much. The game is so capitivating and fun to play alone that I decided to wait until end game before I do multiplayer. Yes, treat this like a MMORPG where early-mid game you should be leveling alone and figuring out how to play. Unfortunately what some of the reviewers say is true. DQH2 is NOT "true" multiplayer where you can explore the -whole- world together. Only story INSTANCES and DUNGEONS. So basically, DQH2 follows a REAL MMORPG type MP experience where you don't really aim to group for early content.
Finally, the last thing that caught my eye in the negative reviews was the question of customization. Even though only one person commented on it I felt the need to address this as I disagree, not strongly, but I do disagree. It becomes apparent that there is a lot of things to customize: you can adjust your stats and abilities through leveling, different weapons give different main abilities, you can upgrade accessories to provide extra benefits, and you can also swap between different classes.
Although I wish the game cost less than 60 USD it has been AN EXTREMELY LONG TIME since I wanted to lose sleep over a game so I would definitely tell my past self to buy this. If you are looking to just run around kill stuff, customize when you're not, and MP mainly when you hit end game, then this is the game for you.

As others have stated, one of the prettiest games out there.  The costumes (which are horrendously overpriced) are very pretty and likely will entice quite a few...after all, this is how they get away with no monthly fees.
However, the true downfall and what kills this game...is the enforced PVP past level 50.  And while some may say "Aw, it's just PVP, it can't be that bad!"  Nope, this games PVP is some of the worst I've ever seen.  It's open world and caters exclusively to that "gank" type PVP'er who you'll never see coming.  It will take you months upon months to get to a point where you'll "survive" a gank, and many more before you can successfully defend against one.
(Edit - To add, there are even costumes which will HIDE the player name so you'll REALLY never see them coming unless you're paying VERY close attention to your surroundings...PLUS, you won't know who it was that killed you.  Naturally, to get this costume the gankers will pay real money for them...so in essence, this is pay to win to some degree.)
Class balance is the core issue, there are a few well-known classes that are confirmed overpowered and need tweaking.  Things like this cannot be allowed in a forced PVP game.
At any rate, you will possibly have fun with it for $5...until you get past 50 and learn the truth of the game.
If you take anything from my review, SAVE your money until you get to that 57-60 level range to decide if you want to drop real money on any of the shop shinies.

Got about 40-45 hours into this game now and I still haven't finished the game storywise. I've found so much to do and explore, not even the grinding for levels when you change class or the farming for some materials bothered me at all. I'll admit I love the Dragon Quest games, every single one of them so I may be a little biased. However, I also believe that I have a decent grasp on what makes a game good and bad. Also one problem I see a lot of people having is crashes or glitches in the game. I've encountered very few glitches and only crashed once and Im pretty sure it was because of other programs I was running at the time. Since that one time in my hours spend playing, I haven't had another crash.
Pros-----
*Great visuals, definately reminds me of the box art and game visuals from all of the previous Dragon Quest games. The environments are not empty and are filled with random objects and monsters as expected from a game where you mow through groups of enemies on a large map.
*The difficulty of the game is completely dependant on you and your ability to read a enemy, this goes doubly when you enter a new area and the monsters are harder. Even more so when you encounter the more difficult monsters in an area or the rare monsters who you have to actively initiate a arena style battle with.
*Simple yet deep combat. There are very few buttons needed to win a fight, most can be won mashing your attack button or using a single spell. This works against masses of easier enemies and the mid range enemies that come in smaller groups. However where the combat really shines is when you fight against the bigger baddies. You have three options when it comes to actively defending yourself. Dodge, Block, or Move (run/jump) out of the way. You have to use your skills and spells effectively against some enemies  in order to win and button mashing will only get you thwacked soundly. Some enemies have elemental weaknesses, rather obvious ones, but adds that layer of strategy to the mix, as they often retaliate after getting stunned by them.
*The voice acting is about what I'd expect from each of the characters a little stilted at times, but no one is perfect. The voices fit well, and I never felt like they never meshed well. I also loved the music as they brought back a lot of the iconic sounds and themes, jingles, and the like. Even some new ones which are nice and I felt like they belonged.
Cons-----
*As was stated, in new areas monsters suddenly get harder as your progress, they do not scale with you at all. Which is fine once your past that area and need to grind out a new class, or farm for materials, but when you are suddenly overwhelmed by even the most basic monsters the first time you enter the new area. It means that the area wasn't scaled correctly for the level and abilities of the characters that will be entering the area. It shouldn't take you 15-20 hits to take down the weakest enemy in the new area when they come in a group of 10-15 along with various other monsters next to them joining in on the fun that is beating you senseless. And the more difficult enemies? Not happening unless you are really good at dodging and blocking and using a lot of heals constantly. It doesn't feel fun when that happens and your forced to go grind a handful of levels before getting to the point where the enemies can be dispatched with relative easy, or at least to the point where you are not getting overwhelmed constantly.
*I love the characters they brought into this world, Some ones we've seen before from Heroes I, and a decent roster of new ones. While I can see why they did that they did with the character choices because of duplicate skill sets or similar play styles to other characters, I still think that having 5 from the same game is a few to many. A little more variety would have been nice.
*The tutorial was a bit short, and never explained how holding down a skill button can charge it to a new level in some cases. (IE: elemental spells, Zap, Zapple, Kazap hold it until it goes to the next spell as it charges.) Maybe it was mentioned, but I don't remember it at all, if I hadn't played the first game I wouldn't have known about it here.
*This is just a small gripe, but the minimap is way to zoomed in, it needs at least 1 more zoom level. Because you either see the entire map, or a very localized area, Something maybe 25% more zoomed out, would have been great. I sometimes found myself lost because the minimap was too zoomed in for me to get my bearings as the minimap often doesn't have any distinguishing features such as location pointers or markers. Which is fine, but you need a larger minimap for navigation, I often found myself with the entire map open while roaming while squinting at the tiny arrow that is you trying to figure out which way I was pointing and where I needed to go.
*Class variety is a bit lacking in this game, you start with warrior, martial artist, mage, priest, and thief. (and two hidden ones) Many of which share weapon types and therefore at least 2 skills with each other, making the class not as unique as it could be. The Dragon Quest franchise has oodles of classes to incorperate into any game they make and they could have diversified a bit and given each class a bit more reason to be played beyond getting the stat boosts for all classes. Also it would make multiplayer a bit more interesting as at the moment you basically see everyone with the same 2-3 classes, with the occasional pc controlled npc.
*On the topic of multiplayer, it works quite well all things considered, but it sorely lacking in the area of any social options, you get a hot bar filled with premade messages, but in the heat of things you cant really get a message off, nor do you usually need to. Also there is no option to try to friend anyone you meet, at least not that I can find.
Conclusion-----
A very good game, not great, but good. It scratches the itch that I have for Dragon Quest and it's world, as I had just finished Dragon Quest 6-8 on the 3DS and can't wait for the next main installment in the main series. It has it's problems as all games do, but not any that in my opinion were game breaking, or soul crushingly terrible that I would have to stop playing over. The story is decently, the characters are fun, the world beautiful, and the combat satisfying. And to top it all off, its Dragon Quest. A bit more involved that Hyrule Warriors and Dynasty Warriors and an overall fun romp through the world of the Seven Realms.

This is a negative review, but it comes with a DISCLAIMER: this game could be worthwhile at a later date. It could mature into an exciting and unique title. That said, on to the review.
A lot of the people complaining about it being an ARK reskin are talking about the gameplay and UI, but it's deeper than that. The server configs are identical, down to the variable names. It was funny in a sad way when I was setting up a server config and noticed all of the variables with "Dino" in their name. Because there's a lack of documentation for setting up servers, I just copy-pasted my ARK dedicated server config into DnL and it worked.
The way it stands now, I think ARK was a starting point for the reinvention of this title. Given time, they may diverge from ARK in meaningful ways and become a game totally distinct from ARK beyond a superficial resemblance. Right now, I don't see myself wanting to play what is little more than an ARK clone when private-server ARK is still appealing and more complete.

I've sunk at least 50 hours into this game (I used to play the demo a lot...I was broke!) and I can honestly say that this is one of the best work-in-progress games I have ever played.
That's not to say that this game is flawless. The games combat system is designed to be extremely punishing. Therefore adding a risk vs. reward element into most things you can do. However, even when equipped with the best gear, it often comes down to random luck. I've flat out shot people in the head, had them survive, stay concious and then shoot through my helmet and kill me. Other times, I've shot people in the leg and had them die. It honestly feels like I'm playing turn-based Call Of Duty when using guns. The melee system is even worse. It doesn't really matter what weapon you have or what armor you're wearing if you face a dogman (or any other creature for that matter) and attempt to melee it you're screwed.
Also, this game being in a post-apocalyptic setting, you have to scavenge for resources (food, water, clothing, armor, etc.). While normally I would be all for this type of mechanic, especially considering the setting, the speed you run through your resources is ridiculous and, at times, can make the game extremely boring as you get stuck in an endless cycle of, find city, scavenge city, use resources found in city, repeat. While this isn't always true, it is for a large majority of the time.
However, the story elements that are slowly being implemented are making this game much more dynamic and the resource system is becoming less and less of an issue.
Where this game shines and puts it head and shoulders about the competition is its realism. Most games shy away from the possibilities of what a post-apocalyptic society could become, but not NEO Scavenger. From the arena, to the gated city of Detroit, this game feels extremely realistic in its setting, something many other games can't claim.
If this game was released today, I'd give it a 6/10. But for an early access game, easily a 8/10.

I quite enjoyed the game at first, but cannot recommend it due to the lack of content and how easy it is.
Once you have built one mega island with every building on it, the only thing that changes about new islands is handicaps and mission events; the game was just too simple for me to enjoy like I enjoy most economy management games.
It's a shame, because the game does do some interesting things with the political side of running a city which other games shy away from, and the artwork for the characters is amazing.
It also has some features which may be leftovers from previous games or something, in that you can select people in your game individually and see info on them as well as various options (mostly involving kidnapping or killing them) similar to dwarf fortress.
I never one needed to actually use this system as, other than mission NPC's, all my people loved me too much.
I completed most of the story missions and tried out some free form games, all my cities quickly reached 80% happyness in all catagories, and my money was always in the hundred thousands. It wasn't particularly challenging once I could afford to quickbuild (it's a button the instantly builds a structure for cash without waiting for a building crew, which shouldn't be in the game IMO) any buildings I wanted and I never once lost an island.
All in all, it's a neat little game that lacks any real challenge and isn't quite deep enough on the economy side to keep me interested past the first few islands.

NEO Scavenger is a rather simple, yet in-depth post-apocalyptic strategy RPG game(woah lots of adjectives). You start off in a Cryo Facility and find yourself roaming a world ravaged by an unknown apocalpyse. The game is turn-based so you have enough time to carefully plan your next move, or end up perishing. The game offers lots of choices as to how you're going to proceed. Fight or Flight? Eat or not? Explore or abandon? The RPG elements are great and there is a lot of detail in the overall health system(pain, blood, temperature...), lots of possible customization, all of it affecting your player(having a rough air filter just might save you from an allergic reaction, or the inhalation of toxic spores). The game takes time to master and lots of luck as well, even after 10 hours I still find new things around the game(randomly generated map, but still unable to scavenge all of it), and still find the dumbest ways to die.
10/10, slipped and fell, died whilst unconscious. (jk) PROTIP: Start with Medic and Botanist Perks.

Pros:
-satisfying combat physics.
-dual class system with 28 unique combinations to build on.
-complex stats system with many damage types and their corresponding DOTS subtypes and resistances to explore. excellent in-game tooltips to help.
-big, beautiful handcrafted world that doesn't feel like a random assortment of tiles and isn't a tolkien ripoff. lots of decent lore and history to find and read too, if you like words.
-tons of quests to do and areas to discover, still finding new stuff at ~250 hours in.
-steam controller support. simply the ideal way to play an arpg. all my buffs on a single button, multi-debuffs on one trigger, cooldown attacks on the other? don't mind if i do.
-guns. gunslinger builds.
-xpac illusionist npc totally separates visual aesthetics from gear stats. wear whatever you need, look however you want.
Cons:
-built on an old limited engine, some performance caps in certain areas.
-no way to move the character around with the thumbstick. add WASD/analog direction support crate plz!
-ridiculous facetank damage + viscous DOTS + resistance debuffs on upper difficulties narrow down build variety into tank/lifesteal/healer and make attribute points choices mostly redundant. put all your points into physique, thank me later.
-upper tier of gear isn't quite varied or wide enough to support the wild amount of creative builds you can bring to the table, also acts as a funnel on end game build types.
-online support is pretty oldschool and not exactly seemless.
-no in-game search on the sprawling devotion points star-chart, which is hard to learn and to use.
-very high difficulty jump between base-game content (Acts 1-4) and xpac content (Acts 5-6). trying to go straight from Act 4 to Act 5 is a good way to get your face wrecked on any difficulty.
Overall, Grim Dawn is my favorite of the existing 'modern' diablo2-alikes. Like all of these games, most of the fun is had in the first half of a characters lifespan while there are tons of interesting build-defining choices to be made. By the time you get to ultimate difficulty, all that's left is the gear grind. If grinding is your thing, it's not so bad in GD - plenty of bosses and chests with high or even guaranteed legendary drop chances. You put the time in and you'll eventually get your perfect gear set. There's a small trading scene if you want to go that route too.
Probably my biggest frustration with the game is the high end loot limitations. Several times I've arrived at ultimate with a character I really enjoyed defining and playing, looked at the loot table for motivation, and discovered that there didn't seem to be any end-game sets or weapons that fit my character concept. This is better with the expansion pack, but still not perfect - the class combination system + the number of damage types you can fit together in a build seems to allow for more variety than the devs had the gear designing imagination, time, or patience for. Some way for players to design and craft their own high end gear would work really well in a game like this, although it would likely be a nightmare to balance.
But Grim Dawn's class combination system is what ultimately keeps me coming back for more - there's always a new combination to experiment with, and levels 1-65ish are consistently a heck of a lot of character tweaking monster sploding fun. I left a review quite some time ago before the recent update, and I figure I should update my review with how I feel about the game lately. I hadn't had a chance to play the update until today, and I have to say, I'm impressed with the new maps, but the new update is still lacking something the game's needed for a while, and that's a rebalancing. Matches with just a few people can feel relatively empty depending on the map size and density, but another map entirely might feel fine with that same amount. If there are a lot of players in any map things really get intense because you can evade one firefight and end up in another, it's all out warfare, but there's also a chance you can die before you really get to have any fun.
The guns are still the same as before the update which I'm disappointed to see, because the Persuader still one shots at mid- to short range. The fun of this game is having an intense ridiculous firefight while diving and sliding around with your opponent in a hail of bullets and trying to keep the reticule focused on them to whittle their health down before they whittle down yours- a fancy DPS race of sorts. All of this fun melts away when you die in a split second because somebody's using the Persuader. I really think it deserves a nerf so firefights with Persuader users can still be fun since you're not dying instantly, more of a challenge rather than an instant death scenario, for both players. I did read that there was an update regarding the Persuader, but it really didn't change much in regards to gameplay, it's still used the same way.
I've never cared much for the music of the game, as I normally play music from other games while I play. While the music additions are cool and fit the tone for the game well, I probably won't be listening to them any time soon.
Honestly, I'm really glad this game's still getting attention, even after over a year of seemingly being forgotten by the developers. It's a really quirky and gimmicky game which can make for some really memorable experiences. There aren't many other games where you can say you did a slo-mo backflip off of a wall and riddled somebody with bullets before sliding past their corpse on your stomach into the next firefight.
Overall, I'm pleased with the new update (balancing aside) and I'm curious to see what future updates can give us. Maybe more characters? A new class? New game types? An offline single-player challenge mode against Bots? Custom soundtrack? It may be a lot to expect from a free game, but a man can dream.

Solid game. I have played more on someone else's computer than what actually shows up for mine. The research system is interesting, and rewards you for not using explosive weapons, as does the engineering. This makes the game more challenging, as explosives will like 99% of the time, assuming no user error, be able to kill most enemies, especially when combined together.
The game on its base level is pretty difficult, though not impossible. It requires good decision making, rapid decision making, and knowing when to sacrifice people's lives in order to accomplish a mission, and when to sacrifice the mission instead. You can get this game on sale pretty often, with all of the dlc bundled in. I can also recommend the dlc, as they are well made, and add additional variety, and options to the gameplay formula.
In the base game you can be expected to face a rapidly escalating battle, especially on your first playthrough, with enemies popping up in different places, and forcing you to change your strategy. You will take losses, and the hardest part is managing who to put at risk, and who not to. There is also a decent character editor available for the game, however I wouldn't suggest you put too much time in to designing the individual characters, unless you have one or two that you will particularly prioritize above all others. I designed a simple uniform of the skul helmet, armor 3, black camo, and it seemed to work fine for the grunts. Playing smartly, without putting units at undue risk, I lost three people in less than ten missions.
RNG will kick your♥♥♥♥♥occasionally, and that is generally the leading cause of my characters dying. But, it also spices things up a bit. When you get a Rookie that gets quite a few lucky shots in, they will begin to snowball, as they begin to level up they will become stronger and stronger, and you should prioritize gearing them up so they can continue becoming stronger. Don't put all of your eggs into one basket, it is possible for an entire squad to be ahnialated, especially if you are playing on the harder difficulties.
The game has solid graphics, a good eery vibe, and sets the tone for a survival story against invading aliens very well. You will build up an ant-farm like base, while managing new recruits, resources, research, and which troops to deploy, and how to outfit them. Combat plays out in a turn-based scenario, where all of your units go, and then all of their's. If you aren't in cover you are dead. If you are in cover and RNGesus decides its your time, you are also dead. As I said earlier, explosives will deny you some of the much needed resources, and I really don't bother with them unless its a life or death situation. If you are about to lose a soldier, it's generally better to take out the enemy with a grenade or rocket, rather than risk losing said soldier.
The game plays well on my ♥♥♥♥♥♥ old computer, and equally well (remember I played it on someone else's high endish computer) on high graphics, as well as low. You will notice some framerate issues if your computer is as ♥♥♥♥♥♥ as mine (can you run it said I can't play it, obviously untrue). The cutscenes are well made, and upgrading technology feels like an important step in securing humanity's future.
For first time players I suggest Ironman Impossible, as just ask anyone on YouTube, it's the easiest setting for the game. If you are wondering which game to buy, Xcom or Xcom 2, I would suggest both if possible, and if only one I would say get Xcom 2. Xcom 2 won't require you to have played #1 to understand, has a better character customization system, and overall has improvements throughout the board.
I would suggest this game for anyone that likes or is the following:
Hardcore Strategy Player
SciFi lover
Alien Killer
Platform Player, like Mario, Underfail, or Sonic, cuz lets be honest you need to play a real game for once :O
Masochist, because boy will there be pain
And finally, if you like games such as Fire Emblem on the handhelds, this game is quite similar to them, at least the older ones where perma death happens, not the newer ones where we wimp out instead.

So, this is Telltale's follow-up to their simple Texas Hold'em game, and it's much better. Their main novelty here is that they have characters from other games, talking while they play cards. If you are really into poker, you probably will get bored quickly, because of how easy the AI is. And, if you are not into poker, but like the characters, you'll get bored even faster, as it's just a poker game.
So, who's this for? I'm not sure. Overall, it's alright, so, if you got it in a bundle, as a gift, or just see it cheap and want to check it out, go for it. But, don't expect too much.

Never touch ironman mode, always get engineers ASAP and spam satellites like you're giving them away at an Elvis concert,  and put your trust in grenades. Follow those rules, and you should soon find yourself having a good time.
More faithful spiritual successors to XCOM exist out there, but a big part of the fun behind XCOM: Enemy Unknown is that the process of tactical micromanagement is scaled back, and the progression towards researching fun gadgets and hardware is expedited.
The expansion pack, Enemy Within, might at first appear to lock all the goodies behind perilously tantalising resource nodes, but most players should be skilled enough to obtain a few meld canisters by the end of the first month, and the actual cost of the facilities and tech needed to convert the new currency to even bigger, shinier toys is cheaper than might be expected. Everybody can now have their very own Mecha Hitler for a low, low cost.
There isn't any point in questioning the logic of XCOM. Yes, the governments of the world are silly for expecting their ultra-elite special counter-invasion task force to fund their own operations through means tantamount to bribery, corruption and smuggling of unregulated organs and explosives to third world countries. It's also absurd that such an organisation as XCOM is only capable of recruiting raw cadets who've barely passed basic training, instead of opening up channels with the Navy SEALS, the SAS, the KGB or something. If it was up to me, then XCOM would only recruit from Nepal. Get some Gurkhas to wreck some grey meat. That said, come the end of the game, the XCOM project does appear to have an excellent knack for selecting psychics, so maybe the strategy of recruiting miopic idiot savants was smart after all.
Lastly, the controls can be very contrived. Sometimes you'll be fighting against the cursor to get onto the right square, as the screen keeps swapping between Z-levels. A control may work better for some people, because if your mouse button is sensitive and you sometimes misclick, then prepare to cry as your cyborg colonel sprints the full distance out into the open and spreads his cheeks for muton sausage.
This game will make you want to drop the dev team into a shark cage dangling above the eldritch shrieking of an ancient cosmic entity, but when RNGesus, or Nuffle, or whoever you pray to for high percentages is on your side, you'll feel such euphoria as your sniper gets an overwatch clutch crit on a stampeding chrysalid. Of course the damage counter will only register a 4 and the alien beast proceeds to go all Starship Troopers on your finest support medic, but hey,

Ive been using Blender on and off for a few years now and Ive recently been getting into UE4 stuff. If you know your way around Blender, its surprising how much you can do and get away with using this software. I was very happy to see this software up on steam.
I was using a student version of 3DS Max for awhile and thought that coming back to Blender would be difficult. I thought that I was going to dread the transition and doubted that Blender was going to have the features I needed. However, After a few weekends of playing with Blender I felt very familiar with the software. I don't regret the transition and the software is also absolutely free. So thats always a plus.
There were also lots of errors with the fbx exporter for awhile, but the export settings im using now seem completely compatible with UE4. Im using version 2.75 right off of Steam and it seems to be working fine. The recent updates have really done well for the fbx features.
Personally, I strongly recommend Blender for any sort of personal project. This software is surprisingly easy to learn and its very fun to get into. Ive been learning lots of basic video game art in my spare time and I feel that Blender has made it much easier. If you like playing with software like I do, Blender is a very good one to get into and its completely free. Pair this 3D software up with a free game engine like UE4 or Unity and the possibilities are endless!

Graphical Appearence: 10/10 – The graphics are really nice, the modern factory-like look really appeals to me.  Excellent ways of customisation and texturing.
Sfx/Music: 9/10 – In this game, music is everywhere. When you’re driving(Never used), In certain missions music is heard and even a DUBSTEP GUN(That sums it up). The 9/10 is because I didn’t like the sounds. It’s loud, indifferent ’pew’ sounds. Even though our main character’s voice is changeable, his voice didn’t really appeal.
Story: 10/10 - Really unique story, kind of impossible, but this is SR. The audio logs(that you collect through steelport) get into the story more deep. The ’simuation’ was a really good idea from the creators. If you listen carefully and care about it, you’ll like this game’s story.
Gameplay:10/10 – Really ’easy’. This kind of OP-ness makes it so that you destroy stuff easily and fast. That is really nice. When I failed csgo comp for the fifth time,  went up to SR to destroy some♥♥♥♥♥♥ Really nice gameplay
Uniqueness:10/10 – Really unique game, never seen these kinds of mechanics. Never tried coop tho, but this ’homie’ mechanic is really appealing. Unique as ♥♥♥♥.
Difficulty: Easy – Easiest story based game I’ve ever seen. You destroy stuff as op as possible, you have all these op superpowers, you really get the chance to beat the living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of people.
Combat:9/10 – Awesome combat mechanics. You can brutally murder people, you can have a shotgun that shoots knockback bullets, a DUBSTEP GUN(again), OP superpowers that make combat easy, but this is a 9/10 because of them. There are many superpowers, so many infact you don’t want to or don’t get the chance to use them. Take the Telekinesis or the Death for above for instance. Nice mechanics tho.
Characters:10/ 10 – Really nice customisation: clothing, accesories, and customisating the main character itself. The crew aka ’saints’ vary a lot of characters. King, The president, Kinzie, Pierce and so on…And you can even look into the side characters’ lives by listening to audio logs. Impressive.
______________________________________________________________________________
Overall: 10/10 If you’re looking for a game that has story, yet has a bit of shooting, combat and fantasy, Buy it NOW.

Grim Dawn is a solid ARPG. I will write my cons and pros list. Its definitely subjective.
PROS
- mobs actually fight back. Unlike Path of Exile, there is no clear speed meta and this is a good thing
- boss loot is rewarding
- atmopshere and lore. Also it has a really nice day/night cycle. The problem is you see it so rarely. Because u have to exit to main menu so often and start new runs for bosses/bounties to reappear.
- a deep skill/devotion system
- arpgs should be easy on normal and hard on last difficulty. Grim Dawn respects that
- addictive
CONS
- almost no deterministic farming. very few legendaries/mythical are related to bosses so the game is not really Solo Self Found friendly anymore even if most of the people play this way. You can play hundreds of hours without getting the set you want. But you can post in trade forums.
- some of the hard bosses are just gear checks and no mechanical fights u can learn and fight them at an earlier moment
- Grim Dawn players are a bit stubborn and fanboys and not really opened mind unfortunately. Yes, it wont affect your playtime that much but...
- alot of players cheat items in this game, post perfect Monster Infrequents and brag about it on youtube (today someone posted a video where you can see he uses a potion which is not even released officialy, he created it with a program. And that program is sticky on grim dawn Tools forum section) It beats the purpose of an arpg. It wont affect you since is mosty a SP game.
- no real End Game like mapping and they wont even think about it. The real end game is farming mats for relics or new components in the expansion
- the multiplayer is not really optimized and it will never be
- Crate doesnt understand urgency. They released their first big patch 5-6 weeks after AoM release. The game lost some momentum now.
Grim Dawn is very good but considering the cons above it might never be great. Remember Torchlight 2 sold at least two times more copies. But I recommend this game and you should buy it if you like quality games.

More faithful spiritual successors to XCOM exist out there, but a big part of the fun behind XCOM: Enemy Unknown is that the process of tactical micromanagement is scaled back, and the progression towards researching fun gadgets and hardware is expedited.
The expansion pack, Enemy Within, might at first appear to lock all the goodies behind perilously tantalising resource nodes, but most players should be skilled enough to obtain a few meld canisters by the end of the first month, and the actual cost of the facilities and tech needed to convert the new currency to even bigger, shinier toys is cheaper than might be expected. Everybody can now have their very own Mecha Hitler for a low, low cost.
There isn't any point in questioning the logic of XCOM. Yes, the governments of the world are silly for expecting their ultra-elite special counter-invasion task force to fund their own operations through means tantamount to bribery, corruption and smuggling of unregulated organs and explosives to third world countries. It's also absurd that such an organisation as XCOM is only capable of recruiting raw cadets who've barely passed basic training, instead of opening up channels with the Navy SEALS, the SAS, the KGB or something. If it was up to me, then XCOM would only recruit from Nepal. Get some Gurkhas to wreck some grey meat. That said, come the end of the game, the XCOM project does appear to have an excellent knack for selecting psychics, so maybe the strategy of recruiting miopic idiot savants was smart after all.
Lastly, the controls can be very contrived. Sometimes you'll be fighting against the cursor to get onto the right square, as the screen keeps swapping between Z-levels. A control may work better for some people, because if your mouse button is sensitive and you sometimes misclick, then prepare to cry as your cyborg colonel sprints the full distance out into the open and spreads his cheeks for muton sausage.
This game will make you want to drop the dev team into a shark cage dangling above the eldritch shrieking of an ancient cosmic entity, but when RNGesus, or Nuffle, or whoever you pray to for high percentages is on your side, you'll feel such euphoria as your sniper gets an overwatch clutch crit on a stampeding chrysalid. Of course the damage counter will only register a 4 and the alien beast proceeds to go all Starship Troopers on your finest support medic, but hey,

This game is utterly amazing.  Don't be put off by the mildly ugly graphics.  You will forget them in no time.  What makes this game mind blowing is that it is a rogue-ish game with permadeath, yet it doesn't feel like it.  Sure, the first few times you play you are going to measure your lifespan in hours, but once you get the hang of it you realize that survival is all up to you and completely possible for very long periods of time.  I am writting this after burning a solid 6 hours on this game in a single sitting.  In that entire time I had thrills, upsets, and close calls, but never died.  This is a rougalike game to be sure, but don't let that cause you to run screaming.
The survival aspects of this game are absolutely awesome.  You find yourself searching for food and water, planning ahead, and deciding when it is worth a risky encounter.  There is no "I am a bad guy" badge on people.  See a fellow stranger in the distance?  It is up to you if you want to use surprise to take out a possible threat, or wave and see if he is friendly and wants to talk.  Do you risk a fire to boil water, knowing it might attract a threat?  When it gets dark, do you stumble blindly looking for a good camp, or take a risky spot in the open and hope for the best?  What do you do when you wake up to find a melon head stolen your weapon and backpack; grab a stick and give chase, stalk them, what?  There are always so many options, and that doesn't even get into the tactical turn based combat!
The combat, while simple on its face is complex and interesting.  Planning is rewarded, but so is on the spot craftiness.   The the game never demands a split second decision, so you have time to ponder your move and roll the dice.  It lets you do so many crafty things and it tends to behave as you would expect.  For instance, imagine you come accross some scary looking person who looks like they want to eat you, and have a host of options.  Do you sneak in close and try and stab him with your trust spear, hoping that this game awesome wound system will let you stun and cripple the guy before he realizes you are there?  Do you try and slip away before he sees  you?  Maybe you decide to bluff and at a distance try pointing your rifle (with no bullets in it) at him, trying to scare him off, if he charges anyways, flip that rifle around and show him the butt of it.  You can jump out of concleament and egg him on, hoping in the rush to get  to you he gives you a solid opening to land the first blow.  Perhaps you get out your old butchers cleaver and start the fight by charging him over onto the ground, and hacking him apart before he can get up.  Hey, he might not even a bad guy, you can always just wave from a distance offering friendly chat and see what he does.
This game is so unassuming, but it is solildly on my top 5 for 2014, and for the value for the price, it is easily #1.  It says "early access", but as far as I can tell, this is a full game.  This game is an absolute gem.  The worst thing about this game is that there are so many things that might scare people off from what is an awesome experience; perm death, ugly graphics, early access, a slightly obscure interface (until you get the hang of it), and a strange theme.  Don't let any of these things scare you off.  This game is amazing!  I can't even imagine what it will be once it is out of early access.  Don't wait for a sale, buy it now.

Good game, but the RNG killed it for me. There are reviews that try to prove that it's "user-sided" that you feel like enemies lucking out and I call BS on that. Why? Missing 12 shots in a row with 70-80% and a stun with 90% is either a bug or BS.
Example: Saved game, one enemy remaining. Flanked with one soldier 78% to hit, hit, 3 of 4 dmg. Yay, let's stun the X-Ray. Moving into point blank range (adjacent field), 90% success. Miss. Really?
Also, I am bloody tired of thin men hitting from 9 squares (no terrain advantage) someone in heavy cover with critical hits (9 dmg) which is an instakill before you can manufacture anything than standard body armour. 99% of the time you will get the feeling that cover actually does nothing for your soldiers as it neither prevents hits, nor massive criticals. Also, I noted that from 28 hits by thin men, all of them were max dmg crits. WTF is this BS? ON ALL DIFFICULTIES!
Additionally, your defense attribute does nothing as well, 60 defense attribute in cover, and your people get smoked with critical hits again from 9+ fields away in medium cover, this is BS. And I don't care if it is a bug or not, it should not effing happen, especially as in the core game, it was not the case, but in enemy within, everything seems buggy, frustrating and plain sh*tty, except for the UI which was improved.
So far, I reloaded the game 9 times, trying to stun that guy, everytime (tried other fields to avoid terrain bug) failed with 90% yet EVERYTIME my soldier with 78% to hit, hits. WHAT?! Hit chances rolled at the damn beginning of the round? Thank you, deinstall.
So far, only observed in "ENEMY WITHIN" but this is BS and an effing joke, this cannot and should not be the point of a strategy game, that I am shown 90% to hit, but RNG established a miss at the beginning of the round. Either that or bug, and at this point I don't give a rat's rear, because if combat is an integral part of a game, hitchances have to work and not be rigged.
Now I also have to talk about other bugs: UI often glitches out, scroll lock bug where you have to save/reload game, often enough you cannot use certain moves for no reason whatsoever (mostly happened on snipers, however) as they are just greyed out (you have postive vision, ammo and 2 movepoints, not affected by any condition, yet all aggressive moves are greyed out, as if you moved, weapon switch does not work, even the moves that are allowed need to be clicked 40 times to work), and of course a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ maneuver UI, often enough you will find yourself clicking to move into position on one side of a wall, in the moment you click, cursor jumps through graphic, you go into cover with your rear TO the enemy on the wrong side of cover.
Also, In "enemy within" you lose items permanently sometimes if soldiers are hospitalized (no feedback from game, so no idea if a  bug or simply a useless new mechanic of the add on).
There is a 50/50 chance you will hate or love this game, I find it an atrocity to find such idiotic bugs in the final version.
A clear, and easily justifiable NO to "enemy within" and a "MEH" to "enemy unknown", because you will find yourself missing 90% of the time with hit chances greater than 78%, which is a joke.

A brutally hard survival game. If you are feeling a masochist, pick this.
Jokes aside, although the only control you have on you caracter is on the inventory management and choosing which actions to perform, I can assure you that this is one of the most complex survival games available in Steam. Due to it's level of difficulty, I suggest you play this on short bursts (as on the first playthroughts you won't last that long anyway :P )
PROS:
-Excellent atmosphere that absorves you into it's post-apocaliptyc setting.
-The sound is great, from the realistic effects to the music.
-Every choice has a consequence, even a choice as deceptevly simple as drinking a bottle of water that you just found
-I would dare to say that the depth of the game's survival mechanics are unparalelled.
-There is an actual main storyline to this game shall you choose to follow it.
CONS:
-It is a very difficult game. I have 6+ hours on this game by the time I am writing this, and I still take a beating every time. I tottaly understand if many people are put off by it.
-The learning curve: I will be honest. This game has TONS of trial and error. Only after the first 5 playthroughs(about 2 hours of playing), you will be able to understand why you have died. From there, the game gets more satisfying, but adding to the complex interface and the fact that the game almost begs you to seek vital information (such as important crafting recipes) to the game's wiki page.
Having said that, if you are looking for a challenge, you certainly have one here. If I were to call this game by other name, it would be Bear Grylls Simulator.

Faster Than Light is a fun and intensive rougelike adventure with elements of strategy and Role-playing. The game puts you at the command post of your own personal space cruiser to save the Federation by destroying the Rebel's Flagship far across the galaxy before they end the Federation forever.
Controls: 8.5/10
FTL has very few controls. Your mouse does most of your work. You have a pause button and a menu button, past that your mouse does nearly everything else. However, as the game progresses, you will use your mouse nonstop in battles. Almost to the point where there is so much to do with just your mouse, you'll make huge mistakes. Hotkeys can help a lot, but you'll have to get used to them and take time away from your trusty mouse. Controls are deceptively simple.
Story: 6/10
FTL's story is of you, your crew, and your spacecraft discovering intel that the Rebels will launch a massive assualt on the Federation's home base far across the galaxy. It is up to you (and seemingly you only) to race toward the Federation's HQ and defend it from the wildly powerful and advance Rebel Flagship before the Rebels crush the base. All and all, the story is a bit lacking. There's only six races in the galaxy you explore and the stories between them are not discussed in much detail. If you die, it's the same thing over again. Short and bittersweet.
Gameplay: 9/10
FTL's gameplay is mostly found in the altercations you have between enemy ships. Otherwise, it's all point and click. The battles are random and sometimes you have the option to battle. The battles are intense and require good timing along with fast hand-eye coordination, strategic thought (take out the shields or the weapons? Or maybe destory their O2 emitter, draining the ship of oxygen?), strong weaponry, and understanding of your enemy. The game also features random events are you traverse the systems. these events can lead you to new ships, scrap (the in-game currency), unique weapons, or your timely doom. As a rougelike adventure, you will die plenty of times and that can be frustrating. You need an understanding of the game and some luck to actually make it through to the end.
Replay Value: 10/10
It's a rougelike game. It is made for you to keep playing.
Final Thoughts/Overall: 8.75/10
FTL is definitely a great, fun game that you will spend hours playing (and loving every moment of it). It has it's annoyances, but they do not ruin the overall greatness of this jewel.

This game is an awesome mix of survival, scavenger, skyrim, and a turn based combat game. The map is huge, consisting of hexagons which may or may not have item already on the ground, indicated by a box. The looking glass indicated scavenging. The tent indicates your camp sites, and finally the red feet indicate whether someone or you have been there recently.
This game is not for the faint of heart. In the beginning, you die frequently and most often by things you wouldn't normally expect. There are NPC who are homicidal and roaming the wilds looking to 'scavenge' off your newly dead body. At first I could only last a few hours, and then I quickly learned the skills necessary to survive longer. My average now is 3 to 5 days. The skill/flaw system can be a little frustrating, and there aren't many of either. It could definitely use more of both to allow a better customization of the characters skills and flaws.
On top of that, there is not a way to customize the characters name, gender, or gender-based clothing, at least none that I have discovered. This is truly a survive or die game. Weather, injuries, cold, hunger, thirst, disease, poison, and combat can all kill you. There are also random hex's that have NPC run stores in which you can trade things for money or for other items. The only city I have found as of yet is Detroit.
The one resounding issue I have with this game is once you are dead... you are dead. There is no way to save unless you want to dink around in your computers files to rig up some kind save system. While the character is still alive, you can save and come back to your one save, but after death it disappears and you have to start over. I don't see a point in that system, but then again.. I didn't make the game.
I think this game has some real potential. It can be frustrating, and seem difficult but failing has helped me learn how to survive longer and pick the skills necessary to survive. There are little things that I think could be corrected like in-game items, or the way in which skills are used.
My favorite skills to use would be Trapping, Botany, Medic, Hiding, Tracking, Electrician, Mechanic, and a few others. I'd like to see a sewing skill and possibly the ability to take/train an animal companion. I know if I were trying to survive, I would try to find a dog to help protect my stuff, and me while sleeping.
I am concerned though that the developers are making the game significantly harder, so I think the option to choose a skill level from safe - ultimate survivor could be used to allow many different people with varied experiences with games like this could play casually or have a challenge. I like being able to play through a game and then go back through it collecting all of the little dodads and whatnot.
In conclusion, I love the basis of this game. I think a few things that need to be changed are the save games, a few additional items in game, a few additional skills and a few changes to how the skills work, a better skill/flaw menu, addition of companions, as well as a difficulty setting.
A bug that I think I have found would be while wearing different shoes, or a single shoe still gives the negative effects of being barefoot. However if the two shoes are the same, the effect goes away.

Tidalis is a a fairly basic action puzzle game with elements of match-3 games and a complete lack of a cohesive vision. The developers seem to have been obsessed with using every single ♥♥♥♥ing idea for a level, block or gamemode they could come up with leading to a mess of under-used options and a bloated, repetitive campaign. It's otherwise well polished (the sounds, music and graphics are all pretty good) but I tired of the game quickly and I suspect most others will too. Yet another game that shows Steam's need for a 'meh' option rather than the binary Yes-No when reviewing. Buy this game only if you love games like this and buy it cheap.

The game has three modes: your typical fast-paced score as much as possible mode, a storylined campaign and a slower puzzle mode that's more about planning ahead.

The score mode won't hold your attention for long unless you're really into this type of game and while it has plenty of options to choose from most just turn the game into a chaotic mess. I haven't tried playing it with another player but I imagine it's a lot of fun as such games often are.

The puzzle mode is pretty much trial and error and the later levels become less a test of problem-solving and more one of memory as you'll have to replicate your previous moves every time you want to try something new. This is tiresome and I couldn't be arsed even finishing it. A button for resetting the level to your last attempt would be a large improvement.
The campaign is fine if somewhat forgettable but rather long at 115 levels most of which feel like filler. Apparently this excessive length was an issue for the developers too since they didn't even bother playtesting the later levels many of which are entirely reliant on luck and can take ♥♥♥♥tons of restarts to complete. I'd single out 99, 102 and 114 as particularly terrible but the end of the game as a whole mistakes frustrating the player for fair difficulty, sadly all to common nowadays. Thankfully there's a skip button but a better solution to this problem is not including ♥♥♥♥ing worthless levels in the first place. There are also a few hidden puzzle levels in the campaign which are generally better than those in the puzzle-level specific mode. The writing is functional, light-hearted and vaguely humorous but it's really just there.
