I remember when I played "Tropico: Mucho Macho Edition" or something like that as a kid on my ghetto♥♥♥♥♥poor people's computer way back in the day. I had no clue what I was doing and the highlight was unlocking cheats and spamming as many soldiers and rebels as I can and observe the massacre. I loved it.
Now, however, I'm an adult. You know what sucks about being an adult? You need more out of games to really enjoy them, yet you don't have the time to enjoy the lengthy ones that try to do just that, give you a lot of game. You know, this series does a good job meeting half way. It's not your typical strategy game that requires mastering a bunch of skills, it's a simple simulation game where you run an island civilization from third world country to first world. You basically do what you should already be doing as an adult, budgetting, but for fun purposes.
You manage your money to buy things that make you money in the long term. You do your best to satisfy people on the way in order to protect your image and seat as the island leader. All the meanwhile, you have various political factions that have expectations from you, and you cannot satisfy EVERYONE so you gotta pick based on long term self gain rather than personal preference sometimes. You gotta spend money on stuff that actually costs you money and does nothing more than satisfy people's needs or desires.
There is a lot of games of this genre that does that. This series, especially this particular title, does it very well however by using humor and a fun atmosphere to make the game feel so enjoyable. It's hard to explain, but this series is just really special unlike others within the genre that sorta go for the same thing as the typical "Sim City" clone.
There is some cons, however. I feel you're not really in control of your population to the extent I'd like. Sometimes, there is even bugs that causes the game to create unnecessary building deletes and the likes. There is DLC that ruins some missions, such as the plant gathering prison for people that are sent to prison. Even though they're prisoners, that structure does not count them as prisoners but as farmers. This is terribly frustrating, but it is one of very few extreme flaws with the game.
I could make a huge wish list of what I'd like to see in the game, but I feel like it is unnecessary. Ultimately, I wish there was more options as a successful dictator/ruler. There is a handful ways of making it, such as tourism or mass amount of economical buildings, or farms, etc. I always feel there should be some evil ways to do it. I always just have a massive amount of plantations and a massive amount of bunkers. This is the only way to be a successful "evil" leader. Enslave the people that refuse to be soldiers and make money off of them. I mean, this is fun but it's so boring and I feel evil can be expanded upon with, perhaps, other consequences that are not game ending.
It's also worth noting these structures I just listed, Bunker and Plantation, are overwhelmingly overpowered. This game isn't pay to win, but those structures definitely make it a lot easier to play. They're both so exploitable, it's sad to see their heart not go into making them balanced.
It's also sad to see that dlc be so expensive. Luckily, I got the complete collection as a discount long ago. In fact, I only owned a handful of DLC from the collection at the time, but they kindly updated my account with their new DLC at the time, meaning I wasn't entitled to some of the DLC they gave me, but they did anyways. I doubt this was intentional, but I just think it's great they didn't attempt to correct that mistake, assuming it was a mistake. Regardless, I feel like most of these dlc's should have been a part of the main game and they could easily have made expansions worth buying instead. The future dlc, or modern times they may have called it (don't remember) is a great example, that's a great one.
The game series also allows map editting. You can basically make your own missions, which gives the player pretty complicated control. You can make virtually every mission you can think of, it's that flexible. You can also check out the maps in their own online thing to download ones made from other players. It's a decent system and I've downloaded maybe twenty maps, but only liked about two of them. I would say that it's a good added touch, but I wish there was some way to have users leave tags and give the ability to search for said tags. I sometimes think certain maps were highly voted for because of reasons that conflicts with my personal play style.
I cannot think of anything else more to say without rambling further. It's a good game for anyone that enjoys this genre. The gameplay is solid, the replay value is great, the flaws are fairly minimal, and the asking price is decent (I'd argue even lower than the game's actual value even despite its age). It has a handful of bugs that are frustrating, but it's good.

This is a fantastic strategy game with a couple minor flaws. Firstly, let me say that I love XCOM. I owned the original UFO Defense for PC and PlayStation, Terror from the Deep, and Apocalypse. I played many reboots including Afterlight and some community made versions as well. This game comes the closest to remaking the original and adds a few nice elements in its own right.
Ill list off the bad first. This game is RNG hell! Try this scenario. You’re down to your last move and have a half dead Muton waiting around the corner. You wisely saved your crit happy, shotgun toting, assault run and gun soldier. You confidently streak towards your adversary with only a slight degree of separation as you stop moving. You check your aim, breathe a sigh of relief at the 98% hit chance. You fire away only to find your Muton buddy laughing furiously as you miss. How did I miss at point blank distance with a shotgun!? Next turn my emboldened Muton friend slaughters my cross eyed soldier with one quick shot to the face. This in turn causes a nearby rookie to freak out and panic. He begins shooting my colonel in the back causing her to bleed out. From this point on in your life, 99% will never be a sure thing again.
Now here is the good. Excellent challenge. This game forces you to think ahead and plan accordingly. Do you think you mastered the game? Try classic or impossible difficulty with ironman enabled. And if that’s not enough try out the long war mod. Both tactical and base management layers offer enough strategy and replayability to keep anyone that likes strategy games entertained for at least two playthroughs. Now add all the alien lore discovered by engaging new aliens and base side research and development, and you have one engrossing experience.
Graphics and sound are fantastic. The game presents in an isometric top down orientation for the tactical aspect. In between turns you can sometimes hear the ominous movements of moving aliens or mortified screams from unsuspecting civilians. Environments are very detailed and there are enough unique maps to not see any repeats on a single play-through. Music is great, but still doesn’t beat the PlayStation soundtrack in my humble opinion.
I highly recommend that any person wanting to experience a great turn based strategy game pick up Enemy Unknown and at least the expansion Enemy Within. Despite the RNG issues, the game is a solid, well thought out attempt to make XCOM relevant again. Fraxis did this game some justice for both stalwart XCOM veterans and new players alike. XCOM 2 has already exceeded my expectations as well. I however think this game belongs in anyone’s collection.

Follow along with the adventures of four valiant hero's, Budget Kirito, Budget Asuna, Budget Lizbeth, and Budget Klien as they journey through “Crappy version of Sword Art Origins” in this heavily redacted carbon copy of Sword Art Online Hollow Realization.
Literally everything in Dragon Quest Heroes II has been laundered from SAO:HR.  At a rate of two cents on the dollar.  The game play, combat system, party system, skill system... everything.  The “Amine style graphics” are Gintama to SAO:HR's Attack on Titan.  The character advancement system is a few cards instead of a deck, and the game world seems like it was designed for seven year old children.
The game mechanics leave you no option but to switch characters and play as your entire party, forcing you out of your hero's body and jarring your suspension of disbelief.  There is no one character through which to inject yourself into the world, even if you wanted to.  And who would want to?
This game is a lazy and uninspired attempt at game design plagiarism that leaves me wishing I had played less than two hours.
If you have played Hollow Realization do not buy Dragon Quest Heroes II.  Disappointment  is all you'll get for your sixty dollars.  If you have not played SAO:HR and DQHII looks like your cup of tea, go buy SAO:HR.

Tidalis is a very cute and highly addictive casual puzzle game with a unique take on a well-known formula. The cutscenes and music are probably a matter of taste (personally, I liked the music but skipped through most of the story), but if you want to just sit down and relax, they create a comfortable and immersive atmosphere. The tutorial does a great job at introducing the game mechanics and there is a huge variety of different game modes. You can even create your own puzzles or play community-created ones. Last but not least, it has full Linux/SteamOS support. If you like games like Tetris Attack or Bejeweled, this is certainly for you.
In campaign mode, however, there is one major issue that you should be aware of: More than other puzzle games I've played, victory is often a matter of mere luck. In some stages the victory conditions are impossible to plan ahead for; on many occasions I had to restart a level several times because the blocks on the board didn't leave any sensible moving options. While in Bejeweled the board is cleared when you're out of moves, this does not happen here. On one occasion, for example, you're supposed to create large combos but at the same time are not allowed to move the majority of blocks. If they're not in a useful position by chance, there's simply nothing you can do, which can be extremely annoying.
If you believe that you can cope with this problem, I recommend this game to you.

Bought this on an impulse and was pleasantly surprised.
Controls are very tight and climbing / sliding etc works as intended. Nothing parkour related is too outlandish, which gives the game a feeling of realism....zombies excluded... The upgrades make you feel like you're actually progressing. Later in the game you can learn skills such as rolling when falling to make almost every drop possible without taking damage, or the ability to coat yourself in gore to camouflage yourself from zombies. New upgrades also effect how you solve game issues. For example, coating yourself in guts then lobbing firecrackers at an enemy patrol group will allow you to safely yank their drop package away while a hoard of infected swarm them.
Graphics are pretty, and it runs well with some tweaking at med/high  for my midgrade laptop. Sounds are well done. Melee attacks are very meaty sounding, explosions and gunfire are thunderous and violent, and infected are at times pretty unsettling with their screams, snarls and wheezes. Melee is very satisfying. Ragdoll animations are beautifully done. Grappling and tossing a zombie charging at you off a rooftop, only to turn around and watch it flip, flop and splatter on adjacent overhangs gives you a sense of power and accomplishment.  Guns are extremely lethal, rightfully so. The damage is countered by the loud noise that will inevitably draw a crowd to your position. Everything feels balanced and well thought out
Voice acting is well done and dialogue seems well written. The quests are pretty enjoyable and after about ten hours in they really start ramping up in scale and difficulty.  Some of the side quests have that quirky fallout new vegas feel to them, the gas mask man as an example. The side quests more often than not give you new weapon blueprints, modifications, and occasionally alter the game world.  This gives you an incentive to branch off the main path, rather than being handed some petty 100% achievement trophy.
Overall I'd give it a honest 9/10. I'm only about 20% done with the story as of 16 hours played,  but its the most fun I've had in a while with a game.

Dying Light started off as an incredibly difficult, slow, and intimidating piece of work. Upon playing some more and becoming more in tune with the game, I realized it is truly a fantastic game. The combat certainly has a learning curve, and at the beginning of the game it is difficult sometimes to kill even one zombie let alone a horde, and the parkour is slow and you tire easy. As you play however, you get better, faster, and stronger. Soon you're able to destroy hordes of zombies and bad humans alike, and suddenly those impossible feats become possible with a little bit of practice. 100% recommend.
In regards to the DLC, the Bozak Horde is actually quite enjoyable. Very difficult, and at times frustrating, but very rewarding especially in co-op. The Following, however, is everything a DLC hopes to be. It puts you into a (HUGE) new map and gives you a car and a new skill; driving. Speeding around the countryside ramming zombies in fields and using nitrus to outrun demolishers is incredibly fun and if I could go back and do it again with the same wonder as the first time playing, I would in a heartbeat.

: The developers packed this game with cool spells, enemies, and craftables; but the progression is awful and grindy, combat is floaty, the gathering is disgusting, and[/b] the game just isn't finished.[/b] The game was pushed out into early access in response to Citadel: Forged with Fire releasing soon.
I was pretty thrilled when I joined a server to be greeted with a character creator, and even a choice of a starter town. There are guards and merchants all over the town. I thought it was all pretty cool,
. I checked under the Skills tab and saw things like survival skills, ranged, melee, cooking, taming, dark magic, light magic, earth magic, and many other skills. However, the magic all starts to go away when you start seeing this game for what it really is; an unfinished mess.
One of the many problems with the game is harvesting, and this one is huge. The games progression, magic, and gameplay revolves heavily around harvesting. The devs made the terrible choice of having the player smack resources repeatedly, up to more than a dozen times, before they get anything. It's random too, so you can hit a tree anywhere from 3 to 20+ times before getting one piece of wood. It almost feels like server lag, but it's intentional to slow player progression. It feels so bad.
Combat. Oh combat. Any reason why it takes 20+ sword hits to kill a rabbit like creature? Any reason why it takes 5+ minutes to smack a sheep to death? Just to slow player progression I'm sure. The devs did include cool spells, however you do have to grind for them. The combat feels unresponsive. Small critters should die when I hit them a few times, but they don't. Like I said, can get some pretty cool spells and items in this game, but it won't be any fun getting there. And I believe it's more about they journey than the destination. This games 'journey' is bad.
The game is riddled with other issues too. Such as bad servers, terrible optimizations, the game runs worse than ARK when it came out. Speaking of ARK, the devs did reuse some things from ARK. Such as the terrible running/breathing sound, rocks, rain, weapons and structures were just reskinned. Utter laziness from the devs on this. The merchants in spawn were all sold out after the server was up for an hour, no spawn protection, bodies are everywhere in the spawn city. PVP is clunky and all over the place.
There's nothing about this that make me want to keep playing this. I wish the devs kept it in the oven much, much longer...

This is absolutely one of the best FPS games of all time! There is no loadout customization, no 15 gamemodes like COD, no quickscopers or campers. This is a very simple game, albeit a fantastic one. If you like Star Wars but not FPS games, this might not be for you. If you like FPS games but not Star Wars, this is definitely worth a try. And if you like both, you will very likely lose yourself in this game for upwards of 50 hours. If you want online gameplay, you have to download gameranger, since the devs stopped supporting online after 9 YEARS! That has to say something about the quality of this game. Once you've done that, you can easily find online lobbies. This is a game where you play as one of the four major factions of the Original trilogy and the Prequel trilogy, and you battle it out on all of the icnoic planets of the Star Wars univserse. Oh, and this is far better than the new Battlefront by Dice.
As long as you enjoy FPS's, the gameplay here is phenonemal and has hundreds of hours of replay value. You can play as a variety of clases for each faction between Droids, the Republic, the Empire and the Rebelion. There are 2 major gamemodes: CTF (1 flag or 2), and Conquest. Conquest is where you fight for command posts, which are basically respawn points on the map. The variety here is low, however it is all you need. In the Galactic Conquest mode, you take turns with the AI to conquer the entire Star Wars galaxy. There is also a campaign, with a very good narrative.
Space battles are also relevant here, and a big part of the gameplay. They are not as good as ground battles, but they are hectic and will provide many more hours of gameplay when supplemented with the ground fighting. They are a little repetitive, but then again so is every FPS.
Finally, you can play as heros every now and again, which are jedi for the faction you are playing as (and also Boba-Fett, who is not a jedi but a hero). Playing as these characters is really fun and makes you feel very OP, which you will be.
This game utilizes all of the classic Star Wars scores composed by John Williams, so needless to say it is great. The only problem with this game's sound is that you will tend to hear a lot of "we captured a command post," or "we lost a command post," from the AI as you play conquest. This gets very old very fast, although it is definitely no major detractor.
For 2005's standards, this game looked pretty good. For 2015-2016 standards, it looks pretty bad. textures are muddy compared to what you see today, and even on max settings it looks nothing like a AAA game today. However, unless yo uare the biggest graphics snob of all time, you will not let this bother you. After all, an FPS doesn't need that good graphics anyway.
Absolutely the best part of this game is the amount of time you can spend playing it. Things start to get repetetive around the 100 hour mark, but you keep playing anyway because the online is always working and you can turn the difficulty up to Elite, which is only for truely elite players. Anyone who plays FPS's knows that repetitiveness in the genre usually just makes you want to play it more, and thats where a lot of this game's draw comes from.
If you like FPS games, you must buy this, especially at a time like now where you can pick it up for 3 bucks. If you like Star Wars, this is probably the best Star Wars game you will ever lay your hands on. The only drawbacks at all are the sub-par graphics and some repetitive audio, but who needs those things when you have as much replay value as this game has to offer? Amazing buy, especially for 10 dollars, or less when it is on sale.

This is a fantastic strategy game with a couple minor flaws. Firstly, let me say that I love XCOM. I owned the original UFO Defense for PC and PlayStation, Terror from the Deep, and Apocalypse. I played many reboots including Afterlight and some community made versions as well. This game comes the closest to remaking the original and adds a few nice elements in its own right.
Ill list off the bad first. This game is RNG hell! Try this scenario. You’re down to your last move and have a half dead Muton waiting around the corner. You wisely saved your crit happy, shotgun toting, assault run and gun soldier. You confidently streak towards your adversary with only a slight degree of separation as you stop moving. You check your aim, breathe a sigh of relief at the 98% hit chance. You fire away only to find your Muton buddy laughing furiously as you miss. How did I miss at point blank distance with a shotgun!? Next turn my emboldened Muton friend slaughters my cross eyed soldier with one quick shot to the face. This in turn causes a nearby rookie to freak out and panic. He begins shooting my colonel in the back causing her to bleed out. From this point on in your life, 99% will never be a sure thing again.
Now here is the good. Excellent challenge. This game forces you to think ahead and plan accordingly. Do you think you mastered the game? Try classic or impossible difficulty with ironman enabled. And if that’s not enough try out the long war mod. Both tactical and base management layers offer enough strategy and replayability to keep anyone that likes strategy games entertained for at least two playthroughs. Now add all the alien lore discovered by engaging new aliens and base side research and development, and you have one engrossing experience.
Graphics and sound are fantastic. The game presents in an isometric top down orientation for the tactical aspect. In between turns you can sometimes hear the ominous movements of moving aliens or mortified screams from unsuspecting civilians. Environments are very detailed and there are enough unique maps to not see any repeats on a single play-through. Music is great, but still doesn’t beat the PlayStation soundtrack in my humble opinion.
I highly recommend that any person wanting to experience a great turn based strategy game pick up Enemy Unknown and at least the expansion Enemy Within. Despite the RNG issues, the game is a solid, well thought out attempt to make XCOM relevant again. Fraxis did this game some justice for both stalwart XCOM veterans and new players alike. XCOM 2 has already exceeded my expectations as well. I however think this game belongs in anyone’s collection.

The devs took what I enjoyed from a classic ARPG like Diablo and made dramatic improvements upon the genre, itself. The dark storyline, engaging lore, versatile/complex combat, character customization, and overwhelming amount of loot keeps me coming back for more. I play this game quite regularly with friends cooperatively. The game is much better with played with others. Worst case, you can always search for a server and join up with randoms, or open your game up for whoever may join and help your cause. You can also trade for hard to find loot to help flesh out the perfect built for your playing style.
Crate Entertainment has done a great job of improving upon the game with periodic patches and solid DLC. You can’t find a better value at this price. This game will give you 100s of hours of entertainment for less than the price of a crappy mixed drink at your local bar! Save a few brain cells and give it a go. You likely won’t be disappointed, and, even if you are, take advantage of Steam’s refund policy. It's a win/win!

Tidalis is a decent little puzzler that could have done with touch controls or a 3DS version - in fact, if you told me that this was a former mobile phone game, I wouldn't doubt you for a second. you see, the object of the game is to chain together blocks by directing a stream of energy through them, but the energy will only move in the direction painted on each block. You can change the directions on each arrowed block, allowing you to set up chains that weren't there before. It gets more complicated from there, with special blocks that stop streams in their tracks, others that need to be smashed on the bottom of the playfield, and others besides.
To be honest, I've found the default difficulty rather easy and relaxing, which is how a casual puzzle game should be IMO - a casual puzzler should never frustrate the player with arbitrary difficulty spikes, it should be the mental equivalent to a light morning jog - only enough exercise to get the blood pumping, and the brain slightly warm. In what I've played of Tidalis, the only place I was continually having difficulty was the "get 7500 pints in 4 minutes" stage, and that's purely because it was pure RNG luck-based bullshoel.
That's the main criticism I have of the game - there's an element of randomness that's slightly unwelcome in a casual environment, though not the same sort that plagues "pay-to-win" crap like Candy Crush Saga, thank goodness. The other gripe I have with the game is the bizarre cutscenes, which are needlessly distracting and try-hard unfunny to boot. but I don't want to sound too harsh on the game - it's a great little time-waster, especially for 79p during a Steam Sale, or as part of an indie bundle (or for free from a Steam friend, thanks Broodje Gezond!). There's some nice, folksy piano/flute-led music there, too, if you're into that kind of thing.
Overall, yeah, I'd recommend it - if you can get it for cheap or free. It's not really worth £4.

Tidalis takes the Tetris genre of games and rips it apart. Tidalis is basically Tetris on steroids.
Like Tetris, multi-colored blocks will fall down your screen at regular intervals. If you match up the blocks correctly they'll be cleared, but if too many blocks stack up (to the top of your screen) you lose. But that is where the similarity ends.
In Tidalis you create "streams" to clear your blocks, and with clever positioning it's possible to use streams to clear blocks all across the play area. As blocks are cleared more streams can be created allowing you to create combos that give you extra points. It's really cool to plan out a chain reaction and see it pay off!
Also, there are about two dozen special blocks to spice up gameplay. Some of these are generally helpful, such as a "quad repeater" -- if one stream goes into the repeater, four come out, meaning you can get some really nice chains or combos going. But some special blocks are generally unhelpful, such as an "idol" block, that will halve the score of any chain that touches it. Usually there are only 1 or 2 special blocks used per level, and you're given a briefing on exactly what they do before the level starts. This is good as it prevents players from getting overwhelmed from the sheer variety possible.
Speaking of variety, there are a ton of different victory conditions to keep things fresh. Remember how I said that quad repeater blocks are generally good? Well how about a level with quad repeaters where the victory condition is to score the smallest chains possible, and the loss condition is to score too many large chains? In that level you'd actually want your streams to avoid the quad repeaters to keep your chains from getting too big!
There are also items that you can use in some levels, for example one item will remove several blocks from the play area and put them in your inventory, allowing you to re-arrange them at your leisure.
There are also many different game modes. For example in "Graviton" game mode your streams are affected by gravity, meaning they do not go up as far, but they go down much further.
Fortunately there are several tutorials for this game, and a Custom Game mode where you can experiment with all the multitude of options.
There is also a Versus mode where you play against other human players, and a Co-operative mode where you work with other human players to beat a level! There is a level editor included so you can create your own levels from scratch!
Finally, there is Adventure mode, which is the main single-player campaign. Whoever heard of a Tetris-genre puzzle game having a single-player campaign with a storyline??? I think that was a pretty nice treat. There are 115 levels in the campaign, with another 100+ optional "Brainteaser" levels. If you get stuck on a level you have the option to skip it, but I'm pleased to say I was able to make it through the whole campaign without having to skip any levels, so the difficulty level was about right. The Brainteaser levels are quite different from normal levels. In Brainteaser mode no blocks fall from the top of the screen, you are only allowed to create one stream, and you have unlimited time to postion your blocks and ponder your one move.
I thought the soundtrack for the game was well done. It is a mix of both cheery and soothing piano tunes.
If there is one criticism it's that the single-player storyline seems to be geared towards young children, but the difficulty level of the puzzles is geared towards adults. But it's not good to be too critical on that point, I'm astounded the game had a storyline at all!
If you like Tetris-style games or really any puzzle games at all you should check out Tidalis.

This is a tough game to review, and whether it's recommended or not depends entirely on the demographic. Tidalis is a supremely polished and smooth game that has a metric ton of features. The trailers and screens don't do justice to the sheer amount of content that the game contains, and it's a nice tonic when compared to the occasional Early Access flop that you see on Steam. There's clearly a lot of love that's gone into the creation of Tidalis.
Fans of puzzle games will find a lot to admire. The gameplay is very solid with a bewildering array of game options. The adventure mode doesn't take itself too seriously, has a decent sense of humour and is as challenging as you want it to be - handicap adjustments can be made at any time, though the default difficulty provides a good test without inducing baldness. The brainteasers offer another dimension, and the level editor is sound. Multiplayer is available in all modes and works well. Special mention to an excellent OST to round things off. Perhaps I'm sounding overly positive, but I was genuinely impressed with the level of quality that this game presented.
That being said, it's ultimately held up by its own genre limitation - if you're a puzzle game fan, particularly match-3 games, then fantastic! I'd urge you to pick this immediately. But for others, it might all get a tad too samey over the course of the game. Despite some varied gameplay mechanics, it all boils down to the same core principle at the end of the day, and if that doesn't sound like your cup of tea then it might not be worth it.
I'd still recommend it as an excellent example of what a good puzzler is all about; depth, difficulty and variety.

DISCLAIMER: I was a beta tester for the game prior to release, and am a "Valued Tester" in the Discord server. I was provided with a beta key during that period, but I purchased the game post-release and have been given no incentive or consideration to write this review.
TL;DR: The game is fun. Buy it.
When I describe Lupinball to people, I say "It's sorta like Duck Game, but with wolves and fireballs instead of ducks and weapons." It gives you a bit of an idea what to expect.
Lupinball is a primarily 2-4 player game (with a single player mode) where each player controls a different bipedal wolf. These wolves collect energy icons that pop up on the field. Up to 3 can be held at once. When one is picked up, the wolf can deploy a shield for a short time, with the shield lasting longer with more spheres. With three, the wolf can deploy a magic fireball. The object of the game is to survive by dodging opposing fireballs while launching yours to hit your opponents. There are also items that pop up from time to time to twist gameplay a bit, like orb blockers (prevent opponents from using shields/fireballs) and one that flips the stage upside-down but leaves controls intact.
This is where the Duck Game comparison comes in. One hit, and you're dead. Once all but one wolf are dead, the stage shifts to the next and the match continues until one player wins enough rounds to win the game. There's a bit less humor in the death scenes compared to Duck Game, but the overall game is very light-hearted, with hilarious loading screen messages relating "fun facts" about wolves, and the characters are very charming. (Bart is best sheep.) Plus, ALL THE WOLF PUNS.
Unlike Duck Game, there are no platforms or jumping. Levels aren't completely random either; each player selects a stage, and the selected stages are played in a random order. When they are complete, players then select additonal stages, and the game continues until a winner is decided. I like this freedom of choice, but I would love to see an "uninterrupted random mode" implemented as an option in the future.
The game handles really well. Movement is smooth (except on stages with elements like wind and ice where impeded movement is the point) and you can even adjust the trajectory of the fireballs for a split second after initiating launch. Each map is unique, and offers its own obstacles, be it slowed down movement (Gailes, Wolphone, Pawcific Ocean) or changing elements like shifting walls and temporary darkness (Wolffer, Moon Estate), to name only a few examples. Gameplay itself is extremely simple; with only movement, shield and fireball launch as your only controls, your mastery of the game will rely on experience more than learning any complicated combos or controls.
You can customize the match options (points to win, friendly fireballs, item appearance, among others) to create the match setting that suits you and your friends best. There are even accessibility options, such as a reduced flash mode and a color-blind mode. And of course, there is online play.
Single player mode flips the rules a bit. You're alone on a map, and you're firing constant fireballs to fill the stage up. You have 30 seconds (extended with each fireball you launch) to keep firing. One hit from one of your own fireballs, and you're out. Once time is up or you die, you are taken to the next stage, repeated until you've played all of the maps in a row. Your score is the amount of fireballs you launched in every stage, totaled up, and there is a global leaderboard for the best score. It's pretty fun, though I would like to see an AI single player mode implemented where you do battle against 1-3 computer opponents.
Dev support is top-notch. The Discord server is active and the community, while young, is already very friendly. Devs hang out there and are dedicated to improving this game and making it a fun experience.
All in all, for 10 bucks (I paid 9 with launch discount), it's a pretty solid game. I think it could earn its place among the many other popular couch multiplayers.

Simple, Basic, Fun
I would totally recommend this to anyone with a few friends who just want to have a bunch of stupid fun. This game doesn't take you on an adventure, it's not trying to be an experience, but what it is is just pure fun. The controls are tight and easy to learn; move with the analog stick, A to shoot fireballs, and B to generate shields... That's it. The multitude of "on pick up use" power ups and differing stage layouts gives a lot of diversity that is fun to revisit time and again.
My only cons with the game is that there is a single player mode, but it's just a "Try to beat the high score" gameplay I'm not a huge fan of, and I'd like to see a wider variety of characters and stages added over time. I know there's only so many colors available to make each fireball unique from another player's, but, perhaps, two toned or multicolored fireballs? And I'd like there to be a option to exclude certain stages from random selection. As fun as the game is there is a stage or two I don't, personally, like. Also a pause menu when playing online with friends (not necessarily with randos).
Those very minor gripes aside, I still think this game is worth your time and it's cheap enough that it's an easy impulse buy. It was made by a small group of people and I think this project was successful, even if I'd like to see certain things added in via patches in future. Give this game a shot.

Dawn of War is Warhammer 40K's first Real-Time Strategy game in the collection of Warhammer 40K videogames.  Since there's quite a bit to say, I'm just going to categorize the different sections of the game.
-Story:  Combining aspects of fantasy and science fiction, you are tasked to lead Gabriel Angelos and the Space Marines known as the Blood Ravens as they take on a campaign to rid the planet of Tartarus of the war-loving, barbaric Orks.  What first starts out as a quest of extermination becomes a more complex conflict as more hostile factions enter the fray and a threat that could endanger the whole galaxy is discovered.  I will refrain from revealing much more about the story, but the campaign ends on a cliffhanger, all the more reason to buy DLC.  While the campaign is only 11 missions long and feels paced a little faster than it probably should be, the game attempts to compensate with each level taking anywhere between 1-2.5 hours, which probably explains why the story may have been rushed.  If you're a veteran of the RTS Genre, you may find the core game's campaign to be easy and manage to clear every level without failure.  Overall it's a story that justifies your actions and explores a small fragment of what it's like to be part of the Imperium of Man if nothing else, but that doesn't make it any less enjoyable.    3.5/5
-Graphics:  The game was made in 2004, as a result the graphics you're going to see are going to be a little dated in contrast to the more modern landscapes and character designs known today, even on the higher settings.  As a result, the textures are going to be rather bland and lacking in detail in some places.  Obvious geometry for the most part isn't too noticeable, however animations are rather rigid and limited and you will probably start seeing the same actions get repeated, especially during the Campaign cutscenes.  Even with all the advancements in graphics throughout the years, Dawn of War ages surprisingly well.  You'll be able to notice the bloodshed, corpses, bullet holes and explosion residue left in craters as the battles rage, even if there are a few limitations.  The buildings are animated, so you'll know if your stuff is damaged, being built or whether something's happening, which is always useful in a fast-paced skirmish where information is vital.  Every faction has their own distinct style that's present in their architecture and Game UI, preventing the player from confusing one side for another. Overall, the game's graphics aren't the best I've seen, but it's pretty remarkable considering what was available at the time.   4/5
-Gameplay:  Dawn of War is one of the simpler RTS games in terms of complexity.  The map is already drawn with every key point identified, however fog of war still exists, ensuring that  reconnaissance is still important.  There are only two resources to collect:  Requisition and Power, with the former being automatically generated (but sped up as you explore the map and claim more points) and the latter requiring the player to construct generators to collect.  Because of how requisition works, one never has to worry about the map being depleted of resources and being unable to build things, although it becomes much more difficult to construct anything when you have less buildings and points to generate resources.  There are also few kinds of units, which allow for simpler yet fewer strategies.  You will only encounter infantry, land vehicles and builders.  Fortunately the game not only classifies infantry as groups that can be reinforced and improved with your resources wherever they're located, it also avoids adding defenseless builders when you attempt to select your army.  There are four factions by default with more added in DLC, each promoting different strategies and play styles, but you're most likely going to be acquainted with the Jack of All Stat Space Marines from the campaign and the tutorial levels.  Speaking of the tutorial, every key aspect playing the game is covered in an easy to understand way that will allow newcomers to at least figure out what they're supposed to be doing.  One thing I will complain about is how limited the camera zooming is, as I tend to be unable to select all of my units that start occupying the entire screen, and at times your units may have difficulty simply going where you request them to, but not very often.  Before I forget, there is one aspect that separates Dawn of War from other Real-Time Strategy games:  Morale.  Yes, the often mistakenly overlooked aspect of war that must be maintained within your ranks.  Morale determines the survival of your units, and once its depleted they will start missing more often than a stormtrooper at point-blank range.  Naturally there are commander units that exist to boost morale and/or break enemy spirit that can be bound to infantry squads and can prove to be dangerous units with enough research and training.  Because of how morale works, it's never a good idea to send in a strike team that's outnumbered.   To summarize everything that was just typed, Dawn of War is one of the less complex RTS games you'll find, but that doesn't make it necessarily easy or boring.  4/5
-Sound:  Everything sounds like what you'd expect it to, weapons, vehicles and all.  Each faction has their own idiosyncratic set of sound cues you'll associate them with.   While it is a minor annoyance to hear your units make an announcement every single time something involving them changes, anything said will always be relevant to the given situation with examples such as “Squad broken!” and “Under fire!”.  Everything your units say is not only standard, but reveals more of the personalities behind the unit type and the faction they hail from.  The background music is usually faint compared to the action, which is a good thing in this case because it doesn't distract from the more important aspect of this game:  Warfare.  While the background music fits the scenario, there isn't much else to say about this limited track.  Aside from the necessary announcements and some extra filler to avoid having the game sound too quiet, sound wasn't much of a focus on this game.  3.5/5
-Replayability:  As games grow older and remain active through time, their replay value gradually diminishes and Dawn of War is no exception.  While the campaign may keep one occupied anywhere between a few days to a week at most, there is no real incentive to play this game for very long.  Skirmish mode may be fun for a few rounds to experiment with other factions and strategies, but aside from that there isn't much to say.  While there might have been an active multiplayer for the core game in the past, hardly anyone tends to roam the lobbies anymore.  Unless you know of other people who own the core game, you may end up never setting foot in the multiplayer community.  Fortunately there are three DLC expansion packs that can add more vitality for the game, with the majority of them being well-received as they incorporate new factions, campaigns and possibly fixes to whatever bugs exist and updates for the graphics.  With what little exists in the core game, DLC is practically a necessity, although it's important to keep in mind that Dawn of War has a sequel where the majority of users have most likely migrated to.  A little distressing, but what do you expect from an old game?  It's a miracle it's still even active.  3.5/5
Summary/TL;DR:
Dawn of War may not be the most complex Real-Time Strategy game out there, but that doesn't make it any less fun.  Overall score:  18.5/25  or 74%*
*Note:  This score is for the core game itself.  The expansion packs have not been evaluated by this user and may change the score.

Movies, theater, and books became art, there is no reason why video games like Braid cannot be as well.

: The developers packed this game with cool spells, enemies, and craftables; but the progression is awful and grindy, combat is floaty, the gathering is disgusting, and[/b] the game just isn't finished.[/b] The game was pushed out into early access in response to Citadel: Forged with Fire releasing soon.
I was pretty thrilled when I joined a server to be greeted with a character creator, and even a choice of a starter town. There are guards and merchants all over the town. I thought it was all pretty cool,
. I checked under the Skills tab and saw things like survival skills, ranged, melee, cooking, taming, dark magic, light magic, earth magic, and many other skills. However, the magic all starts to go away when you start seeing this game for what it really is; an unfinished mess.
One of the many problems with the game is harvesting, and this one is huge. The games progression, magic, and gameplay revolves heavily around harvesting. The devs made the terrible choice of having the player smack resources repeatedly, up to more than a dozen times, before they get anything. It's random too, so you can hit a tree anywhere from 3 to 20+ times before getting one piece of wood. It almost feels like server lag, but it's intentional to slow player progression. It feels so bad.
Combat. Oh combat. Any reason why it takes 20+ sword hits to kill a rabbit like creature? Any reason why it takes 5+ minutes to smack a sheep to death? Just to slow player progression I'm sure. The devs did include cool spells, however you do have to grind for them. The combat feels unresponsive. Small critters should die when I hit them a few times, but they don't. Like I said, can get some pretty cool spells and items in this game, but it won't be any fun getting there. And I believe it's more about they journey than the destination. This games 'journey' is bad.
The game is riddled with other issues too. Such as bad servers, terrible optimizations, the game runs worse than ARK when it came out. Speaking of ARK, the devs did reuse some things from ARK. Such as the terrible running/breathing sound, rocks, rain, weapons and structures were just reskinned. Utter laziness from the devs on this. The merchants in spawn were all sold out after the server was up for an hour, no spawn protection, bodies are everywhere in the spawn city. PVP is clunky and all over the place.
There's nothing about this that make me want to keep playing this. I wish the devs kept it in the oven much, much longer...

NEO Scavenger is an excellent example of survival RPG, bringing to mind other isometric games like UnReal World and Haven and Hearth.  This game masters the eerie, abandoned quality present in Fallout, and is as challenging to navigate.  You will realize the painful cost of each difficult decision.
That said, the game features nothing by way of world building.  You can craft your own ramshackle gear from the broken remnants of the pre-war world and the often hazardous wilderness, but you cannot cultivate, construct defenses, or harvest natural resources apart from sticks, branches, water, and a few edibles.  Everything in the game is slowly decaying, and ultimately, so are you.  If you want a sense that your character has a future other than ending up the corpse someone else scavenges, this is not the game for you.
I can honestly say I feel I've had my money's worth, but I don't think I'll finish the main story line.  This game may well leave you feeling like a murderous hobo, starving, infected, insane, who would gleefully pop out of nowhere and bludgeon some random stranger to death with a tree branch for a shoddy left boot and a plastic shopping bag.  But some people who enjoy the survival genre are looking for just that.

Grim Dawn is definitely one of my favourite games. I love everything about it so far. I believe the game is worth more than Crate Entertainment has priced it at and the expansion adds a staggering amount of content, of which I feel I've hardly scratched the surface.
The environment: Love it. The variety is good and the environments look epic or creepy or epically creepy. The different environments feel natural as you traverse the world of Cairn. The history of the world is detailed and interesting. I like the level of technology in the world. I also enjoy the notes and journals you find along the way.
Character building/progression: very detailed. Great variety with their dual-class system. I feel that almost any combination of dual-class, damage type and weapon choice is possible, though some combinations have more power potential than others. I enjoy the extra layer of Contellations and bonus abilities. There are a lot of possibilities to play with.
Gear: even the basic, non-magical tiers look badass. There are plenty of armour slots to fill and enhancements to play with.
Combat: it's an ARPG. Quick and brutal against hordes of enemies. But, not mindless combat. You may feel like a god of war, but the bosses (of which there are different tiers), and even some hero monsters, can still humble you.
Replay Value: for me, so much replay value. I've logged over 500 hrs at this point and have only taken one character through all the content on Normal and part of Epic - and there's still Legendary difficulty, rogue-like dungeons, and the expansion. I've happily spent a lot of time trying out different class combinations and tinkering with them. When the expansion came out I suppose I could have finished the game on said character (a shotgun wielding pyromancer), but I thought a life-stealing Necromancer with a gigantic 2hander might be fun. I was right.
Conclusion: if you are even flirting with the idea of trying out an ARPG, you should definitely get this game.

It's a more intricate version of chess to me on some level, and aside from the fact all sorts of things can happen with friends in multiplayer, the game causes the player to step it up through varying difficulties and preallocated challenges where some of the behavior is much less transparent on behalf of the AI. Additionally, I've found myself just sitting there, pouring hours into doing things such as becoming supreme overlord dictator of the world. It's a good reminder to me, and perhaps other players, why they should never be placed in such a position of power. The world couldn't handle dictators so overpowered.

I want to love this game, I really really do. I still would suggest it to people who like rogue-like(lite) games, and enjoy the survival because the survival is incredibly well done. I’m akso sure I will play more hours of this as time goes. With that said, my main issue is, unlike a lot of other permadeath games, this one has a story to tell, which might take you a long time to figure out when first playing, and it seems really interesting.
The problem is, very few will ever get to experience that story as no matter how you gear up or character build, your character has the staying power of a lit candle in a hurricane. Little to nothing can stop a low or average enemy from getting in a lucky shot that will knock you out or kill you in one blow, costing you hours of game time. You will lose anything and everything you were working on. Having to re-create a character and starting again with the repetitive cryo facility wake-up scene. I understand this is the concept of this genre, but to have nothing left after working so hard to build up a character and losing 3-5 hours, for me, is frustrating. There are some who may love that, though. Once again, it’s not the permadeath for me, as much as it is the lucky cheap-shot.
There are several mods for it already, though most just give more items and such. There are no saving mods as of yet, and the only way that truly seems to provide a means to see the story is some kind of invulnerability mod. Though removing the challenge entirely isn’t any fun at all. There is also a great mod out there that gives limited repair features that help shift the gameplay.
With that said, the scavenging and survival system is absolutely incredible. Sometimes it can be a little over-complicated when you first play, but as a general rule most recipes make logical sense. Found a shard of glass? Use it as a cutting tool, wrap it with a piece of paper for a makeshift shiv, or use it as a weapon in dire need at the risk of cutting yourself. Found a glass bottle? Smash it and use it to threaten off an enemy. Use clean water or whiskey to sterilize your wounds before using those rags you sterilized in boiled water to stem the bleeding.
The survival is the strongest aspect of this game and it shines over everything. From having to keep warm, to managing your health. Accidentally drank some bad water? Got sepsis from that wound you forgot to clean? You better find a place to hunker down and heal up with that bottle of anti-biotics you found in the locked shed with your makeshift lockpicks. Forage some wood and keep that fire going to stay warm and keep your immune system up, but make sure you set up some noise traps because people and…things can see it burning.
The in-depth survival system makes this an amazing game to enjoy overcoming what I have said above, which is why I still suggest it. To see an indie dev put together a system that a AAA company could never have the creativity to pull off is a breath of fresh air. Tidalis is a casual "falling blocks" puzzler by the developer Arcen Games. The basic premise of Tidalis is that the player must define the orient of each block, fire a beam from one block of a particualr color and that beam travels through like colored blocks in a direct that depends on the player-set orient. If three or more blocks are hit they are elimited. Losing in this game usually is caused by having the game area fill up with blocks although some levels have other special conditions. Win conditions vary per level; they may have the player eliminate a certian number of blocks of a certain color or eliminate a certian number of blocks in a limit number of moves.
I personally didn't enjoy Tidalis or think it's a very well design game. Maybe my limited time in the game suggests I didn't properly give the game a chance, but with the limited scope of a casual game like this the time I spent should be sufficent to determine the quality of a game. The concept of the game might seem good on paper, if you enjoy these sort of games, but actually playing the game failed to inspire or be an enjoyable experience.

The game encourages getting combos. When blocks fall due to the block underneath them being eliminated would also trigger and potentially eliminate additional blocks. In practice, however, the chance that this would happen was fairly rare. One could, however, attempt to tediously line up moves in advance. Again this might sound like a good idea but in a game like this where quickly lining up moves so the board doesn't, this process becomes a mental chore. When triggering a block it will take several seconds for the move to resolve and the player is unable to trigger additional blocks. If falling blocks are trigger the player is often forced to wait for them to impotently resolve before proceeding. Many times the necessary blocks aren't even available and I am required to wait for fate to smile upon me in the form of the blocks that I need. As a result of all of this, the gameplay feels slow, tedious and not particularly satisfying.
Tidalis doesn't support USB controllers - there may be a way to use a controller by adjusting the key bindings but seeing how the game is played I have a hard time seeing how it would work.
If you're looking for a game of this type, there are better options out there.

An interesting casual puzzle game. A little like Tetris but much deeper. Its basic rule is to eliminate 3 blocks of the same colors. The difference is that the block is directional. Player have to adjust the direction of every block to chain the stream through as more blocks as possible. When a set of blocks is eliminated, one or more new streams appear to connect more blocks of different colors. The more sets of blocks are eliminated continuously, the more the combos are. This mechanics makes this game deep, complicated and engrossing. This game uses many different conditions to limit player's move, thus making it much more challenging. Finally, the background music is beautiful. Recommend if you just wanna relax peacefully.

There are parts of this game that I enjoy, and parts that I enjoyed...not so much. I'm not one of those hardcore SR1 or 2 fans who despises the direction the series has gone in, I generally enjoyed SR3. I assure you I have no bias. Warning: SPOILERS!!!
+Great dynamic lighting
-Textures are barely improved from SR3, they are average at best, laughable at worst.
-Some of the animations glitch occasionally (I'm not talking about the intentional story-related glitched NPCs).
+60 fps.
-Lower end machines/cards WILL NOT run this game smoothly: when I originally downloaded SR4, my card couldn't handle it (card in question: Nvidia GTX 650). I was barely hitting 30 fps, steadily running at a jagged 22 fps. Now I've upgraded to an Nvidia GTX 970 and it runs FLAWLESSLY. This is just a warning.
-My game has crashed out of the blue around 4 times, once when I had just completed a mission (it didn't save).
-There isn't a day/night cycle until you unlock it at the end. It stays a gloomy night (I'm assuming to show off the neon alien lights).
+The writing in SR4 is more mature and less goofy when compared to SR3. Many of the jokes are references to classic sci-fi movies.
+Some of the missions [spoilers]place you back in a SR2 setting and there's another where you're fighting STAG from SR3.[/spoilers] It's great for nostalgia.
+In my opinion, the alien invasion/presidency concept is a pretty cool one (I truly wish there was more gameplay as president). The banter back and forth with the villain Zinyak made me laugh. Zinyak is an intellegent foe who isn't over-the-top ridiculous as some villains from SR3 were. He does remind me of a James Bond villain though.
-Some of the loyalty missions became repetitive, even to the point where I turned down the game volume and brought up YouTube or Itunes on another screen and listened to that. Hardcore fans will enjoy rescuing and interacting with the crews on the loyalty missions, but doing the SAME damn thing OVER and OVER wore me out.
+In a few of the missions, you get to [spoilers]go back to a 1950s-style Steelport[/spoilers] and cause destruction with your bare fists, an old pickup truck, and the dubstep gun. This gave me a few laughs and it was nice to see a different side of Steelport without gangsters and crime (even though that's the point of the game).
+HOLY CRAP! [spoilers]SUPER-FREAKING-POWERS!!! I LOVED the addition of superpowers. Being able to run faster than cars and jump higher than buildings[/spoilers] is enjoyable and what, to me, really made me give this game a thumbs up.
-Unfortunately, your [spoilers]super powers[/spoilers] are given to you too early on in the game. It gives the player absolutely NO reason to use cars or to customize said cars.
+The powers you are given are upgradable to the point where you feel like a god.
-I feel like your powers are kind of OP. The game offers no real challenge. I only died like 4 times through my entire playthrough, mainly from stupid mistakes.
+I like the addition of the alien weaponry (including the hilarious, yet kind of pointless, dubstep gun) and the upgrades available for every single gun in the game.
-The weapon customization is lacking. No attachments for weapons, only custom skins; and only a few skins (camos) at that. I would have liked to have seen attachments like lasers or flashlights or grips or anything really.
+The activities spread throughout the city are entertaining and add countless hours of playability on top of the main story and side missions.
-A few times in this game, I got extremely♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ It was mainly because I would keep getting knocked down by lasers from the alien turret. Keep in mind, while youre down, you are losing health and completely vulnerable. In the time it took to recover from a laser bomb, another rpg was headed my way. Even when the explosives resistance was upgraded to the max, it was still frustrating to say the least.
This game is fun as hell and where it falls short, it compensates in other areas. It has a ton of replay value and for $20, it's not a bad price. Naturally, I'd recommend buying this on sale because who wants to spend more money than they have to, but if you can't wait, I think $20 is fair as I've put in 30+ hours so far (on my first playthrough). Buy it, you won't regret it!   --7/10--

Company of Heroes 2 is one of the few RTS games that I genuinely find enjoyable. Much like the original Company of Heroes and Dawn of War II, this is a game that rewards careful tactical consideration and a diverse combined-arms strategy. The campaign is only okay, but the multiplayer (or even simply skirmish matches against the AI) is where this game has great replay value. Be warned, there is no single-copy LAN play, but nowadays you can occassionally find this game on sale and get two copies cheaply, so that is not as much an issue as when the game initially released at full price.
Company of Heroes 2 distinguishes itself from its predecessor by focusing on the eastern front of World War II. The game features two playable armies, the Soviet Union's Red Army and the German Eastern Front army: the Wehrmacht Ostheer. These two teams are different but well-balanced.
In general, the Red Army has the advantage of quantity, such as having larger squads and cheaper vehicles, while the Germans have small squads of elite soldiers and more expensive but stronger vehicles. Because of their strength in numbers, the Soviets can more easily reinforce their units, and can even use their generic conscript soldiers to reinforce other squads on the fly. Meanwhile, the Germans gain technology levels as the fight progresses, unlocking more elite soldiers and more tactical options. Of the two, the Soviets are a bit simpler to play, but neither army lacks for depth.
I am pleased to see that this game has been well-supported since its original launch. With the Western Front Armies expansion, the game has moved in a new direction. Replacing the old level up rewards system, the game now sports a reward drop system called "War Spoils," which allows players to gain items that were previously exclusive to overpriced DLC or pre-orders. Furthermore, the pack adds new Western Front maps and two new armies to the game. Even if you don't own Western Front, you can still play on the maps online, and face both human and AI opponents using the new armies.
The main addition of this expansion is the two new armies, effectively doubling the number of playable teams in the game. These armies are the U.S. Forces and the German Oberkommando West. Like Company of Heroes: Opposing Fronts, the game now has two German armies, but each is unique. Though they still aren't the Panzer Elite of the old game, the German West Army focuses heavily on mechanized forces. Meanwhile, the U.S. is designed as a highly mobile and versatile team, capable of triggering special abilities on the go and outmaneuvering opponents to flank them with relative ease.
Company of Heroes 2 is an impressive game and a worthy sequel to one of the greatest RTS games in PC history. I hope that many others come to enjoy and appreciate this game as I already have, and I recommend it to anyone who will listen wholeheartedly.

Although I have very little time with this game on steam, I put hundreds of hours into the ps2 version.
This is absolutely one of the best FPS games of all time! There is no loadout customization, no 15 gamemodes like COD, no quickscopers or campers. This is a very simple game, albeit a fantastic one. If you like Star Wars but not FPS games, this might not be for you. If you like FPS games but not Star Wars, this is definitely worth a try. And if you like both, you will very likely lose yourself in this game for upwards of 50 hours. If you want online gameplay, you have to download gameranger, since the devs stopped supporting online after 9 YEARS! That has to say something about the quality of this game. Once you've done that, you can easily find online lobbies. This is a game where you play as one of the four major factions of the Original trilogy and the Prequel trilogy, and you battle it out on all of the icnoic planets of the Star Wars univserse. Oh, and this is far better than the new Battlefront by Dice.
As long as you enjoy FPS's, the gameplay here is phenonemal and has hundreds of hours of replay value. You can play as a variety of clases for each faction between Droids, the Republic, the Empire and the Rebelion. There are 2 major gamemodes: CTF (1 flag or 2), and Conquest. Conquest is where you fight for command posts, which are basically respawn points on the map. The variety here is low, however it is all you need. In the Galactic Conquest mode, you take turns with the AI to conquer the entire Star Wars galaxy. There is also a campaign, with a very good narrative.
Space battles are also relevant here, and a big part of the gameplay. They are not as good as ground battles, but they are hectic and will provide many more hours of gameplay when supplemented with the ground fighting. They are a little repetitive, but then again so is every FPS.
Finally, you can play as heros every now and again, which are jedi for the faction you are playing as (and also Boba-Fett, who is not a jedi but a hero). Playing as these characters is really fun and makes you feel very OP, which you will be.
This game utilizes all of the classic Star Wars scores composed by John Williams, so needless to say it is great. The only problem with this game's sound is that you will tend to hear a lot of "we captured a command post," or "we lost a command post," from the AI as you play conquest. This gets very old very fast, although it is definitely no major detractor.
For 2005's standards, this game looked pretty good. For 2015-2016 standards, it looks pretty bad. textures are muddy compared to what you see today, and even on max settings it looks nothing like a AAA game today. However, unless yo uare the biggest graphics snob of all time, you will not let this bother you. After all, an FPS doesn't need that good graphics anyway.
Absolutely the best part of this game is the amount of time you can spend playing it. Things start to get repetetive around the 100 hour mark, but you keep playing anyway because the online is always working and you can turn the difficulty up to Elite, which is only for truely elite players. Pros:
-The idea behind this game was amazing, and this game may be able to reach it's full potential in
the future, but that day is FAR away.
-The game's overall performance isn't great, but it's also not bad.
-The animations and models are actually pretty good.
There aren't many more good things that I can say about this game right now however.
Cons:
-The graphics are awful, nothing like the screenshots.
-The gameplay is bland and feels virtually identical to ARK: Survival Evolved, and the few
new mechanics that this game has (Magic, Factions, an actual Perk Tree, etc.) are just boring
and don't feel like they've been fully fleshed out yet.
-The menus, specifically the inventory and options menus, are practically just copy and pasted
from ARK.
-The controls are terrible, half of the actions weren't even bound to a key by default and those
that were either didn't work at all or were impractical.
-The character customization is really awkward due to the use WAY to many sliders.
-There are three playable races in this game, humans, elves, and dwarves, these races are
literally nothing more than a saved preset however and they don't have anything other than
slight differences in appearance differentiating them.
-Some of the models are just slight edits of creatures from ARK, including the dragon on the
main ♥♥♥♥ing menu.

Conclusion:
This game is terrible at present which is suprising due to the fact that it's been in development
for several years.
I was really hyped for this game, but I have been severely let down.
Note:
I am completely aware that Snail Games owns Studio Wildcard, but
in my personal opinion, that does not justify practically remaking ARK.

I don't normally write serious reviews. I'm one of those undesirable♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that uploads the "11/10 uninstall function works great" review, but
will be my exception. You have no idea how hard it will be for me to not write "I murdered a naked guy while wearing a clown mask", but I will get through it, for this amazing game.
Let's start with the basics; you're some random guy (avoiding spoilers) that has just woken from cryogenic sleep during the apocalypse somewhere around the city of Detroit. After a friendly interaction with a lovely creature known as a "Dogman", you step outside to  experience the outside world of Michigan... and dang, it's cold. Like, "Oh my God I can't feel my feet and I'm feeling really sleepy" cold. After a few deaths and several hours of learning the basics (don't eat random berries or mushrooms you find unless  you know they aren't poisonous, that guy with the broken bottle really wants to eat your leg, and yes, it's cold, put some pants on) you really get into this game.
As others have said, however, an ungodly amount of time can be spent on this game, and it can never be taken back. In a sense, it's like
. You spend 3 hours finding a weapon, finding your friends wherever they are on the map, and end up faffing around until some gruesome death by either a glitching zombie or a player that only speaks Russian.
In the beginning, you get used to dying. After a while, however, you end up living longer and longer, until one life lasts you hours of real life time. Everything is peachy until that one night you decide to sleep in a forest and forget to set up a noise trap or hide, and you're stabbed to death by some plague-ridden nutcase in your sleep. After a day or two of angry avoidance of the game, you decide to give it a second chance, innocently, you pour more hours into it, only to die in a similar manner. It's a beautiful circle of life (death)!
With such extensive content already and more updates to come, NEO Scavenger is one of my favorite games of all time. I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys hardcore survival games, and/or murdering innocents with his/her bare hands whilst wearing nothing but a Ronald McDonald lookalike mask and a hospital gown. So i loaded up some much played(as you can see) civ v today and several hours in i noticed something unfortunate and to my eyes wholly unacceptable. The siege units became tissue paper...which diminishes any tactics in the game(they have starcraft and warcraft and other zerg games, we dont need this one to become one). I will support this premise first with math and then with logic.
Math: Pikeman str 16 gets hit str str 42 city for (40-50) damage repeatadly
trebuchet str 12x1.66(double cover) + 200% city bonus(does not say attack only but as you will see clearly is atm ie nerf)=60str...one would think 10 damage...actual damage taken 50..sometimes 75. Meaning? Just 12x1.66 from double cover should be 20. 20 should take 25 percent less damage than the 16 str pikeman meaning 30-38 damage....IF you ignore the city bonus, so clearly the city bonus is being ignored on defense. Nevermind that that does not fully cover the amount of damage seige are taking from cities but at a minimum this is the case.
Said seige unit is also sitting in a citadel and so should be getting another 100% defense....it isnt. So, it is in fact taking EXTRA damage from the city not just ignoring a bonus that to wording, logic, and previous mechanics was and should be applying.
Now aside from the whole, these are their own rules they are breaking thing why should we care? Seige units add depth to the game. With the current mechanics there is really no reason to build them. They are more an uninformed player trap than anything else. if you are supoosed to zerg...and only zerg and siege gets hit for as much and more damage versus the thing they are designed to fight why would you not simply pile on the more generally useful land units. Tactical game without tactics...junk.
If the game was like this the whole time i woulda had my 2 hour refund. As of right now, do not recommend.

TLDR: "Medium" RPG elements and hack 'n slash combat make this a really fun game.
This is a hack and slash reminiscent of Dynasty warriors, but it has enough RPG elements that set it apart. It also has light crafting elements (i.e. use monster drops to 'upgrade' accessories) and the grinding is quite pleseant. The class system is a lot more than I was expecting as well.
As you level you are awarded points that you can put into your character that give you bonuses (+amount health, mana, strength etc.) as well as grant you skills (i.e. special moves, magic, buffs etc.) to mess around with. There are also points that you can invest into your characters that carry over from profession to profession so you get a feeling of progression even if you change classes.
You also have weapons proficiencies that grant you stat buffs to your entire party which you can add and swap out when you reach a set limit as you get more of them. You can also change back to a previous profession and you keep all the points you invested into said unlocks and the level of that profession (and can respec if you want a different build). It's very fluid and fun and awards you trying out new weapons and professions.
Overall, I'm enjoying this game very much and if you like 'light' (more like medium) RPG elements and hack n' slash, I would definitely recommend this game. The nostalgia from the older games is great too (they use the same sound effects for many of the monster's iconic moves and spell sounds).

Company of Heroes 2 is one of the few RTS games that I genuinely find enjoyable. Much like the original Company of Heroes and Dawn of War II, this is a game that rewards careful tactical consideration and a diverse combined-arms strategy. The campaign is only okay, but the multiplayer (or even simply skirmish matches against the AI) is where this game has great replay value. Be warned, there is no single-copy LAN play, but nowadays you can occassionally find this game on sale and get two copies cheaply, so that is not as much an issue as when the game initially released at full price.
Company of Heroes 2 distinguishes itself from its predecessor by focusing on the eastern front of World War II. The game features two playable armies, the Soviet Union's Red Army and the German Eastern Front army: the Wehrmacht Ostheer. These two teams are different but well-balanced.
In general, the Red Army has the advantage of quantity, such as having larger squads and cheaper vehicles, while the Germans have small squads of elite soldiers and more expensive but stronger vehicles. Because of their strength in numbers, the Soviets can more easily reinforce their units, and can even use their generic conscript soldiers to reinforce other squads on the fly. Meanwhile, the Germans gain technology levels as the fight progresses, unlocking more elite soldiers and more tactical options. Of the two, the Soviets are a bit simpler to play, but neither army lacks for depth.
I am pleased to see that this game has been well-supported since its original launch. With the Western Front Armies expansion, the game has moved in a new direction. Replacing the old level up rewards system, the game now sports a reward drop system called "War Spoils," which allows players to gain items that were previously exclusive to overpriced DLC or pre-orders. Furthermore, the pack adds new Western Front maps and two new armies to the game. Even if you don't own Western Front, you can still play on the maps online, and face both human and AI opponents using the new armies.
The main addition of this expansion is the two new armies, effectively doubling the number of playable teams in the game. These armies are the U.S. Forces and the German Oberkommando West. Like Company of Heroes: Opposing Fronts, the game now has two German armies, but each is unique. Though they still aren't the Panzer Elite of the old game, the German West Army focuses heavily on mechanized forces. Meanwhile, the U.S. is designed as a highly mobile and versatile team, capable of triggering special abilities on the go and outmaneuvering opponents to flank them with relative ease.
Company of Heroes 2 is an impressive game and a worthy sequel to one of the greatest RTS games in PC history. I hope that many others come to enjoy and appreciate this game as I already have, and I recommend it to anyone who will listen wholeheartedly.

The apology for Dead Island we all wanted.
I got this gifted, and having just finished the main games' story and all the side missions, I can vouch for this being super amazing. Coop-ing with a friend, I've enjoyed slaughtering my way through zombies combined with neat parkouring. So many great moments, so many laughs. It also has a good mechanic for changing between single player story and playing it with someone, and from what I've heard you can actually play 4 people at a time. Any competitions are optional, as are plenty of side missions, which is a good thing as the game is letting you decide where and when to go anywhere you like.
Starting out can be tough, seeing you have no special skills to defeat the gnawing dead wanting you for their last supper. The games' brilliance, however, lies in letting you get points ALSO FOR RUNNING AWAY and AVOIDING danger, as well as combating enemies, so you always feel like you're winning and getting stronger by leveling up three different skill trees.
This helps greatly with any frustration you might experience when dying many times over. You always have the choice of just running away and you'll get better at running, climbing and parkouring the more you practice - as in PLAYER skill, not just character skill. So it's a win/win most of the time. The occasional slip from a ledge or grabbing hold of the wrong parkour point is only minor and doesn't in the slightest detract from a superb game.
Definitely worth your money and your time, this is one of the best and funniest game experiences I've had in a while. Get this and enjoy it alone or with friends - I guarantee super good times either way.
Edit: I just finished the expansion and my review may as well count for that as well. Add some cool and fun buggies to the already fun gameplay and we are all set for zombie survival.

Once you add "devotions," the variety of builds is staggering.
