One of if not the best indie game I've played, 9/10. Think rogue-like game where you control the crew of a spaceship. You can move them around, repairing or boosting systems. You also control power distribution, and can boost shields, weapons, or hyperdrive (if you need to flee quicker). You can also buy various upgrades for both your crew, your ship and the weapons. All these things allow for a suprising amount of customisability despite each playthrough being quite short.
Pros -
Indie game means low price, which it's more than worth
Interesting mechanic of controlling the crew rather than the ship directly - if you get boarded either send you crew to fight or vent that room to space
Lot of customisability
Short(ish) playthroughs mean its handy as a pick-up-and-play
Cons - There isn't THAT many random events, enough to have 3/4 unique playthroughs but after than the odd one will be familiar - still has more replayability than a lot of games
Endgame is ridiculous, expect to have to play through half a dozen times just to reach the final boss, just to get annihilated by them.

BDO is a game that always intrigued me for the longest time. I have never really been into MMO's before, but I first tried the game when they did a free week trial, just before the steam release of the game. I found the combat enjoyable, and I liked what I saw of the game even if I only reached level 27 or so on that character.
When it released on steam I purchsed the game and started over again, trying new classes but it never got its teeth stuck in me. I found making money was convoluted and there was a lot of depth to the game. I put it down and didn't touch it until this week.
I started again, making a new character, this time determined to stick it out past my confusion and start learning things as I went, taking things slow. I found a really solid guide on youtube by
where he goes over the basics.
One of the things I would HIGHLY reccommend is watching this video a few times to understand everything that he says, he covers a lot but it is worth it.
I really like this game as I can play it as hardcore or as casual as I want. I set my character up to fish or process stuff I gathered the night before, and then I work on IRL stuff. I can check back, see if I need to do something different or take my stuff to my storage to keep going. Then when I am done or I want to take a break I can go play this game hardcore. The entire time I feel like I am making progress on my character.
The game also incentivize you to take on multiple characters, without the need for going through the whole story to unlock anything. You make it past the tutorial level, then you are free to do as you please. Even better, the more characters you have past a certain threshold, the more money the game gives you everyday. Yes, the game gives you money everyday for playing the game and having multiple characters.
I haven't even begun to scratch this games inner workings, and I am happy I stuck it out this week. I'm gonna be playing this game for the next little bit.
The only downsides I have encountered is that pets are almost a must if you are gonna focus on combat, which is a pretty decent way to get money. Pets will pick up things every 10 seconds, but you can upgrade them to pick up every 4 seconds which is a huge bonus. Even more you can equip up to 5 of them. Thankfully its not too expensive to get one, about $10 for most of them. I also seem to have somewhat crappy performance on my machine. I am running an i7 5820K 1070TI 16 GBs of RAM and running the game on an SSD and I am getting around 70 FPS on very high settings. Which seems kind of low to me, but its still playable.
all in all, I'd say the game is an 8/10.

Blender is a fantastic program for the budding graphic artist. It is packed full of features that many other free modeling packages miss and has the power to create stunning images and video.
I don't know of any other package that allows you to make a full 3D video, edit movie and sound clips, render out beautiful scenes with such a large set of effects and build games all in one place.
There have been a few complaints about the interface and, I admit the learning curve is steep. However, once you learn to use it the interface can be your greatest ally. It gives you the power to define how you use the program. Don't let the few people complaining stop you from trying it out.
I started out in 3DS Max, have used Maya and SoftImage. Of all these programs, I find I enjoy working in Blender the most.

Over the 100 hours I've played this game I've found things I like in it but overall, it has serious flaws.
Pros:
1. Good to pass time in it. Matches are long but they don't feel like eternity.
2. The gameplay is diverse in strategies.
Cons - or what's broken:
1. Diplomacy and the behaviour of the leaders are ridiculous - not unrealistic but more like every leader have their periods. This would be just a minor annoyance but there's more:
2. Combat. The AI sux at combat. It can loose a great advantage at anytime because it leads its army like an idiot. It often happens that I beat a 2-3x as large civ which has a 3-4x as large army due to poor strategies. Of course, you can just increase the "difficulty" which will give more and more resources to the AI but it won't improve its algorithms.
3. Besieging - can you imagine a normal city standing with 2 units of crossbowmens against 4 units of cannons and 2 units of rifflemens? Some cities regenerate more HP than what 3 cannons can fire...
4. The AI cheats from normal(prince) difficulty. It often happens that when I conquer multiple cities of a civ - including their capitals - they spawn HUGE armies out of nowhere - while having a positive income and a lot of money. On the other hand when I lose a city I know I'm in trouble. Some civs constantly lose wars against me but still manage to "spare" more resources.
5. Science victory and intercontinental wars - they take waaaay too much time and they're really boring until the end. Playing on continents against a few civs is better.
6. There are too much resources to "manage" and they're really there just to waste your time.
7. The keyboard layout is bad because it uses arrow keys instead of WASD by default. Ergonomy is important.
8. The overlay of the interface looks bad and isn't comfortable.

This is a game I was hoping would exist for a long time.
The glory and grandeur of founding and expanding your own civilization is captured by Sid Meier's brilliant game design.
The rules are fairly straightforward but definitely take lots of repetition to master. It will take most people many games before they feel like they are building a civilization that is worth the test of time. You can choose a multitude of starting leaders, and Sid Meier has some very enlightened choices, such as the Pre-Columbian civilizations (not savages) that existed prior to European contact.
Different leaders have different starting statistics that aid their progress in varied ways. This adds some flavor to a game that is otherwise fairly clockwork in execution.
The graphics are just a tad bit cartoonish for my tastes but I think they appeal to most people. Overall, it's a great strategy game and worth hours of your time.
9/10

Arnold Ray "Bake" McBride (born February 3, 1949 in Fulton, Missouri), also nicknamed "Shake n' Bake" and "The Callaway Kid", is a former Major League Baseball outfielder, known primarily as a member of the Philadelphia Phillies' teams of the late 1970s and early 1980s. Selected in the 37th round in 1970 as the 811th player,[1] he made his major league debut for the St. Louis Cardinals in 1974, finishing the season with 173 base hits, 30 stolen bases, and a .309 batting average, and was named the National League's Rookie of the Year, the first Cardinal to earn the award since Bill Virdon in 1955. On June 15, 1977, McBride was traded, with Steve Waterbury, by the St. Louis Cardinals to the Phillies for Tom Underwood, Dane Iorg, and Rick Bosetti.
On February 16, 1982, McBride was traded to the Cleveland Indians for Sid Monge. On November 7, 1983, he was granted free agency, but chose to retire from baseball.

Black Desert Online
First off, do not expect to get anywhere in this game without putting hours into it, whether those hours are active or afk skilling, you will need to do both.
Now onto the review.
Black Desert Online is one of the best mmorpg's I have played to date. Seeing as i've been gaming since I was young, and kind of an MMORPG wh*re, I have played my fair shares. There is no "main" quest line. Quest are categorized into different types, Black Spirit, Life, Exploration/Trade etc. Each quest you complete gives you experience into your "Contribution Points" (CP) experience bar. You will need these Contribution Points (CP) to establish yourself in this game. You will use the CP to invest into certain nodes to send your workers to.. And yes you have workers. They will gather resources for you as you play the game and they have a whole leveling system of their own. Quest reset daily and your CP, workers, and pets are account bound so alts are an incentive in this game. There is so much about this game that you will need at least 5k hrs to get a good holding. If you want to game/afk your life away, this is the game to do it.

One of the more 'middle-range' Artifex Mundi hidden object games on Steam.
I say more middle range because although it is on a newer version of their game engine and has some of the nice more well rounded UI and UX enhancements and very pretty art (other than the characters), I found overall the story/setting and game play to be a bit more stilted and less enjoyable than some of the others. It is nice to see one without a 'Play in expert mode' achievement though.
The games 'unique' element is the detective mode. You are given a hidden object search with 9 'clues', but it doesn't label what they are.. you are given hints in casual and advanced mode via cursor highlights but I imagine this would have been quite hard if you started straight into expert mode as they don't initially make it very clear how it works.. I also found her 'conclusions' based on the evidence found to be extremely hard to believe.. it supports the story but some of it is barely logical =)
I appreciated that the hidden object puzzles all made good use of real word items and for the most part were fairly logical in sizing and placement (objects that would be on a desk were on a desk for example). While games that mix it up can be quite fun (See the Amazing Adventures series by SpinTop/Popcap) it is all good as long as it is consistent and there are some games that just do it for one or two objects which I just find frustrating.. it's not a clever trick.. it just makes the logic of the world seem even more stupid.
While the hidden object games seem logical, most of the other puzzles seem outright bizzare to be fitting into the world and whie there is some supernatural/mythological elements to explain some of these, others just wouldn't make sense beyond 'the game wants me to put this here to open that'.. which I generally don't mind, but when so much else is trying to make sense it comes across a little inconsistent.
Hidden object puzzle to logic/block sliding/roating/other puzzles is probably 3/1ish.. it felt like there were a lot more hidden objects in this one than some of the more recent games - and to be honest it was quite a nice mix. I felt there was an over-use of the rotating puzzle though.
I often find that since these games have introduced the ability to jump between map points quickly and easily (love it) that sometimes, as in this game, I just open the map up each time I do something and jump to the next point with an 'active' flag. This game seemed to have some fairly random non-connected scenes that encouraged this behaviour and once you begin it can be hard to stop. This is in contrast to other examples such as 'Left Behind - No one on board' where it just 'felt right' to navigate naturally between scenes.
Unfortunately there were a couple of scenes that were hard to find. I think this was due to the points on the map being the start of one or two scenes, so there is a marker that there is something to do there, but you can miss the connector to the next scene because unlike the later games not all scenes are accessible from the map. This also results in indoor locations disabling the use of the map - this is different to when they disable selections on the map because it is inaccessible - and it just feels weird to be told.. no.. you're inside the library - you can't go to the museum now unless you walk through three rooms back to the main door and teleport from the street.
STORY INFORMATION FOLLOWS:
I'm not sure if it was the attempt to have the game based in a more 'American' setting and it just coming off wrong or what, but the writing and language used seemed more stilted. Structurally it just felt.. weird.
There are some unsympathetic sympathetic characers, you can tell from the later notes and things that you are meant to feel bad for their situation and/or that they are trying to make the best of their bad situation but the writing of the notes hidden throughout the game is quite a contrast to the dialogue as though written by two different people who perhaps had different ideas, the dialogue writer making them hard boiled and unforgiving and the note writer trying to justify it but it just doesn't work together.
I do sometimes get the feeling in Artifex Mundi hidden object games that I'm meant to have known something before the game tells me, and I activate a puzzle or do something out of order and then it's not until I go and do something else that the 'back story' is filled in and it clicks for me.. which in their newer stuff is handled a lot better.
There were a few instances in this game where it was like 'I need a lens for the projector' which is great and all - but I'm currently at the point where I don't even see a need for the projector itself yet. It felt sometimes like it was taking away my opportunity to go 'AHA - I need to go back to that projector because now I have these slides that will tell me more'.
:STORY INFORMATION ENDS
This is one for those who want more hidden object searches over logic puzzles - there is no way to skip the hidden object searches by substituing mahjong/dominoes etc (as other Artifex Mundi games have done).
This game is one of the shorter ones that I have played recently, and though I don't think I'll replay it straight away to get the achivements I missed (the hidden ?'s, and the achievement for getting all achievements), it didn't make me feel like I wouldn't want to go through it again in order to do so.
It looks like another 9Clues game will be released soon and having now played this one I look forward to it and am hoping it will make use of some of the UX and story sensibilities of the more recent games.

First steam review. In short, Imagine Grand Theft Auto, Ratchet and clank, And infamous all had a baby. They called it Saints row 4. This game has the best aspects of all those games and it executed it very well.
Pros:
Smooth running
Good Comedy
Amazing customization
Good appeal to male and female gamers
Good weapons
Cons:
Still has some bugs. Such as objectives and youreslf getting stuck in walls forcing you to restart. I'd say I had to restart the mission due to bugs about 20 times total at the time of writing this review.
Crashes to desktop. The developers programmed the game to auto start after a crash or force close though. Which is a nice feature, but still crashes here and there nonetheless. I'd say it did this 7 times total at the time of this review.
Low replay value after 100% completion.
Other than getting your wanted level up and fighting enemies that way. No incentive to start a new game.
Gives you option to alter voice, but poor voice slider. Lower and higher voices sound distorted and electronic.
Not a hard game.
I bought the game with all the dlc pack and as soon as I had the dubstep gun and the "bling element" the game was no longer a challenge by any means.
Boss fights are a joke
Seriously, I was not scared or pulling my hair out over ANY of the bosses in this game. I would usually just spawn a UFO and 1 hit kill the boss with rockets. Or just pull out my dubstep gun.
VERY FEW AIR UTILITY LIKE GUN USAGE
I know this sounds like a little aspect of the game but I'll explain why it's on here. You have super powers in the game. (which you can use in the air) one of which includes super jumping. You can jump insanely high off the ground and glide, but cannot shoot your guns in the air, or stop in the air by any means. so that means if you want to use a rocket launcher and your enemy is on elevated ground you better have damn good prediction aiming on your moderate speed moving rocket.
Car usage is a joke.
If you're into the driving aspect of saints row or gta, this game is definitely not for you. Sure you can use cars. Highjack them. Fly into them. etc. like normal. But when you can run 5x as fast as a car, and ignore unit collision as well while running. There's not need. Not to mention you can super jump and glide across half the map 10x faster than any car in this game.
Overall
I like this game. And I do recommend it. But get it on sale. With all the dlc to it. Otherwise you might be disappointed with the game since there's so much dlc content. I haven't played the other saints row game due to the rumors of being identical to GTA but as a standalone game I had fun. I read it's not as fun if you've played Saints row 3 due to repeated content.

Overcooked is a great local co-op game. It is pretty straight forward, so almost anyone can play (I've played with 5 of my non-gamer friends and only 1 of them didn't immedetely get a hang of the controls). It's got a cute little plot to go along with the game, just enough so you have a reason to progress, but not enough so you feel like it's forcing a plot on a game that really isn't focused on the story. Most importantly though, the stages of the game are fun. Each one has its own weird mechanic, or a twist on one you learned previously, so levels don't get repetetive. The only mechanic I really hated was the    ice levels, but even they weren't too bad. Also, you probably want a controller to play this game, it's not required, but playing it with a controller is really the best way to play. Lastly, and this should be obvious but I'll say it anyway. Don't play this game by yourself. You can, but it really wasn't meant to be played alone. I found you could have a bit of fun trying to play the game by turning on shared controller and then playing two people at once, but still, make sure you have friends to play with most of the time.

Tropico 4 is one of the games that I originally started playing on the xBox 360. I didn't really know what to expect, Simulators are not really my thing, however I was very plesently surprised by this game, I started with the modern times campaign, from early 1950s through to launching a rocket in modern times. There are options as to how you manage your people from being a dictator and getting the secret police involved, to allowing democracy to run its course (and you'll probably be voted out).
It's a fun building simulator, not along the lines of Anno, which by the way is graphically stunning, it's a bit more light hearted, which is one of the things that attracted me to it, I was hooked, it is a game that you can lose track of time in quite easily, unless like me you a Mrs that gets very angry, I was spending more time on the game and not paying any attention to her (I still don't pay her any attention, but we are married now so she has no choice).
Somethings on this game are quite frustrating the looped music being one of them so I recommend you quickly go into the audio options and drop that volume down to 0. The other thing that is slightly frustrating is the partial controller support, Since the game is out on the 360 as well, just carry it across to the PC users as well, I appreciate not everyone likes to use a controller, but I am lazy and I am one of those rare breeds that sometimes finds a controller a little easier to use then a keyboard and mouse.
The missions are a little repetitive at times, you know that you will spend most of the time exporting to Russia, USA or China, you also know that someone is going to want a bribe, that said though it is a nice quirky game that if you put some hours into it will reward you. I picked this up a a humble bundle for next to nothing and for the rewardability you get from the game it's a definite recommendation from me.
Good graphics, smooth controls, overall decent story. Ya, I'd give it a 5/7 for sure

This game is a great survival RPG for anyone who wants an unforgiving, challenging, and heavily replayable game. The gameplay is very enjoyable, and I find it interesting how realistic this game is. The developers really have put in time to make sure that true human necessities are represented, such as food, a warm place to sleep, something to drink, and a means of protecting yourself. You're almost guaranteed to not do well on your first playthrough, but that's one of the best things about the game. As you keep playing, you learn more and more about what you need to do and what to look for & avoid, and you constantly get better at it. If you've played Don't Starve, you'll see similar gameplay aspects in NEO Scavenger.
If you're a fan of the original Fallout games, if you like survival games, or if you like truly tough games that take time and effort to succeed at, you'll surely enjoy this game.

This is a pretty good addition to the HO/adventure genre.  The plot is reasonably good, the music and voice acting are done better than some (not perfect, mind you, but decent), and it's graphically well made.  The "detective scene" portions are, as far as I can tell, unique to this game and it's nice to see some variation in a genre that tends to reuse and overuse the same types of puzzles constantly.
One problem I can see is the length; I clocked in at 2.6 hours with only about 2 of those hours being in the first playthrough (the rest was going back to grab a missed achievement, since I'm crazy like that).  At this short of a play time, it does not warrant the full $9.99 price tag, but if you can find a decent sale, it's completely worth it.
The other potential "con" to the game is that the HO scenes are not at all challenging and the puzzles are also relatively simple to complete.  If you're a veteran HO gamer looking for challenging puzzles, this isn't what you're looking for.  But if you're interested in a casual, simple game that won't take too much brain-power to get through, you'll probably like it.
TL;DR: this a fun, short, and casual game that is worth picking up on sale.

There are lots of opportunities too where you could easily kill one of them, or change the way things played out in Westeros. Basically, to avoid spoilers, let's make a comparison: in this game, you're like one of the giraffes in the intro of The Lion King. You can see a bunch of the plot happening, but you don't really do anything. You're just there, as background padding, with a barely interesting story, because you basically don't exist.
Nothing you do changes anything even in the self-contained story, and that's a pretty big downside for Telltale; I know their choices are usually fake, but in this one they FEEL fake. You get two options, for example: "Don't stab this guy" and "Stab this guy". Regardless of which you pick, you don't stab him. Then why'd you let me make a choice at all? It didn't even have to be a fatal stab, at least make my character do what I told him to do.
Other downsides include that only two of the plots are interesting. The young woman Forester - I can't even remember her name - has an extremely tedious plot that'll make you groan every time you return to it. She's the extreme version of unimportant choices, as she's constantly mingling with the rich and powerful, but fails to even impact her own story.
Overall, I wouldn't recommend this, even to fans of the show. It's very, very weak.

I am unsure as of what genre exactly this is...Telltale games tell you a story with interactive elements.
In this particular case they tell you the story of a comparably unknown house in the Game of Thrones / Song of fire and Ice universe.
The stories/chapters are told in a movie/film like manner and sometimes you will be presented either with quick push decsions (eg. in a fight) where failing to do so will end by you being dead and then scene being repeated or with conversation choices when talking to some characters.

So after all, for me it appears to be rather a film/movie with some interactive elements of nuisance than a game (RPG style where your decision actually make a difference and you appear to have different outcomes).
And for this price I cannot really recommend it.
So, my recommendation...only buy when really interested in the GoT lore and when on sale.

2-3 Hours in:
TL;DR: Combat, visuals are highly satisfying and fun. Storyline and voice acting could use a lot of work.
Black Desert Online is fun. It has been a while since I've experienced such a satisfying combat system, where you genuinely feel awesome rolling through the game. The combat chaos reminds me a great deal of Diablo, if you played Diablo from over your character's shoulder. Combat is action based, direction and key or mouse clicks affect your character's chosen attack. Combat is quick, flashy, and a bit chaotic, but highly entertaining and satisfying.
BSO's visuals are stunning, bright, and colorful. The world is gorgeous, and sports dynamic weather, a day/night cycle, and an open setting rife for exploration. I have, thus far, not seen a fast travel system, and it appears everyone travels by horse, donkey, or foot. The players are able to set their characters to travel automatically along a specified path (to quests, waypoints, etc.)
The game mechanics are a little confusing at first. There is a lot to take in. I'll let you know how that changes with some more time invested.
I would not pursue this game specifically for its story. The voice acting is painful and the storyline is not delivered well. They focused on telling a world-story, as opposed to concerning the storyline more with the player. There is something going on with the player's connection with dark energy and the dark shadow sprite that feeds you some of your quests.
Quests: A weird hybrid of running to and from quest givers and automatically being given and turning in quests from your companion dark shadow sprite. Not sure, exactly, why there are two different forms of quest givers, but it does not bother my personally. It may bother other players, though.

Super Amazing Wagon Adventure is a bizarre, but extremely addictive experience—a deceptively simple shmup/roguelike hybrid where every fork in the road offers a wealth of random events.  Its deliberately minimalistic graphics are not only a reflection of the edutainment game it parodies, but also the old-school gameplay mechanics from which much of its difficulty is derived—only one weapon can be used at a time, and the game is programmed to only process two
from the player at once, which leads to the quintessential choice between playing offensively or defensively...or, in other words, moving in one direction and attacking, or moving in two directions.
Does this come across as clunky sometimes?  Do the Atari-esque graphics hold it back in some regards?  Maybe.  But at a meager three dollars, the game offers a surprising amount of depth.  I would definitely recommend it to anyone looking for a light-hearted shmup experience.

Half life 2 is the sequel to the original Half-life that came out way back in 1998, and boy does it deliver.
Half-Life was as good as it was because it was innovative as hell, had some satisfying as heck gunplay, a slightly interesting story, wonderful imagery and bad♥♥♥♥♥fights. This game's a bit of a different horse entirely, but it's still just as good.
The visuals of this game, even to this day, hold up fantastically. Nothing looks really blurry unless you get really close and start zooming in, the models are very rich and detailed, the water looks really good even to today's standards and the art direction as well as level design are wonderful.
The Half-Life series is known to innovate, and Half-Life 2 did not disappoint. The physics are extremely advanced to the point where I've never found a game that handles it better to this day, the gun-play is simply improved over the predecessor, and the new mechanics, enemies, story, enviroments, and everything else that make this game unique are fantastic. Half-way through the game you get a ''gravity gun'' which allows you to manipulate physics objects. It's a bit of a gimmick but it's without a doubt the best gimmick I've ever seen, and stupidly fun to use.
Storywise, this game 1-upped its predecessor by a mile and has a script worthy of a plethora of awards. I won't spoil anything, but Half-Life 2 takes place in a dystopian future where the entire human race is under alien control. The characters are rich, have their own arcs  and are, simply put, very well written and interact with each other nicely. The way that Half-Life 2 handles "cut-scenes" is by having characters move around you and do their thing whilst you're left in full control of the situation. This simple fact immerses you into the game a whole lot more than a regular cut-scene and caused me to genuinely care about each and every one of these rich and detailed characters.
Level design is great. The world's fun to explore and play through, there's tiny little secrets everywhere and there's fun physics puzzles splayed all around. The world feels real, there's npc's everywhere and I never once got lost.
Seriously one of my favorite games ever. A true classic.

Two cases: You enter an arcade where there has been a slaughter by the fanatically religious Blue Frogs. A man croakes to you to help him. I write this review having played and beaten XCOM: Enemy Unknown and the expansion XCOM: Enemy Within.
Enemy Unknown is a fabulous remake of the original XCOM. Turnbased strategy, resource management, base development, character development, loss of characters...all of it adds up to a great gaming experience. Another huge plus is, being a Mass Effect fan, XCOM is where a lot of the inspirtation for ME came from, meaning playing this was like going back into a favorite universe in a whole new way.
The only downside, really, was that the game was somewhat simple and short, being a remake of an older game from a few generations back.
Enemy Within removed that downside, adding some substance and flavor to the game and rebalancing several aspects of gameplay. Also added were two new tech trees: Genetic Modification and Cybernetic Modification. Both are fun to explore and use in game and add quite a lot of depth to the game. Unlike many expansions, Enemy Within feels like a completed game, and most of the new features are integrated into the game pretty well. Also, from what I have seen of XCOM 2, the story line progresses from Enemy Within moreso than from Enemy Unknown, adding some relevance to the expansion.
Overall, XCOM was a fantastic experience that was just plain fun. Highly recommended to any and all fans of Sci Fi, Turnbased Strategy, Tactical Strategy, Mass Effect, and gaming in general.

If you're not familiar with the Telltale way of making games - its basically a heavily story driven adventure, where you can choose the outcomes of scenes mixed in with modest playable quick time event's.

It's debatable how much the story really changes depending on your choices, though to be honest - not many "branching" games actually deviate much from a fairly defined course. I've played the first chapter twice, making totally different choices and it still ended up with the same result.
I'd be hard pressed to think of any game that is truly that narratively flexible. So in the end it comes down to whether  non canon characters and events in Game Of Thrones is of interest to you, assuming that this doesn't actually tie into the tv show somehow when it hits the final stretch. There is an element to it that might be canon - time will tell.
Personally I found it just as brutal, and uncompromising as the tv show, and written reasonably well. It's not like the tv show is Shakespeare, and though I've never read the books - I doubt they are either. And so it wasn't a bad way to spend around 10 hours.
On the plus side the voice acting is excellent, and does feature a number of cast members. On the downside the graphics can look very ropey in places, and the animation is very stiff.
I enjoyed it, but it's probably quite a marmite kind of game.

This game gives me mixed feelings, so I will be brief:
The artistic direction of 9 Clues is fantastic. Like a lot of HoGs, the visuals are very much high up on the list of important aspects, and here the game does not disappoint.
HOWEVER
With a very thin storyline, and a protagonist who flips between being a detective genius, followed by being a naive victim to quite possibly the worst-kept secret of all in this game: the main antagonist - I find it very difficult to recommend this game to anyone but the most dedicated of HoG-lovers.
Yes, these games don't hinge on storyline, but really what follows when you boot this game is a tiny amount of story, followed by a bout of kleptomania as you 'collect' everything that's not nailed down, and attempt to rescue your friend. The puzzles are fairly straightforward, which is fine - I assume I'm not the target audience here - but often the puzzles have zero bearing on the game's plot, instead just serving as unnecessary hurdles.
I know there are plenty of fans of the genre, and I am - alas - not one of them, as such I am a tad biased.
If you see this game in a sale - do by all means pick it up for a bit of casual enjoyment, but don't expect anything too challenging.

The promise of Telltale's games - your choices matter - is simply not true in this game.
Without spoiling much, the best example of choices not mattering is when you are confronted by an enemy from your past. This guy has done terrible things to your loved ones, but your instructions are explicit - put the enmity aside. So when your enemy starts goading you into a fight, it feels like a great choice - swallow your pride or take your vengeance.
Except it doesn't matter. You can't avoid the fight, you can't run away, and you're forced to kill your enemy in self-defense. You can't even just refuse to kill him, because your enemy will pick a stick up off the ground and stab you to death with it (not an exaggeration). You can get a witness to vouch for your story, you can get the commander to BELIEVE THIS WITNESS, but you are punished for this death no matter what you do.
If that sounds like fun to you, then you'll get 10 fun hours out of the Game of Thrones Telltale game because the entire game is filled with choices like these.
If that doesn't sound like fun to you, I encourage you to stay away or watch the game for free on YouTube. It honestly works much better as a passive story than in one where your choices cannot change what happens to your characters.
P.S. I will commend the voice acting and graphics in this game - the team did a great job bringing the Game of Thrones world to life and having the show's voice actors greatly helped with the immersion. For me, that's just not enough to recommend a game if the gameplay is weak.

Best MMO combat ever in my opinion: shatters the WoW model of many abilities with a concrete rotation to follow. Instead, you are given a variety of different attacks and combinations to use in your own creative sequences. The result is closer to Dynasty Warriors style combat, but with more variety of ability choices. Graphics are the best I've seen in an MMO as well: they remind me alot of the Witcher 3 art and environmental styles. Gearing and getting a mount is even easier than WoW (I compare alot of features to WoW as I am a former junkie): in about 4 hours of gameplay as a complete noob, I still managed to earn over 1 million silver and buy a mount and some nicer gear. I only plan on playing this game casually, so I can't speak to the endgame. I have only dipped my toes into crafting and professions, but they seem deep. Ditto for the player housing model (you can own dozens of properties in towns throughout the game, and customize the interior completely).
Overall, this game seems to take a lot of old MMO concepts, polish them up, and add some nice new features as well. For $11 CDN with no additional sub fees, I have already gotten my money's worth out of this game and have much more to do in it yet.

Overcooked is a great local co-op game. It is pretty straight forward, so almost anyone can play (I've played with 5 of my non-gamer friends and only 1 of them didn't immedetely get a hang of the controls). It's got a cute little plot to go along with the game, just enough so you have a reason to progress, but not enough so you feel like it's forcing a plot on a game that really isn't focused on the story. Most importantly though, the stages of the game are fun. Each one has its own weird mechanic, or a twist on one you learned previously, so levels don't get repetetive. The only mechanic I really hated was the    ice levels, but even they weren't too bad. Also, you probably want a controller to play this game, it's not required, but playing it with a controller is really the best way to play. Lastly, and this should be obvious but I'll say it anyway. Don't play this game by yourself. You can, but it really wasn't meant to be played alone. I found you could have a bit of fun trying to play the game by turning on shared controller and then playing two people at once, but still, make sure you have friends to play with most of the time.

The visuals...oh the visuals. One of the finest examples of graphical quality and fluid gameplay I've ever played. The optimization is impeccable and really shows. My PC isn't a weak one, but for what I get to look at I'm always surprised that it runs as smooth as it does. Combat is always a pleasure as I slice, dice, pound and smash through the hordes of undead while vaulting over obstacles, climbing buildings and zipping around with my grapling hook.
I only wish they would make a shooter with the same tech they made this game with, or greatly expand upon the gunplay and firearm customization mechanics. I just wish there were more games made to look and feel like this one - but it's time for the compliment/critique sandwich.
As for the size of the maps of both the vanilla game and the DLC, I felt there could have been more content/missions. The distress calls made by survivors are always the same - either they're being attacked by bad guys or by the infected. It can feel a little empty, even while doing missions. Even in the tightly-packed city areas, I feel a certain lack of atmosphere and character. It can really feel like just a playground for the likes of me and my insane cardio.
The story could have been injected with a bit more intrigue and depth as well. If the developers were aiming more towards it being more of a straightforward zombie-killing simulator, they got it. Those of us who crave a deeply story-driven experience will come away wanting more.
Overall I wouldn't hesitate to recommend this game to anyone. Combining the visuals, gameplay and overall replayability, I give this game a solid 8.5/10.

First of all, I haven't recommended this game because the combat mechanics design is flawed.  The consequence is that the player loses soldiers due to the design, not for gameplay reasons, which takes a lot of fun out of the game.  So it's a "No" from this reviewer.
Most the missions are simple firefights at a distance which the design can handle, but when it comes to combat in confined spaces the design fails.  Lack of an overwatch model that works can make it easy to walk up to soldiers with impunity and shoot them, even when the defender is covering the area the attacker advances from.  The defender stands there like a stunned mullet and gets shot.
Another issue is the repeated use of the same maps.  Rather than implement some randomness which would force the player to use their brain and devise a tactical plan, the game has a small set of maps.  So, like mice in a maze, players learn the solution and develop a "play book" for each map, with each step of the soldiers choreographed in advance.  This becomes dull and boring.
Unlike the original games, the alien ships lack any real challenge.  Attacking an alien ship is probably the easiest part of the game.  Because overwatch doesn't work, opening a door is never a dangerous action and the attacker gets the first shot which is unrealistic.
The technology research design is also over-simplified which makes it uninteresting.
The horror aspects of the earlier games have been dumbed down.  The aliens themselves are not very threatening.  The floating brains of the original game have been replaced with spider-like creatures.  The alien soldiers have been changed from lizard men into fat roly-poly types who can't shoot.  Mechs make an appearance but that's stuff for the kiddies.
There are 3 difficulty levels.  Normal is where I played 70 battles, killed 800 aliens and lost 3 soldiers (because I used some rookies late game). This level is far too easy. Classic is where the game obviously cheats to add difficulty. In my sporting activities I never liked the cheaters. An improved AI would have been a better design choice.  The third level is Impossible - for the masochists.
In summary, the game is more like playing chess than a wargame.  And as such, it falls short on imaginative gameplay and fun.

NEO Scavenger is a rogue-like survival game that was originally made in Flash.
You control a character with amnesia or a version of memory loss, it is your job to make sure you survive in the vast post-apocalyptic landscape filled with mutants and raiders. The game involves turn-based combat and crafting which both give the game that unique gameplay style that makes it stand out amongst other titles. (May not sound like it, but it really is different)
The game is hard, I really do mean hard. The rogue-like genre means that when you die or lose in game you will need to restart from the beginning, it also means that each map is procedurally generated and so there will never be the same items or NPC's in a single location. With the difficulty aside the game is really fun with a lot of replayability, there is no real storyline yet but it will be soon implemented according to the dev.
At the time of writing this review it is still in the beta stage of development and also in Early Access, from what I have seen and played it is one of the few Early Access games that haven't disappointed me.

Pros:
+$10 initial cost, this is a bargain for an MMO.
+Decent optimization settings for laptops, great graphics if you can afford to run them.
+Great combat system, combo based, kind of feels like dark souls with the over-telegraphed enemy attacks and evasion skills to dodge them.
+Doesn't require a whole party of friends to play, the game is largely a single-player adventure with options to make clans or form guilds if you really want to.
Cons:
(-) The game gives you 30 days of "Rookie" log-in rewards that basically make the game more enjoyable, or should I say "actually playable"? Well after the first 30 days, expect to pay $20-$40 every month if you want to enjoy the game, or be like me and don't pay anything at all if you can put up with a bit more of a grind.
(-) The graphics might be good, but the servers are absolutely terrible. Expect very very frequent outtages, lag spikes, you name it.
(-) Combat = great. Leveling up? Not so much. Leveling is exponential in this game. Getting from 1-50 is somewhat of a breeze, and is actually considered the tutorial of the game. Getting from 50-56 is the equivalent of doing it all over again. I'm not sure what the highest level player is, but ever since the game came out, even with extremely dedicated players, the highest is at about 62. What really matters about a character however, isn't so much your level, but your gear. Decent gear takes a long, long time to get. You can either save up your in-game money to buy it straight off the auction house, or torture yourself with this horrible upgrading scheme where you buff up your items based on RNG. It's soooo bad.
(-) No friends, no problem. Right? Well... what if you have friends? Tough luck. There is NO player trading in this game. If you have the idea of getting 3 or 4 people together and making a small guild, having a great time and all saving up to buy something awesome, or pooling your in-game money together to get the less active members new gear... well throw that idea out the window. This game FORCES you to fly it solo. The most player-player interaction you can even do in this game is partying up to fight monsters, or going PvP. Neither of it is really any fun, or game changing.
-- Tl;dr  --
It's just not worth it.

It's a real shame. This game is great, BUT... ...it gets ruined by useless features that contribute absolutely nothing to the game.
Combat mechanics are one of the best I've seen in an MMO and the skills are awesome and feel impactful.
The lore and quests are below average, but I never considered them important since this is a sandbox game. It's just a side thing in a world where you do what you please.
The worst part of this game, however, is the AFKing. Even if you want to play this game casually, you are forced to keep the game running in the background. You want carrying capacity? Let your character carry load in a loop to build it up. Want to level up life skills? Let your character do the profession AFK. Etc. This was gamebreaker for me. I want to enjoy the game when I want, I hate being forced into some kind of full time AFK simulator just to be able to enjoy the game.
Another big downside for me in the game is that there are features behind the pay wall, which I really cannot agree when the game is buy to play, regardless how low the price is. The main issue I've had with this is that you have to buy pets in order to get the autoloot feature. Good luck looting each corps individually otherwise. And if I had played further, there would probably be more things needed to purchase like inventory slots to avoid frustration.
All in all, the game is great, but due to purchasable features and forced AFK it's not worth getting into.

This game brings all the festivity of Christmas with the combination of Jewel Quest.  The idea here is that you need to match up 3 of the same item (like silver bells or santa hats).  The design choices are lovely and this game makes me want to sing Joy to the world. It's colorful, it's festive and it has beautiful visuals and it has a fun story to keep things interesting. It's also the kind of game that makes me a little hungry because it has such delights like candy canes and gingerbread men!
You start off as the new mayor of a christmas type of town but there isn't much time to get things ready. The guy there to help you (and also give you quests to complete by purchasing the tasks) is something akin to a Christmas Elf. Yep you purchase the tasks.   Such as decorating Christmas trees, building a snowman, etc... The various things the helper says during this game are amusing, such as what he says when you finally put the ice cream shop in. I could almost hear Santa Clause himself coming to town. So basically after each level you earn a certain reward of coins which you can use towards completing the tasks set up for you, most tasks take 2 or more gameplay in order to get the necessary amount of coins.
The levels get tougher as you go along, some only give you a certain amount of time, while others provide you with limited number of turns or matching up different items.  You do have some help. As of writing this review I had two of the three available power-up item helpers.  One is a four way santa rocket that sends rockets in all directions, going up, down, left and right of that specific column.  The other power up i had was explosives which i could buy with gems.  You earn a certain amount of gems by completing quests.
8 out of 10.
The soundtrack has more than one selection and its perfect for this type of game. One of the tracks is "Joy to the world".  Keeps the festive spirit bright with good tidings while I do combos to collect the goal for the quest.  I would have liked it if there was a little more music to the game like a rendition of Frosty the Snowman or maybe Rudolph the Red Nosed Reindeer.  But the music provided was satisfactory enough to hold my attention to each jolly jingle that played in my ears.
9 out of 10.
The game mechanics are incredibly simple. You simply use the left mouse button to swap between objects. A very young child could play this with relative ease.
However. since I am talking about the game mechanics I would like to inform the developer of something that I came across during one of my replays.  In a specific instance of one of the timed levels (and this was with maybe 60 or so on the time clock) I came across a problem.  The game froze at a point where you get the option to restart. I couldn't click it, i couldn't click the secondary option. I could not get ctrl/alt/del to quit the game, i pressed escape with zero luck, I had to hit the F12 key just to exit the game at that point.   And for the wondering mind, I was using a mac when I played.
That was the only problem I have come across from your game.
Now, on with the
For how easy the mechanical aspect of this game is I give it a 10 out of 10.
The eye candy in this game is Huge.  I loved every colorful thing that I saw.  The details to every visual aspect are spot on and I recommend gamers taking a look for themselves at all the colorful creations this game has to offer.  The visuals are breathtakingly beautiful.  I feel like a kid in a candy store.  The visuals are so well done. Between the hues of trees and the selective colors for presents and shops, the game truly brings out a dazzling array of gorgeous stuff to look at.
10 out of 10.
The first thing I must inform gamers here is that there is an option to purchase more gems for explosives and the like, but the prices (in real cash) are reasonable. The overall gameplay is fun and I would recommend this as a Family friendly game that anybody who likes Christmas, or Jewel Quest or even just to try it out for themselves.  The game truly is fun and the challenge is in trying to match up three like objects.
I enjoyed myself and I get this good Christmas feeling that you will too.

The visuals...oh the visuals. One of the finest examples of graphical quality and fluid gameplay I've ever played. The optimization is impeccable and really shows. My PC isn't a weak one, but for what I get to look at I'm always surprised that it runs as smooth as it does. Combat is always a pleasure as I slice, dice, pound and smash through the hordes of undead while vaulting over obstacles, climbing buildings and zipping around with my grapling hook.
I only wish they would make a shooter with the same tech they made this game with, or greatly expand upon the gunplay and firearm customization mechanics. I just wish there were more games made to look and feel like this one - but it's time for the compliment/critique sandwich.
As for the size of the maps of both the vanilla game and the DLC, I felt there could have been more content/missions. The distress calls made by survivors are always the same - either they're being attacked by bad guys or by the infected. It can feel a little empty, even while doing missions. Even in the tightly-packed city areas, I feel a certain lack of atmosphere and character. It can really feel like just a playground for the likes of me and my insane cardio.
The story could have been injected with a bit more intrigue and depth as well. If the developers were aiming more towards it being more of a straightforward zombie-killing simulator, they got it. Those of us who crave a deeply story-driven experience will come away wanting more.
Overall I wouldn't hesitate to recommend this game to anyone. Combining the visuals, gameplay and overall replayability, I give this game a solid 8.5/10.

Half life 2 is the sequel to the original Half-life that came out way back in 1998, and boy does it deliver.
Half-Life was as good as it was because it was innovative as hell, had some satisfying as heck gunplay, a slightly interesting story, wonderful imagery and bad♥♥♥♥♥fights. This game's a bit of a different horse entirely, but it's still just as good.
The visuals of this game, even to this day, hold up fantastically. Nothing looks really blurry unless you get really close and start zooming in, the models are very rich and detailed, the water looks really good even to today's standards and the art direction as well as level design are wonderful.
The Half-Life series is known to innovate, and Half-Life 2 did not disappoint. The physics are extremely advanced to the point where I've never found a game that handles it better to this day, the gun-play is simply improved over the predecessor, and the new mechanics, enemies, story, enviroments, and everything else that make this game unique are fantastic. Half-way through the game you get a ''gravity gun'' which allows you to manipulate physics objects. It's a bit of a gimmick but it's without a doubt the best gimmick I've ever seen, and stupidly fun to use.
Storywise, this game 1-upped its predecessor by a mile and has a script worthy of a plethora of awards. I won't spoil anything, but Half-Life 2 takes place in a dystopian future where the entire human race is under alien control. The characters are rich, have their own arcs  and are, simply put, very well written and interact with each other nicely. The way that Half-Life 2 handles "cut-scenes" is by having characters move around you and do their thing whilst you're left in full control of the situation. This simple fact immerses you into the game a whole lot more than a regular cut-scene and caused me to genuinely care about each and every one of these rich and detailed characters.
Level design is great. The world's fun to explore and play through, there's tiny little secrets everywhere and there's fun physics puzzles splayed all around. The world feels real, there's npc's everywhere and I never once got lost.
Seriously one of my favorite games ever. A true classic.

So this game is probably one of the most fun co-op games I've played, and it has the added bonus of being so simple that almost anyone can pick up a controller and start playing. I've played it a good bit two others, and the first few worlds are really enjoyable like that. Having a full group of four people is even more fun. Some of the later kitchens are clearly meant for four people, and don't really work too well with three. The competitive mode is really fun, but does not require quite as much strategy as the campaign mode does (at least what I can tell).
The visuals are nothing fancy, but have enough charm to make them work. The music is top notch in my opinion. The stage design is chaotic and creative. It has a huge focus on throwing these really inefficient kitchen designs at you, but almost all of them work well to keep things fun. I will say dealing with the shenanigans of kitchens in the middle of streets or icebergs becomes particularly amusing when you're playing with a bunch of engineering students.
There are a few issues with regards to camera positioning or being able to drop crucial items in unreachable locations, but they only show up once or twice.
In short, the fun of this game comes from coming up with strategies to deal with crazy kitchen layouts working as a team to make culinary masterpieces. If you've got two or three friends to play with, I would highly recommend this game, even at full price.

This is actually a pretty swell hidden-object game. If you don't like the genre, this is certainly not going to change your mind, as it's pretty by-the-numbers.
However, it's a well-polished example, and even combines with more point-and-click adventure elements, which are a nice change of pace from hidden-object all day everyday. The music is great and the ambience is unsettling, the graphics are well-drawn and the story, while not great, is decent enough.
It's probably not a game for the "hardcore gamer", as the puzzles themselves are pretty easy, and you should be able to power through them without much trouble. But it's a nifty little game to chill with an afternoon :)
Also, the game - as with many other hidden-object games - is a great way for people not very proficient in English to learn some new words. I spent 5 minutes searching for a fingernail before realizing that "nail" is also something that you can use with a hammer. Yes, I'm an idiot.
On Mac the game seems to have a broken integration with Apple Game Center (so just press 'Cancel' when asked to log in), and once or twice I ran into bugs that actually left puzzles unsolvable, but overall I still recommend 9 Clues for into hidden-object games or "light games" in general.

NEO Scavenger is a rogue-like survival game that was originally made in Flash.
You control a character with amnesia or a version of memory loss, it is your job to make sure you survive in the vast post-apocalyptic landscape filled with mutants and raiders. The game involves turn-based combat and crafting which both give the game that unique gameplay style that makes it stand out amongst other titles. (May not sound like it, but it really is different)
The game is hard, I really do mean hard. The rogue-like genre means that when you die or lose in game you will need to restart from the beginning, it also means that each map is procedurally generated and so there will never be the same items or NPC's in a single location. With the difficulty aside the game is really fun with a lot of replayability, there is no real storyline yet but it will be soon implemented according to the dev.
At the time of writing this review it is still in the beta stage of development and also in Early Access, from what I have seen and played it is one of the few Early Access games that haven't disappointed me.

This game can feel like it's out to get you, designing the specific scenario that will make all your schemes and plans crumble in the manner of a couple seconds. Got great shields and upped your evasion to hopefully dodge those pesky missles? Well then, how about a few mantis beamed directly into your doors and shield room. Whats that? You only have engi? How unfortunate...
The best part of the entire situation though I'm going to steal from the youtube review Pyrion Flax gave the game, but really it's not that this game has anything against you. For one thing it's a computer program. and even better it's procedurely generated. That means that whatever situation it throws you in when you least expect it is completely random. The only thing you can take from this is that this game doesn't hate you, fate itself hates you. Honestly I have restarted this game more than any other game I believe I own, even Xcom. It's one of those games I suggest doing it on easy mode unless you get really good at the game or just want to hate youself.
In the end though, it's a masterfully done game. The way it both frustrates you and draws you in at the same time is mind boggling. The graphics are pretty well done for a 2D game, and honestly I can hardly see how they could be done better in 3D. It has pretty much infinite replayability, and even new content now and then. If you're into strategy and space games this is a must have really.
It's not perfect, there are a couple things I would like to see, probably the most important being a more noticeable warning light when you're oxygen is running out. I have actually killed my crew several times because I didn't notice they were all suffocating to death until it was too late. I've even gone a few jumps before realizing my ship was devoid of air. It can be a problem, but honestly if this is the biggest complaint I can come up with about the game then I'll deal with it. It even has mods, which I can't say I've tried yet

Don't be fooled by my Steam hours -
I've used it for hundreds before it came to Steam.
If you don't know what you're looking at, it's a 3D modeling and Animation program, much like 3DS MAX, Maya or Cinema 4D.
It has it's own problems, but it's still being developed and it's FREE. Absolutely FREE.
The Blender Foundation is an open-source compamy, which means it only runs off income like donations and products from their Blender store (T-Shirts, Flash Drives, ect.).
This program can easily be put up there with proffesional programs like 3DS MAX or Maya.
It's still under development, and it's GUI (called a gooey, folks) is a bit crowded, but nothing that can't be fixed.
It's renderer, called Cycles, is a bit slow but can be freestyle or photorealistic.
Blender has a game engine(which is currently primitive, but that's changing this year), VFX tracking and support, great animation tools(different, but up to par with Maya), great modeling tools, and flexible materials and rendering.
What are you waiting for? Go download it!

So this game is probably one of the most fun co-op games I've played, and it has the added bonus of being so simple that almost anyone can pick up a controller and start playing. I've played it a good bit two others, and the first few worlds are really enjoyable like that. Having a full group of four people is even more fun. Some of the later kitchens are clearly meant for four people, and don't really work too well with three. The competitive mode is really fun, but does not require quite as much strategy as the campaign mode does (at least what I can tell).
The visuals are nothing fancy, but have enough charm to make them work. The music is top notch in my opinion. The stage design is chaotic and creative. It has a huge focus on throwing these really inefficient kitchen designs at you, but almost all of them work well to keep things fun. I will say dealing with the shenanigans of kitchens in the middle of streets or icebergs becomes particularly amusing when you're playing with a bunch of engineering students.
There are a few issues with regards to camera positioning or being able to drop crucial items in unreachable locations, but they only show up once or twice.
In short, the fun of this game comes from coming up with strategies to deal with crazy kitchen layouts working as a team to make culinary masterpieces. If you've got two or three friends to play with, I would highly recommend this game, even at full price.

This game is fantastic. If you are looking for an outstanding Star Wars game, this is definately one to check out. It much better game when compared to the EA reboot, and a much better value.
Pros:
- While the multiplayer has been taken out (although you can play multiplayer through third parties), the game still has plenty to do. I am 5 hours in and still have not completed the first galactic conquest. More about this later.
- Galactic Conquest is the greatest mode in this game. The premise is for your side to control all the planets in the galaxy. This is through taking out enemy fleets and capturing enemy planets. You can also purchase higher ranking troops for in-game currency and get bonuses to help you in-battle. Overall, great mode.
- No Micro-Transactions. Enough said.
- Mod support. This game is overflowing with content, but you can still add more. Plenty of mods to keep you playing this game for hours and hours.
- Heroes. Heroes are special characters that are associated with a side. Some for the rebels include Obi-Wan and Chewbacca. I find great fun in running around as Obi-Wan and throwing my lightsaber at stormtroopers. Great Addition.
- Multiple Views. The game can be viewed in first or third-person. It's those little additions that count.
- This may seem unprofessional, but there are so many more that i have yet to discover.
Cons:
- If you are coming to pc from console, the graphics may seem outdated. While you can download graphical overhauls, that may not be as convenient. Me personally, i love the graphics.
Verdict:
10/10
If you are a fan of Star Wars, and don't mind minimally dated graphics, you will love this game.

Very good local multiplayer game. Play as up to 4 players, everyone selects a cook and off you go. Set in a kitchen with hazards that get harder every level. You start with the task to cook a soup. All you have is a Stove, a cooking board with a knife and a chest of supplies (Tomatoes, onion, potatos etc.). After you get your first task you have to coordinate together to cook the meal and send it out. While the one player provides the supplies and washes the dirty plates, the other player has to cut and throw the food into the pot on the stove. After it finished cooking you put it on a plate and send it out. BUT CAREFUL! Don't let your food overcook or a big fire will break out wich you have to put down first.
Later in the game the levels get significantly harder. Moving tables, flying fireballs and moving ice platforms are just some of the hazards. Coordinate with your team to complete the levels and cook for the FLYING SPAGHETTI MONSTER, which is your endboss.
You can also play this game in Singleplayer but you have to control 2 cooks which is not as fun as it is in multiplayer.
Pros:
+ Very fun local multiplayer

+ Challenging

Dawn of war is your typical RTS style game in that its involves base building, unit building, and upgrades. What set it apart from everything in the market is the universe it is set in. 40K is extremely dark and beautiful at the same time, it is set in the 41st millennium of man where we have set foot all over our known galaxy. We find Aliens of the typical fantasy worlds, elves, orcs, demons but they are all their own empires stretching across the stars. With other factions thrown in, such as Chaos, the galaxy is one huge warzone. Game play is paced for small squads play to epic armies going all in and tho the unit counts may be lower than that of AoE or StarCraft a few squads of well armed marines can take a whole base in a matter of minutes. It is a great start to what turns into a 4 piece series that add more factions of the universe and a great intro to not only the digital games but the table top as well. On that note the table top may not be paced at its digital counter part but the units mirror each other to great detail. Fans of the table top will fall in love with this game in no time. Campaign is a good story line and shows just hopeless this era in the future can be and how the Space Marines will do everything it takes to win and bring glory to Empire.

I wanted to keep this review relatively short, but that did not end up happening. There is a reasonable amount to say about Half Life, so here are some pros and cons:
Pros:
-Still looks good in 2017. Not polished, but good.
-Physics engine doesn't feel all that dated considering this is a 13-year-old game.
-Long, enjoyable campaign with an immersive story and characters that you end up caring about
-Variety of gameplay mechanics made possible with its (at-the-time) innovative physics engine and (relative) diversity of weaponry makes this game easily replayable
-Old-school fps mentality where you have to ration ammo and health forces you to think about future encounters
-Diverse landscapes
-Memorable experience. Game feels like more than merely the sum of its parts. This was also the case with Half Life 1, where you could probably point to any single aspect of that game and then show me a game that came out at the time which exceeded it in at least that aspect. But as a whole, many of those games were forgettable and not greater than the sum of their parts. Hence, Half Life 1 and 2 are classics, especially in the fps genre, where a garbage story is pretty much the norm.
Cons:
-If I were super picky, I would say the graphics look a bit blocky today and character models could use work. But this isnitpicking. For its age, it's rather good.
-My biggest gripe is this: weapon diversity. I know I said relative weapon diversity was a pro, but when compared to games even part of the older generation, like its predecessor Half Life 1 or Quake 2, there is no question to me that there were more interesting and diverse weapons there. Some of what was in Half Life 1 is gone here.
-At the end of Half Life 1, we had Xen. I know this is something a lot of people didn't like, but I think it was also something a lot of people thought gave the game some needed diversity and change of pace from the regular game environments. There is nothing of this sort in Half Life 2 exactly, as we are restricted to human environments. This is also sort of nitpicking though, as Half Life 2 actually has quite a diverse set of environments.
-Some of the weapons just don't feel as responsive as they should. The MP5 felt very clunky and inaccurate in Half Life 1. Unfortunately, this is the same case with Half Life 2.
-Once you get that alien blaster (sorry, I forget its name), just about every other weapon becomes obsolete.
However, the story, characters and long play time make for a very good game. It's not perfect by any stretch of the imagination, but as far as fps games go, is one of the best even to this day. There is a reason why people keep wanting Valve to release Half Life 3 or Episode 3 or whatever it is that they were planning on. 9/10

Part of the fun though is trying over and over again to see what happens. Every time you travel to the next point on your map within a given sector you will get a random event which could range from enemies, to allies, to randomly finding a useful weapon add-on for your ship. The randomness is what this game is all about. It's like playing a slot machine, you just want to give it one more spin before giving up just to see how lucky you can get.
All in all, if you want to be challeneged but have fun while doing so, and want a game with massive replay value that keeps feeling fresh, give this game a shot. Your money will be well spent for the time you will burn playing this!

When Dawn of War first came out, I remember just being floored by it's visuals. The opening cinematic in paritcular, was at the time, quite impressive. Warhammer 40k was something I had never heard of, and so to go from StarCraft to this darker, and grittier world was right up my gutter. The campaign was short, but it was quickly followed up by several expansions that kept the game fresh and fun. Playing it again now, I was surprised to see how little of that experience had changed. Sure, the game runs at 1024 by 768, and the graphics seem less impressive, but the mechanics of developing your squad and gathering resources through the continual conquering of your enemies really made this game a blast. At the end of the day, it's all about how much fun you're having, and this game is a lot of fun offline and online. It should be said that the campaign tells a story that is nothing special in terms of actual content or twists, but it is fantastically well told with voice actors who truly breathe life into the mythical Space Marines. This game is in a class of it's own and showed the world that there was room for another Sci Fi RTS could standout from C&C and StarCraft. A must own.

At this point with a few reviews already under my belt, I've somewhat run out of things to say about hidden object games (or HOGs). With how many there are and the near identical formula used as their base, unless it's appalling or extraordinary I find myself scratching my head for something more elaborate and articulated to say than "it's good for fans of the genre". Artifex Mundi's games however are something of an exception to that rule, as more than most casual developers they've shown a desire to strive to better their games with each release, reusing the same basic template but refining it along the way.
9 Clues: The Secret of Serpent Creek so far as I've explored their catalog is the best example of Artifex taking criticism to heart and using it to turn out a more enjoyable, polished experience. The narrative is a fairly predicable Scooby Doo-esq mystery, in a mysterious town full of odd people that seem just a little too obsessed with snakes. It didn't surprise me, nor is it especially well written, but there's a very typical Artifex charm in the way the story plays out as if they know it's derivative but it's the best they can do so they're still going to give it their all to make it entertaining. The voice acting is a significant step up from what they've managed in the past, perhaps thanks to the fact that the characters presented are so strange that any stilted exchange or bizarre inflection becomes a part of the character instead of sounding like an intern was pulled in at the last moment to record a few lines.
The hidden object scenes themselves, though as usual something of a treat on the side to the main casual adventure game meal, feel more logical in how they're placed and presented. Gone are the random cascades of junk shoved into random corners of the environment, replaced with a handful of scenes that make sense in the narrative (though it's still a little hard to believe anywhere in the world is quite so cluttered with pieces of machinery scattered all throughout the town). And perhaps most worthy of note is the addition of fast travel at long last, which eliminates the tedious back tracking which is already thankfully minimized do to the shorter, but much tighter experience.
So yes, it would be easy to simply say 9 Clues is a great HOG and you should certainly give it a chance whether you're already a fan of the genre of not, but I think it's worth pointing out the areas Artifex Mundi has put in the effort to improve their game in a genre so lacking in inspiration or often considered to be of a high quality. It's going to be hard to go back to their older games I've yet to play, but it also has me excited moving forward seeing how dedicated they are to making their games as excellent as they can be. HOG developers of the world, take note!

I wanted to keep this review relatively short, but that did not end up happening. There is a reasonable amount to say about Half Life, so here are some pros and cons:
Pros:
-Still looks good in 2017. Not polished, but good.
-Physics engine doesn't feel all that dated considering this is a 13-year-old game.
-Long, enjoyable campaign with an immersive story and characters that you end up caring about
-Variety of gameplay mechanics made possible with its (at-the-time) innovative physics engine and (relative) diversity of weaponry makes this game easily replayable
-Old-school fps mentality where you have to ration ammo and health forces you to think about future encounters
-Diverse landscapes
-Memorable experience. Game feels like more than merely the sum of its parts. This was also the case with Half Life 1, where you could probably point to any single aspect of that game and then show me a game that came out at the time which exceeded it in at least that aspect. But as a whole, many of those games were forgettable and not greater than the sum of their parts. Hence, Half Life 1 and 2 are classics, especially in the fps genre, where a garbage story is pretty much the norm.
Cons:
-If I were super picky, I would say the graphics look a bit blocky today and character models could use work. But this isnitpicking. For its age, it's rather good.
-My biggest gripe is this: weapon diversity. I know I said relative weapon diversity was a pro, but when compared to games even part of the older generation, like its predecessor Half Life 1 or Quake 2, there is no question to me that there were more interesting and diverse weapons there. Some of what was in Half Life 1 is gone here.
-At the end of Half Life 1, we had Xen. I know this is something a lot of people didn't like, but I think it was also something a lot of people thought gave the game some needed diversity and change of pace from the regular game environments. There is nothing of this sort in Half Life 2 exactly, as we are restricted to human environments. This is also sort of nitpicking though, as Half Life 2 actually has quite a diverse set of environments.
-Some of the weapons just don't feel as responsive as they should. The MP5 felt very clunky and inaccurate in Half Life 1. Unfortunately, this is the same case with Half Life 2.
-Once you get that alien blaster (sorry, I forget its name), just about every other weapon becomes obsolete.
However, the story, characters and long play time make for a very good game. It's not perfect by any stretch of the imagination, but as far as fps games go, is one of the best even to this day. There is a reason why people keep wanting Valve to release Half Life 3 or Episode 3 or whatever it is that they were planning on. 9/10

This will be long winded.
I am an old dude, my first time gaming was age 8 in 1979 when my Dad brought home an Atari 2600 (love Space Invaders hate pong because my older brother beat me everytime).
Then in the early '80s my Dad bought a Vic20, I now coded my own games! Then came a CBM64, I still coded my own games but they looked better!
Then I did some console stuff for years and then I got a job in a PC shop in 1995. I bought a PC and bugger me were they expensive then. I got into this new internet thing and started playing PC games, the first game I was mad on was Half Life. Then at the end of 1999 came this game called Quake 3. I played the demo on 56k and was fully into it. February 2000 and my little brother gives me a legit copy of Quake 3 and I install it and I have just moved into a new flat that has ISDN!  (ISDN was a British thing in the late 1990s early 2000s, it was 64k internet rather than the 56k norm) and I play Quake 3 and I love it.
I played Q3 until 2006, various mods (including one that was the Quake 3 version of Team Fortress Classic (WFA for life!) and legit Pro clans in legit leagues (hi Clanbase).
The Q3 scene died off a little and I got into the Team Fortress 2 beta and that was my new jam.
I played Quake live in a browser when it came out and enjoyed it but my heart had gone to TF2.
Now it is on Steam and I am pretty pleased. I'm not as fast as I used to be but I'm still above average and I'm glad to see Railgun Instagib still a choice, because overall that it my favourite game mode.
So, Quake 3 overall? Fast, precise and infuriating; yet wonderful because of this.
